items.d: Heat lets more current flow through an NTC thermistor.

items.t: A PTC thermistor has higher resistance when it gets hotter.
items.d: Heat holds current back more in a PTC thermistor.

items.t: Thermistors can work as temperature sensors.
items.d: The circuit reads the resistance and turns that into a temperature.

items.t: A circuit breaker is a safety switch that opens when current is too high.
items.d: It protects wires from a current bigger than they are meant to carry.

items.t: A circuit breaker can be reset and used again. A blown fuse cannot.
items.d: After it trips, you can switch it back on once things are safe.

items.t: A breaker allows a brief small surge, like a motor starting, but trips on a big one.
items.d: A fridge motor may draw extra current for a moment. A real overload is much bigger.

items.t: Alessandro Volta built the first battery, the voltaic pile, in 1800.
items.d: His pile was the first battery that made current from a chemical reaction.

items.t: Volta's pile was a stack of copper and zinc discs with salty paper between them.
items.d: The paper was soaked in brine, which is salty water.

items.t: A battery is made of one or more cells that make electricity.
items.d: A small flashlight cell is one cell. Bigger batteries join cells together.

items.t: The minus end of a battery is where electrons come out.
items.d: They leave the minus end, travel around the circuit, and return at the plus end.

items.t: A rechargeable battery can be used up and charged again, many times.
items.d: A charger pushes current back in, so the battery is ready to work again.

items.t: Electric current is measured in amperes, named after Andre-Marie Ampere.
items.d: An ammeter is the tool that measures how much current is flowing.

items.t: In direct current, charge flows one way. In alternating current, it keeps reversing.
items.d: Direct current is called DC. Alternating current is called AC.

items.t: Voltage is the push between two points. People also call it electric pressure.
items.d: Like a pump pushing water around pipes, voltage pushes charge around a circuit.

items.t: The volt is named for the Italian physicist Alessandro Volta.
items.d: A voltmeter measures the voltage, the push, between two points.

items.t: A switch is closed when its contacts touch, and open when they are apart.
items.d: Closed means on, because current can flow. Open means off. The simplest switch is only on or off.

items.t: A push-button switch springs back when you let go.
items.d: A doorbell works like that. You press it, it clicks on, then it springs off.

items.t: A capacitor stores energy by collecting charge on two surfaces close together.
items.d: The earliest capacitors were glass jars of water, called Leyden jars.

items.t: A capacitor can block steady direct current but let alternating current pass.
items.d: A steady flow charges it up and then stops. A flipping flow keeps moving.

items.t: A transistor can act as a switch that electricity turns on or off.
items.d: A tiny signal can control a much bigger one. The first working transistor was made in 1947.

items.t: Static electricity is an imbalance of electric charge on or inside a material.
items.d: Rub a balloon on your hair and the charge makes it stick to the wall.

items.t: When two materials touch, electrons can move from one material to the other.
items.d: That moving charge is what makes things feel zappy afterwards.

items.t: Rubbing materials together is the main cause of the static electricity we notice every day.
items.d: Sliding down a plastic slide can leave your hair standing up.

items.t: Static charge can make your hair stand up.
items.d: Each hair gets the same kind of charge, and like charges push each other apart.

items.t: A balloon rubbed on hair picks up extra electrons, so it becomes negatively charged.
items.d: That charge lets the balloon stick to a wall for a while.

items.t: Foam packing peanuts can cling to a cat's fur because of static electricity.
items.d: Charged things attract light, uncharged things nearby.

items.t: A static spark happens when built-up charge suddenly escapes. This is an electrostatic discharge.
items.d: You may feel a tiny snap after walking on a carpet and touching a door handle.

items.t: A lightning bolt is like an ordinary static spark, only much bigger.
items.d: Both are charge jumping across a gap to even things out.

items.t: Dry air lets static charge build up more easily than damp air.
items.d: That is why you get more zaps in dry winter weather.

items.t: Static charge stays on an object until it can flow away as a current or discharge.
items.d: Touching a metal doorknob gives it a path, so you feel the little zap.

items.t: The word electron comes from elektron, the Greek word for amber.
items.d: People noticed that rubbing amber could give it an electric charge.

items.t: In 1600, William Gilbert found that glass, wax and sulphur also make static when rubbed, not just amber.
items.d: So static is not special to amber. Many materials do it.

items.t: Charles Du Fay found two kinds of electric charge.
items.d: He named them after glass and resin.

items.t: A triboelectric series lists materials by the charge they tend to gain when rubbed.
items.d: Johan Wilcke made one in 1757.

items.t: A photocopier uses static electricity to put toner powder in the right places on paper.
items.d: This process is called xerography.

items.t: Inside a copier, a drum is given an even coat of static charge first.
items.d: A thin wire gives the drum its charge before copying starts.

items.t: Early copier drums used selenium, which holds charge in the dark but loses it when light hits it.
items.d: So bright parts of a page can wipe the charge away.

items.t: A copier shines light from your page onto the drum, leaving a hidden pattern of charge.
items.d: This invisible pattern is called a latent image.

items.t: Copier toner is a fine powder that gets a static charge by rubbing against tiny carrier particles.
items.d: It is the same rubbing trick as a balloon on hair.

items.t: Charged toner sticks to the parts of the drum with the opposite charge, which makes the picture show up.
items.d: Static attraction is doing the drawing.

items.t: A copier moves toner from the drum onto paper using pressure and static attraction.
items.d: The powder jumps from the drum to the page.

items.t: Lightning heats the air around it to about 30,000 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is several times hotter than the surface of the Sun.

items.t: Thunder is the sound of air that was heated so fast by lightning that it made a shock wave.
items.d: The air shoves outward very quickly, and we hear a boom.

items.t: The main current surge in a lightning bolt can move at up to one third the speed of light.
items.d: Light moves about 300,000 km each second.

items.t: Lightning strikes somewhere on Earth about 44 times every second.
items.d: That adds up to nearly 1.4 billion flashes every year.

items.t: The most common kind of lightning stays inside the clouds.
items.d: Many flashes never reach the ground at all.

items.t: Airplanes are hit by lightning fairly often, but strikes are generally not dangerous to them.
items.d: So a flash near a plane is rarely a problem.

items.t: A lightning rod is a metal rod on a building that helps protect it from lightning.
items.d: It gives lightning an easy path to follow.

items.t: Most lightning rods are made of copper or a mix of metals that contains copper.
items.d: Copper carries electricity very well.

items.t: Benjamin Franklin came up with the lightning rod in 1749.
items.d: He wanted to protect buildings from lightning.

items.t: A lightning rod must be connected to the ground to work.
items.d: The wire leads the electricity into the earth.

items.t: On a flat roof, lightning rods are usually placed around the edge.
items.d: Several rods spread around the roof protect the whole building.

items.t: Sharp points start electric discharges more easily because the electric field is stronger at the tip.
items.d: This is why lightning rods have pointed tops.

items.t: St. Elmo's fire is a blue or violet glow that can appear on tall pointed things like ship masts in storms.
items.d: The air itself glows as electricity leaks from the point.

items.t: A Van de Graaff generator uses a moving belt to pile up charge on a hollow metal dome.
items.d: It is often used in science museums.

items.t: If you touch a Van de Graaff generator, your hair stands out because each hair has the same charge.
items.d: Like charges push apart, so the hairs spread out.

items.t: A small tabletop Van de Graaff generator can make about 100,000 volts.
items.d: That is high voltage, but it carries only a tiny current.

items.t: Large Van de Graaff generators in open air can reach about 5 million volts.
items.d: Robert Van de Graaff invented the machine in 1929.

items.t: A Leyden jar is a glass jar with metal foil on the inside and outside. It can store electric charge.
items.d: It was an early way to hold static electricity.

items.t: The Leyden jar was the first way to store electric charge in large quantities.
items.d: Ewald von Kleist and Pieter van Musschenbroek discovered it independently in the 1740s.

items.t: Benjamin Franklin concluded that a Leyden jar stores its charge in the glass, not the water.
items.d: Before that, many people thought the water inside held it.

items.t: Electric eels are not true eels. They are more closely related to knifefish and catfish.
items.d: They just look a bit like eels.

items.t: An electric eel stacks about 6,000 special cells in a row, like batteries, to make a strong shock.
items.d: The cells add their small voltages together.

items.t: An electric eel can give shocks of up to about 860 volts to stun its food.
items.d: Its electric organs are made from changed muscle cells.

items.t: Electric eels have poor eyesight, so they sense their surroundings with electric signals.
items.d: This sense is called electrolocation.

items.t: Electric eels get most of their oxygen by gulping air at the water's surface.
items.d: Even though they live in water, they must come up to breathe.

items.t: A platypus has almost 40,000 electric sensors on its bill to find food.
items.d: They are arranged in stripes along the bill.

items.t: Sharks are the most electrically sensitive animals known.
items.d: They can sense the faint electric fields given off by other animals.

items.t: Messages travelling along your nerves are tiny electrical signals.
items.d: One whole signal takes only a few thousandths of a second.

items.t: Magnetism comes from moving electric charges.
items.d: Moving charges create magnetic effects around them.

items.t: Each spinning electron acts like a tiny magnet.
items.d: Electrons are tiny parts of atoms.

items.t: Iron, cobalt, and nickel can be strongly magnetic.
items.d: Many of their electrons act like tiny magnets pointing the same way.

items.t: Moving molten metal in Earth's outer core helps make its magnetic field.
items.d: The moving metal creates electric currents deep inside Earth.

items.t: Earth's magnetic poles are not at its geographic poles.
items.d: Magnetic north and the North Pole are in different places.

items.t: Cooling rocks can save a record of Earth's magnetic field.
items.d: Scientists study these rocks to learn where magnetic poles used to be.

items.t: Earth's magnetic poles have switched places hundreds of times.
items.d: This has happened since Earth formed.

items.t: A compass needle lines up with Earth's magnetic field.
items.d: This helps travelers find directions.

items.t: Electric current through a coil of wire creates a magnetic field.
items.d: This is the basic idea behind an electromagnet.

items.t: An electromagnet's field vanishes when its current is switched off.
items.d: Unlike a permanent magnet, it can be turned on and off.

items.t: The Sun sends a stream of charged particles called the solar wind.
items.d: This stream flows outward through the solar system.

items.t: Earth's magnetosphere shields us from harmful charged particles in space.
items.d: It acts like a giant magnetic shield around our planet.

items.t: Solar particles can make glowing auroras near Earth's poles.
items.d: Earth's magnetic field guides the particles toward polar regions.

items.t: During magnetic storms, energy follows Earth's field lines into the upper atmosphere.
items.d: That energy can create bright auroras.

items.t: Huge aurora displays need the Sun's and Earth's magnetic fields to line up just right.
items.d: That special alignment does not happen all the time.

items.t: A burst of material from the Sun can supercharge Earth's magnetosphere.
items.d: Such a burst is called a coronal mass ejection.

items.t: MRI scanners use strong magnets to line up protons in the body.
items.d: Protons are tiny particles found inside atoms.

items.t: An MRI uses radio waves to knock lined-up protons out of place.
items.d: Sensors detect energy as the protons line up again.

items.t: Body tissues respond at different speeds inside an MRI scanner.
items.d: These differences help doctors tell one type of tissue from another.

items.t: Maglev trains float above their tracks using magnets.
items.d: They move without rolling on ordinary train wheels.

items.t: Some maglev trains are pulled upward toward a steel rail.
items.d: A feedback system keeps a steady gap between the train and track.

items.t: Some maglev systems create electric currents in the track.
items.d: The resulting magnetic attraction and repulsion lift the train.

items.t: In 1820, Hans Christian Orsted showed that electric current makes a magnetic field.
items.d: A nearby current moved a compass needle.

items.t: William Sturgeon invented an electromagnet in 1824.
items.d: His magnet weighed about 200 grams and could lift about 4 kilograms.

items.t: Joseph Henry made powerful electromagnets using many layers of insulated wire.
items.d: One of his magnets could support 936 kilograms.

items.t: An iron core can make a coil's magnetic field thousands of times stronger.
items.d: The core is placed inside the wire coil.

items.t: More current makes an electromagnet stronger.
items.d: Changing the current lets people adjust the magnet's strength.

items.t: Giant electromagnets can lift heavy pieces of scrap iron and steel.
items.d: Switching off the current lets the metal go.

items.t: Electromagnets work inside motors, generators, speakers, and maglev trains.
items.d: Electricity and magnetism help each of these machines work.

items.t: Navigation compasses appeared in China by 1088.
items.d: Shen Kuo described them during the Song dynasty.

items.t: Early compass makers magnetized iron needles with lodestone.
items.d: Makers struck the needles with a lodestone.

items.t: True north and magnetic north are usually different directions.
items.d: The angle between them is called magnetic declination.

items.t: A gyrocompass uses a fast-spinning wheel to find true north.
items.d: Iron in a ship's hull does not disturb it.

items.t: A compass stops showing one clear direction very close to a magnetic pole.
items.d: The needle may begin to drift instead.

items.t: Near Earth's magnetic poles, a compass needle tilts up or down.
items.d: This tilt is called magnetic inclination.

items.t: A map line where a compass points exactly toward true north is called an agonic line.
items.d: Along that line, magnetic declination is zero.

items.t: A motor turns when a magnetic field pushes on a wire carrying current.
items.d: The push makes the motor's rotor spin.

items.t: A commutator flips a motor's current every half turn.
items.d: This keeps the motor spinning in the same direction.

items.t: Michael Faraday built the first electromagnetic generator in 1831.
items.d: It was called the Faraday disk.

items.t: Power station generators can be spun by steam, gas, or moving water.
items.d: Turbines provide the turning motion.

items.t: Moving a magnet and a wire circuit past each other can produce voltage.
items.d: This effect, called induction, is the idea behind generators.

items.t: A transformer passes energy between two coils using a magnetic field.
items.d: The two circuits do not need a metal wire connecting them.

items.t: A transformer needs changing current to work.
items.d: Changing current creates the changing magnetic field it uses.

items.t: Transformers raise voltage to reduce heating losses in power lines.
items.d: This helps electricity travel far from power stations to homes.

items.t: A speaker uses a magnet and an electric coil to move its cone.
items.d: The moving cone pushes air and makes sound waves.

items.t: A moving-coil speaker works like a microphone in reverse.
items.d: A speaker makes sound from a signal, while a microphone makes a signal from sound.

items.t: Some bacteria contain chains of tiny magnetic crystals.
items.d: The crystals, called magnetosomes, act like a compass needle.

items.t: Green aurora light comes from oxygen at lower altitudes.
items.d: Oxygen at the highest aurora altitudes can glow red.

items.t: Nitrogen molecules can give auroras blue and purple colors.
items.d: Different gases and heights help paint an aurora's colors.

items.t: An electron is thousands of times lighter than a proton.
items.d: A proton is about 1,836 times heavier than one electron.

items.t: J. J. Thomson discovered the electron in 1897.
items.d: He found it while studying glowing beams called cathode rays.

items.t: In metals, outer electrons can move around freely. That is why metals carry electricity so well.
items.d: This is why wires are made of metal, like copper.

items.t: The number of protons in an atom's nucleus decides which element it is.
items.d: An atom with 1 proton is hydrogen. An atom with 6 protons is carbon.

items.t: Protons and neutrons are made of even tinier particles called quarks.
items.d: A proton has two up quarks and one down quark.

items.t: There are six kinds of quark: up, down, charm, strange, top and bottom.
items.d: The top quark was the last one found, in 1995.

items.t: The word quark comes from a line in a book by James Joyce: "Three quarks for Muster Mark!"
items.d: Scientist Murray Gell-Mann picked the funny word for the new particle.

items.t: Quarks are never found alone. They always stick together inside bigger particles.
items.d: Three quarks together make a proton or a neutron.

items.t: James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. It has no electric charge.
items.d: Neutral means it is not positive or negative.

items.t: Neutron stars contain neutrons packed as tightly as matter in an atom's nucleus.
items.d: This makes neutron stars extremely dense.

items.t: In 1909, tiny particles fired at gold foil sometimes bounced straight back. Scientists were amazed.
items.d: This led Rutherford to discover that atoms have a tiny, dense nucleus.

items.t: The Standard Model lists 17 basic particles. Twelve of them are matter particles.
items.d: It is like a periodic table, but for the smallest known particles.

items.t: Matter particles come in three generations: six quarks and six particles called leptons.
items.d: Everyday matter uses only the first generation.

items.t: Three of nature's four forces work by swapping particles.
items.d: Photons carry electromagnetism, gluons carry the strong force, and W and Z bosons carry the weak force.

items.t: The Higgs boson was announced at CERN on 4 July 2012.
items.d: Two big experiments, ATLAS and CMS, both saw it.

items.t: Particles get their mass by interacting with the Higgs field.
items.d: Photons do not interact with it, so light has no mass.

items.t: The Large Hadron Collider is a 27-kilometre ring of magnets near Geneva.
items.d: It sits in a tunnel about 100 metres underground.

items.t: The LHC's magnets are cooled to about -271 degrees Celsius, colder than outer space.
items.d: This cold lets the magnets become superconductors.

items.t: Two particle beams race in opposite directions around the LHC at nearly the speed of light.
items.d: They travel in separate beam pipes.

items.t: Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN in 1989.
items.d: He first built it to help scientists share their work.

items.t: Every particle of matter has an antiparticle with the same mass but the opposite charge.
items.d: The antiparticle of the electron is called the positron.

items.t: When matter meets matching antimatter, they destroy each other and release energy.
items.d: Scientists call this annihilation.

items.t: Carl Anderson discovered the positron, the anti-electron, in 1932.
items.d: It has the electron's mass but a positive charge.

items.t: Hospital PET scanners use positrons, which are a kind of antimatter.
items.d: Doctors use PET scans to see inside the body.

items.t: Dark matter makes up about 27% of the universe. We find it by its gravity.
items.d: We cannot see it, but it pulls on stars and galaxies.

items.t: Ordinary matter, including stars and galaxies, makes up about 5% of the universe.
items.d: The rest is dark matter and dark energy.

items.t: Trillions of neutrinos from the Sun zoom through your body every second, and you never notice.
items.d: They almost never bump into anything.

items.t: Einstein published his theory of special relativity in 1905.
items.d: It changed how scientists think about space and time.

items.t: Light in empty space has the same speed for everybody, however fast they are moving.
items.d: This surprising idea is a key part of special relativity.

items.t: Einstein's equation E = mc² shows that mass and energy are equivalent.
items.d: A tiny amount of mass can be converted into a lot of energy.

items.t: Light in empty space travels at exactly 299,792,458 metres per second.
items.d: That is about 300,000 km every second.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth. Moonlight takes only about 1.3 seconds.
items.d: The Moon is much closer to us than the Sun.

items.t: Einstein's general relativity says gravity comes from curved space and time.
items.d: Mass and energy curve spacetime, changing how objects move.

items.t: Clocks tick a little slower near heavy objects. GPS satellites have to allow for this.
items.d: Without the fix, GPS would slowly lose track of where you are.

items.t: In 1919, a solar eclipse showed that the Sun bends starlight, just as Einstein predicted.
items.d: The news made Einstein famous around the world.

items.t: Gravity can bend light, so a faraway galaxy can look stretched or appear in several copies.
items.d: This is called gravitational lensing.

items.t: Gravitational waves are ripples in space and time. LIGO first detected them on 14 September 2015.
items.d: They came from two black holes crashing together.

items.t: A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that even light cannot escape.
items.d: That is why it looks black.

items.t: A black hole as heavy as the Sun would pull on planets just like the Sun does.
items.d: Planets would keep orbiting as before.

items.t: The Event Horizon Telescope showed the first picture of a black hole on 10 April 2019.
items.d: It was the black hole in a galaxy called M87.

items.t: The Sun makes energy by joining hydrogen nuclei to make helium. This is called fusion.
items.d: That energy gives us sunlight and warmth.

items.t: Henri Becquerel discovered radioactivity in 1896 when uranium made a photo plate go dark.
items.d: The plate was wrapped in black paper, but it still got marked.

items.t: A half-life is the time a radioactive material takes to lose half of its activity.
items.d: After two half-lives, one quarter of the starting activity remains.

items.t: Superconductors have exactly zero electrical resistance when very cold.
items.d: Kamerlingh Onnes first saw this in mercury in 1911.

items.t: A superconductor pushes magnetic fields out, so it can float above a magnet.
items.d: This is called the Meissner effect.

items.t: Max Planck's work on glowing hot objects in 1900 helped start quantum physics.
items.d: He found that energy comes in tiny chunks.

items.t: Light and electrons can act like waves or like particles, depending on the experiment.
items.d: Scientists call this wave-particle duality.

items.t: Lasers and transistors depend on quantum physics.
items.d: Transistors are tiny switches used in computer chips.

items.t: Quantum tunneling lets tiny particles slip through barriers that seem too strong to cross.
items.d: It even helps the Sun shine.

items.t: Air rushing from a balloon pushes the balloon in the opposite direction.
items.d: A balloon rocket flies because the escaping air pushes it.

items.t: Repeating an experiment helps check whether its result is accurate.
items.d: Try the same test several times and compare what happens.

items.t: Inertia is an object's tendency to resist a change in its motion.
items.d: A resting ball stays still until a force pushes it.

items.t: When all forces on an object cancel out, its motion stays steady.
items.d: The total force is then zero, even if several forces are acting.

items.t: The same push accelerates a lighter object more than a heavier one.
items.d: An empty cart speeds up more easily than a loaded cart.

items.t: A bigger push gives an object a bigger acceleration.
items.d: Push a toy car harder, and its speed changes more quickly.

items.t: Force tells how quickly momentum changes. Momentum is mass times velocity.
items.d: A force can change an object's speed or direction.

items.t: A jet engine sends hot gas backward, and the reaction pushes the engine forward.
items.d: The forward push is called thrust.

items.t: Sound moves through a solid by shaking the tiny particles in it.
items.d: Each vibrating particle passes the shake to nearby particles.

items.t: In a string phone, the listening cup turns string vibrations into sound in the air.
items.d: Those air vibrations reach your ear as sound.

items.t: A scratching sound can seem louder through a solid desk than through the air.
items.d: Place an ear on the desk while someone gently scratches the other end.

items.t: Soft materials absorb more sound than hard materials.
items.d: A soft material soaks up more sound than a hard, solid one.

items.t: Sound waves lose strength as they travel farther.
items.d: A string phone usually sounds fainter when its string is longer.

items.t: A simple string phone uses two cups joined by a tight string or wire.
items.d: The string must stay taut so vibrations can travel along it.

items.t: The bottom of a string phone cup acts like a diaphragm.
items.d: It changes sound waves into vibrations that travel along the string.

items.t: Changing tension in a string phone makes waves travel along the string.
items.d: The waves carry the speaker's sound toward the other cup.

items.t: A string phone can turn a corner if an extra can is placed at the corner.
items.d: The extra can helps pass the vibrations around the bend.

items.t: On an equatorial sundial, hour lines are spaced 15 degrees apart.
items.d: Earth turns about 15 degrees each hour.

items.t: A sundial's shadow maker must point parallel to Earth's axis to keep correct time.
items.d: This sloping part is called a gnomon.

items.t: On many sundials, hour line spacing changes with latitude.
items.d: A dial designed for one place may not tell time correctly far away.

items.t: A sundial shows sun time, which may differ from clock time.
items.d: Corrections are needed to compare its shadow with an official clock.

items.t: The equation of time describes a correction between sundial time and clock time.
items.d: The size of this correction changes during the year.

items.t: A sundial's shadow edge tilts by an angle equal to the place's latitude.
items.d: At a latitude of 40 degrees, the edge tilts 40 degrees from horizontal.

items.t: Daylight saving time shifts clocks, so a sundial reading needs an extra adjustment.
items.d: The Sun does not change its path when people move their clocks.

items.t: A gnomon is the still part of a sundial that casts a shadow.
items.d: The shadow moves across marked lines as Earth turns.

items.t: At Florence Cathedral, a spot of sunlight marks midday and the summer solstice.
items.d: The moving sunlight acts like a giant calendar and clock.

items.t: A spinning top stays balanced because spinning helps stabilize its motion.
items.d: This stabilizing behavior is called the gyroscopic effect.

items.t: A tilted top's axis can trace a circle around the upright direction.
items.d: This circular motion of the axis is called precession.

items.t: Friction steals energy from a spinning top, making it wobble more.
items.d: The wobble grows as the top slows down.

items.t: A top spinning steadily and upright is said to be in the sleep position.
items.d: It can look almost still even though it is spinning quickly.

items.t: A tippe top can flip over when it spins fast enough.
items.d: Its stem turns downward while its rounded body rises.

items.t: A top's tiny tip touches little of the floor, which keeps friction low.
items.d: Less contact can help the top spin for longer.

items.t: Squeezing a Cartesian diver bottle shrinks its air bubble and makes the diver denser.
items.d: The denser diver sinks. Release the bottle, and it can rise again.

items.t: Trapped air makes a Cartesian diver slightly buoyant, so it floats.
items.d: Buoyant means the water gives it enough upward push to stay up.

items.t: Squeezing a closed water bottle sends extra pressure throughout the water.
items.d: This spreading of pressure is called Pascal's principle.

items.t: A fluid pushes up on an object with a force equal to the displaced fluid's weight.
items.d: This rule is called Archimedes' principle.

items.t: A floating object pushes aside fluid equal to its own weight.
items.d: A floating toy weighing 100 grams displaces 100 grams of water.

items.t: A large ship floats because its hull pushes aside enough water to match its weight.
items.d: The wide, deep hull spreads the ship's mass over a large volume.

items.t: Water pressure increases with depth.
items.d: The bottom of a submerged object is pushed harder than its top.

items.t: Buoyancy makes an object underwater seem lighter than it really is.
items.d: Water's upward push supports part of the object's weight.

items.t: At a steady temperature, squeezing gas into less space raises its pressure.
items.d: This relationship between gas pressure and volume is Boyle's law.

items.t: Halving a gas's volume doubles its pressure if its temperature stays steady.
items.d: For example, 2 litres at 1 unit of pressure becomes 1 litre at 2 units.

items.t: Cushioning an egg drop stretches out the stopping time and reduces the force.
items.d: Soft padding lets the egg slow down over a longer time.

items.t: Terminal velocity is the top speed an object reaches while falling through a fluid.
items.d: At this speed, resistance stops the object from speeding up more.

items.t: A parachute has a low terminal velocity because it has a large area for its mass.
items.d: Its broad shape meets lots of air resistance.

items.t: In Heron's fountain, falling water compresses air that pushes another jet of water up.
items.d: The fountain uses water flow and air pressure, and it eventually stops.

items.t: A hole near the bottom of a water bottle squirts faster than a hole higher up.
items.d: Water pressure is greater farther below the surface.

items.t: A draining bottle's water jet slows as the water level falls.
items.d: Less water above the hole means a slower exit speed.

items.t: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that still acts like that element.
items.d: Everything from air to apples is made of atoms.

items.t: Most of an atom's mass is packed into its tiny nucleus.
items.d: The nucleus sits at the center of the atom.

items.t: Protons are positively charged particles inside an atom's nucleus.
items.d: The number of protons tells you which element the atom is.

items.t: Neutrons have no electric charge and sit in an atom's nucleus.
items.d: A neutron is about as heavy as a proton.

items.t: Electrons are negatively charged particles found around an atom's nucleus.
items.d: Electrons help atoms join and react with one another.

items.t: An element's atomic number equals the number of protons in each of its atoms.
items.d: Every carbon atom has 6 protons, so carbon's atomic number is 6.

items.t: Each element has a short chemical symbol.
items.d: O means oxygen, C means carbon and Fe means iron.

items.t: The periodic table lists elements in order of atomic number.
items.d: Each step across the table adds one proton.

items.t: Elements in the same periodic table column often behave in similar ways.
items.d: Lithium, sodium and potassium share a column, and all are soft, shiny metals.

items.t: A molecule forms when two or more atoms join with chemical bonds.
items.d: A water molecule contains three atoms joined together.

items.t: A compound contains two or more different elements chemically joined.
items.d: Water is a compound made from hydrogen and oxygen.

items.t: The oxygen gas in air is mostly made of molecules with two oxygen atoms.
items.d: Its chemical formula is O2.

items.t: Each water molecule contains two hydrogen atoms and one oxygen atom.
items.d: That is why water's formula is H2O.

items.t: Each carbon dioxide molecule has one carbon atom and two oxygen atoms.
items.d: Its formula is CO2, and you breathe some out.

items.t: Table salt contains sodium ions and chloride ions in a 1 to 1 ratio.
items.d: Its chemical formula is NaCl.

items.t: An ion is an atom or group of atoms with an electric charge.
items.d: It becomes charged by losing or gaining electrons.

items.t: An atom that loses electrons becomes a positive ion.
items.d: A sodium atom can lose one electron to become a sodium ion.

items.t: An atom that gains electrons becomes a negative ion.
items.d: A chlorine atom can gain one electron to become a chloride ion.

items.t: A covalent bond forms when atoms share electrons.
items.d: Hydrogen and oxygen share electrons in a water molecule.

items.t: An ionic bond is the attraction between positive and negative ions.
items.d: This attraction holds sodium and chloride ions together in salt.

items.t: Isotopes are atoms of one element with different numbers of neutrons.
items.d: All carbon isotopes have 6 protons, but their neutron counts can differ.

items.t: A solid keeps its own shape and volume.
items.d: Its particles stay close together and vibrate in place.

items.t: A liquid keeps its volume but takes the shape of its container.
items.d: Juice changes shape when poured from a carton into a glass.

items.t: A gas has no fixed shape or volume.
items.d: Air spreads out to fill a balloon.

items.t: Melting changes a solid into a liquid.
items.d: An ice cube melts into liquid water as it warms.

items.t: Freezing changes a liquid into a solid.
items.d: Liquid water becomes ice in a freezer.

items.t: Evaporation happens when particles escape from a liquid's surface.
items.d: A wet pavement slowly dries even when the water is not boiling.

items.t: Boiling happens throughout a liquid, not only at its surface.
items.d: Bubbles of water vapor form throughout boiling water.

items.t: Condensation changes a gas into a liquid.
items.d: Water vapor can form drops on the outside of a cold glass.

items.t: Sublimation changes a solid directly into a gas.
items.d: Snow can slowly disappear on a cold, dry day without first melting.

items.t: Deposition changes a gas directly into a solid.
items.d: Water vapor can form ice crystals as frost on a cold surface.

items.t: Plasma is a gas-like state containing charged particles.
items.d: Stars are mostly plasma.

items.t: Heating matter usually makes its particles move faster.
items.d: Warm food gives off smells faster because particles move and spread more quickly.

items.t: A gas can be squeezed into a smaller space more easily than a liquid.
items.d: Pushing a blocked bicycle pump compresses the trapped air.

items.t: Density tells how much mass is packed into a certain volume.
items.d: A stone is usually denser than an equal-sized piece of foam.

items.t: Ice is less dense than liquid water, so it floats.
items.d: Ice cubes stay near the top of a drink.

items.t: Water expands when it freezes.
items.d: The same amount of water takes up more space as ice.

items.t: A pure substance has a fixed composition and its own set of properties.
items.d: Pure water always contains hydrogen and oxygen in the same ratio.

items.t: A mixture contains substances together without chemically joining them.
items.d: A bowl of cereal and fruit is a mixture whose parts remain easy to see.

items.t: A solution is a mixture that looks the same throughout.
items.d: Salt can spread evenly through water to make a clear solution.

items.t: A solute dissolves in a solvent.
items.d: In sugar water, sugar is the solute and water is the solvent.

items.t: Concentration tells how much solute is in a certain amount of solution.
items.d: More drink powder in the same amount of water makes a stronger solution.

items.t: A saturated solution cannot dissolve more solute at that temperature.
items.d: Extra sugar stays at the bottom once the water has dissolved all it can.

items.t: Stirring can make a solid dissolve faster.
items.d: Sugar dissolves faster when stirred because fresh water keeps reaching it.

items.t: Hot water can dissolve more sugar than the same amount of cold water.
items.d: Temperature can change how much of a substance will dissolve.

items.t: Crystals can form when particles in a solution arrange into a pattern.
items.d: Salt crystals may appear as salty water slowly evaporates.

items.t: Oil and water do not mix evenly.
items.d: After shaking, oil droplets usually join and rise into a separate layer.

items.t: A suspension has particles that may settle when left still.
items.d: Muddy water clears slowly as some soil sinks to the bottom.

items.t: A colloid has tiny particles spread through another substance.
items.d: Milk contains tiny fat droplets and proteins spread through water.

items.t: Filtering can separate an insoluble solid from a liquid.
items.d: A coffee filter traps solid grounds while the liquid passes through.

items.t: Evaporation can separate a dissolved solid from water.
items.d: When salt water evaporates, the salt remains behind.

items.t: Distillation separates substances by boiling and then condensing vapor.
items.d: Water vapor can be cooled and collected apart from dissolved salt.

items.t: Paper chromatography can separate some mixtures of colored dyes.
items.d: Some marker inks spread into several colors as water moves up paper.

items.t: A magnet can help separate iron from a mixture.
items.d: A magnet can lift iron filings away from sand.

items.t: An alloy is a mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements.
items.d: Alloys can have different properties from the elements used to make them.

items.t: Brass is an alloy made mainly from copper and zinc.
items.d: It often has a golden color and is used for musical instruments.

items.t: Steel is made mostly from iron with carbon and sometimes other elements.
items.d: Changing the mixture can make different kinds of steel.

items.t: Air is a mixture of gases, not a single substance.
items.d: Dry air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen.

items.t: A chemical reaction rearranges atoms into new substances.
items.d: The atoms remain, but their bonds and partners can change.

items.t: Mass is conserved during a chemical reaction in a closed container.
items.d: The total mass before and after the reaction stays the same.

items.t: Bubbles, a color change or a new solid can be clues that a reaction occurred.
items.d: One clue alone does not always prove that a new substance formed.

items.t: A temperature change can be a clue to a chemical reaction.
items.d: Some reactions warm their surroundings, while others cool them.

items.t: A catalyst speeds up a reaction without being used up overall.
items.d: Enzymes act as catalysts for many reactions in your body.

items.t: Many reactions need some starting energy called activation energy.
items.d: A spark supplies starting energy when a gas stove is safely switched on.

items.t: An exothermic reaction releases energy to its surroundings.
items.d: Disposable hand warmers get warm as iron powder inside slowly rusts.

items.t: An endothermic reaction takes in energy from its surroundings.
items.d: Photosynthesis stores energy from sunlight in sugar.

items.t: Burning is a chemical reaction that usually involves oxygen.
items.d: A candle flame releases heat and light as wax vapor reacts with oxygen.

items.t: Photosynthesis changes carbon dioxide and water into glucose and oxygen.
items.d: Plants use light energy to power this chemical process.

items.t: Many cells use oxygen to release energy from food.
items.d: This process produces carbon dioxide and water.

items.t: Iron rusts when it reacts with oxygen in the presence of water.
items.d: Keeping an iron tool clean and dry helps slow rusting.

items.t: Salty water can make iron rust faster.
items.d: Dissolved ions help electric charges move during the rusting process.

items.t: Silver can tarnish by reacting with sulfur compounds in the air.
items.d: The reaction forms a dark coating on the silver's surface.

items.t: Copper can slowly form a green patina after reacting with air and water.
items.d: The coating is made of new copper compounds.

items.t: The pH scale tells how acidic or basic a water-based solution is.
items.d: A pH meter or indicator paper can measure it.

items.t: Acidic solutions have a pH below 7 on the common pH scale.
items.d: Lemon juice is acidic because it contains citric acid.

items.t: Basic solutions have a pH above 7 on the common pH scale.
items.d: A solution of baking soda and water is mildly basic.

items.t: Pure water is neutral, with a pH of 7 at about 25 degrees Celsius.
items.d: Neutral means it is neither acidic nor basic.

items.t: A chemical indicator changes color depending on acidity.
items.d: Indicator paper can show whether a solution is acidic or basic.

items.t: Red cabbage contains pigments that can act as a pH indicator.
items.d: The pigments show different colors in acidic and basic liquids.

items.t: An acid and a base can react to form a salt and water.
items.d: This kind of reaction is called neutralization.

items.t: Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when it reacts with an acid.
items.d: The gas forms the bubbles when baking soda meets lemon juice.

items.t: Yeast can turn sugars into carbon dioxide and other substances.
items.d: The gas makes bubbles that help bread dough puff up.

items.t: Baking powder contains ingredients that can produce carbon dioxide gas.
items.d: The bubbles help cakes and muffins rise while baking.

items.t: Heat changes the shape and links of proteins in an egg.
items.d: This chemical change turns a runny egg white firm.

items.t: Starch grains swell and thicken mixtures when heated with water.
items.d: Starch can make soup or sauce less runny.

items.t: Browning toast creates new flavors through reactions between sugars and proteins.
items.d: These are called Maillard reactions.

items.t: Caramelization happens when sugar molecules change as they are heated.
items.d: The change creates brown colors and new flavors.

items.t: A soap molecule has a water-loving end and an oil-loving end.
items.d: This lets soap connect oily dirt with water.

items.t: Soap can surround grease in tiny droplets that water carries away.
items.d: That is why washing works better with soap than with water alone.

items.t: Detergents lower water's surface tension.
items.d: This helps water spread through fabric and reach dirt.

items.t: Hard water contains noticeable amounts of dissolved calcium and magnesium ions.
items.d: These minerals can leave a pale scale inside a kettle.

items.t: A polymer is a large molecule built from many smaller repeating units.
items.d: Many plastics are polymers with long chains of repeating parts.

items.t: Cellulose is a natural polymer found in plant cell walls.
items.d: Paper and cotton contain lots of cellulose.

items.t: Rubber contains long polymer chains that can uncoil when stretched.
items.d: The chains help a rubber band return toward its original shape.

items.t: Glass is a solid, not a liquid that slowly flows.
items.d: Its particles are locked in place but lack the neat pattern of a crystal.

items.t: Diamond and graphite are different forms of the element carbon.
items.d: Their carbon atoms are arranged differently, giving them different properties.

items.t: Noble gases react very little with other elements.
items.d: Helium, a noble gas, is used to fill some balloons.

items.t: Pure water conducts electricity poorly, but dissolved ions improve conduction.
items.d: Salt water conducts better because its moving ions carry electric charge.

items.t: Each column of the periodic table is a group. A group is also called a family.
items.d: Elements stacked in one column belong to the same family.

items.t: There are 18 groups, numbered from left to right.
items.d: Group 1 is on the left. Group 18 is on the right.

items.t: Elements in the same group have similar traits.
items.d: They often share a similar look and similar chemistry.

items.t: Groups can be named for the top element, or have a special name.
items.d: The halogens are a family with their own special name.

items.t: Potassium is in group 1 because it has one outer electron.
items.d: That outer electron is its valence electron.

items.t: Calcium is in group 2 because it has two outer electrons.
items.d: Those two are its valence electrons.

items.t: Elements become more metallic as you go down a group.
items.d: Metallic character grows toward the bottom of the column.

items.t: Nonmetal character is strongest toward the top right of the table.
items.d: It increases from the bottom left toward the top right.

items.t: Noble gases were unknown when Mendeleev made his first table.
items.d: His first table had no group 18.

items.t: The alkali metals are lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium, and francium.
items.d: Hydrogen is not counted in this family.

items.t: Alkali metals are soft enough to cut with a knife.
items.d: A knife can slice them because the metal is so soft.

items.t: All alkali metals react with water, and heavier ones react more.
items.d: A light one reacts, and a heavier one reacts more strongly.

items.t: Alkali metals are kept under oil so air cannot reach them.
items.d: Without the oil, they would react with the air.

items.t: Each alkali metal has one outer electron it gives away easily.
items.d: When that electron leaves, the atom becomes a positive ion.

items.t: Each alkali metal has its own special flame colour.
items.d: Scientists use those colours to tell the metals apart.

items.t: Alkali metals are never found as pure metal in nature.
items.d: In nature they are always part of a salt.

items.t: Lithium, an alkali metal, is used in batteries.
items.d: It can be the anode, one part that helps the battery work.

items.t: Sodium lamps often light the streets of cities.
items.d: These lamps use glowing sodium vapour to make light.

items.t: The alkaline earth metals are beryllium, magnesium, calcium, strontium, barium, and radium.
items.d: All six belong to group 2 of the periodic table.

items.t: Alkaline earth metals are shiny, silvery-white, and somewhat reactive.
items.d: You would notice their bright silvery shine.

items.t: The family name comes from oxides once called alkaline earths.
items.d: Most metals in the family were named after those oxides.

items.t: Alkaline earth metals react less than the alkali metals do.
items.d: Both families react, but alkali metals react more readily.

items.t: Calcium helps build the bones of animals with backbones.
items.d: Calcium salts give bone its structure.

items.t: Magnesium is found in chlorophyll, the green pigment in plants.
items.d: Green leaves hold magnesium inside this pigment.

items.t: Strontium carbonate is used to colour fireworks red.
items.d: Makers add this strontium compound for a red display.

items.t: Chalk, limestone, gypsum, and anhydrite contain calcium.
items.d: All four are common natural materials that have calcium in them.

items.t: Calcium is used to make cheese, mortar, and cement.
items.d: You meet it in food and in the mortar between bricks.

items.t: The word halogen means salt former.
items.d: These elements join with metals and form salts.

items.t: Halogens make salts such as table salt and calcium fluoride.
items.d: Table salt is sodium chloride, a metal joined with a halogen.

items.t: Chlorine is a gas, bromine is a liquid, and iodine is a solid.
items.d: At room temperature this family shows three states of matter.

items.t: Iodine was found when purple fumes condensed into black crystals.
items.d: Those black crystals were solid iodine.

items.t: Chlorine and bromine help disinfect drinking water and pools.
items.d: Both are used so the water stays clean enough to use.

items.t: Fluoride in drinking water is used to help prevent tooth decay.
items.d: This is called water fluoridation, and it protects teeth.

items.t: The body needs a tiny trace of iodine to make thyroid hormones.
items.d: You do not need much, but that little bit is important.

items.t: Noble gases hardly react with other elements.
items.d: Their chemical reactivity is extremely low.

items.t: Noble gases are stable because the outer electron shell is full.
items.d: With a full shell, they have little need to form bonds.

items.t: The noble gases make up group 18 of the periodic table.
items.d: The whole family shares that one group.

items.t: Noble gases have no colour, smell, or taste, and they do not burn.
items.d: You cannot see, smell, or taste them, and they do not catch fire.

items.t: Noble gases glow in their own colours inside discharge lamps.
items.d: Each gas in the family can shine with its own colour.

items.t: Helium gives lift to balloons and blimps.
items.d: Its buoyancy helps them float in the air.

items.t: Liquid helium cools the magnets inside MRI scanners.
items.d: MRI machines use it to keep their magnets very cold.

items.t: Neon is a noble gas that gives lamps a popular orange glow.
items.d: Fill a lamp with neon and it glows orange.

items.t: In a neon-style sign, the gas inside decides the colour.
items.d: A different gas can make the tube glow a different colour.

items.t: Neon tubes can be bent into curving letters or pictures.
items.d: The tube is shaped first, then used to form a sign.

items.t: Transition metals are the metals of the d-block, and they conduct electricity.
items.d: Current can flow through a wire made of one of these metals.

items.t: Mercury is a transition metal that is liquid at room temperature.
items.d: In a warm room it flows, while most metals stay solid.

items.t: Iron is a transition metal that can be magnetic.
items.d: Metallic iron can act as a magnet.

items.t: Many transition metal compounds are coloured.
items.d: Electrons moving between energy levels make the colours.

items.t: The first evidence of helium was a bright yellow line in sunlight.
items.d: Scientists saw that line on 18 August 1868.

items.t: Helium boils at a lower temperature than any other element.
items.d: You have to make it very cold before it becomes a liquid.

items.t: On 6 March 1869, Mendeleev presented his periodic table to the Russian Chemical Society.
items.d: That date is often remembered as the birth of the periodic table.

items.t: Mendeleev wrote that many elements were still waiting to be discovered.
items.d: Gallium and germanium were among the elements found later.

items.t: Mendeleev said the whole periodic table came to him in a dream.
items.d: He wrote that in the dream, all the elements fell into place.

items.t: Mendeleev predicted three missing elements and gave them temporary names like ekasilicon.
items.d: He described how each one should behave before anyone found it.

items.t: The element mendelevium is named after Dmitri Mendeleev.
items.d: It is a lab-made element.

items.t: Henry Moseley found each element has one more unit of charge in its nucleus than the one before.
items.d: Today we call that number the atomic number.

items.t: Moseley found a regular math link between an element's X-rays and its atomic number.
items.d: This gave scientists a reliable way to count the places in the table.

items.t: Moseley predicted that elements 72 and 75 were still undiscovered.
items.d: His X-ray method pointed to gaps in the periodic table.

items.t: In the early 1800s, Johann Döbereiner grouped some elements into sets of three called triads.
items.d: He noticed the elements in each set behaved in similar ways.

items.t: In a Dobereiner triad, the middle element's atomic weight is about the average of the other two.
items.d: It was an early clue that elements follow hidden patterns.

items.t: John Newlands noticed that element patterns repeat every eight places, like notes in music.
items.d: He compared it to a musical scale, where the eighth note repeats.

items.t: Mendeleev's 1869 table put the 63 known elements in order of atomic weight.
items.d: Today we know 118 elements, almost twice as many.

items.t: A popular story says Mendeleev played a card game with element cards on long train trips.
items.d: The story is told as chemical solitaire. It helps picture how he sorted elements.

items.t: Mendeleev's predicted eka-aluminium was found in 1875 and is now called gallium.
items.d: Its discovery showed his table could see into the future.

items.t: When the noble gases were found, they were placed together in their own new column.
items.d: This showed the table could grow without breaking its pattern.

items.t: William Ramsay and Lord Rayleigh showed that argon from the air was a brand-new element.
items.d: It was hiding in plain sight in the air all around us.

items.t: Copper beads about 8,000 years old have been found in Turkey.
items.d: They were found at Çatalhöyük and date from about 6000 BC.

items.t: Hennig Brand made phosphorus from urine. It was the first element with a recorded discoverer and date.
items.d: Before that, nobody wrote down who found an element.

items.t: In 1789 Antoine Lavoisier wrote the first modern list of elements, with 33 entries.
items.d: He even listed light and heat by mistake, since they are not elements.

items.t: Humphry Davy used electricity to split compounds and found metals like sodium and calcium.
items.d: Sodium and calcium had never been seen as pure metals before.

items.t: Kirchhoff and Bunsen suggested finding new elements by studying the colors of light they give off.
items.d: An element can produce a distinctive pattern of colored lines.

items.t: Caesium was found by its two bright blue lines of light, and rubidium followed months later.
items.d: Both were found using the same color-spotting method.

items.t: Bernard Courtois found the element iodine in the ashes of burned seaweed.
items.d: Seaweed soaks up iodine from seawater.

items.t: Gallium was found in 1875 by a French chemist who spotted two violet lines in light from a zinc ore.
items.d: He used a tool called a spectroscope to see them.

items.t: Gallium is named after Gallia, the Latin name for France.
items.d: Its discoverer was French and named it for his homeland.

items.t: Gallium melts at about 30 degrees Celsius, so a solid piece can melt in your hand.
items.d: Its melting point is just above room temperature.

items.t: Gallium's first measured density did not match Mendeleev's prediction, so he asked for a re-test.
items.d: The corrected number matched his forecast.

items.t: Clemens Winkler found germanium in 1886 and named it after his homeland, Germany.
items.d: He first wanted to call it neptunium, but that name was taken.

items.t: Germanium's measured properties closely matched what Mendeleev had predicted for ekasilicon.
items.d: Another gap in the table was filled by a real element.

items.t: Helium was first seen in sunlight during a solar eclipse in 1868, as a yellow line no known element made.
items.d: It was spotted in the Sun before anyone found it on Earth.

items.t: Helium is named after Helios, the Greek word for the Sun.
items.d: It was the first element found somewhere other than Earth.

items.t: Technetium was the first mostly man-made element. Its name comes from a Greek word for artificial.
items.d: It is element 43, and Mendeleev had predicted it in 1871.

items.t: Marie Curie named the element polonium after her homeland, Poland.
items.d: She and her husband Pierre announced it in 1898.

items.t: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911.
items.d: She was also the first woman to win a Nobel Prize.

items.t: Glenn Seaborg helped discover ten elements, including plutonium, americium and curium.
items.d: He was a chemist who spent his life exploring heavy elements.

items.t: Seaborg suggested that the actinides form their own row, which is placed below the lanthanides.
items.d: That is why the periodic table has two floating rows at the bottom.

items.t: Four elements are named after one Swedish village called Ytterby.
items.d: They are yttrium, ytterbium, terbium and erbium.

items.t: Nihonium, element 113, was the first element discovered by a team in Asia.
items.d: The team at Japan's RIKEN institute saw only three atoms in total.

items.t: Oganesson, element 118, is the last element in the seventh row of the periodic table.
items.d: It is named after the physicist Yuri Oganessian.

items.t: Tennessine, element 117, is named after the US state of Tennessee.
items.d: Its discovery used a target made in Tennessee and a beam made in Russia.

items.t: Meitnerium, element 109, is named after the physicist Lise Meitner.
items.d: She helped discover nuclear fission and the element protactinium.

items.t: Copernicium, element 112, is named after the astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus.
items.d: Copernicus changed how people viewed the world.

items.t: Hafnium is named after Hafnia, the Latin name for Copenhagen, where it was found.
items.d: It filled the gap at element 72 that Moseley had pointed out.

items.t: Rhenium was named in 1925 after the Rhine river, using its Latin name, Rhenus.
items.d: Rhenium is element 75.

items.t: Marguerite Perey discovered francium in 1939 in Paris and named it after France.
items.d: It was the last element first found in nature, not made in a lab.

items.t: Astatine's name comes from a Greek word meaning unstable.
items.d: It is the rarest natural element, with less than a gram in all of Earth's crust.

items.t: Argon is named from the Greek word argos, meaning lazy.
items.d: It hardly reacts with anything. It makes up about 1 percent of air.

items.t: The periodic table now has 118 known elements. The first 94 are found in nature.
items.d: The other 24 only exist when scientists make them in labs.

items.t: Today's periodic table lists elements by atomic number, the number of protons in the nucleus.
items.d: Mendeleev used weight instead. Moseley's work led to the change.

items.t: Iron is the most common element on Earth by mass.
items.d: Much of Earth's iron is deep inside the planet.

items.t: Iron is the fourth most common element in Earth's crust.
items.d: The crust is Earth's rocky outer layer.

items.t: Pure iron is a shiny, silvery-grey metal.
items.d: Its smooth surface can look like a mirror.

items.t: Iron melts at about 1,538 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is far hotter than a kitchen oven.

items.t: Iron is magnetic.
items.d: Magnetised iron helped people make some of the earliest compasses.

items.t: Iron in your body helps your blood carry oxygen.
items.d: An adult body contains about 4 grams of iron.

items.t: A freshly exposed surface of pure copper is pinkish-orange.
items.d: Its surface can change colour over time.

items.t: Copper carries heat and electricity very well.
items.d: That is one reason copper is used in electrical wires.

items.t: Copper is soft and bendy enough to be pulled into wire.
items.d: This ability to stretch into wire is called ductility.

items.t: Copper can grow a thin surface layer that protects the metal below.
items.d: Corrosion is slow damage. This layer helps stop more of it.

items.t: People have used copper for at least 10,000 years.
items.d: It was one of the earliest metals used by people.

items.t: Aluminium is about one-third as dense as steel.
items.d: That makes aluminium light for its size.

items.t: Aluminium is the most common metal in Earth's crust.
items.d: Only oxygen and silicon are more common elements there.

items.t: Aluminium quickly grows a super-thin protective oxide skin.
items.d: The invisible layer protects the metal underneath.

items.t: Aluminium carries heat and electricity well.
items.d: It can be used in electrical wires.

items.t: Aluminium looks silvery and reflects light well.
items.d: A smooth aluminium surface can bounce back lots of light.

items.t: Aluminium is soft and easy to shape.
items.d: It can be drawn out or pushed through a shaped opening.

items.t: Aluminium is not magnetic.
items.d: An ordinary magnet will not attract a piece of pure aluminium.

items.t: Gold is the most malleable metal.
items.d: Malleable means easy to hammer, even into thin gold leaf.

items.t: Gold can be drawn into a wire only one atom wide.
items.d: Gold can stretch into amazingly thin wires.

items.t: Gold is very dense.
items.d: One cubic centimetre of gold has a mass of about 19.3 grams.

items.t: Gold is one of the least reactive chemical elements.
items.d: That means gold hardly changes when it meets other chemicals.

items.t: Most metals are grey or silvery, but gold is slightly reddish-yellow.
items.d: Its unusual colour helps make gold easy to recognise.

items.t: Gold is used in electrical connectors because its surface stays clean.
items.d: Tiny gold parts are found inside computerised devices.

items.t: Gold carries heat and electricity well.
items.d: This is useful in some electronic parts.

items.t: Silver carries electricity better than any other metal.
items.d: It conducts electricity even better than copper.

items.t: Silver is one of the best heat conductors of all materials.
items.d: Heat can travel through silver very quickly.

items.t: Silver reflects light better than any other metal.
items.d: This makes it useful in special mirrors and window coatings.

items.t: Silver slowly turns black when it reacts with sulfur in the air.
items.d: This dark surface coating is called tarnish.

items.t: Silver has long been used for jewellery and tableware.
items.d: It can be polished to a brilliant white shine.

items.t: Traditional photographic film and paper use silver compounds.
items.d: A compound here is a chemical made with silver.

items.t: Silver can be drawn into a wire only one atom wide.
items.d: Like gold, it stretches into wire very easily.

items.t: Zinc has the chemical symbol Zn and atomic number 30.
items.d: Atomic number 30 means each zinc atom has 30 protons.

items.t: Zinc is hard and brittle at most temperatures.
items.d: When warmed to 100 to 150 degrees Celsius, it becomes bendable.

items.t: Zinc is used in electrical batteries.
items.d: The metal helps some batteries produce electric current.

items.t: Your body needs a tiny amount of zinc.
items.d: Zinc is an essential trace element for humans.

items.t: Tin is soft enough to cut with little force.
items.d: It is a silvery-white metal that is easy to shape.

items.t: A bar of tin can make a crackling sound when bent.
items.d: This curious sound is called tin cry.

items.t: Tin melts at about 232 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is a low melting temperature for a metal.

items.t: Food cans are often steel covered with a thin layer of tin.
items.d: Tin-plated steel is widely used for food packaging.

items.t: Pure titanium is as strong as some steels but less dense.
items.d: It is useful when something needs to be both strong and light.

items.t: Pencil "lead" is not lead. It is graphite, a soft form of carbon.
items.d: Graphite is soft enough to leave a dark streak on paper when you write.

items.t: Diamond is the hardest natural material known.
items.d: It is made of carbon, the same element as the graphite in a pencil.

items.t: Diamond is highly transparent, while graphite is dark.
items.d: The atoms are joined in different patterns, so they look and feel very different.

items.t: Graphite, a form of carbon, can carry electricity.
items.d: Most nonmetals cannot, so graphite is a special case.

items.t: All known life on Earth is built from carbon compounds.
items.d: Plants, animals and people all have carbon in their bodies.

items.t: Scientists can find how old once-living things are by measuring carbon-14.
items.d: This is called radiocarbon dating. It can help date old wood and bones.

items.t: Carbon-14 has a half-life of about 5,700 years.
items.d: Half of it changes into something else in that time, like a very slow clock.

items.t: Carbon is used in the iron and steel industry to smelt iron.
items.d: Smelting means getting metal out of the rock it is found in.

items.t: Hydrogen sulfide gives rotten eggs their stinky smell.
items.d: It is a gas that contains the element sulfur.

items.t: When sulfur burns, it melts into a red liquid and makes a blue flame.
items.d: Grown-ups use special labs to study this safely. Do not try it at home.

items.t: Sulfur is used to make matches and to protect plants from pests.
items.d: It is an ingredient in matches, insecticides and fungicides.

items.t: The biggest use of sulfur is making sulfuric acid.
items.d: Sulfuric acid is an important chemical used in many factories.

items.t: The blue colour of the gemstone lapis lazuli comes from sulfur.
items.d: Sulfur-containing ions inside the stone give it its blue colour.

items.t: Sulfur does not dissolve in water.
items.d: Stir yellow sulfur powder in water and it just stays as powder.

items.t: Phosphorus was discovered in 1669 by a German alchemist named Hennig Brand.
items.d: Alchemists were early experimenters who came before modern chemists.

items.t: Phosphate minerals are the main part of your bones and teeth.
items.d: That means phosphorus helps keep your smile strong.

items.t: Phosphorus is a key nutrient that plants need to grow.
items.d: Farmers add phosphorus fertiliser to the soil to help crops.

items.t: Phosphorus is part of DNA, RNA and the energy molecule ATP.
items.d: DNA is the instruction book inside your cells.

items.t: About 78 percent of Earth's air is nitrogen gas.
items.d: Only about one fifth of air is oxygen.

items.t: Nitrogen gas has no colour and no smell.
items.d: You are breathing lots of it right now and cannot tell.

items.t: Nitrogen turns into a liquid at about minus 196 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is far colder than any freezer.

items.t: Liquid nitrogen looks a lot like water.
items.d: It is clear and runny, but it is extremely cold.

items.t: Nitrogen is a building block of proteins.
items.d: Every living thing has nitrogen in its amino acids, which make proteins.

items.t: About half of the world's food depends on nitrogen fertilisers made in factories.
items.d: Nitrogen helps crops grow big and healthy.

items.t: Nitrogen gas is used in food packaging to keep oxygen out.
items.d: Bags of snacks are often filled with it.

items.t: Most of Earth's crust is made of silicate minerals.
items.d: Silicate minerals contain silicon and oxygen, and they make up many rocks.

items.t: Silicon is used to make computer chips.
items.d: Chips like these are inside phones and most modern gadgets.

items.t: Egyptians were making glass with silica at least 3,500 years ago.
items.d: Silica is found in sand.

items.t: Borosilicate glass handles sudden temperature changes better than ordinary glass.
items.d: It is used in science lab glassware and some baking dishes.

items.t: The six common metalloids are boron, silicon, germanium, arsenic, antimony and tellurium.
items.d: Metalloids sit in a diagonal band on the periodic table.

items.t: Metalloids look like metals but mostly act like nonmetals.
items.d: They are shiny but brittle, so they snap instead of bending.

items.t: Nonmetals are usually poor at carrying heat and electricity.
items.d: That is why wires are made of metal and wrapped in plastic.

items.t: Carbon can form different structures called allotropes.
items.d: Diamond and graphite are allotropes of carbon.

items.t: A carbon atom can form up to four bonds with other atoms.
items.d: This lets carbon link into many different structures.

items.t: Carbon has been known since ancient times.
items.d: Charcoal and soot are familiar carbon rich materials.

items.t: Diamond is the hardest known natural mineral.
items.d: It scores 10, the highest number on the Mohs hardness scale.

items.t: In diamond, each carbon atom bonds to four other carbon atoms.
items.d: The bonds point toward the corners of a shape called a tetrahedron.

items.t: Volcanic eruptions carried diamonds toward Earth's surface.
items.d: Many arrived inside rocks called kimberlites.

items.t: Diamonds are weighed in carats. One carat equals 0.2 grams.
items.d: A 5 carat diamond has a mass of 1 gram.

items.t: Diamonds sparkle because they bend light strongly.
items.d: The scientific name for this light bending is refraction.

items.t: Graphite is very soft, scoring only 1 to 2 on the Mohs scale.
items.d: That softness helps graphite leave marks on paper.

items.t: Graphite has thin carbon layers that can slide over one another.
items.d: Imagine pages in a book slipping across each other.

items.t: The name graphite comes from a Greek word meaning to draw or write.
items.d: The name was created in 1789.

items.t: Graphite can carry electricity along its flat carbon layers.
items.d: Some of its electrons can move freely along those layers.

items.t: Hot melted glass does not stick easily to graphite.
items.d: That makes graphite useful for tools used in glassmaking.

items.t: Graphene is a honeycomb sheet of carbon atoms only one atom thick.
items.d: Its atoms form a flat pattern of linked hexagons.

items.t: Graphene is the world's thinnest two dimensional material.
items.d: It is just one carbon atom thick.

items.t: Graphene absorbs only about 2.3% of the light reaching it.
items.d: So a graphene sheet is nearly see-through.

items.t: Graphene was isolated in 2004 using graphite and sticky tape.
items.d: Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov used tape to peel away very thin layers.

items.t: Experiments with graphene earned two scientists the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics.
items.d: The winners were Andre Geim and Konstantin Novoselov.

items.t: A C60 buckyball contains 60 carbon atoms.
items.d: Its cage has 20 hexagons and 12 pentagons.

items.t: Buckyballs are named after architect Buckminster Fuller.
items.d: Their carbon cages resemble his rounded geodesic domes.

items.t: Scientists discovered buckyballs in 1985.
items.d: The discovery team worked at Rice University and the University of Sussex.

items.t: A space telescope spotted C60 and C70 buckyballs in cosmic dust in 2010.
items.d: The telescope was NASA's Spitzer Space Telescope.

items.t: Carbon nanotubes are tiny cylinders only a few nanometres wide.
items.d: Some can grow several centimetres long.

items.t: A single walled carbon nanotube is extremely narrow.
items.d: It is about a 100,000th of the width of a human hair.

items.t: Charcoal is made by strongly heating wood with very little air.
items.d: This process is called pyrolysis.

items.t: Artists can draw with charcoal made from grapevines.
items.d: This drawing material is called vine charcoal.

items.t: One gram of activated carbon can have over 3,000 square metres of surface area.
items.d: Countless tiny pores create this enormous hidden surface.

items.t: About 78 percent of dry air is nitrogen.
items.d: In 100 cups of dry air, about 78 cups are nitrogen.

items.t: About 21 percent of dry air is oxygen.
items.d: Oxygen is the gas your body uses when you breathe in.

items.t: Earth's air has five main layers above you.
items.d: From low to high: troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, exosphere.

items.t: About 80 percent of the air's mass sits in the lowest layer.
items.d: That layer is the troposphere, the air closest to the ground.

items.t: Food packs often hold nitrogen so oxygen stays out.
items.d: Nitrogen does not react with the food, so snacks keep longer.

items.t: About half the world's food depends on fertiliser from air.
items.d: The fertiliser is nitrogen taken from air and turned into plant food.

items.t: Every living thing contains nitrogen, including you.
items.d: It helps build proteins and DNA, the plans inside each cell.

items.t: Liquid nitrogen boils at about minus 196 degrees Celsius.
items.d: Water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, so this is much colder.

items.t: By mass, oxygen is the most common element in Earth's crust.
items.d: Most of it is locked inside rocks, joined to other elements.

items.t: Liquid oxygen is a light sky blue.
items.d: As a gas, oxygen is invisible. As a liquid, it looks light blue.

items.t: A strong magnet can hold liquid oxygen between its poles.
items.d: Liquid oxygen is pulled by magnets, unlike most everyday things.

items.t: Most oxygen in our air comes from photosynthesis.
items.d: Sunlight splits water, and oxygen is released into the air.

items.t: The ozone layer holds ozone, a form of oxygen, high in the stratosphere.
items.d: From up there it absorbs harmful ultraviolet light coming from the Sun.

items.t: Argon's name comes from a Greek word meaning lazy.
items.d: Argon got that name because it hardly reacts with anything.

items.t: Argon is the third most common gas in Earth's air.
items.d: It makes up a bit less than 1 percent, after nitrogen and oxygen.

items.t: Argon inside light bulbs protects the hot filament.
items.d: It keeps oxygen away, so the thin glowing wire does not burn up.

items.t: Helium is the second-lightest element, after hydrogen.
items.d: Only hydrogen is lighter than helium.

items.t: Helium is the second most common element in the universe.
items.d: In all of space, only hydrogen is more common than helium.

items.t: Helium was found in sunlight before it was found on Earth.
items.d: During an 1868 eclipse, a yellow line showed a new element named for the Sun.

items.t: Helium has the lowest boiling point of any element.
items.d: It stays a gas until it is colder than every other element.

items.t: At normal air pressure, helium stays liquid right down to absolute zero.
items.d: It becomes solid only at about 25 times the pressure of sea-level air.

items.t: Helium lifts balloons and airships.
items.d: Fill a balloon with helium and it floats up into the sky.

items.t: On Earth, helium is collected from natural gas.
items.d: In some gas fields it can be up to about 7 percent of the gas.

items.t: Helium that leaks into the air drifts away into space.
items.d: It does not fall back, so the supply we collect is not replaced.

items.t: A little helium changes your voice for a short time.
items.d: The new sound does not last. Your usual voice soon returns.

items.t: Bacteria in pea and bean roots capture nitrogen from air.
items.d: These rhizobia live in root nodules and make nitrogen plants can use.

items.t: Neon glows reddish orange in electric signs.
items.d: When electricity flows through neon gas, it shines that colour.

items.t: Only about 1 part in 55,000 of air is neon.
items.d: Neon is a tiny trace in air, so it takes a lot of air to collect.

items.t: Hydrogen is the lightest element of all.
items.d: No other element on the periodic table has a smaller mass.

items.t: Hydrogen is the most common element in the universe.
items.d: There is more hydrogen in space than any other element.

items.t: Hydrogen gas has no colour, no smell, and burns easily.
items.d: You cannot see it or smell it, but a flame can light it.

items.t: Hydrogen's name means water-former.
items.d: Burning hydrogen makes water, which is why the Greek name fits.

items.t: The Sun and other stars are made mainly of hydrogen.
items.d: In stars, hydrogen is so hot that it becomes plasma, a fourth state of matter after solid, liquid and gas.

items.t: Halve a gas's space, at the same temperature, and pressure doubles.
items.d: Keep the same amount of gas. Pressure 2 becomes 4 when the space is halved.

items.t: Your breathing follows Boyle's law.
items.d: Larger lungs lower the pressure, so air flows in. Smaller lungs push air out.

items.t: Gases expand when you heat them and shrink when you cool them.
items.d: A balloon in a warm room looks fuller than one left in the cold.

items.t: Your body makes carbon dioxide, and you breathe it out.
items.d: Blood carries this gas to your lungs, and then you exhale it.

items.t: At sea level, standard air pressure is 101,325 pascals.
items.d: That equals a column of mercury about 760 millimetres tall.

items.t: Air pressure gets lower the higher you climb.
items.d: On a high mountain, less air pushes down than at the seashore.

items.t: The air above one square centimetre has a mass of about 1 kilogram.
items.d: The column runs from the ground all the way to the top of the air.

items.t: A cold fizzy drink holds more carbon dioxide than a warm one.
items.d: Warm the drink and the gas escapes sooner, so it goes flat.

items.t: Dry ice is solid carbon dioxide that turns straight into gas.
items.d: This happens at about minus 78.5 degrees Celsius, with no liquid stage.

items.t: A hot air balloon rises because the air inside is less dense.
items.d: The same amount of space holds less warm air than cool air, so the balloon floats.

items.t: People first flew freely in a hot air balloon in 1783.
items.d: The flight was in Paris on 21 November 1783.

items.t: Noble gases such as helium, neon, and argon hardly react.
items.d: Their outer electron shells are full, so they rarely form compounds.

items.t: Some restaurants freeze ice cream with liquid nitrogen.
items.d: Fast freezing makes tiny ice crystals, so the ice cream is smooth.

items.t: One litre of liquid nitrogen becomes about 694 litres of gas.
items.d: At 20 degrees Celsius it expands so much it must not be sealed tight.

items.t: The ozone layer is mostly about 15 to 35 kilometres up.
items.d: Most of that ozone sits in the lower part of the stratosphere.

items.t: Ozone absorbs about 97 to 99 percent of medium-frequency ultraviolet light.
items.d: The layer soaks up nearly all of that sunlight before it reaches the ground.

items.t: The top of water acts like a stretchy skin. This is called surface tension.
items.d: Surface molecules pull harder on their neighbours beside and below them.

items.t: Water striders can stand on water because of surface tension and long, water-repelling legs.
items.d: They look like they skate across a pond.

items.t: Water drops are roughly round because the surface layer pulls them inward.
items.d: Look at a raindrop on a window. It makes a little dome.

items.t: Bubbles are round because surface tension pulls them into a sphere.
items.d: A soap bubble floating in the air is almost a perfect ball.

items.t: Cohesion is the pull between molecules of the same kind. It holds water molecules together.
items.d: It is why a drop of water clings together instead of spreading out.

items.t: Adhesion is water being attracted to other things and sticking to them.
items.d: Water drops stick to a window instead of sliding off at once.
