The 64th square in the doubling chessboard puzzle holds 2^63 grains.
The total in the doubling chessboard puzzle is one less than 2^64.
items.d: The sum is 2^64 - 1 because the squares hold 1, 2, 4, 8, and so on.

items.t: Scientific notation uses powers of 10 to shorten huge or tiny numbers.
items.d: 320,000 can be written as 3.2 x 10^5.

items.t: In standard scientific notation, the front number is at least 1 but less than 10.
Calculators may use E to show a power of 10.
Scientific notation makes very large or small numbers easier to compare.
items.d: 10^8 is ten times 10^7 because its exponent is one greater.

items.t: In modern English, a billion is 10^9 and a trillion is 10^12.
items.d: A billion is 1,000,000,000. A trillion has three more zeros.

items.t: A million is 1,000,000, or 10^6.
items.d: Some places name larger numbers differently, but a million stays the same.

items.t: A nine-year-old named Milton Sirotta coined the word googol in 1920.
items.d: He made up the name for the huge number 10^100.

items.t: A googol is 1 followed by 100 zeros.
items.d: A googolplex is even bigger: 1 followed by a googol of zeros.

items.t: A googol is far larger than the estimated particle count of the observable universe.
items.d: A googol is 10^100, while the particle estimate is around 10^80.

items.t: One order of magnitude means a change by about a factor of 10.
items.d: About 100 is one order of magnitude greater than about 10.

items.t: The numbers 2 and 2,000,000 differ by six orders of magnitude.
items.d: Multiplying 2 by 10 six times gives 2,000,000.

items.t: An order-of-magnitude estimate rounds a quantity to the nearest power of 10.
items.d: A rough size might be written as 10, 100, 1,000, or another power of 10.

items.t: Kilo means 10^3, mega means 10^6, and giga means 10^9.
items.d: Those powers equal 1,000, one million, and one billion.

items.t: Tera means 10^12, while peta means 10^15.
items.d: A peta-unit is 1,000 times as large as a tera-unit.

items.t: Milli, micro, and nano describe very small metric amounts.
items.d: Milli is 10^-3, micro is 10^-6, and nano is 10^-9.
Each number is double the one before it.

items.t: Two raised to the tenth power is 1,024.
items.d: 2^10 = 1,024, which is close to kilo's value of 1,000.

items.t: A byte with 8 bits can hold 2^8 different values.
Most computers represent numbers in binary, or base two.
items.d: Binary place values are powers of 2, such as 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16.

items.t: You can arrange a square number of dots into a perfect square grid.
items.d: Sixteen dots make a 4 by 4 grid because 4^2 = 16.

items.t: Adding consecutive odd numbers from 1 always makes a square number.
A square number can end only in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6, or 9.
items.d: A whole number ending in 2, 3, 7, or 8 cannot be a square.

items.t: A square with side length n has an area of n^2.
items.d: A square with 6 cm sides has area 6^2 = 36 square centimetres.

items.t: The volume of a cube is its side length raised to the third power.
items.d: A cube with 3 cm sides has volume 3^3 = 27 cubic centimetres.

items.t: The first five positive cubes add to 225, a perfect square.
Exponential growth speeds up because each increase depends on the current amount.
items.d: Repeated doubling goes 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32.

items.t: Doubling time is how long a growing amount takes to become twice as large.
items.d: With a one-day doubling time, 5 becomes 10 after one day.

items.t: Bacteria splitting can show doubling growth: one becomes two, then four, then eight.
items.d: After three doublings, 1 x 2^3 = 8.

items.t: If pond plants double daily and cover the pond on day 30, day 29 is only half covered.
items.d: The last doubling changes one-half of the pond into one whole pond.

items.t: One million equals 1,000 x 1,000 and also 100 cubed.
One million seconds is about 11.57 days.
items.d: Big numbers can feel different when they measure time instead of objects.

items.t: A mole, a chemistry counting unit, contains exactly 6.02214076 x 10^23 particles.
items.d: This huge count is called the Avogadro number.

items.t: A light-year is a distance of about 9.46 trillion kilometres.
items.d: Scientific notation writes that distance as about 9.46 x 10^12 km.

items.t: A repeating decimal has digits that settle into a pattern and repeat forever.
items.d: Example: 1/3 = 0.333... The digit 3 never stops.

items.t: Some decimals repeat a whole block of digits, not just one digit.
items.d: 3227/555 = 5.8144144144... The block 144 repeats forever.

items.t: A decimal that ends, like 0.25, is called a terminating decimal.
items.d: 1/4 = 0.25. After the 5, every digit is zero, so we can stop.

items.t: Every fraction turns into a decimal that either ends or repeats.
A fraction in simplest form repeats if its bottom number has a prime factor besides 2 and 5.
items.d: 1/3 repeats because 3 is not 2 or 5. 1/20 ends, since 20 = 2 x 2 x 5.

items.t: The fraction 1/7 is 0.142857142857... A block of 6 digits repeats forever.
items.d: The block is 142857. Then it starts again: 142857 142857...

items.t: The fraction 1/9 is 0.111... The digit 1 repeats forever.
The fraction 1/11 is 0.090909... A block of two digits repeats.
items.d: The block is 09. It goes 09 09 09 and never stops.

items.t: Pi is about 3.14159. It is the circle's distance around divided by its distance across.
items.d: Wrap a string around a can, then divide by the can's width. You get about 3.14.

items.t: Archimedes showed that pi is between 223/71 and 22/7.
items.d: That is between 3.1408 and 3.1429, so pi is about 3.14.

items.t: The fraction 22/7 is a handy way to estimate pi, but it is not exact.
items.d: 22 / 7 is about 3.1429. Pi is about 3.1416.

items.t: Try this: 1/3 = 0.333... Multiply both sides by 3 and you get 0.999... = 1.
Place value means a digit's worth depends on where it sits in the number.
items.d: In 3.45, the 4 is worth 4 tenths, or 0.4.

items.t: The part of a decimal to the left of the dot is the whole number part.
items.d: In 7.25, the whole number part is 7.

items.t: Simon Stevin brought decimal fractions into everyday use in the 1500s.
items.d: He was a Flemish mathematician who helped make decimals common in daily life.

items.t: Many countries, mostly English-speaking, use a dot as the decimal separator.
items.d: For example, 3 and 5 tenths can be written as 3.5.

items.t: When a number is exactly halfway, like 2.5, we need a rule to round it.
items.d: The usual school rule, round half up, sends 2.5 to 3.

items.t: Round half to even sends a tie like 2.5 to the nearest even whole number.
items.d: 2.5 becomes 2, and 3.5 becomes 4.

items.t: A major computer standard uses round half to even for binary numbers.
items.d: This method is also called statistician's rounding.

items.t: Truncating a number means chopping off the extra digits without rounding.
items.d: Truncating 4.89 to a whole number gives 4. Rounding gives 5.

items.t: A stock index once showed about half its correct value because numbers were chopped, not rounded.
items.d: It started at 1000, and after 22 months showed about 520.

items.t: Canada stopped producing pennies in 2012.
items.d: Canadian banks stopped giving out pennies in 2013.

items.t: With 5 cent rounding, a total ending in 1 or 2 cents is rounded down.
items.d: Example: $3.52 becomes $3.50.

items.t: With 5 cent rounding, a total ending in 3 or 4 cents is rounded up.
items.d: Example: $3.53 becomes $3.55.

items.t: With 5 cent rounding, totals ending in 0 or 5 cents do not change.
Unit price is the cost of one single unit, like one litre or one kilogram.
items.d: If 2 kg cost $6, the unit price is $6 / 2 = $3 per kg.

items.t: Unit price helps you compare prices.
items.d: 500 pens for $2000 is $4 each. That costs less per pen than $5 each.

items.t: India changed to decimal money on 1 April 1957.
items.d: Before that, 1 rupee was 16 anna, 64 pice or 192 pie.

items.t: France once tried a day with 10 hours, each with 100 minutes. People did not like it.
items.d: The rule was cancelled in 1795.

items.t: The word percent comes from the Latin words per centum.
items.d: Those words mean “by the hundred.”

items.t: The % sign grew from a shortened way of writing the Italian words per cento.
items.d: Per cento means “for a hundred.”

items.t: A percentage is a number or ratio written as a fraction of 100.
To turn a ratio into a percent, multiply its value by 100.
One whole is 100%. Half of a whole is 50%.
items.d: If 6 of 12 marbles are blue, 6/12 = 50%.

items.t: One percent is one hundredth of a whole.
items.d: 1% of 300 is 3 because 300 / 100 = 3.

items.t: Ten percent is one tenth of a whole.
items.d: 10% of 70 is 7 because 70 / 10 = 7.

items.t: To find 5%, find 10% and divide it by 2.
items.d: 10% of 80 is 8, so 5% of 80 is 4.

items.t: To find 20%, find 10% and double it.
A 25% discount removes one quarter of the original price.
items.d: 25% of $40 is $10, so the sale price is $30.

items.t: A 10% discount means you pay 90% of the original price.
items.d: 90% of $50 is $45, so the discount saves $5.

items.t: A 30% discount means 30 parts out of 100 are taken away.
items.d: 30% of $20 is $6, so the new price is $14.

items.t: Always ask what whole amount counts as 100%.
items.d: Five red beads could be 50% of 10 beads or 25% of 20 beads.

items.t: Percent changes are usually measured from the starting value.
items.d: A rise from 50 to 60 is 10/50 = 20%.

items.t: A 10% rise followed by a 10% fall does not return to the start.
items.d: 100 rises to 110, then falls by 11 to 99.

items.t: A change from 10% to 15% is 5 percentage points.
items.d: It is also a 50% rise compared with the starting 10%.

items.t: A ratio compares amounts in a chosen order.
items.d: With 8 oranges and 6 lemons, oranges to lemons is 8:6.

items.t: The order of a ratio matters.
items.d: If cats to dogs is 2:3, then dogs to cats is 3:2.

items.t: Simplify a ratio by dividing every part by the same common factor.
items.d: 40:60 becomes 2:3 after both parts are divided by 20.

items.t: A proportion says that two ratios are equal.
items.d: 6:8 and 3:4 form a proportion because 6/8 = 3/4.

items.t: Equal ratios can help you scale a recipe.
items.d: If juice to water is 1:3, then 2 cups of juice need 6 cups of water.

items.t: A rate compares quantities measured in different units.
items.d: Travelling 120 km in 2 hours gives a rate of 60 km per hour.

items.t: Euclid described a ratio as a comparison of two amounts of the same kind.
items.d: You can compare 2 m with 6 m as the ratio 1:3.

items.t: The word ratio comes from a Latin word meaning reason.
items.d: Early translators used it for the Greek word logos.

items.t: A map scale compares map distance with matching ground distance.
items.d: A scale of 1:100 means 1 cm on the map stands for 100 cm outside.

items.t: On a 1:50,000 map, 1 cm represents 500 m on the ground.
Map scales can be written in words, as ratios, or as fractions.
items.d: A ratio scale of 1:1,000 is also the fraction 1/1,000.

items.t: Small-scale maps cover big areas.
items.d: That is because their scale fraction is small, such as 1/100,000,000.

items.t: A town plan can be large-scale while a world map is small-scale.
items.d: A town might use 1:10,000, while a world map might use 1:100,000,000.

items.t: Unit price tells you the cost of one standard unit.
items.d: If 4 kg costs $12, the unit price is $3 per kg.

items.t: Comparing unit prices can reveal which pack costs less per unit.
items.d: Six rolls for $12 cost $2 each. Eight for $20 cost $2.50 each.

items.t: Shops often show the unit price on the shelf label below an item.
items.d: Look for a price such as cost per kilogram or cost per litre.

items.t: A tip can be a percentage of the bill.
items.d: A 10% tip on a $30 bill is $3.

items.t: A service charge may already be added as part of a restaurant bill.
items.d: Check the bill before calculating any separate tip.

items.t: A square has an aspect ratio of 1:1.
items.d: Its width and height are equal, such as 5 cm by 5 cm.

items.t: Older TVs commonly used a width-to-height ratio of 4:3.
items.d: A 40 cm wide picture in this ratio is 30 cm high.

items.t: Widescreen TVs and most laptops use a 16:9 aspect ratio.
items.d: A picture 32 cm wide in this ratio is 18 cm high.

items.t: International paper sizes such as A4 use a side ratio of about 1.414:1.
items.d: The exact ratio is the square root of 2 to 1.

items.t: A gear ratio can be calculated from the teeth on the gears.
items.d: A 10-tooth gear and a 20-tooth gear have a tooth ratio of 1:2.

items.t: An output gear with fewer teeth turns faster but has less turning force.
items.d: Gear size changes speed and turning force in opposite ways.

items.t: In a gear chain, the first and last gears set the overall ratio.
items.d: Gears between them can change the direction of turning.

items.t: Bicycle chain drives use the same ratio maths as gears.
items.d: Different front and rear sprockets change how far the wheel turns.

items.t: The golden ratio is about 1.618.
items.d: It is irrational, so its decimal digits never end or settle into a repeating pattern.

items.t: In a regular pentagon, diagonal length divided by side length is the golden ratio.
items.d: If a side is 1 unit, a diagonal is about 1.618 units.

items.t: Ratios of neighbouring Fibonacci numbers get closer to the golden ratio.
items.d: 13/8 = 1.625, which is close to 1.618.

items.t: Pi is the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter.
items.d: For every circle, circumference / diameter is about 3.14159.

items.t: Eighteen-karat gold is 18 parts gold out of 24, which is 75% gold.
items.d: 18/24 simplifies to 3/4, and 3/4 = 75%.

items.t: In a group of just 23 people, it is more likely than not that two share a birthday.
items.d: About 50.7% chance. It feels too small, but chance is surprising!

items.t: With 70 people in a room, it is almost certain that two of them share a birthday.
items.d: The chance is about 99.9%, even though a year has 365 days.

items.t: If there are only 365 possible birthdays, 366 people guarantee a shared birthday.
items.d: There are more people than possible birthdays, so at least two must match.

items.t: Shared birthdays come up fast because 23 people make many pairs: 253 different pairs.
items.d: 23 x 22 / 2 = 253 pairs. Each pair is a chance for a match.

items.t: In the Monty Hall game, switching doors wins the prize 2 times out of 3. Staying wins only 1 time out of 3.
items.d: Your first pick is right 1/3 of the time. Switching wins the other 2/3.

items.t: Marilyn vos Savant said to switch doors. Thousands of readers wrote that she was wrong, but she was right.
items.d: Many of the letters came from people with advanced math degrees.

items.t: The famous mathematician Paul Erdos only believed the Monty Hall answer after seeing a computer simulation.
items.d: Even great mathematicians can be fooled by probability.

items.t: To see why switching wins, imagine a million doors. Your first pick is very unlikely to be right.
items.d: If all but one other door is opened, that last closed door is very likely the winner.

items.t: On a standard die, the numbers on opposite faces always add up to 7.
items.d: 1 is opposite 6, 2 is opposite 5, and 3 is opposite 4. Check your own die!

items.t: Game players write 2d6 for 'roll two six-sided dice' and d20 for 'roll one twenty-sided die'.
items.d: 3d4 would mean rolling three four-sided dice.

items.t: Two ordinary dice give 36 equally likely results. The sum 7 is the most common, showing up 6 times out of 36.
The sums 2 and 12 are the hardest to roll with two dice. Each can happen in only 1 way out of 36.
items.d: Only 1+1 makes 2, and only 6+6 makes 12.

items.t: Sicherman dice use 1,2,2,3,3,4 and 1,3,4,5,6,8, but have the same sum chances as normal dice.
items.d: They are the only such pair using positive whole numbers.

items.t: A standard deck has 52 cards: 13 ranks in each of four suits, hearts, diamonds, clubs and spades.
In a combination, order does not matter. Choosing 5 cards from 52 can be done in 2,598,960 ways.
items.d: Holding A, K, Q, J, 10 is the same hand in any order.

items.t: Probability is a number from 0 to 1. Impossible is 0, certain is 1, and a fair coin landing heads is 1/2.
items.d: 1/2 is the same as 50%.

items.t: With a fair die, the chance of rolling a 1 or a 2 is 1/6 + 1/6 = 1/3. The chance of not rolling a six is 5/6.
items.d: Add chances for either-or. Subtract from 1 for not.

items.t: A coin has no memory. After four heads in a row, the chance of heads on the next flip is still 1/2.
items.d: Past flips do not change the next one.

items.t: The chance of five heads in a row is 1/32, but only before you start flipping.
items.d: After four heads, the fifth flip is still 1/2.

items.t: As you flip a fair coin many times, the share of heads tends to get closer to 1/2.
items.d: This is called the law of large numbers.

items.t: The average value of a fair six-sided die roll is 3.5, even though you can never roll a 3.5.
The number of ways to line up n different things is n factorial, written n!.
items.d: 3 things can be lined up 3 x 2 x 1 = 6 ways.

items.t: A 52-card deck has about 8 x 10^67 possible orders.
items.d: A well-shuffled deck is probably in an order that never existed before.

items.t: In Pascal's triangle, each number is the sum of the two numbers directly above it.
items.d: Row 1 2 1 gives the next row 1 3 3 1, since 1+2=3 and 2+1=3.

items.t: In Penney's coin game, the second player can always pick a pattern more likely to appear first.
items.d: If the first player picks HTH, picking HHT wins with 2-to-1 odds.

items.t: Efron's four special dice beat each other in a circle. Each die beats the next with chance 2/3.
items.d: Like rock paper scissors, but with dice.

items.t: No strategy has an advantage against a rock paper scissors player who chooses randomly.
items.d: When both players choose randomly, ties happen 1/3 of the time.

items.t: If you take 3 socks from a drawer of only black and blue socks, you are sure to get a matching pair.
items.d: Two of the three must share a color.

items.t: Gerolamo Cardano, a doctor and gambler, wrote an early probability book around 1564.
items.d: It was published in 1663.

items.t: Drop a short needle on a floor with parallel lines. Its chance of crossing a line involves pi.
items.d: Many drops can be used to estimate pi.

items.t: Polygons are named by their number of sides.
items.d: A shape with 7 sides is a 7-gon, also called a heptagon.

items.t: A heptagon has 7 sides. It is sometimes called a septagon.
items.d: Count 7 straight sides and 7 corners.

items.t: A nonagon has 9 sides. It is sometimes called an enneagon.
items.d: A 9-gon has 9 sides and 9 corners.

items.t: An 11-sided polygon is called a hendecagon or an undecagon.
items.d: You can also simply call it an 11-gon.

items.t: The inside angles of an n-sided simple polygon total (n - 2) x 180°.
items.d: For a hexagon, (6 - 2) x 180° = 720°.

items.t: A regular polygon has equal sides and equal inside angles.
items.d: A regular pentagon has 5 equal sides and 5 equal angles.

items.t: A concave polygon has an inside angle greater than 180°.
items.d: That large angle makes part of the shape look as if it caves in.

items.t: A star polygon has sides that cross in a regular pattern.
items.d: A five-pointed pentagram is one example.

items.t: Bees build honeycomb from many hexagonal cells.
items.d: Each cell has 6 sides, and the cells fit together.

items.t: Cooling lava can form tightly packed columns with hexagonal ends.
items.d: A hexagon has 6 sides.

items.t: An equilateral triangle has 3 equal sides.
items.d: Sides of 5 cm, 5 cm, and 5 cm make an equilateral triangle.

items.t: An isosceles triangle has 2 sides of equal length.
items.d: Sides of 4 cm, 4 cm, and 6 cm can make an isosceles triangle.

items.t: A scalene triangle has 3 sides with different lengths.
items.d: Sides of 3 cm, 4 cm, and 5 cm make a scalene triangle.

items.t: A right triangle has one 90° angle.
items.d: A 90° angle looks like the square corner of a sheet of paper.

items.t: An acute triangle has 3 angles smaller than 90°.
items.d: Angles of 50°, 60°, and 70° form an acute triangle.

items.t: An obtuse triangle has one angle greater than 90°.
items.d: Angles of 100°, 40°, and 40° form an obtuse triangle.

items.t: The 3 inside angles of a flat triangle always total 180°.
Triangles are sturdy because their 3 side lengths fix their angles.
items.d: That is why triangle shapes are useful in strong frames.

items.t: Any 2 sides of a triangle together must be longer than the third side.
items.d: Lengths 3, 4, and 5 work because 3 + 4 is greater than 5.

items.t: A triangle's outside angle equals its 2 far inside angles added together.
items.d: If the far angles are 70° and 50°, the outside angle is 120°.

items.t: Every angle in an equilateral triangle is 60°.
An equilateral triangle has 3 lines of mirror symmetry.
items.d: Each mirror line passes through a corner and the opposite side.

items.t: Six equilateral triangles fit around one point.
items.d: Each angle is 60°, and 6 x 60° = 360°.

items.t: An equilateral triangle is a regular polygon.
items.d: Its 3 sides are equal, and its 3 angles are equal.

items.t: A Reuleaux triangle is curved and has the same width in every direction.
items.d: A circle also has the same width in every direction.

items.t: A Reuleaux triangle has 3 curved sides that bulge outward.
items.d: Start with an equilateral triangle and replace its sides with arcs.

items.t: A Reuleaux triangle can turn inside a square while touching all 4 sides.
items.d: This idea is used in drill bits that make nearly square holes.

items.t: The 4 inside angles of a simple quadrilateral total 360°.
A square has 4 equal sides and 4 right angles.
items.d: Each right angle measures 90°.

items.t: A rectangle has 4 right angles.
items.d: Its angles total 4 x 90° = 360°.

items.t: A parallelogram has 2 pairs of parallel sides.
items.d: Opposite sides point in the same direction and never meet.

items.t: A kite has 2 pairs of equal sides next to each other.
items.d: Its 2 diagonals cross at a 90° angle.

items.t: A quadrilateral has 2 diagonals joining opposite corners.
items.d: Draw both diagonals to connect each corner to the corner across from it.

items.t: A square is a regular quadrilateral.
items.d: All 4 sides and all 4 angles are equal.

items.t: Squares tile a flat surface with no gaps.
items.d: Four 90° corners meet to make 360° around one point.

items.t: A square's diagonal is its side length times the square root of 2.
items.d: A square with side 5 cm has a diagonal of exactly 5 x √2 cm.

items.t: A square has 2 equal diagonals that cross at its center.
items.d: Each diagonal joins one corner to the opposite corner.

items.t: A rhombus is a quadrilateral with 4 equal sides.
items.d: A rhombus does not need to have right angles.

items.t: A rhombus with right angles is a square.
items.d: It has 4 equal sides and four 90° angles.

items.t: A rhombus's diagonals cross at right angles and cut each other in half.
items.d: Their crossing makes four 90° angles.

items.t: In a parallelogram, opposite sides and opposite angles are equal.
items.d: If one angle is 70°, the angle across from it is also 70°.

items.t: A parallelogram's diagonals cut each other in half.
items.d: Their crossing point is the midpoint of both diagonals.

items.t: Rectangles, rhombuses, and squares are special parallelograms.
items.d: Each one has 2 pairs of parallel sides.

items.t: Any parallelogram can tile a flat surface without gaps.
items.d: Slide copies beside one another to cover the surface.

items.t: A trapezoid has at least one pair of parallel sides called bases.
items.d: The bases can have different lengths.

items.t: A trapezoid in North America is called a trapezium in Britain.
items.d: The same shape can have different names in different places.

items.t: An isosceles trapezoid has equal legs and a line of mirror symmetry.
items.d: Its 2 nonparallel sides have the same length.

items.t: A trapezoid's midsegment equals the average length of its 2 bases.
items.d: With bases of 6 cm and 10 cm, the midsegment is (6 + 10) / 2 = 8 cm.

items.t: A pentagon has 5 sides.
items.d: Its name comes from Greek words linked to five angles.

items.t: The inside angles of a simple pentagon total 540°.
items.d: Use the polygon rule: (5 - 2) x 180° = 540°.

items.t: A right angle is a quarter turn. It measures exactly 90 degrees.
items.d: The corner of a book is a right angle. Four of them make a full turn: 4 x 90 = 360.

items.t: An acute angle is smaller than 90 degrees.
items.d: A 30 degree slice is acute because 30 is less than 90. The point of a pencil can look acute too.

items.t: An obtuse angle is bigger than 90 degrees but smaller than 180.
items.d: 120 degrees is obtuse. It is past a square corner (90) but not yet a straight line (180).

items.t: A straight angle is 180 degrees, which is half a turn.
items.d: It looks like a straight line. Two right angles make one: 90 + 90 = 180.

items.t: A reflex angle is bigger than 180 degrees but smaller than 360.
items.d: 270 degrees is reflex. It is three right angles: 3 x 90 = 270, more than a half turn.

items.t: A full turn is 360 degrees. Another name for it is a perigon.
items.d: Two straight angles make a full turn: 180 + 180 = 360. You face the same way you started.

items.t: Complementary angles add up to 90 degrees.
items.d: In a right triangle the two small angles add to 90. If one is 28 degrees, the other is 90 - 28 = 62.

items.t: Supplementary angles add up to 180 degrees.
items.d: Side by side they form a straight line. If one is 125 degrees, the other is 180 - 125 = 55.

items.t: When two lines cross, the opposite angles are equal.
items.d: If one angle is 35 degrees, the opposite angle is 35. The angle next to it is 180 - 35 = 145.

items.t: Parallel lines are straight, stay in one plane, and never meet.
items.d: They stay the same distance apart. If the gap is 2 metres here, it is still 2 metres far ahead.

items.t: Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle of 90 degrees.
items.d: A wall and the floor meet this way. Neighbouring sides of a square or a rectangle do too.

items.t: The shortest path from a point to a line meets the line at 90 degrees.
items.d: To reach a straight fence the shortest way, walk straight at it so your path makes a right angle.

items.t: On a compass, the north-south line and the east-west line are perpendicular.
items.d: North to east is 90 degrees. Turn that way four times and you face north again: 4 x 90 = 360.

items.t: A line crossing two parallel lines makes matching corner angles equal.
items.d: Look at the same corner at each crossing. If the top-right angle is 72 degrees at one, it is 72 at the other.

items.t: Between parallel lines, the inside angles of a Z shape are equal.
items.d: These are alternate interior angles. If one is 58 degrees, the other angle in the Z is 58.

items.t: Between parallel lines, same-side inside angles add to 180 degrees.
items.d: If one of them is 68 degrees, the one on the same side is 180 - 68 = 112.

items.t: Join the ends of a circle's diameter to any point on the circle. That angle is 90 degrees.
items.d: The point can be anywhere on the circle except the two ends of the diameter. It makes a right angle every time.

items.t: A clock's minute hand turns 6 degrees every minute.
items.d: In 15 minutes it moves 15 x 6 = 90 degrees, a right angle. In 30 minutes it moves 30 x 6 = 180.

items.t: A clock's hour hand turns 0.5 degrees every minute.
items.d: It moves 360 degrees in 12 hours, or 720 minutes. 360 / 720 = 0.5. In one hour that is 60 x 0.5 = 30 degrees.

items.t: In 12 hours, a clock's hands overlap 11 times, not 12.
items.d: Include the overlap at the start of the 12 hours, but not the one at the very end. That gives 11, not 12.

items.t: At 8:00, the smaller angle between the clock hands is 120 degrees.
items.d: 0.5 x (60 x 8 minus 11 x 0) = 240. Since 240 is over 180, the angle is 360 - 240 = 120.

items.t: The inside angles of a triangle add up to 180 degrees.
items.d: A triangle has 3 sides. (3 - 2) x 180 = 180. So 50 + 60 + 70 = 180.

items.t: The four inside angles of any simple four-sided shape add up to 360.
items.d: Simple means the sides do not cross. Try 60 + 80 + 100 + 120. That equals 360.

items.t: The inside angles of a simple pentagon add up to 540 degrees.
items.d: Simple means the sides do not cross. (5 - 2) x 180 = 540, and 90 + 100 + 110 + 120 + 120 = 540.

items.t: Each inside angle of a regular pentagon is 108 degrees.
items.d: All five match. 5 x 108 = 540, the same as the pentagon's angle total. 108 = 90 + 18.

items.t: Each inside angle of a regular hexagon is 120 degrees.
items.d: 360 / 3 = 120. Honeycomb cells are hexagons, a shape that uses space and wax well.

items.t: Each inside angle of a regular octagon is 135 degrees.
items.d: 8 x 135 = 1,080. Check with (8 - 2) x 180 = 6 x 180 = 1,080. A stop sign has this shape.

items.t: Walk around a convex polygon and the outside turns add up to 360 degrees.
items.d: Convex means no dents. A square turns 90 degrees at each corner: 4 x 90 = 360.

items.t: At each corner, the outside angle and the inside angle add to 180.
items.d: If the inside angle is 120 degrees, the outside angle is 180 - 120 = 60.

items.t: One radian is the angle that cuts off an arc as long as the radius.
items.d: Picture a pizza slice whose crust is as long as one straight side. That slice's angle is one radian.

items.t: Opposite angles of a parallelogram are equal.
items.d: If one corner is 65 degrees, the corner directly across from it is 65 degrees too.

items.t: Neighbouring angles of a parallelogram add up to 180 degrees.
items.d: If one angle is 65 degrees, the angle beside it is 180 - 65 = 115. Then 65 + 115 = 180.

items.t: The diagonals of a rhombus cross each other at right angles.
items.d: Diagonals join opposite corners. They meet at 90 degrees and split each other in half.

items.t: A diagonal of a rhombus cuts the corner angles exactly in half.
items.d: A diagonal joins opposite corners. An 80 degree corner splits into 40 + 40 = 80.

items.t: A square's diagonals cross at 90 degrees and cut corners into 45 degrees.
items.d: Diagonals join opposite corners. Half of the 90 degree corner is 45, and 45 + 45 = 90.

items.t: A rectangle has four right angles, one at every corner.
items.d: Each corner is 90 degrees. Add them: 90 + 90 + 90 + 90 = 360.

items.t: A triangle with sides 3, 4, and 5 always has a right angle.
items.d: 3 x 3 = 9 and 4 x 4 = 16. Then 9 + 16 = 25, and 5 x 5 = 25. The right angle is between sides 3 and 4.

items.t: Earth's axis is tilted by about 23.4 degrees, and that tilt causes the seasons.
items.d: A quarter of a right angle is 90 / 4 = 22.5 degrees. Earth's tilt is just a little more than that.

items.t: Latitude is an angle from the equator: 0 degrees there, 90 degrees at the poles.
items.d: The North Pole is 90 degrees north of the equator, one right angle. The South Pole is 90 degrees south.

items.t: One degree of latitude covers about 111 km on the ground.
items.d: From the equator to a pole is 90 degrees. 90 x 111 = 9,990 km, close to 10,000 km.

items.t: The Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn sit at about 23.4 degrees latitude.
items.d: They match Earth's tilt. The two tropics are about 23.4 + 23.4 = 46.8 degrees apart.

items.t: The Sun and the full Moon each look about half a degree wide.
items.d: That is about 30 arcminutes. Your little finger at arm's length is about 1 degree, roughly twice as wide.

items.t: The Sun appears to move about 15 degrees across the sky each hour.
items.d: 360 degrees split into 24 hours is 360 / 24 = 15. On an equatorial sundial, hour lines are 15 degrees apart.

items.t: A mirror reflects light so the incoming angle equals the outgoing angle.
items.d: Measure from a line at 90 degrees to the mirror. Light that comes in at 25 degrees leaves at 25 degrees.

items.t: A rainbow's brightest light appears about 42 degrees from the point opposite the Sun.
items.d: 42 degrees is just under half a right angle. Half of 90 is 45, and 45 - 42 = 3.

items.t: In gradians, a right angle is 100 units and a full circle is 400.
items.d: A straight line is 200 gradians. Half a right angle is 45 degrees, which is 50 gradians. 4 x 100 = 400.

items.t: 360 divides evenly by every whole number from 1 to 10 except 7.
items.d: 360 / 8 = 45 and 360 / 9 = 40. But 7 x 51 = 357, which is 3 less than 360, so 7 does not fit.

items.t: One degree is 60 arcminutes, and one arcminute is 60 arcseconds.
items.d: So one degree is 60 x 60 = 3,600 arcseconds. A right angle is 90 x 3,600 = 324,000 arcseconds.

items.t: One radian is about 57.3 degrees.
items.d: That is a bit less than 60. Two radians are about 57.3 x 2 = 114.6 degrees, more than a right angle.

items.t: In an isosceles triangle, angles opposite the equal sides are equal.
items.d: If the angle between the equal sides is 40 degrees, each base angle is (180 - 40) / 2 = 70.

items.t: A parallelogram's area is its base times its height.
items.d: Base 8 cm and height 5 cm: 8 x 5 = 40 square cm.

items.t: Cut a parallelogram along a diagonal and you get two identical triangles.
items.d: If the parallelogram is 40 square cm, each triangle is 40 / 2 = 20 square cm.

items.t: To find a trapezoid's area, add its two parallel sides, halve that, then multiply by the height.
items.d: Sides 6 and 10, height 4: (6 + 10) / 2 x 4 = 8 x 4 = 32 square cm.

items.t: Make every length in a flat shape twice as long. Its area becomes 4 times as large.
items.d: A 3 cm square has area 9 square cm. A 6 cm square has area 36 square cm.

items.t: A circle's area is pi times its radius times itself. Double the radius and the area becomes 4 times as large.
items.d: Radius 1 gives about 3.14. Radius 2 gives about 12.56, exactly 4 times the area.

items.t: The square metre is the standard unit of area. It is a square 1 metre on each side.
items.d: 1 square metre = 100 cm x 100 cm = 10,000 square cm.

items.t: Heron's formula finds a triangle's area when you only know its three sides.
items.d: Sides 4, 13 and 15: half the perimeter is 16. Then 16 x 12 x 3 x 1 = 576, and the square root is 24.

items.t: The volume of a cuboid, a cylinder or any prism is its base area times its height.
items.d: A box with a 5 cm by 4 cm base and height 3 cm: 5 x 4 x 3 = 60 cubic cm.

items.t: A cone holds exactly one third as much as a cylinder with the same base and height.
items.d: If a cylinder holds 30 cubic cm, the matching cone holds 30 / 3 = 10 cubic cm.

items.t: Around 300 BCE, a Greek book called Euclid's Elements gave exact volume rules for cones, pyramids and spheres.
items.d: That is over 2,300 years ago, and the rules are still taught in school today.

items.t: One litre is the same as 1,000 cubic centimetres. A cubic metre holds 1,000 litres.
items.d: A 10 cm cube holds 10 x 10 x 10 = 1,000 cubic cm, which is exactly 1 litre.

items.t: Archimedes probably measured odd-shaped objects by dunking them in water and watching the water level rise.
items.d: The volume of the displaced water equals the object's volume.

items.t: When a shape grows, its surface grows with the square of the scale, but its volume grows with the cube.
items.d: Triple a cube's sides: surface grows 3 x 3 = 9 times, volume 3 x 3 x 3 = 27 times.

items.t: An elephant is not just a giant mouse. Its legs need far thicker bones to carry its heavy body.
items.d: Weight grows with volume, but bone strength grows more slowly.

items.t: Cutting a solid into small pieces gives it much more surface, so powders can react faster than lumps.
items.d: Cut a 1 cm cube into 8 small cubes: surface grows from 6 to 8 x 1.5 = 12 square cm.

items.t: A trapezoid's midsegment joins the middles of its slanted sides. Its length is the average of the two bases.
items.d: Bases 6 and 10: the midsegment is (6 + 10) / 2 = 8.

items.t: A trapezoid's area equals its midsegment length times its height.
items.d: Midsegment 8, height 4: 8 x 4 = 32. It matches the other trapezoid area rule.

items.t: In every parallelogram, opposite sides are equal and the two diagonals cut each other exactly in half.
items.d: Both diagonals cross at the middle point of the shape.

items.t: Join the midpoints of the sides of any four-sided shape and you always get a parallelogram with half the area.
items.d: Midpoints of a square of area 100 make a square of area 50.

items.t: A rectangle and a rhombus are both special kinds of parallelogram.
items.d: A rectangle has four right angles. A rhombus has four equal sides.

items.t: Any pyramid's volume is one third of its base area times its height, whatever shape the base is.
items.d: Square base 6 by 6 and height 5: 36 x 5 / 3 = 60 cubic cm.

items.t: A pyramid's surface area is its base area plus the areas of all its triangle faces.
items.d: A square pyramid has 1 square base and 4 triangle faces to add up.

items.t: About 3,700 years ago, Egyptians wrote a math problem on the volume of a pyramid with its top cut off.
items.d: It is in the Moscow Mathematical Papyrus, a very old scroll.

items.t: The Moscow Mathematical Papyrus has 25 problems. Seven are geometry, including areas of triangles.
items.d: Its geometry problems include finding triangle areas.

items.t: A sphere's volume is exactly two thirds of the volume of the cylinder that fits snugly around it.
items.d: If the cylinder's volume is 3 cubic cm, the sphere's volume is 2 cubic cm.

items.t: Cavalieri's principle: two solids with the same cross-section area at every height have the same volume.
items.d: Think of two stacks made from the same number of equal coins. Their volumes match.

items.t: Slide a stack's layers sideways and its volume stays. A leaning cylinder holds as much as a straight one.
items.d: A leaning stack of coins has the same volume as a straight one.

items.t: In 5th-century China, Zu Chongzhi and his son used an idea like Cavalieri's to find the volume of a sphere.
items.d: That was more than 1,000 years before Cavalieri.

items.t: A cylinder's volume is pi times radius squared times height. A leaning cylinder has the same rule.
items.d: Radius 2 cm, height 5 cm: about 3.14 x 4 x 5 = 62.8 cubic cm.

items.t: A straight cylinder's curved side has area 2 times pi times radius times height. It unwraps to a rectangle.
items.d: A can label with radius 5 cm and height 10 cm: 2 x 3.14 x 5 x 10 = 314 square cm.

items.t: For a polygon with corners on grid dots, area = inside dots + half the edge dots - 1.
items.d: A 2 by 2 square: 1 inside, 8 on the edge. 1 + 4 - 1 = 4 square units.

items.t: Each side of the Great Pyramid of Giza's base is about 230 metres long.
items.d: Its base is about 230 x 230 = 52,900, so roughly 53,000 square metres.

items.t: In a tangram square of area 1, each big triangle is 1/4. The small square is 1/8.
items.d: Two big triangles are 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2 of the whole square.

items.t: Of all shapes with the same perimeter, the circle holds the most area. Ancient Greeks knew this.
items.d: A 40 cm loop of string: as a square it holds 100 square cm, as a circle about 127.

items.t: A sphere has the smallest surface area for its volume.
items.d: Surface tension helps small water drops become round, a shape with very little surface.

items.t: A cube's surface area is 6 times its side squared, because it has six equal square faces.
items.d: Side 3 cm: each face is 9, so 6 x 9 = 54 square cm.

items.t: A sphere's surface area is 4 times pi times radius squared. It also equals pi times diameter squared.
items.d: Diameter 10 cm: 3.14 x 10 x 10 = about 314 square cm.

items.t: A hectare equals the area of a square 100 metres on each side: 10,000 square metres.
items.d: A hectare is about 2.5 acres. Ten of them make 100,000 square metres.

items.t: An acre is about 4,047 square metres, which is roughly 40 percent of a hectare.
items.d: An acre was once the land one farmer with oxen could plough in a day.

items.t: In a right triangle, the square of the longest side equals the squares of the other two sides added.
A standard 6.1 m (20-foot) shipping container holds about 33 cubic metres; a 12.2 m one holds about 67.5.
items.d: The longer container is twice as long, so it holds about twice as much.

items.t: Only 3 regular polygons tile a floor alone: equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons.
items.d: Bathroom tiles are often squares or hexagons.

items.t: Any triangle, and any four-sided shape, can tile a flat floor with no gaps or overlaps.
items.d: Make copies of the same shape and they will always fit together.

items.t: A circle is all points in a flat plane that are equally far from one center point.
items.d: If every edge point is 4 cm from the center, the radius is 4 cm.

items.t: Pi is the circumference of any circle divided by its diameter.
items.d: A circumference of 31.4 cm and diameter of 10 cm give 31.4 / 10 = 3.14.

items.t: To find a circle's circumference, multiply its diameter by pi.
items.d: Using pi as 3.14, a 6 cm diameter gives 3.14 x 6 = 18.84 cm.

items.t: Pi is irrational. Its decimal digits continue forever without repeating a pattern.
items.d: The start is 3.14159, but there is no final digit.

items.t: NASA uses 3.141592653589793 for its most accurate trips between planets.
items.d: That version of pi has 15 digits after the decimal point.

items.t: NASA's pi is amazingly precise, even for a circle about 64 billion km across.
items.d: Its calculated edge would be off by only about a little finger's width.

items.t: Just 37 decimal places of pi are enough for a circle as wide as the visible universe.
items.d: Its calculated circumference would be accurate to about one hydrogen atom's width.

items.t: Earth's circumference is roughly 40,100 km.
items.d: One quarter of that distance is about 40,100 / 4 = 10,025 km.

items.t: Eratosthenes measured a Sun shadow angle of about 7.2 degrees in Alexandria.
items.d: At the same moment, the Sun shone straight down a well in Syene.

items.t: An angle of 7.2 degrees is one fiftieth of a full circle.
Eratosthenes used shadows and distance to estimate Earth's circumference.
items.d: The city distance was about 5,000 stadia, so 5,000 x 50 = 250,000 stadia.

items.t: Archimedes trapped pi between two fractions using polygons with 96 sides.
items.d: He showed that 223 / 71 is less than pi, and pi is less than 22 / 7.

items.t: An ancient Babylonian tablet used 25/8 as an estimate of pi.
An ancient Egyptian papyrus suggests about 256/81 for pi.
In 263, Liu Hui bounded pi with polygons of 96 and 192 sides.
items.d: The second polygon had 192 / 96 = 2 times as many sides.

items.t: Zu Chongzhi found that pi lies between 3.1415926 and 3.1415927.
items.d: The two bounds differ by just 0.0000001.

items.t: The fraction 355/113 is a remarkably close estimate of pi.
In 1424, Al-Kashi calculated 16 correct decimal digits of pi using a huge polygon.
items.d: His polygon had about 805 million sides.

items.t: Johann Lambert proved that pi is irrational in 1768.
items.d: That means no fraction of two whole numbers, such as 22/7, equals pi.

items.t: You cannot square a circle using only a compass and a straightedge.
items.d: Squaring a circle means drawing a square with exactly the same area.

items.t: William Jones used the Greek letter pi for the circle ratio in 1706.
items.d: The symbol pi is shorter than writing circumference / diameter.

items.t: Leonhard Euler helped make the symbol pi popular in the 1700s.
items.d: He used it in works published in 1736 and 1748.

items.t: A diameter is the longest chord in a circle.
items.d: In a circle of radius 5 cm, the diameter is 2 x 5 = 10 cm.

items.t: A chord is a straight line joining two points on a circle.
items.d: A diameter is a special chord that passes through the center.

items.t: An arc is a connected piece of a circle's curved edge.
items.d: Half of a 360-degree circle is a 180-degree arc.

items.t: A sector is the region between two radii, like a pizza slice.
items.d: If four equal sectors fill the circle, each angle is 360 / 4 = 90 degrees.

items.t: A circle segment is enclosed by a chord and the arc joining its ends.
items.d: The chord is straight, while the arc is curved.

items.t: A tangent is a straight line that touches a circle at exactly one point.
items.d: Unlike a chord, a tangent does not cross through the circle.

items.t: Among shapes with the same perimeter, a circle encloses the greatest area.
items.d: If each boundary is equally long, the circle holds the most space inside.

items.t: The area of a circle is pi times its radius squared.
items.d: With radius 3 cm, the area is pi x 3 x 3 = 9pi square centimetres.

items.t: Doubling a circle's radius makes its area four times as large.
items.d: Radius 3 gives 9pi, while radius 6 gives 36pi. Then 36pi / 9pi = 4.

items.t: A circle has the same area as a certain triangle made from its measurements.
items.d: Use the circumference as the triangle's base and the radius as its height.

items.t: An angle from both ends of a diameter to another point on the circle is always 90 degrees.
items.d: That is a right angle, like the corner of a square.

items.t: A circle is a special ellipse whose two focus points share the same place.
items.d: Its eccentricity is 0, so it is not stretched in any direction.

items.t: On an ellipse, the distances to its two foci always have the same total.
items.d: If the distances are 4 cm and 7 cm, their fixed total is 4 + 7 = 11 cm.

items.t: A planet's orbit is approximately an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.
items.d: The Sun is usually not at the exact center of the ellipse.

items.t: A ray leaving one focus of an ellipse can reflect through the other focus.
items.d: This focusing effect helps explain how an elliptical whispering gallery works.

items.t: You can draw an ellipse with string looped around two pins.
items.d: Keep the string tight with a pencil while tracing the curve.

items.t: A circle viewed from a sideways angle looks like an ellipse.
items.d: A round plate can look oval when you tilt it.

items.t: Eccentricity measures how stretched an ellipse is.
items.d: A circle has eccentricity 0. Values closer to 1 make a more stretched ellipse.

items.t: Inside a parabola, light parallel to its axis reflects to one focus.
items.d: Rays coming in along that direction meet at the same point.

items.t: With no air drag, a thrown object's path under steady gravity is a parabola.
items.d: Galileo showed why the path curves instead of staying straight.

items.t: Parabolic mirrors are used in reflecting telescopes and satellite dishes.
items.d: Their curved shape directs parallel rays toward one focus.

items.t: Car headlight reflectors use parabola shapes.
items.d: Light starting near the focus reflects outward in nearly parallel rays.

items.t: A parabola can be formed by slicing a cone with a plane parallel to its side.
items.d: Changing the slice changes the curve made on the cone.

items.t: A Reuleaux triangle is a curved triangle with constant width.
items.d: The distance across it stays the same in every direction.

items.t: Every constant-width curve has perimeter equal to pi times its width.
items.d: For width 5 cm, the perimeter is 5pi cm, about 15.7 cm.

items.t: A cycloid is traced by a point on a circle rolling along a straight line.
items.d: A marked point on a rolling wheel rises, curves forward, and returns to the ground.

items.t: On a cycloid-shaped slide, every starting point reaches the bottom in the same time.
items.d: Starting higher means going farther, but the steeper beginning adds speed sooner.

items.t: The area beneath one cycloid arch is three times the rolling circle's area.
items.d: If the circle's area is 8 square centimetres, the arch area is 3 x 8 = 24.

items.t: A tessellation covers a flat surface with shapes. There are no gaps and no overlaps.
items.d: Bathroom floor tiles are a tessellation.

items.t: Only three regular polygons tile a flat surface alone: equilateral triangles, squares and regular hexagons.
items.d: Their equal sides and angles fit together with no gaps.

items.t: Regular pentagons cannot tile a flat surface on their own.
items.d: Their corner angles do not fit a full turn, so gaps appear.

items.t: People used tessellations in Ancient Rome and in Islamic art.
items.d: Many old floors and walls still show these patterns.

items.t: Mathematicians proved a hexagon grid splits an area into equal cells using the least wall length.
items.d: Thomas Hales proved it in 1999.

items.t: Reflection symmetry means one half of a shape is a mirror image of the other half.
items.d: The mirror line is called the line of symmetry.

items.t: Translational symmetry means a pattern looks the same after you slide it along.
items.d: A row of fence posts or a border pattern works this way.

items.t: A glide reflection is a flip across a mirror line plus a slide along that line.
items.d: Footprints in sand are a good example.

items.t: A regular polygon with n sides has n-fold rotational symmetry.
items.d: A square looks the same 4 times in one turn. A hexagon, 6 times.

items.t: There are exactly 17 kinds of repeating wallpaper patterns. Evgraf Fedorov showed this in 1891.
items.d: Every repeating wallpaper pattern fits one of these 17 types.

items.t: A Penrose tiling covers a flat surface but never repeats. No slide ever matches it to itself.
items.d: Roger Penrose studied these tilings in the 1970s.

items.t: Escher called his tiling art the Regular Division of the Plane.
items.d: His tilings use animal shapes that fit together with no gaps.

items.t: Mandala is a Sanskrit word meaning circle.
items.d: Mandalas spread their design evenly from the centre.

items.t: Self-similarity means a pattern repeats at smaller and smaller sizes.
items.d: A fern frond looks like a tiny copy of the whole fern.

items.t: Romanesco broccoli has buds made of smaller buds in spirals. It is a natural fractal.
items.d: The number of spirals is a Fibonacci number.

items.t: To make a Koch curve, split a line in three and swap the middle part for a pointed bump.
items.d: Helge von Koch described it in 1904.

items.t: The Koch snowflake's area approaches 8/5 of the starting triangle's area.
items.d: That limit is 1.6 times the area of the first triangle.

items.t: The Sierpinski triangle is made of three half-size copies of itself.
items.d: Its fractal dimension is about 1.585.

items.t: The Sierpinski carpet splits a square into 9 equal squares, removes the middle one, then repeats.
items.d: Wacław Sierpinski introduced it in 1916.

items.t: A leap year has 366 days. The extra day is February 29.
items.d: Years that divide by 4, like 2028, are usually leap years. 2028 / 4 = 507.

items.t: A year is about 365.2422 days, not a whole number. Leap years fix the leftover bit.
items.d: Leftover is about 0.25 days a year. 4 years x 0.25 = about 1 extra day.

items.t: The year 2000 was a leap year, but 1900 was not.
items.d: Century years only count if they divide by 400. 2000 / 400 = 5, but 1900 / 400 = 4.75.

items.t: A person born on February 29 is called a leapling.
items.d: They were born on the extra day in a leap year.

items.t: Our calendar skips 3 leap days every 400 years to stay accurate.
items.d: In 400 years, 100 leap days would be expected. 100 - 3 = 97 real leap days.

items.t: Earth takes about 365 days and 6 hours to circle the Sun. Four years fall about one day short.
items.d: Using the rounded figure, 4 years x 6 hours = 24 hours, about one day.

items.t: Without leap years, seasons would slowly drift away from their usual calendar dates.
items.d: In one place, a summer month could eventually become a winter month.

items.t: Mars has leap years too. A Martian year is about 668.6 sols, so some years have 669.
items.d: A sol is one Martian day. Six of every ten Martian years have 669 sols.

items.t: In countries that switched in 1582, Thursday 4 October was followed by Friday 15 October.
items.d: Those calendars skipped the dates from 5 to 14 October.

items.t: Today's calendar averages 365.2425 days a year. The older Julian calendar averaged 365.25.
items.d: The difference is 365.25 - 365.2425 = 0.0075 days a year.

items.t: Britain and its empire switched calendars in 1752 and skipped 11 days.
items.d: Eleven dates were removed from September 1752.

items.t: The year 46 BC had 445 days. It was nicknamed the last year of confusion.
items.d: A normal year has 365 days. 445 - 365 = 80 extra days to fix the calendar.

items.t: The legendary early Roman calendar began in March and had ten months and 304 days.
items.d: January and February were added to the Roman calendar later.

items.t: September, October, November and December were once the 7th to 10th months.
items.d: Their names come from Latin numbers. Then January and February were added, so the names no longer match.

items.t: July is named after Julius Caesar. Before that it was called Quintilis.
items.d: Quintilis was renamed July in Julius Caesar's honor in 44 BCE.

items.t: August is named after Emperor Augustus. It used to be called Sextilis.
items.d: Sextilis was renamed in Emperor Augustus's honor in 8 BCE.

items.t: The Moon takes about 29.5 days to go from new Moon to new Moon. That is where months come from.
items.d: 29.5 x 2 = 59 days, so two Moon cycles last about 59 days.

items.t: Seven months have 31 days, four have 30, and February has 28 or 29.
A rhyme helps with month lengths: 'Thirty days hath September.'
items.d: It names April, June, September and November as the 30-day months.

items.t: A week is exactly seven days, which is 604,800 seconds.
items.d: 7 days x 24 hours x 60 minutes x 60 seconds = 604,800 seconds.

items.t: Days of the week are named after the Sun, the Moon and five planets.
items.d: Sunday is Sun day and Monday is Moon day.

items.t: Tuesday through Friday are named after the Germanic figures Tiw, Woden, Thor and Frige.
items.d: Thursday means "Thor's day."

items.t: Saturday means "Saturn day." It is the English day name kept directly from the Romans.
items.d: The other Roman planet names were replaced with Germanic names in English.

items.t: In 1973, mathematician John Conway invented a trick to find the weekday of any date in your head.
items.d: It is called the Doomsday rule. He could answer in about two seconds.

items.t: In any year, 4/4, 6/6, 8/8, 10/10 and 12/12 all fall on the same day of the week.
items.d: In 2025, all of them fell on a Friday. Check it on a calendar!

items.t: Our calendar repeats exactly every 400 years, which is 146,097 days.
items.d: 146,097 / 7 = 20,871, so it is a whole number of weeks.

items.t: Since 1967, a second has used 9,192,631,770 cycles of radiation from caesium-133.
items.d: The radiation is linked to a change between two energy states in the atom.

items.t: A second was once defined as 1/86,400 of a day.
items.d: 24 hours x 60 minutes x 60 seconds = 86,400 seconds in a day.

items.t: A day is exactly 86,400 seconds in the standard system of units.
items.d: 24 x 60 = 1,440 minutes, and 1,440 x 60 = 86,400 seconds.

items.t: A day measured by the stars is about 4 minutes shorter than a 24-hour day.
items.d: It is 23 hours and 56 minutes. 24 hours - 4 minutes = 23 hours 56 minutes.

items.t: The Moon's pull slowly slows Earth's spin. Days get about 2 milliseconds longer every 100 years.
items.d: A millisecond is one thousandth of a second, so the change is tiny.

items.t: About 500 million years ago, a day on Earth lasted only about 20 hours and 40 minutes.
items.d: Earth spun faster then, so there were more days in a year.

items.t: A leap second once made a minute 61 seconds long to keep clocks matched to Earth's spin.
items.d: Between 1972 and 2016, 27 leap seconds were added to world time.

items.t: On a sundial, the Sun seems to move about 15 degrees each hour.
items.d: 24 hours x 15 degrees = 360 degrees, a full circle.

items.t: a.m. and p.m. come from Latin. They mean 'before midday' and 'after midday'.
items.d: 7 a.m. is before midday. 7 p.m. is in the evening, after midday.

items.t: On a 24-hour clock, hours go from 00 to 23.
Time zones run from UTC-12:00 to UTC+14:00.
items.d: That is a spread of 26 hours, because 12 + 14 = 26.

items.t: China uses just one time zone, UTC+8, even though it is wide enough for five.
items.d: So when the Sun rises in the east, the far west still shows the same clock time.

items.t: The International Date Line runs roughly along the 180 degree meridian, bending around some islands.
items.d: Cross it going west and the calendar jumps ahead one day.

items.t: Kiritimati in Kiribati is at UTC+14. It sees each new day first.
items.d: The island is 14 hours ahead of UTC, so New Year arrives there before almost anywhere.

items.t: Greenwich Mean Time is the yearly average of when the Sun crosses the Prime Meridian each day.
items.d: The Prime Meridian is 0 degrees longitude, in Greenwich, London.

items.t: "Spring forward, fall back" tells you which way to move the clocks.
items.d: In spring, clocks move ahead one hour. In autumn, they move back one hour.

items.t: The Chinese calendar follows the Moon and adds leap months, so New Year moves each year.
items.d: Leap months help keep the calendar matched with the seasons.

items.t: The ancient Egyptians had 12 months of 30 days, plus 5 extra days.
Computers often count seconds from 1 January 1970. This start is called the Unix epoch.
items.d: The count starts at midnight UTC.

items.t: Speed is distance divided by time. A cyclist who goes 30 m in 2 s is moving at 15 m/s.
items.d: 30 / 2 = 15 metres per second.

items.t: Driving 80 km in 1 hour, or 320 km in 4 hours, both give an average speed of 80 km/h.
One metre per second is about 3.6 km per hour.
items.d: 10 m/s is about 10 x 3.6 = 36 km/h.

items.t: Venus takes 243 Earth days to rotate once, longer than its 225-Earth-day year.
items.d: 243 - 225 = 18 Earth days longer.

items.t: Mercury's year is 88 Earth days, but one sunrise to the next takes 176 Earth days.
items.d: 176 / 88 = 2, so a Mercury day is two Mercury years.

items.t: Binary uses only two digits, 0 and 1.
items.d: Computers can represent numbers using just these two digits.

items.t: Each binary digit is called a bit.
items.d: The word bit is short for binary digit.

items.t: Counting in binary goes 0, 1, 10, 11, 100, 101.
items.d: After 1 there is no digit 2, so you start a new place: 10 means two.

items.t: In binary, each place is worth double the place before it.
items.d: Places are worth 1, 2, 4, 8, 16. So 1101 is 8 + 4 + 1 = 13.

items.t: Computers use binary because it is easy to build with electronic circuits.
items.d: Two circuit states can represent 0 and 1.

items.t: In 1937 George Stibitz built a binary adding machine on his kitchen table. He called it Model K.
items.d: K stood for Kitchen.

items.t: In Roman numerals, I is 1, V is 5, X is 10 and M is 1,000.
items.d: So XVI is 10 + 5 + 1 = 16.

items.t: Roman numerals are usually added up letter by letter.
Sometimes, a smaller Roman numeral before a larger one is subtracted.
items.d: IX is 10 - 1 = 9, and XL is 50 - 10 = 40.

items.t: The biggest number in standard Roman numerals is 3,999.
items.d: It is written MMMCMXCIX.

items.t: The year 1900 in Roman numerals is MCM.
Hexadecimal uses the letters A to F for the values 10 to 15.
items.d: So A is 10, B is 11, and F is 15.

items.t: One byte, which is 8 bits, can be written with just two hex digits.
items.d: For example, 2C is one byte.

items.t: Twelve can be shared evenly by 2, 3, 4 and 6. Ten can only be shared by 2 and 5.
items.d: 12 / 3 = 4 and 12 / 4 = 3, with nothing left over.

items.t: Twelve times twelve, which is 144, is called a gross.
Twelve cubed is called a great gross.
You can count to 12 on one hand by touching your thumb to each finger bone.
items.d: Each finger has 3 bones, and 4 fingers x 3 bones = 12.

items.t: There are 12 months in a year and 12 inches in a foot.
items.d: Twelve shows up in our everyday world all the time.

items.t: A Sumerian abacus appeared about 4,500 years ago.
items.d: That is between about 2700 and 2300 BC.

items.t: Base 5 probably started because we have five fingers on each hand.
items.d: In base 5 you only use the digits 0 to 4.

items.t: In base 5, the number twenty-five is written 100.
items.d: Places are worth 1, 5 and 25, so 100 means one 25.

items.t: The French word for 80, quatre-vingts, really means four-twenties.
In tally marks, the fifth stroke goes across the other four. It looks like a five-bar gate.
items.d: Counting 15 takes three gates.

items.t: Tally marks are grouped in fives so they are easy to read.
items.d: Counting 5, 10, 15 is quicker than counting 1 by 1.

items.t: We still use base 60 today. An hour has 60 minutes and a minute has 60 seconds.
items.d: 60 x 60 = 3,600 seconds in one hour.

items.t: A circle has 360 degrees. That is six sixties.
The number 60 can be divided evenly by twelve different numbers.
Maya numbers used a dot for 1, a bar for 5 and a shell for zero.
items.d: Two dots and a bar make 7.

items.t: Our digits 0 to 9 use place value. A digit's worth depends on where it sits.
items.d: In 505, the first 5 is 500 and the last 5 is just 5.

items.t: A normal magic square of size n has sum n x (n squared + 1) / 2 on every line.
items.d: For a 4 by 4 square: 4 x (16 + 1) / 2 = 34.

items.t: The smallest normal magic square is 3 by 3. Every row, column, and diagonal adds to 15.
items.d: The numbers 1 to 9 total 45, and 45 / 3 = 15.

items.t: Every normal 3 by 3 magic square is a turn or flip of the same basic square.
items.d: Turning or reflecting the square changes its look, but each line still adds to 15.

items.t: There are exactly 880 different normal 4 by 4 magic squares.
items.d: Each one uses 1 to 16, with every row and column adding to 34.

items.t: The Tower of Hanoi with n disks needs at least 2 to the power n, minus 1 moves.
items.d: With 4 disks, the fewest moves is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 - 1 = 15.

items.t: Moving a 64-disk Tower of Hanoi once per second would take about 585 billion years.
items.d: The minimum is 2 to the power 64, minus 1 moves.

items.t: Edouard Lucas presented the Tower of Hanoi puzzle in 1883 using a playful pen name.
items.d: He used the pen name N. Claus de Siam.

items.t: The best method for the four-peg Tower of Hanoi was not proved until 2014.
items.d: Adding one peg makes the puzzle much harder to study.

items.t: The map of all Tower of Hanoi positions forms a pattern like a Sierpinski triangle.
items.d: This repeating shape is a fractal, with smaller triangles inside larger ones.

items.t: A proper Sudoku needs at least 17 starting clues.
items.d: With fewer than 17 clues, a standard 9 by 9 Sudoku cannot have just one solution.

items.t: There are exactly 6,670,903,752,021,072,936,960 completed 9 by 9 Sudoku grids.
items.d: That is about 6.67 sextillion different grids.

items.t: Sudoku was probably designed by Howard Garns and appeared in 1979 as Number Place.
items.d: Its first known magazine version used an English name.

items.t: A number puzzle became popular in Japan in 1984. In 1986 its name was shortened to sudoku.
items.d: The shorter name was easier to say and remember.

items.t: The Japanese word sudoku roughly means "digit-single."
items.d: Each digit appears once in every row, column, and 3 by 3 box.

items.t: A completed Sudoku is a special kind of Latin square.
items.d: It follows the Latin square row and column rules, plus a rule for each 3 by 3 box.

items.t: Every Sudoku row, column, and 3 by 3 box must contain the digits 1 to 9.
items.d: A digit cannot repeat within any one of those groups.

items.t: In knights and knaves puzzles, knights always tell the truth and knaves always lie.
items.d: Use each statement to work out which kind of speaker could have said it.

items.t: Logician Raymond Smullyan coined the name "knights and knaves" in 1978.
items.d: His name helped make this family of truth-and-lie puzzles well known.

items.t: Knights and knaves puzzles happen on an imaginary island with two kinds of people.
items.d: Everyone is either a truthful knight or a lying knave.

items.t: A two-guard puzzle can be solved by asking what the other guard would say, then doing the opposite.
items.d: Both guards point you toward the same wrong choice, so reverse their answer.

items.t: Some knights and knaves puzzles add normals, who may tell either truth or lies.
items.d: A normal person's statement alone does not reveal whether it is true.

items.t: A classic river puzzle asks a farmer to move a wolf, a goat, and a cabbage across.
items.d: The wolf cannot be left with the goat, and the goat cannot be left with the cabbage.

items.t: Old river crossing puzzles appear in a manuscript traditionally credited to Alcuin.
items.d: The earliest surviving copies of this puzzle collection are from the 9th century.

items.t: In the bridge and torch puzzle, four people cross two at a time using one torch.
items.d: The torch must travel with each crossing, so someone may need to bring it back.

items.t: The pigeonhole principle says more items than boxes means one box gets at least two items.
items.d: Put 4 balls into 3 boxes, and some box must hold 2 or more balls.

items.t: Three socks chosen from only black and blue socks must include a matching pair.
items.d: With 3 socks but only 2 colors, one color must appear at least twice.

items.t: Among 367 people, at least two must share a birthday.
items.d: There are at most 366 possible birthdays, but there are 367 people.

items.t: In any group of at least two people, two people have shaken the same number of hands.
items.d: This is a surprising use of the pigeonhole principle.

items.t: If 10 people each shake hands once with everyone else, there are 45 handshakes.
Handshake totals are triangular numbers, which can be arranged as triangular dot patterns.
items.d: For 4 people, 3 + 2 + 1 = 6 handshakes.

items.t: John Venn introduced his diagrams in a paper published in 1880.
items.d: Overlapping shapes can show which things belong to one set, several sets, or none.

items.t: Euler diagrams came before Venn diagrams.
items.d: Both use shapes to show sets, but their rules are not exactly the same.

items.t: A complete Venn diagram for three sets has eight regions, including the outside.
items.d: Three sets make 2 x 2 x 2 = 8 possible in-or-out combinations.

items.t: The Konigsberg puzzle asked for a walk crossing each of the city's seven bridges exactly once.
items.d: The challenge was about choosing a route, not measuring distance.

items.t: Leonhard Euler proved in 1736 that the seven bridges walk was impossible.
items.d: He studied how land areas were connected instead of drawing every possible route.

items.t: Euler's solution to the seven bridges puzzle helped begin graph theory.
items.d: A graph uses points and connecting lines to model routes and networks.

items.t: In the Monty Hall puzzle, switching doors wins the car two thirds of the time.
items.d: Switching has a 2 in 3 chance, while staying has a 1 in 3 chance.

items.t: The Monty Hall problem is named after a game show host.
items.d: Its surprising answer comes from probability, not from the door positions.

items.t: Paul Erdos accepted the Monty Hall answer after seeing a computer simulation.
items.d: Repeating a puzzle many times can reveal how often each strategy wins.

items.t: The sliding 15 puzzle was invented by Noyes Palmer Chapman, a postmaster in New York.
items.d: Its numbered tiles slide around one empty space.

items.t: Exactly half of all possible starting positions in a sliding tile puzzle are unsolvable.
items.d: Legal tile moves can reach only one of two groups of arrangements.

items.t: Any solvable 15 puzzle can be finished in at most 80 single-tile moves.
items.d: Some starting positions need all 80 moves when every move is counted separately.

items.t: The eight queens puzzle has 92 different solutions.
items.d: Place 8 queens so no two share a row, column, or diagonal.

items.t: A knight's tour visits every square of a chessboard exactly once.
items.d: The path uses only a knight's L-shaped chess move.

items.t: Gauss quickly found that 1 + 2 + 3 and so on through 100 equals 5,050.
items.d: Pair 1 with 100, 2 with 99, and so on. There are 50 pairs of 101.

items.t: With 23 people, the chance that at least two share a birthday is about 50.7 percent.
items.d: There are 253 pairs of people to compare, so a match is more likely than it first seems.

items.t: The zebra puzzle uses clues about five houses to find who owns the zebra and who drinks water.
items.d: A grid can track each house's clues and rule out impossible matches.

items.t: A light-year is a distance, not a time.
items.d: It is how far light travels in one year, about 9.5 trillion kilometers.

items.t: A parsec is a distance used by astronomers.
items.d: One parsec is about 3.26 light-years.

items.t: Looking far into space also means looking into the past.
items.d: We see a star 100 light-years away as it looked 100 years ago.

items.t: Stars twinkle because moving air bends their light.
items.d: Earth's atmosphere makes the light shift slightly from moment to moment.

items.t: Planets usually twinkle less than stars.
items.d: Their tiny disks of light are steadier when seen through moving air.

items.t: A star's color gives a clue to its surface temperature.
items.d: Blue stars are hotter than red stars.

items.t: A star can look bright because it is powerful, close, or both.
items.d: Distance changes how bright a star appears from Earth.

items.t: Nearly every star you can see without a telescope is in our Milky Way galaxy.
items.d: Other galaxies are much farther away and usually look like faint patches.

items.t: A constellation is a named area of the sky with a star pattern.
items.d: Its stars may be very different distances from Earth.

items.t: Astronomers divide the whole sky into 88 official constellations.
items.d: Together, they work like a map of the sky.

items.t: The Northern and Southern Hemispheres see different parts of the sky.
items.d: Some constellations never rise above the horizon in the other hemisphere.

items.t: Different constellations are easy to see in different seasons.
items.d: Earth faces different directions at night as it travels around the Sun.

items.t: From some places on Earth, a circumpolar constellation never sets below the horizon.
items.d: It seems to circle a sky pole during the night.

items.t: Polaris appears close to the north sky pole.
items.d: In the Northern Hemisphere, it can help observers find north.

items.t: Polaris is not the brightest star in the night sky.
items.d: Sirius appears brighter from Earth.

items.t: The Big Dipper is an asterism, not an official constellation.
items.d: Its seven bright stars are part of Ursa Major.

items.t: The ecliptic is the Sun's yearly path across our sky.
items.d: The Moon and planets also appear close to this path.

items.t: The zodiac constellations lie along the ecliptic.
items.d: The Sun appears to pass in front of them during the year.

items.t: Moon phases repeat about every 29.5 days.
items.d: This is the time from one new Moon to the next.

items.t: At new Moon, the Moon appears close to the Sun in our sky.
items.d: Its sunlit half faces mostly away from Earth.

items.t: At full Moon, Earth is roughly between the Sun and Moon.
items.d: The side facing Earth appears fully lit.

items.t: At a quarter Moon, half of the Moon's visible face looks lit.
items.d: The name describes how far the Moon is through its monthly cycle.

items.t: A waxing Moon shows more of its lit side each night.
items.d: It changes from new Moon toward full Moon.

items.t: A waning Moon shows less of its lit side each night.
items.d: It changes from full Moon toward new Moon.

items.t: People around the world see the same Moon phase at the same moment.
items.d: The phase may look tilted differently from different places.

items.t: Earthshine can faintly light the dark part of a crescent Moon.
items.d: Sunlight reflects from Earth to the Moon and back to us.

items.t: A lunar eclipse happens when the Moon passes through Earth's shadow.
items.d: Earth blocks some sunlight that would normally reach the Moon.

items.t: A lunar eclipse can happen only at full Moon.
items.d: That is when the Moon can pass behind Earth compared with the Sun.

items.t: Eclipses do not happen every month because the Moon's orbit is tilted.
items.d: The Moon usually passes above or below the needed line.

items.t: The Moon rises about 50 minutes later each day on average.
items.d: Its motion around Earth changes where it appears against the stars.

items.t: A full Moon rises near sunset and sets near sunrise.
items.d: It appears roughly opposite the Sun in the sky.

items.t: The Moon looks about half a degree wide in the sky.
items.d: Your little finger at arm's length can cover it easily.

items.t: The Moon illusion makes a low Moon look larger than a high Moon.
items.d: Its actual size in the sky changes very little during one night.

items.t: The bright side of the Moon always points toward the Sun.
items.d: Even when the Sun is below the horizon, this can reveal its direction.

items.t: The Sun's faint outer atmosphere is called the corona.
items.d: It becomes visible around the blocked Sun during a total solar eclipse.

items.t: Stars make energy by squeezing hydrogen together to make helium.
items.d: This process is called nuclear fusion.

items.t: A stable star balances two effects.
items.d: Gravity pulls inward while hot gas and radiation push outward.

items.t: Stars begin inside cold clouds of gas and dust.
items.d: Gravity can pull parts of a cloud together into dense clumps.

items.t: A protostar is a young, warming clump that may become a star.
items.d: It becomes a star when fusion begins in its center.

items.t: Stars spend most of their lives in the main sequence stage.
items.d: During this stage, they fuse hydrogen into helium.

items.t: A star's mass strongly affects how its life unfolds.
items.d: Mass changes its temperature, brightness and lifetime.

items.t: Massive stars use their fuel faster than smaller stars.
items.d: Although they have more fuel, they usually have shorter lives.

items.t: A red giant is a star whose outer layers have greatly expanded.
items.d: Its surface cools as the star grows larger.

items.t: A Sun-like star can leave behind a white dwarf.
items.d: A white dwarf is the hot, dense core left after outer gas drifts away.

items.t: A white dwarf can hold about a star's mass in an Earth-sized sphere.
items.d: Its matter is packed extremely tightly.

items.t: Some massive stars finish with a brilliant explosion called a supernova.
items.d: The blast can scatter newly made elements into space.

items.t: A neutron star is the crushed core left by some supernovas.
items.d: It packs more mass than the Sun into a sphere about the size of a city.

items.t: A pulsar is a spinning neutron star that sends out beams.
items.d: The beams can appear as regular pulses when they sweep past Earth.

items.t: A black hole has a boundary called an event horizon.
items.d: Past this boundary, not even light can escape.

items.t: Black holes do not pull in everything around them like vacuum cleaners.
items.d: Far away, their gravity acts like the gravity of any object with the same mass.

items.t: A binary star system contains two stars orbiting each other.
items.d: Many stars are members of pairs or larger groups.

items.t: In an eclipsing binary, one star regularly passes in front of the other.
items.d: The system's combined light dims in a repeating pattern.

items.t: A variable star changes in brightness over time.
items.d: It may swell, shrink, pulse, or be partly blocked by a companion.

items.t: An open cluster is a loose group of stars born from one cloud.
items.d: Open clusters are often found in a galaxy's disk.

items.t: A globular cluster is a crowded, round group of old stars.
items.d: Some contain hundreds of thousands of stars.

items.t: A nebula is a cloud of gas and dust in space.
items.d: Some nebulae form stars, while others contain material shed by stars.

items.t: An emission nebula glows because nearby hot stars energize its gas.
items.d: The Orion Nebula is a well-known example.

items.t: A reflection nebula shines by scattering nearby starlight.
items.d: Its gas and dust do not make their own visible light.

items.t: A dark nebula blocks light from stars behind it.
items.d: It can look like a dark shape against a bright background.

items.t: Stars formed much of the carbon and oxygen found in the universe.
items.d: Stellar processes build elements from lighter particles.

items.t: A star's spectrum can reveal which elements are in its atmosphere.
items.d: Each element leaves a special pattern of lines in the light.

items.t: A brown dwarf is not massive enough for steady hydrogen fusion.
items.d: It is more massive than a planet but less massive than a true star.

items.t: A spiral galaxy has a flat disk, a central bulge and winding arms.
items.d: Its arms often contain gas, dust and young stars.

items.t: An elliptical galaxy looks round or oval.
items.d: It usually has less cool gas and dust than a spiral galaxy.

items.t: An irregular galaxy has no simple spiral or oval shape.
items.d: Gravity from nearby galaxies can help distort its form.

items.t: The Milky Way belongs to a group of galaxies called the Local Group.
items.d: The group includes the Andromeda Galaxy and dozens of smaller galaxies.

items.t: The Andromeda Galaxy is about 2.5 million light-years away.
items.d: Under a dark sky, it can be seen without a telescope as a faint smudge.

items.t: The center of the Milky Way lies toward the constellation Sagittarius.
items.d: Thick dust clouds hide much of it from visible-light telescopes.

items.t: Infrared and radio waves can pass through some space dust.
items.d: They help astronomers study regions hidden from visible light.

items.t: A supermassive black hole sits at the center of the Milky Way.
items.d: It is called Sagittarius A* and has about four million Suns of mass.

items.t: Galaxies gather into groups and clusters because of gravity.
items.d: Clusters can contain hundreds or thousands of galaxies.

items.t: The universe is expanding.
items.d: On very large scales, the space between distant galaxy groups grows.

items.t: Light from many distant galaxies is shifted toward redder wavelengths.
items.d: This redshift helps show that the universe is expanding.

items.t: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old.
items.d: Astronomers estimate this using expansion and ancient light.

items.t: The cosmic microwave background is faint light from the early universe.
items.d: It now reaches us mostly as microwaves from every direction.

items.t: A quasar is a brilliant center of a distant galaxy.
items.d: Gas falling toward a supermassive black hole releases enormous energy.

items.t: An asteroid is a rocky or metallic object that orbits the Sun.
items.d: Asteroids are much smaller than planets.

items.t: Most known asteroids orbit in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.
items.d: Jupiter's gravity helped stop them from joining into one planet.

items.t: Asteroids in the main belt are usually far apart.
items.d: A spacecraft can cross the belt without weaving through crowded rocks.

items.t: A comet has a nucleus made of ice, dust and rock.
items.d: Its frozen materials warm as the comet approaches the Sun.

items.t: A comet can grow a glowing cloud and tails near the Sun.
items.d: The cloud around its nucleus is called a coma.
