items.t: In 1572, Tycho saw a bright star appear where none had been seen before.
items.d: It became brighter than every other star and planet in the sky.

items.t: Tycho is often called the greatest astronomer before the telescope.
items.d: He measured the sky with his eyes and special tools, without a telescope.

items.t: The king of Denmark offered Tycho the island of Hven so he could build an observatory.
Tycho named his castle observatory Uraniborg, after Urania, the muse of astronomy.
Tycho imagined the Sun going around Earth while the other planets go around the Sun.
items.d: It was a mix of the old and new ideas.

items.t: Johannes Kepler was born in 1571 in Weil der Stadt, in what is now Germany.
Kepler is best known for his three laws of planetary motion.
items.d: They describe how planets travel around the Sun.

items.t: Kepler worked out his laws by studying Tycho Brahe's careful observations of Mars.
Kepler made the Rudolphine Tables, lists of where stars and planets would be.
items.d: They were made to replace older, less accurate tables.

items.t: In October 1604 Kepler watched a bright new star appear in the evening sky.
Kepler wrote Somnium, a story about a fantastic trip to the Moon.
items.d: It is an early example of science fiction.

items.t: Kepler's book Harmonice Mundi was published in 1619.
Galileo was born in Pisa in 1564.
items.d: He grew up to use the telescope in a brand new way.

items.t: Galileo built an improved telescope and found Jupiter's four biggest moons.
Galileo saw that Venus has phases, just like our Moon.
items.d: He saw it change shape through his telescope.

items.t: Through his telescope, Galileo saw mountains and craters on the Moon.
Galileo studied sunspots, the dark spots on the Sun.
items.d: Never look at the Sun without proper eye protection.

items.t: Galileo noticed that a pendulum keeps the same beat even when it swings a little wider or narrower.
Galileo saw that the Milky Way is made of a huge number of stars packed close together.
items.d: From far away, they look like a glowing cloud.

items.t: The Galilean moons were the first moons found anywhere beyond Earth.
Ganymede, one of Galileo's moons, is the biggest moon in the solar system.
items.d: It is even bigger than the planet Mercury.

items.t: Io, another moon Galileo found, is the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
Isaac Newton was born at Woolsthorpe Manor, a small hamlet in Lincolnshire, England.
Newton's famous book, the Principia, was first published in 1687.
Newton figured out the laws of motion and the law of universal gravity.
Newton used gravity math to explain Kepler's laws of planet motion.
Newton built the first reflecting telescope, which uses a mirror instead of a lens.
Newton showed that a prism splits white light into the colors of a rainbow.
Newton helped invent calculus, a kind of math for studying things that change.
Newton ran the Royal Mint and made British coins more accurate and safer.
Newton was president of the Royal Society from 1703 to 1727.
Edmond Halley mapped the stars of the southern sky.
Halley helped pay to print Newton's great book, the Principia.
Halley saw that watching Venus cross the Sun could help measure distances in space.
Halley once dived 18 meters deep in the River Thames using a diving bell.
Halley's Comet takes about 76 years to go around the Sun.
Halley's Comet will come back in 2061.
Edmond Halley correctly predicted that a comet would return in 1758.
items.d: That comet is now named after him.

items.t: Halley's Comet was last seen from Earth in 1986.
Dust from Halley's Comet makes two meteor showers each year, in May and October.
items.d: They are the Eta Aquarids and the Orionids.

items.t: William Herschel found the planet Uranus on 13 March 1781.
items.d: It was the first planet discovered since ancient times.

items.t: The Hubble Space Telescope was deployed by the space shuttle Discovery in 1990.
Hubble orbits about 483 km above Earth.
items.d: That is about 300 miles above Earth.

items.t: Hubble's main mirror is 2.4 metres across.
items.d: That is 94.5 inches across.

items.t: Hubble travels around Earth at about 27,000 km per hour.
Hubble discovered moons around Pluto and watched a comet hit Jupiter.
Hubble's first pictures were blurry. Astronauts added corrective optics in 1993.
items.d: The new optics helped Hubble make sharp pictures.

items.t: Astronauts flew five missions to service Hubble from 1993 to 2009.
Cecilia Payne showed that stars are made mainly of hydrogen and helium.
In 1925, Cecilia Payne earned Radcliffe College's first astronomy PhD.
An astronomer first doubted Payne's hydrogen result, then later reached the same answer.
In 1956, Payne-Gaposchkin was the first woman promoted to full professor within Harvard Arts and Sciences.
A talk about a 1919 eclipse expedition inspired Cecilia Payne to study astronomy.
Henrietta Leavitt identified 1,777 variable stars in the Magellanic Clouds.
items.d: Variable stars change in brightness over time.

items.t: Leavitt found that brighter Cepheid stars pulse more slowly than dimmer ones.
Leavitt's discovery made Cepheid stars useful for measuring distances to other galaxies.
items.d: Their pulse rate helps astronomers work out their true brightness.

items.t: Henrietta Leavitt was deaf and worked as a human computer at Harvard Observatory.
items.d: A human computer studied information and performed calculations.

items.t: Vera Rubin found that stars near a spiral galaxy's edge orbit about as fast as stars nearer its centre.
Rubin's galaxy studies gave strong evidence for dark matter, mass that cannot be seen directly.
Astronomer Vera Rubin worked for years with instrument maker Kent Ford.
items.d: Their tools helped them measure how fast stars orbit in galaxies.

items.t: In 2019, a telescope was renamed the Vera C. Rubin Observatory.
In 1967, student Jocelyn Bell spotted an odd mark on chart paper. It was the first known pulsar.
The first pulsar signal was nicknamed LGM-1. It actually came from a spinning neutron star.
In 2018, Jocelyn Bell Burnell gave her entire $3 million prize to help more students study physics.
At age 19, Chandrasekhar calculated a white dwarf's mass limit during a voyage to England.
items.d: The limit is about 1.4 times the Sun's mass.

items.t: Chandrasekhar shared the 1983 Nobel Prize for studying how stars are built and change.
NASA's Chandra X-ray Observatory is named after astronomer Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar.
Carl Sagan helped create the 13-part TV series Cosmos in 1980.
items.d: It introduced astronomy to hundreds of millions of viewers.

items.t: Carl Sagan urged NASA to take the Pale Blue Dot photo of Earth from about 6 billion km away.
items.d: In the picture, our whole planet looks like a tiny speck.

items.t: Carl Sagan helped choose the sounds and images placed on the Voyager Golden Record in 1977.
Sagan's research helped show why Venus is extremely hot.
items.d: A runaway greenhouse effect traps a great deal of heat there.

items.t: Katherine Johnson graduated from college at age 18 with degrees in mathematics and French.
Katherine Johnson calculated the path for Alan Shepard's 1961 spaceflight.
items.d: Shepard became the first American to travel into space.

items.t: John Glenn asked Katherine Johnson to check a computer's calculations before his orbital flight.
Katherine Johnson's backup charts helped guide Apollo 13 safely home in 1970.
In 1924, Edwin Hubble found Cepheid stars in Andromeda and showed it lies beyond the Milky Way.
In 1929, Hubble showed that farther galaxies move away faster.
items.d: This relationship is evidence that the universe is expanding.

items.t: Edwin Hubble created a system for classifying galaxies that astronomers still use.
In 1927, Georges Lemaitre argued that galaxies moving apart show the universe is expanding.
Lemaitre's 1931 primeval atom idea became the first form of the Big Bang theory.
Webb studies infrared light and has a five-layer sunshield.
items.d: The shield protects the telescope from heat and infrared radiation.

items.t: Annie Jump Cannon arranged star types as O, B, A, F, G, K, M. Astronomers still use this order.
Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930 at age 24 using a blink comparator.
items.d: The device helped him compare pictures of the night sky.

items.t: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson discovered the cosmic microwave background in 1964.
Cosmic microwave background light was released about 380,000 years after the Big Bang.
items.d: It comes from when the young universe first became transparent.

items.t: LIGO first detected gravitational waves in 2015 from two merging black holes.
items.d: The waves had travelled about 1.3 billion light-years.

items.t: In 1995, Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz announced a planet orbiting a Sun-like star.
items.d: 51 Pegasi b circles its star in about 4.2 days.

items.t: Astronomers published the first picture of a black hole, called M87*, in 2019.
A light-year is how far light travels in one Earth year.
items.d: It measures distance, even though the name sounds like a time.

items.t: One light-year is about 9 trillion kilometres.
items.d: That is about 6 trillion miles, a huge distance even for light.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 8.3 minutes to reach us.
items.d: We see the Sun as it was 8.3 minutes ago.

items.t: The nearest large galaxy, Andromeda, is about 2.5 million light-years away.
items.d: Light from Andromeda takes about 2.5 million years to arrive.

items.t: Violet light waves are the shortest we can see. Red are the longest.
items.d: Violet is about 380 nanometres, a tiny length. Red is about 700.

items.t: Each colour in a rainbow is a different wavelength of light.
items.d: Red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet are different waves.

items.t: Hotter objects shine in shorter waves, so their colour changes.
items.d: As something heats up, the light it gives off shifts colour.

items.t: Light's spectrum runs from long radio waves to short gamma rays.
items.d: Our eyes see only a small part of this huge range of light.

items.t: One parsec is about 3.26 light-years.
items.d: Ten parsecs is about 32.6 light-years, because 10 times 3.26 is 32.6.

items.t: The Moon drifts about 3.8 centimetres farther from Earth each year.
items.d: Scientists time laser pulses that bounce off mirrors on the Moon.

items.t: Light moving away from us gets stretched. That is called redshift.
items.d: Stretching makes the light waves longer than they started.

items.t: Light moving toward us gets squeezed. That is called blueshift.
items.d: Squeezing makes the light waves shorter than they started.

items.t: As space expands, light from far galaxies is stretched redder.
items.d: Astronomers call this stretch cosmological redshift.

items.t: A bigger redshift means the light has travelled farther.
items.d: More redshift means a longer trip for that galaxy's light.

items.t: On the largest scales, farther galaxies move away faster.
items.d: That overall pattern is called Hubble's law.

items.t: Hubble's law was the first clear sign the universe is expanding.
items.d: Edwin Hubble published the key galaxy observations in 1929.

items.t: Parallax looks biggest in views taken about six months apart.
items.d: Earth is then on opposite sides of its orbit around the Sun.

items.t: The farther a star is, the smaller its parallax shift.
items.d: A nearby star seems to jump more as Earth moves around the Sun.

items.t: In 1838, Friedrich Bessel measured the parallax of 61 Cygni.
items.d: He used that tiny sky shift to work out the star's distance.

items.t: Parallax is a nearby thing seeming to shift against far ones.
items.d: Hold a thumb out and switch eyes. It hops. Stars do that too.

items.t: Right ascension and declination are sky longitude and latitude.
items.d: Together they give every sky point a steady map address.

items.t: One hour of right ascension equals 15 degrees.
items.d: Two hours equal 30 degrees, because 2 times 15 is 30.

items.t: An astronomical unit is about the average Earth-Sun distance.
items.d: It is defined as exactly 149,597,870,700 metres.

items.t: In empty space, light moves at exactly 299,792,458 metres a second.
items.d: That rounds to about 300,000 kilometres per second.

items.t: No signal or energy can travel faster than light in empty space.
items.d: Light speed is the limit for carrying news across space.

items.t: In 1676, Ole Romer showed that light takes time to travel.
items.d: He learned this by watching Jupiter's moon Io.

items.t: The Milky Way galaxy is about 100,000 light-years across.
items.d: Even light would take about 100,000 years to cross it.

items.t: Astronomers use a ladder of methods to measure space distances.
items.d: Each step is checked against the method from the step before.

items.t: A standard candle is an object whose true brightness is known.
items.d: Compare that with how bright it looks, and you get distance.

items.t: Henrietta Leavitt linked a Cepheid's pulse rate to brightness.
items.d: Time the pulses, and you learn how bright the star truly is.

items.t: A galaxy cluster can bend passing light, like a giant lens.
items.d: Astronomers call this effect a gravitational lens.

items.t: A perfect gravity lens can make a distant light look like a ring.
items.d: That bright circle is called an Einstein ring.

items.t: Eratosthenes measured Earth's size using shadows in two cities.
items.d: On his measuring day, Syene had no shadow. In Alexandria the shadow angle was about 7.2 degrees.

items.t: In 1919, eclipse teams tested whether gravity bends starlight.
items.d: Arthur Eddington and Frank Dyson led those observations.

items.t: A moving clock is measured to tick slower than a resting clock.
items.d: To a resting watcher, the moving clock runs slow.

items.t: In 1971, atomic clocks flew around Earth to test relativity.
items.d: Hafele and Keating carried them east and west on airliners.

items.t: In empty space, everyone measures the same speed of light.
items.d: Move fast or sit still, and light still passes at that speed.

items.t: Gravity is mass bending space and time.
items.d: The bigger the mass, the more it bends space and time.

items.t: GPS has to include special relativity to help us navigate.
items.d: Special relativity is part of how those satellites guide us.

items.t: Helium was first seen in 1868 as a yellow line in sunlight.
items.d: Jules Janssen saw it during a total solar eclipse in India.

items.t: Helium was first trapped on Earth in 1895 by William Ramsay.
items.d: That was about 27 years after the yellow line was seen in the Sun.

items.t: A star's spectrum can reveal its ingredients and temperature.
items.d: Splitting the starlight shows which elements are in the star.

items.t: Dark lines in the Sun's rainbow come from absorbing elements.
items.d: Kirchhoff and Bunsen matched those lines to lab elements.

items.t: On the magnitude scale, brighter stars have smaller numbers.
items.d: Magnitude 1 is exactly 100 times brighter than magnitude 6.

items.t: A fist held at arm's length covers about 10 degrees of sky.
items.d: You can use that fist to roughly measure spaces between stars.

items.t: The Sun and the Moon look about the same size in our sky.
items.d: Their angular size, the patch of sky they cover, is about equal.

items.t: The Sun is a star.
items.d: It looks much bigger than other stars because it is much closer to Earth.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: In empty space, light travels about 300,000 kilometers in one second.

items.t: Earth takes about a year to go around the Sun.
items.d: Earth spins as it travels, so different places get daylight at different times.

items.t: The Moon shines by reflecting sunlight.
items.d: As the Moon goes around Earth, we see different amounts of its sunny side.

items.t: The Moon spins once in about the same time it takes to go around Earth.
items.d: That is why we see nearly the same side of the Moon from Earth all the time.

items.t: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks some of the Sun's light from reaching Earth.
items.d: People in the Moon's shadow can see the Sun partly or fully covered.

items.t: Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun.
items.d: It takes about 88 Earth days to go around the Sun once.

items.t: Venus takes longer to spin once than it takes to go around the Sun.
items.d: One spin takes about 243 Earth days. One trip around the Sun takes about 225.

items.t: Mars owes much of its red color to rusty dust.
items.d: Some of the iron in its rocks and dust has reacted with oxygen, like rust on an old bike.

items.t: Mars has two small moons.
items.d: Their names are Phobos and Deimos.

items.t: Jupiter is the biggest planet in our solar system.
items.d: The Great Red Spot you can see in pictures of Jupiter is a huge storm.

items.t: Saturn's rings are made mostly of pieces of ice.
items.d: The pieces stay in motion, circling Saturn.

items.t: Uranus spins almost on its side.
items.d: Picture a spinning top that keeps spinning while tipped almost all the way over.

items.t: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to circle the Sun.
items.d: It is the farthest of the eight planets from the Sun.

items.t: We live in a galaxy called the Milky Way.
items.d: A galaxy is a huge group of stars, gas and dust held together by gravity.

items.t: The eight planets in order from the Sun are Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune.
items.d: Earth is the third planet in that line.

items.t: Our solar system is the Sun and everything that travels around it.
items.d: That includes eight planets, their moons, dwarf planets, asteroids and icy objects.

items.t: The Sun and the planets formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
items.d: They grew inside a spinning cloud of gas and dust.

items.t: Earth's average distance from the Sun is about 150 million kilometers.
items.d: Nonstop at 100 kilometers per hour, the drive would take more than 170 years.

items.t: If the Sun were a basketball, Earth would be a tiny seed about 25 meters away.
items.d: On this model, the Moon is a speck about 7 centimeters from Earth.

items.t: The four planets closest to the Sun are rocky worlds.
items.d: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars all have solid ground.

items.t: Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune are giant planets.
items.d: They are much bigger than Earth and have no solid ground to stand on.

items.t: Jupiter and Saturn are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
items.d: These light gases are the main ingredients of those two giant planets.

items.t: The Sun holds more than 99 percent of the solar system's material.
items.d: All the planets and moons together are only a small share.

items.t: So far, Earth is the only place we know that has life.
items.d: Spacecraft look for water and chemical clues, but they have not found living things elsewhere.

items.t: About 109 Earths could fit side by side across the Sun.
items.d: The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometers across.

items.t: The Sun has about 1.3 million times Earth's volume.
items.d: Volume tells how much space something takes up.

items.t: Deep in the Sun, hydrogen nuclei join to form helium and release energy.
items.d: That energy eventually reaches us as light and heat.

items.t: The Sun's surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius.
items.d: The core is far hotter, about 15 million degrees Celsius.

items.t: Sunspots are darker patches on the Sun.
items.d: They are cooler patches linked to the Sun's magnetism, but they are still very hot.

items.t: The Sun blows a stream of particles called the solar wind.
items.d: These particles stream far past the planets. Some help create auroras on Earth.

items.t: Earth's seasons happen because the planet is tilted.
items.d: The tilt is about 23.5 degrees. The half leaning toward the Sun has summer.

items.t: Earth is closest to the Sun in January.
items.d: It is farthest in July. The difference is small and does not cause the seasons.

items.t: Earth has a magnetic field that reaches far into space.
items.d: Compass needles line up with it. It also guides many particles from the Sun.

items.t: Auroras are colorful lights in the sky near Earth's poles.
items.d: They appear when particles from space hit gases high in the air. Green is the most common color.

items.t: From space, Earth looks mostly blue, with white clouds.
items.d: Oceans cover most of the surface, and clouds swirl above green and brown land.

items.t: Some Mars rovers were lowered by a rocket platform.
items.d: After a parachute slowed them, the platform hovered and set the rover down on cables.

items.t: Mercury is the smallest of the eight planets.
items.d: It is about 40 percent wider than Earth's Moon.

items.t: From sunrise to sunrise on Mercury takes about 176 Earth days.
items.d: Daylight lasts about 88 Earth days, then night lasts about 88 more.

items.t: Mercury has almost no air to hold in heat.
items.d: Daytime can reach about 430 degrees Celsius. Night can drop to about minus 180.

items.t: Some deep craters at Mercury's poles hold water ice.
items.d: Their floors never get sunlight, so the ice can stay frozen.

items.t: Venus is almost the same size as Earth.
items.d: It is only a little smaller, but a thick blanket of air makes it very different.

items.t: Venus is the hottest planet, hotter even than Mercury.
items.d: Thick carbon dioxide air traps heat. The surface is about 460 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Air pressure on Venus is about 90 times the pressure on Earth.
items.d: The air is so heavy that a spacecraft needs to be very strong to work there.

items.t: Venus spins in the opposite direction from Earth.
items.d: Because of that backward spin, the Sun rises in the west and sets in the east.

items.t: Venus is the brightest planet in our sky.
items.d: People call it the Morning Star or the Evening Star, but it is a planet, not a star.

items.t: Thick clouds hide the rocky surface of Venus.
items.d: Spacecraft used radar, which can see through clouds, to map the ground.

items.t: Mars takes about 687 Earth days to go around the Sun.
items.d: One Earth year is about 365 days, so Mars takes almost two Earth years.

items.t: A day on Mars is only a little longer than a day on Earth.
items.d: It lasts about 24 hours and 37 minutes.

items.t: Mars has a thin atmosphere made mostly of carbon dioxide.
items.d: Its pressure is under one hundredth of Earth's, far too thin to breathe.

items.t: Mars is usually very cold.
items.d: A typical temperature is about minus 60 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Gravity on Mars is about 38 percent as strong as on Earth.
items.d: An object would feel about 38 percent as heavy on Mars as it does on Earth.

items.t: Mars has ice caps at both poles.
items.d: They contain frozen water and frozen carbon dioxide, also called dry ice.

items.t: Mars has dry riverbeds and old lake bottoms.
items.d: They show that liquid water flowed there a long time ago.

items.t: Dust storms on Mars can grow huge.
items.d: Some spread across much of the planet and hide the surface for weeks.

items.t: Sunsets on Mars can look blue.
items.d: Fine dust scatters light so the glow around the setting Sun looks blue.

items.t: The biggest volcano in the solar system is on Mars.
items.d: Olympus Mons is more than twice as tall as Mount Everest and hundreds of kilometers wide.

items.t: Mars has a canyon system thousands of kilometers long.
items.d: Valles Marineris is about 4,000 kilometers long, far longer than the Grand Canyon.

items.t: Phobos races around Mars in about 8 hours.
items.d: It moves so fast that, from Mars, it rises in the west and sets in the east.

items.t: Jupiter spins so fast that its day lasts about 10 hours.
items.d: The quick spin makes Jupiter a little wider around the middle than from top to bottom.

items.t: Jupiter's stripes are bands of clouds.
items.d: Neighboring bands blow in opposite directions in very strong winds.

items.t: At Jupiter's cloud tops, gravity is about 2.5 times Earth's.
items.d: An object there would feel about 2.5 times as heavy as it does on Earth.

items.t: Jupiter's four biggest moons were discovered in 1610.
items.d: Galileo Galilei found Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto with a telescope.

items.t: Ganymede is the biggest moon in the solar system.
items.d: This moon of Jupiter is wider than the planet Mercury.

items.t: Two Voyager spacecraft left Earth in 1977 to visit the giant planets.
items.d: Each one carries a disk of sounds and pictures, a greeting from Earth.

items.t: Io, a moon of Jupiter, has many active volcanoes.
items.d: Jupiter's gravity squeezes Io as it orbits, heating the inside until rock melts.

items.t: Europa's surface is a cracked shell of ice.
items.d: The cracks and magnetic clues are strong signs of a salty ocean under the ice.

items.t: Saturn's average density is less than the density of water.
items.d: Its average density is about 70 percent of water's.

items.t: Saturn's rings are very wide but amazingly thin.
items.d: They stretch tens of thousands of kilometers, yet many parts are only about 10 meters thick.

items.t: A giant six-sided cloud pattern surrounds Saturn's north pole.
items.d: Strong winds around the pole help form this unusual shape.

items.t: Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere.
items.d: Its air is mostly nitrogen. It is so cold that methane, a gas on Earth, forms lakes.

items.t: Enceladus shoots jets of water ice into space.
items.d: A spacecraft flew through the spray and found water vapor and ice grains.

items.t: A probe named Huygens landed on Titan in 2005.
items.d: It touched down on Saturn's largest moon and sent photos back from the surface.

items.t: Uranus takes about 84 Earth years to orbit the Sun.
items.d: One year on Uranus lasts about as long as 84 years on Earth.

items.t: Methane gas makes Uranus and Neptune look blue.
items.d: Methane soaks up red light, so the light that bounces back looks blue or blue-green.

items.t: Neptune has some of the fastest winds in the solar system.
items.d: Those winds can blow at more than 1,000 kilometers per hour.

items.t: Triton orbits Neptune backward.
items.d: It circles opposite Neptune's spin. Its surface is colder than minus 200 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Pluto is a dwarf planet, smaller than Earth's Moon.
items.d: It usually orbits beyond Neptune. It shares that icy region with many other objects.

items.t: Pluto takes about 248 Earth years to go around the Sun.
items.d: Earth goes around the Sun 248 times while Pluto goes around once.

items.t: Pluto has five known moons.
items.d: The biggest, Charon, is so large that they both orbit a point in the space between them.

items.t: A spacecraft flew past Pluto in 2015.
items.d: New Horizons saw icy mountains, a bright heart-shaped region and a plain of nitrogen ice.

items.t: Ceres is a dwarf planet in the asteroid belt.
items.d: It orbits between Mars and Jupiter and is the largest object there.

items.t: The asteroid belt is mostly empty space.
items.d: The rocks are far apart. Together they hold much less material than the Moon.

items.t: Some asteroids share Jupiter's path around the Sun.
items.d: Called Trojans, they travel in groups ahead of Jupiter and behind it.

items.t: Spacecraft have brought pieces of asteroids back to Earth.
items.d: Scientists study those old rocks to learn what the planets formed from.

items.t: The Moon is about 384,000 kilometers from Earth.
items.d: At 100 kilometers per hour, nonstop, the trip would take about 160 days.

items.t: The Moon is about one quarter as wide as Earth.
items.d: Earth is about 13,000 kilometers across, and the Moon is about 3,500.

items.t: Gravity on the Moon is about one sixth as strong as on Earth.
items.d: An object would feel about one sixth as heavy on the Moon as it does on Earth.

items.t: The Moon has almost no air.
items.d: Without air, there is nothing to breathe, so astronauts carry oxygen in their suits.

items.t: Daylight on the Moon lasts about two weeks.
items.d: Night lasts about two weeks too. A full day there is about as long as a month on Earth.

items.t: The far side of the Moon is not always dark.
items.d: It gets two weeks of sunshine, just like the side that faces Earth. We just cannot see it from here.

items.t: The dark patches on the Moon are plains of old lava.
items.d: Long ago people thought they were seas. They are really dry rock.

items.t: Footprints on the Moon can last a very long time.
items.d: There is no wind or rain to erase them.

items.t: Water ice sits in shadowed craters near the Moon's poles.
items.d: The Sun never shines on those floors, so the ice stays frozen.

items.t: The Moon is slowly moving away from Earth.
items.d: It drifts about 4 centimeters farther each year. Mirrors left on the Moon help measure this.

items.t: A lunar eclipse happens when Earth blocks sunlight from the Moon.
items.d: The Moon can look reddish because Earth's air bends some red light into the shadow.

items.t: From the Moon's near side, Earth looks big and bright.
items.d: Earth is wider than the Moon, and its clouds reflect a lot of sunlight.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin was the first person to orbit Earth.
items.d: He flew on April 12, 1961. His trip around the planet took about 108 minutes.

items.t: Valentina Tereshkova was the first woman in space.
items.d: She orbited Earth in 1963, flying for almost three days.

items.t: Neil Armstrong was the first person to walk on the Moon.
items.d: The Apollo 11 landing was in July 1969. Buzz Aldrin stepped out soon after Armstrong.

items.t: Twelve Apollo astronauts walked on the Moon.
items.d: Six landings between 1969 and 1972 each had two people walk on the surface.

items.t: Apollo crews brought about 380 kilograms of Moon rocks to Earth.
items.d: Labs on Earth still study those rocks to learn what the Moon is made of.

items.t: Apollo crews took about three days to reach the Moon.
items.d: Then a small lander flew down while the main ship stayed in orbit around the Moon.

items.t: The International Space Station orbits about 400 kilometers up.
items.d: It goes around Earth about once every 90 minutes.

items.t: The space station travels at about 28,000 kilometers per hour.
items.d: Crews see about 16 sunrises during a single day on Earth.

items.t: Astronauts float because they are falling around Earth.
items.d: Gravity still pulls. They fall together with the station, so their feet do not press down.

items.t: Astronauts exercise for about two hours each day in orbit.
items.d: Their bodies do less work against gravity, so exercise keeps muscles and bones strong.

items.t: In orbit, water forms round floating blobs.
items.d: Because it is falling with the station, it is not pulled flat. It clings together as a ball.

items.t: The sky looks black in space even when the Sun is out.
items.d: There is no air to scatter sunlight. On Earth, that scattering makes the sky blue.

items.t: A rocket moves forward by pushing gas out the back.
items.d: The gas pushes back on the rocket just as hard, and that push lifts it.

items.t: Most of a rocket at liftoff is propellant.
items.d: Propellant includes fuel and an oxidizer. Empty tanks and used stages drop away during flight.

items.t: Many rockets head east to get a boost from Earth's spin.
items.d: The ground itself is moving east, fastest near the equator.

items.t: A returning crew capsule uses a heat shield, then parachutes.
items.d: The shield takes the heat of rushing into the air. Parachutes slow the final fall.

items.t: A small helicopter named Ingenuity flew on Mars.
items.d: In 2021 it made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet. Its blades spun fast in the thin air.

items.t: The Sun is about 1.4 million kilometers wide.
items.d: That is about 100 times wider than Earth.

items.t: The Sun holds about 99.8 percent of all the mass in our solar system.
items.d: All the planets, moons, and other objects share the remaining 0.2 percent.

items.t: It would take more than 330,000 Earths to match the Sun's mass.
items.d: The Sun is incredibly heavy compared with our planet.

items.t: The Sun is about 1,000 times as massive as Jupiter, our biggest planet.
items.d: Jupiter is giant, but the Sun is much, much bigger.

items.t: Almost 1,000 Jupiters could fit inside the Sun.
items.d: Jupiter is the biggest planet, and the Sun still dwarfs it.

items.t: Our Sun is an average-sized star. Some stars are smaller, and some are up to 1,000 times wider.
Many stars have a partner star, but our Sun travels alone.
items.d: More than half of all stars live in groups of two or more.

items.t: The Sun is a giant ball of hydrogen and helium.
items.d: Its own gravity holds it together in a round shape.

items.t: The Sun is a yellow dwarf star, a common kind of star in our galaxy.
items.d: Dwarf here just means medium-sized, not tiny.

items.t: The Sun is really white, even though it can look yellow from Earth.
items.d: Earth's air scatters some of its light, so it looks yellow or orange to us.

items.t: Gravity at the Sun's surface is about 28 times stronger than gravity on Earth.
items.d: A child who weighs 30 kg here would feel as heavy as 840 kg there.

items.t: The Sun's average density is only a little greater than water's.
items.d: It is much denser inside and much thinner near the outside.

items.t: The center of the Sun is about 15 million degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is hotter than anything we can make on Earth for everyday use.

items.t: The Sun's visible surface is about 5,500 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That sounds hot, but it is cool compared with the Sun's core.

items.t: The Sun's outer atmosphere is much hotter than its surface, reaching about 2 million degrees Celsius.
items.d: Scientists are still studying why this happens.

items.t: The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old.
items.d: It formed from a giant spinning cloud of gas and dust.

items.t: The cloud that made the Sun squeezed together, spun faster, and flattened into a disk.
items.d: Our planets later formed in that disk.

items.t: The Sun is a little less than halfway through its life.
items.d: It will keep shining for about another 5 billion years.

items.t: The Sun will spend about 10 to 11 billion years as a main-sequence star.
items.d: Our Sun is a calm, long-lasting star.

items.t: The Sun is slowly getting brighter, by about 1 percent every 100 million years.
items.d: That change is far too slow for anyone to notice.

items.t: The Sun will eventually become a small, hot star called a white dwarf.
items.d: That change will happen about 5 billion years from now.

items.t: The Sun has already used up nearly half of the hydrogen in its core.
items.d: It still has plenty left for billions of years.

items.t: The Sun shines because of nuclear fusion in its core.
items.d: In fusion, hydrogen is squeezed together to make helium.

items.t: The Sun's huge mass creates strong gravity and enormous pressure inside it.
items.d: That pressure, plus the heat, lets fusion happen in the core.

items.t: Every second, the Sun's core turns about 600 billion kilograms of hydrogen into helium.
items.d: That is a lot of hydrogen, but the Sun is so big it can keep going.

items.t: Every second, the Sun turns about 4 billion kilograms of matter into energy.
items.d: That energy is what shines out as sunlight.

items.t: In the Sun's main fusion chain, about 0.7 percent of the starting mass turns into energy.
items.d: A tiny bit of mass makes a huge amount of energy.

items.t: In 1.5 millionths of a second, the Sun gives off more energy than people use in a whole year.
items.d: The Sun is an amazing power plant.

items.t: The Sun's fusion makes tiny ghostly particles called neutrinos.
items.d: About 65 billion pass through every square centimeter facing the Sun each second.

items.t: The Sun's core is about 150 grams per cubic centimeter, around 8 times denser than gold.
items.d: Yet it is still a hot gas, not a solid.

items.t: The core holds roughly half of the Sun's mass.
items.d: It is only the innermost quarter of the Sun by distance.

items.t: Most of the Sun's energy is made in a small region around its center.
items.d: About 91 percent is made within the inner fifth of the Sun's radius.

items.t: The Sun has layers, with the core in the middle.
items.d: Outside the core are the radiative zone and then the convection zone.

items.t: In the radiative zone, energy travels outward as radiation.
items.d: This layer is just outside the core.

items.t: Energy can take about 170,000 years to travel from the core to the top of the convection zone.
items.d: It bounces around like a pinball.

items.t: After leaving the Sun's surface, sunlight needs only about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: The slow part of the trip is inside the Sun.

items.t: In the convection zone, large bubbles of hot plasma rise toward the Sun's surface.
items.d: Big bubbles of hot gas rise toward the surface, like boiling soup.

items.t: The Sun's surface has bubbling cells called granules.
items.d: Each granule is about 1,000 kilometers across.

items.t: A granule on the Sun lasts only about 20 minutes.
items.d: Then a new one bubbles up in its place.

items.t: The photosphere is the Sun's visible surface, the part that gives off the light we see.
items.d: It is only about 400 kilometers thick.

items.t: The chromosphere's name comes from Greek words meaning sphere of color.
items.d: The name comes from Greek.

items.t: The chromosphere looks red because its hydrogen glows at a red wavelength.
items.d: Glowing hydrogen gas makes the red color.

items.t: The word corona is Latin for crown.
items.d: It is usually hidden by the Sun's bright surface.

items.t: The Sun spins once about every 25 days at its equator and every 36 days near its poles.
items.d: It is a ball of gas, so different parts spin at different speeds.

items.t: The Sun takes about 230 million years to travel once around the Milky Way.
items.d: It moves together with the whole solar system.

items.t: The Sun's gravity holds the whole solar system together.
items.d: It keeps every planet moving in its path.

items.t: The Sun is about 150 million kilometers from Earth.
items.d: That distance is the length of the trip sunlight makes in 8 minutes.

items.t: The closest star to the Sun is Proxima Centauri.
items.d: It is a small red dwarf star.

items.t: Activity on the Sun creates space weather that can travel about 150 million km to Earth.
Space weather can damage satellites and cause electrical blackouts on Earth.
Solar wind comes from the Sun's hot outer atmosphere, called the corona.
Earth's atmosphere and magnetic field shield us from most of the solar wind.
Earth's magnetic field stretches into a long tail on the side facing away from the Sun.
Energy from a solar flare travels through space at the speed of light.
A huge solar eruption that often comes with a flare is called a coronal mass ejection.
Northern lights near the North Pole are also called aurora borealis.
Southern lights near the South Pole are also called aurora australis.
Oxygen can make auroras glow green or red. Nitrogen can make them blue or purple.
Solar particles follow Earth's magnetic field lines toward the poles, where they make auroras.
Auroras are not only on Earth. They have also been seen on Jupiter and Saturn.
Sunspots are cooler areas on the Sun where magnetic fields are tightly packed.
A sunspot can remain on the Sun for a few days or for several months.
Sunspots are usually about 1,600 to 161,000 km across.
The number of sunspots rises and falls during the Sun's roughly 11-year cycle.
People have watched and recorded sunspots for more than 1,000 years.
Sunspots look dark because they are cooler than the brighter surface around them.
A solar flare is an intense burst of light and other radiation on the Sun.
Solar flares are the most powerful explosions in our solar system.
Each step up in solar flare class means about 10 times more energy.
Light from a solar flare takes about 8 minutes to reach Earth.
A coronal mass ejection is a huge cloud of charged gas that erupts from the Sun.
One coronal mass ejection can blast billions of tonnes of material into space.
A fast coronal mass ejection can reach Earth in as little as 15 hours.
Some coronal mass ejections spread across millions of kilometers in space.
Solar storms can heat Earth's upper atmosphere, adding drag to some satellites.
The solar wind is charged gas flowing outward from the Sun in every direction.
Solar wind forms a vast magnetic bubble called the heliosphere around the planets.
The spinning Sun winds its magnetic field into a giant shape called the Parker spiral.
About every 11 years, the Sun's north and south magnetic poles switch places.
Coronal holes release a fast stream of solar wind.
Auroras appear when electrons collide with gases high in Earth's atmosphere.
Auroras usually form about 80 to 500 km above Earth's surface.
Auroras form two oval rings around Earth's magnetic poles.
items.d: During a major magnetic storm, the glowing ovals spread farther from the poles.

items.t: Auroras are easiest to see around 60 to 75 degrees north or south latitude.
The darkest center of a sunspot is called the umbra.
Scientists began numbering solar cycles with Solar Cycle 1 in 1755.
The busiest part of a sunspot cycle is solar maximum. The quietest is solar minimum.
A geomagnetic storm is a major disturbance in the magnetic region around Earth.
Geomagnetic storms can disturb GPS and radio signals and affect electric power grids.
A coronal mass ejection can make a compass needle wander during a geomagnetic storm.
Green is the most common color seen in Earth's auroras.
Jupiter's main auroras are linked to charged gas from its volcanic moon Io.
The solar wind is made mostly of electrons, protons, and alpha particles.
Solar wind and sunlight help make a comet's tail point away from the Sun.
Mercury is the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest planet in our solar system.
items.d: It is only a little bigger than Earth's Moon.

items.t: Mercury is a little more than a third as wide as Earth.
items.d: Its radius is about 2,440 km.

items.t: Mercury is about 58 million km from the Sun on average.
items.d: Sunlight takes about 3 minutes to get there.

items.t: A year on Mercury lasts only 88 Earth days.
items.d: If you lived there, you would have a birthday about every three months!

items.t: Mercury is the fastest planet in the solar system.
items.d: It zooms around the Sun at nearly 47 km every second.

items.t: Mercury spins slowly. One spin takes about 59 Earth days.
One sunrise to the next sunrise on Mercury lasts 176 Earth days.
items.d: That is twice as long as its year!

items.t: Mercury spins nearly upright, so it has almost no seasons.
Daytime on Mercury can reach about 430 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is hotter than a pizza oven.

items.t: Nights on Mercury can drop to about minus 180 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is colder than any place on Earth!

items.t: Mercury has no moons and no rings.
Mercury is the second densest planet, after Earth.
Mercury has a huge metal core that makes up most of the planet's width.
items.d: The core's radius is about 2,074 km.

items.t: Mercury's rocky outer shell is only about 400 km thick.
Mercury's Caloris Basin is a giant impact basin about 1,550 km across.
Mercury has cliffs up to about 1.6 km high.
items.d: They formed as the planet cooled and shrank.

items.t: Mercury may have water ice at its north and south poles.
items.d: Some spots there never see sunlight.

items.t: Mercury has no real atmosphere, only a very thin layer called an exosphere.
Mercury's magnetic field is only about 1% as strong as Earth's.
Some craters on Mercury are named after famous artists, musicians and authors, like Dr. Seuss.
Mercury is named after the swiftest of the ancient Roman gods.
People have known about Mercury since ancient times.
items.d: You can see it without a telescope.

items.t: Mariner 10 was the first spacecraft to use a gravity assist to change its path.
items.d: It used Venus's gravity to swing toward Mercury.

items.t: Mariner 10 flew past Mercury three times.
items.d: Its pictures covered nearly half of the planet.

items.t: Mariner 10 found that Mercury has a weak magnetic field.
MESSENGER was the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury.
items.d: It orbited the planet for four years.

items.t: MESSENGER found that the ice near Mercury's poles is mostly water ice.
BepiColombo is a joint mission of Europe's ESA and Japan's JAXA.
items.d: It carries two orbiters to study Mercury.

items.t: BepiColombo flew past Earth once, Venus twice and Mercury six times on its way.
items.d: It uses these flybys to adjust its path.

items.t: Venus is the hottest planet in our solar system.
items.d: Its surface is about 467 degrees Celsius.

items.t: Venus is hotter than Mercury, even though it is farther from the Sun.
items.d: Its thick air traps heat like a blanket.

items.t: Venus is about 12,104 km wide, almost the same size as Earth.
items.d: That is why it is often called Earth's twin.

items.t: Venus spins backward compared with Earth, so the Sun rises in the west.
A day on Venus is a little longer than a year on Venus.
items.d: It spins once in 243 Earth days, but circles the Sun in 225.

items.t: Venus is tilted only about 3 degrees, so it has no noticeable seasons.
Air pressure on Venus's surface is about 93 times what it is on Earth.
items.d: It feels like being deep under the sea.

items.t: Venus's air is mostly carbon dioxide, and its clouds are made of sulfuric acid.
Winds at the tops of Venus's clouds can blow about 360 km per hour.
Venus has no moon and no rings.
Venus has thousands of volcanoes.
Venus's tallest mountain is about 11 km high, taller than Mount Everest.
Venus has strange round, flat-topped volcanic domes called pancake domes.
items.d: Some are up to 62 km wide.

items.t: Venus has far fewer impact craters than Mercury.
Venus is the third brightest object in our sky, after the Sun and the Moon.
Venus is named after the Roman goddess of love and beauty.
items.d: It is the only planet named after a female god.

items.t: Mariner 2 was the first spacecraft to visit another planet.
items.d: It flew past Venus on 14 December 1962.

items.t: Magellan used radar to see through the thick clouds of Venus.
items.d: Radar let it map the surface.

items.t: Magellan was launched from the Space Shuttle Atlantis in 1989.
Akatsuki was the first Japanese spacecraft to orbit Venus.
items.d: It studied the planet's atmosphere.

items.t: Venus Express found that Venus lost large amounts of water into space.
items.d: This took place over billions of years.

items.t: Earth is about 12,756 kilometers wide at the equator.
Earth is about 150 million kilometers from the Sun on average.
Sunlight takes about eight minutes to reach Earth.
Earth takes about 365.25 days to travel once around the Sun.
Earth spins once in about 23.9 hours.
Air near Earth's surface is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen.
Earth's ocean covers about 71% of the planet's surface.
The ocean holds about 97% of all the water on Earth.
Earth's spin and molten metal core help create its magnetic field.
Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago.
Earth is the only planet in our solar system with exactly one moon.
Earth is the third planet from the Sun.
Earth is the biggest of the four rocky planets nearest the Sun.
On land, Earth's rocky crust is about 30 kilometers deep on average.
Earth's outer shell is divided into huge plates that keep moving.
Earth's atmosphere blocks much of the Sun's harmful radiation.
Earth's solid inner core is made of iron and nickel.
items.d: Its temperature can reach about 5,400 C.

items.t: The Moon is about 384,400 kilometers from Earth on average.
The troposphere rises about 12 kilometers above Earth on average.
items.d: It is the lowest layer of the atmosphere.

items.t: Most of Earth's weather happens in the troposphere.
The troposphere is the atmosphere's densest layer.
items.d: The layers above press down on it.

items.t: Most airplane flights take place in the troposphere.
The stratosphere stretches from about 12 to 50 kilometers above Earth.
The ozone layer is in the stratosphere.
items.d: It protects us from harmful ultraviolet rays from the Sun.

items.t: The stratosphere has almost no clouds or weather.
The mesosphere stretches from about 50 to 80 kilometers above Earth.
The top of the mesosphere is the coldest place in the Earth system.
Most meteors burn up in the mesosphere.
items.d: Their bright trails can look like shooting stars.

items.t: The atmosphere's highest clouds form near the top of the mesosphere.
items.d: They are called noctilucent clouds.

items.t: The thermosphere reaches from about 80 to 700 kilometers above Earth.
Auroras can glow in the thermosphere.
The International Space Station orbits Earth in the thermosphere.
The exosphere is Earth's outermost atmosphere layer.
items.d: It stretches from about 700 to 10,000 kilometers up and has no weather.

items.t: The exosphere has no sharp top. It slowly fades into space.
Greenhouse gases help keep Earth warm enough for life.
items.d: Without them, the average surface temperature would be about -20 C.

items.t: Apollo 17 astronauts took the Blue Marble photo on December 7, 1972.
items.d: They photographed Earth while traveling toward the Moon.

items.t: The Blue Marble photo clearly shows almost all of Africa's coastline.
Voyager 1 took the Pale Blue Dot picture of Earth on February 14, 1990.
In the Pale Blue Dot picture, distant Earth looks about one pixel wide.
Earth's magnetosphere is a huge bubble shaped a little like a comet.
The solar wind is a steady stream of charged particles from the Sun.
Earth's magnetosphere helps shield our planet from particle radiation.
Auroras have different names near each pole.
items.d: Northern lights are aurora borealis. Southern lights are aurora australis.

items.t: Auroras form when solar particles meet gases in our atmosphere near the poles.
Aurora colors come from glowing gases.
items.d: Oxygen shines green or red, while nitrogen shines blue or purple.

items.t: Earth is the only planet in our solar system known to support life.
The Moon is about 384,400 kilometres from Earth.
items.d: That is the average space between the Moon and Earth.

items.t: About 30 Earths could fit between Earth and the Moon.
items.d: The gap is much wider than the Moon looks in the sky.

items.t: The Moon is less than a third as wide as Earth.
items.d: Its radius is about 1,740 kilometres.

items.t: Each year the Moon drifts about 2.5 centimetres farther from Earth.
items.d: That is about one inch a year, which is very slow.

items.t: The Moon takes about 27 days to travel once around Earth.
items.d: That trip is a little shorter than a calendar month.

items.t: You would weigh about one-sixth as much on the Moon.
items.d: Someone who is 30 kilograms on Earth would feel as heavy as 5 kilograms.

items.t: In full sun, the Moon's ground heats to about 127 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is hotter than water boiling at 100 degrees Celsius.

items.t: In darkness, the Moon's ground falls to about minus 173 degrees Celsius.
items.d: A kitchen freezer is only about minus 18 degrees Celsius.

items.t: The Moon's crust is thinner on the near side than the far side.
items.d: It is about 40 kilometres thick on the near side and up to 60 on the far side.

items.t: The Moon's solid iron core has a radius of about 240 kilometres.
items.d: Melted iron about 90 kilometres thick surrounds that solid core.

items.t: Most of the Moon's melted-rock ocean turned solid in about 100 million years.
items.d: That was early in the Moon's life, soon after it formed.

items.t: Space rocks keep striking the Moon and digging craters.
items.d: Asteroids, meteoroids, and comets all leave marks on the ground.

items.t: Lava filled the Moon's dark plains about 4.2 to 1.2 billion years ago.
items.d: Those plains are the dark patches you can see from Earth.

items.t: India's Chandrayaan-1 found water on the Moon in 2008.
items.d: It was the first mission to show clearly that the water was there.

items.t: The Moon's gravity helps make the tides in Earth's oceans.
items.d: Its pull is a big reason the sea rises and falls each day.

items.t: The Moon has almost no air, just a very thin sprinkle of particles.
items.d: Those particles are knocked loose from the ground.

items.t: The Moon has no volcanoes erupting today.
items.d: Long ago it was flooded with flowing lava.

items.t: The Moon is like a time capsule from about 4.5 billion years ago.
items.d: Cold empty space has kept its ancient surface well preserved.

items.t: Ancient ice hides in Moon craters that never see the Sun.
items.d: Those deep shadows stay cold enough to hold the ice.

items.t: The same side of the Moon always points toward Earth.
items.d: The Moon turns once each time it orbits, so we see one face.

items.t: From Earth we can see about 59 percent of the Moon over time.
items.d: A small wobble lets a little extra land peek around the edge.

items.t: The Moon's far side has more craters and fewer dark lava plains.
items.d: Lava covered up many old craters on the side facing Earth.

items.t: Apollo 8 astronauts were the first people to see the far side with their own eyes.
items.d: That happened in December 1968, on the Apollo 8 mission.

items.t: Chang'e 6 brought the first samples back from the Moon's far side.
items.d: The spacecraft returned to Earth in June 2024.

items.t: The Moon is the fifth-largest moon in the solar system.
items.d: No other moon is so large compared with its planet.

items.t: The Moon is the second-densest moon in the solar system.
items.d: Only Jupiter's moon Io is denser.

items.t: The Moon has no planet-wide magnetic field like Earth.
items.d: Only some patches of its crust are magnetic.

items.t: Gravity is a bit stronger over some giant impact basins.
items.d: These places of extra pull are called mascons.

items.t: The Moon's dark plains are called maria, which means seas.
items.d: The name is Latin, but these seas contain no water at all.

items.t: Dark lava plains cover about 16 percent of the Moon.
items.d: Most of them lie on the side that faces Earth.

items.t: The dark plains look dark because their rock is rich in iron.
items.d: Iron-rich rock reflects less light than the pale highlands.

items.t: The Ocean of Storms is the Moon's largest lava plain.
items.d: Its science name is Oceanus Procellarum, and it is dry rock.

items.t: Tycho crater is about 85 kilometres wide and 4.7 kilometres deep.
items.d: It is named after Tycho Brahe, a Danish astronomer.

items.t: Tycho is a young crater, formed about 108 million years ago.
items.d: Bright rays of tossed rock stretch about 1,500 kilometres from it.

items.t: The South Pole-Aitken basin is about 2,500 kilometres across.
items.d: It is one of the largest impact craters in the solar system.

items.t: The Moon's lowest ground is in the South Pole-Aitken basin.
items.d: Those spots are about 9 kilometres below the average height.

items.t: The Moon's iron core is small for a rocky world.
items.d: Its core is under a quarter of the Moon's radius. Many rocky worlds have a core about half their radius.

items.t: Pale rock formed the Moon's first crust about 4.4 billion years ago.
items.d: That light-coloured rock is called anorthosite.

items.t: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo match Earth rocks very closely.
items.d: That close match is a clue that the Moon and Earth share material.

items.t: The Moon's mass is only about 1.2 percent of Earth's mass.
items.d: If Earth were 100 kilograms, the Moon would be about 1.2 kilograms.

items.t: A chunk of the Moon is lighter than the same-sized chunk of Earth.
items.d: One cubic metre of the Moon averages about 3,344 kilograms. Earth averages about 5,514.

items.t: A spacecraft must go about 2.38 kilometres per second to leave the Moon.
items.d: Escaping Earth takes about 11.2 kilometres per second.

items.t: The Moon reflects only about 12 percent of the sunlight hitting it.
items.d: Its surface is quite dark, even when the full Moon looks bright.

items.t: Moon dust is sharp and jagged, not smooth like Earth dust.
items.d: The grains were never worn smooth the way Earth dust is.

items.t: Tiny impacts both grind Moon rock into dust and weld bits together.
items.d: Micrometeorites, which are very small space rocks, do this work.

items.t: Moon dust carries an electric charge, so it sticks to surfaces.
items.d: Charged grains cling on instead of falling away.

items.t: A large moonquake can shake for up to an hour.
items.d: Very little there soaks up the shaking, so it goes on and on.

items.t: Some moonquakes start when sunlight returns after the long night.
items.d: The crust had been cold for about two weeks, then it expands.

items.t: Chang'e 4 was the first spacecraft to land softly on the far side.
items.d: It landed in Von Karman crater, about 180 kilometres wide, on 3 January 2019.

items.t: Chang'e 5 found lava rock about 1.96 billion years old.
items.d: It landed near Mons Rumker, a big volcanic area on the Moon.

items.t: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun.
items.d: It comes after Mercury, Venus and Earth.

items.t: Mars is about half as wide as Earth.
items.d: Its radius is about 3,390 km, roughly half of Earth's.

items.t: A day on Mars is about 24.6 hours long, very close to a day on Earth.
items.d: A Mars day is called a sol.

items.t: A year on Mars lasts 687 Earth days, almost twice as long as an Earth year.
items.d: One Mars year equals about 669.6 sols.

items.t: Mars is tilted about 25 degrees, almost the same as Earth, so it has seasons.
items.d: Its tilt gives Mars distinct seasons.

items.t: Seasons on Mars last longer than seasons on Earth.
items.d: That is because Mars takes longer to go around the Sun.

items.t: Mars is about 1.5 times as far from the Sun as Earth is.
items.d: Sunlight takes about 13 minutes to reach Mars.

items.t: Mars is cold. Its average temperature is about minus 65 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is far below freezing, like a super freezer.

items.t: Temperatures on Mars can reach about 20 degrees Celsius and fall to about minus 153 degrees.
items.d: Mars has a very large temperature range.

items.t: Mars has a thin atmosphere. It is mostly carbon dioxide, with some nitrogen and argon.
items.d: About 95 out of every 100 bits of air are carbon dioxide.

items.t: Surface air pressure on Mars is only about 0.6% of Earth's.
items.d: That means the Martian atmosphere is very thin.

items.t: Mars looks red because iron in its rocks and dust has rusted.
items.d: Rust is also what turns an old bike orange-brown.

items.t: Mars has two small moons, Phobos and Deimos.
items.d: Both moons are much smaller than Mars.

items.t: Phobos and Deimos are shaped like potatoes, not balls.
items.d: They are too small for gravity to squeeze them round.

items.t: Mars has no global magnetic field today.
items.d: Some old rocks in its south are magnetized, so it may have had one long ago.

items.t: Long ago, rivers, lakes and seas covered parts of Mars.
items.d: Scientists see old river valleys and lakebeds from billions of years ago.

items.t: Water ice lies just under the surface near the poles of Mars.
items.d: Scientists have found this buried ice in the polar regions.

items.t: Dust storms on Mars can cover much of the planet.
items.d: The dust can take months to settle down.

items.t: Mars has dust devils, spinning columns of dust that can look like tornadoes.
items.d: Some are several kilometers tall.

items.t: Olympus Mons on Mars is the biggest volcano in our solar system.
items.d: Its base is about as big as the state of Arizona.

items.t: Olympus Mons is about three times as tall as Mount Everest.
items.d: It rises about 26 km above the plains around it.

items.t: Olympus Mons is a shield volcano, shaped like the big volcanoes of Hawaii.
items.d: It has a very broad shape with gentle slopes.

items.t: Olympus Mons grew so huge because Mars has no moving crust plates.
items.d: Lava kept piling up in the same spot for a very long time.

items.t: Valles Marineris on Mars is the biggest canyon in our solar system.
items.d: It is about 3,870 km long, and up to about 9.3 km deep.

items.t: Valles Marineris means Mariner Valleys. It is named after the Mariner 9 spacecraft.
items.d: Mariner 9 found it in 1971 and 1972.

items.t: The Tharsis bulge is a giant raised area on Mars, about 5,000 km across.
items.d: It holds the biggest volcanoes in the solar system.

items.t: Hellas Planitia is a giant crater on Mars, about 2,300 km wide.
items.d: A huge space rock hit Mars about 4 billion years ago.

items.t: Gravity on Mars is only about 38% as strong as gravity on Earth.
items.d: A child weighing 30 kg on Earth would feel about as heavy as 11 kg on Mars.

items.t: Mars has two permanent ice caps, one at each pole.
items.d: They are named Planum Boreum in the north and Planum Australe in the south.

items.t: Sunsets on Mars look blue near the Sun.
items.d: Fine dust in the air lets blue light through more easily.

items.t: The daytime sky on Mars looks yellow to orange away from the Sun.
items.d: Earth's sky is blue because our air is different.

items.t: In Mars winter, some carbon dioxide freezes at the poles as dry ice.
items.d: This changes the air pressure across Mars by about 25% over the year.

items.t: Sound is much quieter on Mars, and it travels more slowly than on Earth.
items.d: The air is so thin that it carries sound poorly.

items.t: Long ago, Mars was warm enough for water to flow on its surface for a long time.
items.d: Liquid water could remain on the surface for extended periods.

items.t: NASA's MAVEN spacecraft found that Mars lost most of its air to space.
items.d: The solar wind, a stream of particles from the Sun, helped strip it away.

items.t: Most of the water on Mars today is probably frozen in its polar caps.
items.d: Mars once had much more water long ago.

items.t: A standard trip from Earth to Mars takes about nine months.
items.d: The exact travel time depends on the spacecraft and its path.

items.t: A radio message from Mars takes about 3 to 22 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: The wait changes because the two planets keep moving.

items.t: The distance between Earth and Mars keeps changing.
items.d: It ranges from about 54 million km to about 400 million km.

items.t: NASA's MOXIE experiment made oxygen from carbon dioxide in Mars's air.
items.d: It produced about 122 grams of oxygen in total.

items.t: Oxygen made on Mars could help astronauts breathe and help rockets burn fuel.
items.d: That could mean carrying less material from Earth.

items.t: Martian soil contains chemicals called perchlorates that are hazardous to living things.
items.d: Future visitors would need to handle the soil carefully.

items.t: Phobos is the larger of Mars's two moons.
items.d: It measures about 27 by 22 by 18 km.

items.t: Phobos zooms around Mars about three times every day.
items.d: It circles Mars much faster than our Moon circles Earth.

items.t: Phobos is slowly moving closer to Mars, by about 1.8 meters every hundred years.
items.d: In about 50 million years it may crash or break apart.

items.t: Phobos has a huge crater called Stickney.
items.d: The crater is about 9.5 km wide.

items.t: Seen from Mars, Phobos rises in the west and sets in the east.
items.d: It does this twice in every Mars day.

items.t: Deimos takes about 30 hours to circle Mars.
items.d: The small moon measures about 15 by 12 by 11 km.

items.t: Perseverance launched in July 2020 and landed on Mars in February 2021.
Perseverance searches Mars for signs of ancient life.
Perseverance landed in Jezero Crater, which is about 45 kilometres wide.
Long ago, rivers flowed into Jezero Crater and formed a lake.
Perseverance has collected more than two dozen different rock samples.
Each rock core collected by Perseverance is about 1.3 centimetres wide.
Perseverance has two microphones that record real sounds from Mars.
Perseverance's MOXIE experiment made oxygen from carbon dioxide in the Martian air.
The Ingenuity helicopter travelled to Mars under the belly of Perseverance.
Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another planet.
The Ingenuity helicopter completed 72 flights on Mars.
Curiosity launched in November 2011 and landed on Mars in August 2012.
The Curiosity rover explores a place on Mars called Gale Crater.
Curiosity is about the size of a small SUV.
Curiosity stands about as tall as a basketball player.
Curiosity has a robotic arm about 2.2 metres long.
In Mars gravity, Curiosity weighs about 337 kilograms.
Curiosity uses a laser to study tiny spots on rocks from a distance.
items.d: The laser turns a pinpoint of rock into vapor so instruments can examine it.

items.t: Curiosity has a drill that collects powdered rock for testing.
Curiosity uses 17 cameras to explore Mars.
Curiosity carries 10 science instruments.
Curiosity has climbed about 1 kilometre up the slopes of Mount Sharp.
Spirit and Opportunity were identical twin rovers.
Spirit and Opportunity searched Mars for signs of water from long ago.
The Spirit rover landed on Mars on January 3, 2004.
Opportunity landed on Mars on January 24, 2004, three weeks after Spirit.
Opportunity drove about 45 kilometres across Mars.
Spirit drove about 7.7 kilometres across Mars.
Martian wind blew dust off Opportunity's solar panels, helping the rover keep going.
Spirit landed in Gusev Crater, which may once have held a lake.
Opportunity last sent a message to Earth on June 10, 2018, during a huge dust storm.
Spirit and Opportunity sent Earth more than 300,000 raw images.
Mars Pathfinder landed on Mars on July 4, 1997.
Sojourner was the first Mars rover and weighed about 10.6 kilograms.
Sojourner stood only about 30 centimetres tall.
Pathfinder bounced about 15 times on giant airbags when it landed.
items.d: The protected spacecraft bounced across Mars like a giant beach ball.

items.t: Pathfinder's landing airbags inflated about 100 metres above the ground.
The Pathfinder lander was named the Carl Sagan Memorial Station.
The Sojourner rover was named after Sojourner Truth.
Pathfinder's lander sent Earth more than 16,500 images.
Viking 1 made the first truly successful landing on Mars.
Viking 1 landed on Mars on July 20, 1976.
Viking 1 took the first photograph from the surface of Mars.
The two Viking landers sent back about 4,500 photos of their landing sites.
The Viking landers scooped up Martian soil and tested it for signs of life.
The Viking 1 lander kept working until November 11, 1982.
The Viking orbiters mapped about 97 percent of Mars's surface.
InSight landed on Mars on November 26, 2018.
InSight landed on a flat, smooth plain called Elysium Planitia.
InSight had a robotic arm about 1.8 metres long.
Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun.
items.d: Start at the Sun and count outward. Jupiter comes in at number five.

items.t: Jupiter is about 11 times wider than Earth.
items.d: Its radius is about 69,911 kilometers, from the center out to the edge.

items.t: Jupiter has about 318 times the mass of Earth.
items.d: Mass means how much material is packed into the planet.

items.t: Jupiter's volume is about 1,321 times Earth's volume.
items.d: You would need 1,321 Earths to fill the same amount of space.

items.t: Jupiter is the largest planet in the solar system.
items.d: It holds more than twice the material of all the other planets combined.

items.t: Jupiter is about 778 million kilometers from the Sun, on average.
items.d: That is about 5.2 times as far from the Sun as Earth is.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 43 minutes to reach Jupiter.
items.d: The light leaves the Sun and travels a long way before it arrives.

items.t: A day on Jupiter lasts only about 9.9 hours.
items.d: That is the shortest day of any planet, because Jupiter spins so fast.

items.t: One year on Jupiter lasts about 12 Earth years.
items.d: Jupiter needs about 4,333 Earth days to go once around the Sun.

items.t: Jupiter's axis is tilted by only about 3 degrees.
items.d: The tilt is so small that Jupiter does not have extreme seasons.

items.t: Jupiter formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
items.d: It grew from gas and dust left over after the Sun formed.

items.t: Jupiter's atmosphere is mostly hydrogen and helium.
items.d: The clouds there are made of ammonia and water.

items.t: Jupiter is a gas giant with no solid surface.
items.d: There is no ground to stand on. The planet is a deep ball of gas.

items.t: Jupiter is a bit like a star, but it never got big enough to light up.
items.d: Stars shine because they are very heavy. Jupiter is not heavy enough to shine like the Sun.

items.t: You can see Jupiter from Earth with only your eyes.
items.d: No telescope is needed. People have known it since ancient times.

items.t: Jupiter spins so fast that it bulges at the equator.
items.d: The radius at the equator is 7% longer than the radius at the poles.

items.t: Winds at Jupiter's equator can reach about 539 kilometers per hour.
items.d: That is about 335 miles per hour.

items.t: Jupiter's three main cloud layers together are about 71 kilometers thick.
items.d: From the top cloud to the bottom cloud is only about 44 miles.

items.t: Galileo's probe measured pressure about 23 times Earth's.
items.d: Deep in Jupiter, the gas presses much harder than air does here.

items.t: Eight huge spinning storms circle Jupiter's north pole.
items.d: They form an octagon. Five more form a pentagon at the south pole.

items.t: Jupiter's stripes reach about 3,000 kilometers under the clouds.
items.d: Juno learned this by measuring Jupiter's pull of gravity.

items.t: Most of Jupiter's lightning flashes near the poles.
items.d: Those storms drop softball-sized hail made of ammonia and water.

items.t: In 2017, Jupiter's Great Red Spot was 16,350 kilometers wide.
items.d: That width is about 1.3 times the diameter of Earth.

items.t: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a high-pressure storm.
items.d: Clouds in the spot swirl counter-clockwise.

items.t: The Great Red Spot lies about 22 degrees south of the equator.
items.d: That puts the giant storm in Jupiter's southern half.

items.t: As of 2008, the Great Red Spot spun once about every 4.5 Earth days.
items.d: That is about 11 days on Jupiter.

items.t: About a century before 2004, Jupiter's Great Red Spot was far bigger.
items.d: It was about 40,000 kilometers long, and it has been shrinking.

items.t: No one knows for sure why Jupiter's Great Red Spot is red.
items.d: The cause of that red color is still a mystery.

items.t: The roots of the Great Red Spot reach about 320 kilometers deep.
items.d: Juno measured the storm and found it goes about 200 miles down.

items.t: Jupiter has a Little Red Spot and a Great Red Spot.
items.d: The little storm is about half the size of the great one.

items.t: Voyager 1 took a close photo of the Great Red Spot in 1979.
items.d: The picture was made as the spacecraft flew past Jupiter.

items.t: Jupiter's rings were first seen on March 4, 1979.
items.d: Voyager 1 found the third ring system known in the solar system.

items.t: Jupiter's rings come in four parts.
items.d: A halo, a main ring, and two gossamer rings, which are very thin.

items.t: Jupiter's main ring is about 6,500 kilometers wide.
items.d: That is about half as wide as Earth is across.

items.t: Jupiter's ring dust is knocked off its small inner moons.
items.d: Space rocks hit four tiny moons, and the dust they raise makes the rings.

items.t: Jupiter's magnetic field is 16 to 54 times as strong as Earth's.
items.d: A compass follows Earth's field. Jupiter's field is far stronger.

items.t: Jupiter's magnetic tail stretches nearly 1 billion kilometers.
items.d: The tail streams behind Jupiter and reaches toward Saturn's orbit.

items.t: The Sun could fit inside Jupiter's huge magnetic bubble.
items.d: The Sun's glowing corona would fit too, with room to spare.

items.t: Jupiter's magnetic bubble would look giant from Earth.
items.d: If we could see it, it would look five times larger than the full Moon.

items.t: Jupiter has auroras, like Earth's northern and southern lights.
items.d: Jupiter's auroras are hundreds of times more energetic than Earth's.

items.t: Jupiter's auroras glow at both poles all the time.
items.d: They do not fade away, though some days they shine brighter.

items.t: Volcanoes on the moon Io feed a doughnut of plasma around Jupiter.
items.d: Plasma is a gas made of charged particles.

items.t: NASA's Juno spacecraft launched on August 5, 2011.
items.d: A large rocket carried it into space from Florida.

items.t: Juno went into orbit around Jupiter on July 4, 2016.
items.d: Its main engine fired for 35 minutes to begin that orbit.

items.t: Juno was the first solar-powered NASA craft built to work this far out.
items.d: No earlier NASA craft ran on sunlight so far from the Sun.

items.t: A Galileo probe entered Jupiter on December 7, 1995.
items.d: It entered the atmosphere at about 47.6 kilometers per second.

items.t: The Galileo probe sent data for 58 minutes.
items.d: Then heat stopped its radio, after those measurements were sent.

items.t: Io has hundreds of volcanoes. It is the most volcanically active world in our solar system.
items.d: Imagine a moon that is always erupting somewhere!

items.t: Some volcanoes on Io shoot lava fountains dozens of kilometers into the sky.
Io has lakes of melted rock on its surface.
items.d: They are filled with molten rock, not water.

items.t: Io is only a little bigger than Earth's Moon.
Io is about one-quarter as wide as Earth.
Io's eruptions can be seen with large telescopes on Earth.
Io's volcanoes cover its surface with new material so fast that it has few big craters.
items.d: Comets and asteroids can't keep up with the lava.

items.t: In 1979, the Voyager 1 spacecraft spotted the first signs of Io's volcanoes.
Io is pulled and squeezed by Jupiter's huge gravity and by nearby moons. This heats it up.
items.d: That heat helps power all those volcanoes.

items.t: Most of what we know about Io comes from a spacecraft called Galileo.
Europa is the fourth largest of Jupiter's moons.
Europa probably has a saltwater ocean hidden under its icy shell.
items.d: Scientists have strong evidence for this.

items.t: NASA launched the Europa Clipper spacecraft on October 14, 2024.
items.d: Its job is to study Jupiter's icy moon Europa.

items.t: Europa Clipper is the largest spacecraft NASA has ever built for a planet mission.
Galileo was the spacecraft that taught us most of what we know about Europa.
Ganymede is the largest moon in our solar system.
Ganymede is bigger than the planet Mercury.
items.d: A moon bigger than a planet!

items.t: Ganymede has a saltwater ocean underground.
items.d: It may hold more water than all of Earth's surface water.

items.t: Ganymede is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field.
Ganymede's magnetic field makes ribbons of glowing gas near its poles.
items.d: These glowing lights are called auroras.

items.t: Ganymede may be built in layers, like a club sandwich.
Ganymede has a core made of metal iron.
Ganymede looks brownish-gray because rock and ice are mixed together.
Callisto is the most heavily cratered object in our solar system.
Callisto is Jupiter's second-largest moon and the third-largest moon in the solar system.
Galileo Galilei found Callisto and Jupiter's other three biggest moons in 1610.
items.d: He used an early telescope.

items.t: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto are Jupiter's four largest moons. They are called the Galilean moons.
items.d: They are named after Galileo, who first saw them.

items.t: Jupiter has more than 100 moons.
Titan is Saturn's largest moon. It is the only moon known to have a thick atmosphere.
Titan has clouds, rain, rivers, lakes and seas.
items.d: But they are made of liquid methane and ethane, not water.

items.t: Besides Earth, Titan is the only place known to have liquid on its surface.
Pioneer 11 was the first spacecraft to explore Titan.
items.d: It flew through Saturn's system on September 1, 1979.

items.t: NASA's Dragonfly is a flying machine planned to explore many places on Titan.
Titan is larger than the planet Mercury.
Christiaan Huygens discovered Titan in 1655.
Some of Saturn's small moons are shaped like potatoes or ravioli.
Enceladus is only about 500 kilometers wide.
Enceladus has the whitest, most reflective surface in the solar system.
Enceladus is very cold. Its surface is about minus 201 degrees Celsius.
Fountains of icy water and gas shoot out from Enceladus.
items.d: Their spray forms one of Saturn's rings, called the E ring.

items.t: Enceladus has an ocean inside it, under a thick shell of ice.
Mimas is the smallest and innermost of Saturn's major moons.
Mimas is probably made almost entirely of water ice.
Cassini was the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn.
items.d: It launched on October 15, 1997.

items.t: Cassini found that Titan has methane rivers that run into a methane sea.
One side of Iapetus is as dark as coal.
Iapetus has a chain of mountains about 10 kilometers high along its middle.
Iapetus always shows the same face to Saturn.
Rhea is the second-largest moon of Saturn.
Hyperion is the largest of Saturn's moons that are not round.
Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second-largest planet.
Saturn is about 120,500 km wide at its equator, about nine times wider than Earth.
Saturn is the only planet in our solar system with an average density lower than water.
Saturn is mostly made of hydrogen and helium.
Saturn has a dense core of iron and nickel, surrounded by rocky material.
Saturn has no true solid surface where a spacecraft could land.
Saturn has about 95 times as much mass as Earth.
Saturn bulges at its equator, so it looks slightly squashed.
Saturn's upper clouds are made of ammonia ice.
Saturn sends out about 2.5 times as much energy as it receives from the Sun.
One day on Saturn lasts only about 10.7 hours.
One year on Saturn lasts about 29.4 Earth years.
Saturn is tilted about 26.7 degrees, so it has seasons.
Saturn is about 1.4 billion km from the Sun on average.
Sunlight takes about 80 minutes to travel from the Sun to Saturn.
Winds near Saturn's equator can reach about 500 metres per second.
A giant storm called the Great White Spot appears about once every Saturn year.
Saturn formed about 4.5 billion years ago.
Four robotic spacecraft have visited Saturn.
People have watched Saturn since prehistoric times.
Saturn has seven main rings, with spaces between them.
Saturn's rings are made of chunks of ice and rock.
Saturn's ring system stretches as far as about 282,000 km from the planet.
Saturn's main rings are only about 10 metres thick.
Ring particles range from tiny dust grains to chunks as big as a house.
The 4,700 km wide Cassini Division separates Saturn's A and B rings.
Galileo saw Saturn's rings in 1610, but he could not tell what they were.
Galileo thought Saturn's rings looked like ears on the planet's sides.
Christiaan Huygens realized that a thin, flat ring surrounds Saturn.
In 1675, Giovanni Cassini discovered gaps dividing Saturn's rings.
James Clerk Maxwell showed that the rings contain many separate orbiting particles.
Moving outward from Saturn, the three main rings are C, B, and A.
Saturn's rings are about 99.9 percent water ice.
The B ring is Saturn's largest, brightest, and most massive ring.
Some parts of Saturn's B ring block more than 99 percent of passing light.
The tiny moon Pan travels inside a 325 km wide gap in the A ring.
The moon Daphnis helps keep the narrow Keeler Gap clear.
Saturn's narrow F ring can change in just a few hours.
