Voyager images revealed dark features called spokes in Saturn's B ring.
The huge, faint Phoebe ring was discovered in 2009.
Saturn's extremely wide E ring spans about 300,000 km.
Saturn's rings look edge-on from Earth every 13 to 15 years.
Saturn has a six-sided cloud pattern called the hexagon around its north pole.
Saturn's hexagon is nearly 25,000 km across, about two Earths wide.
The hexagon reaches about 100 km below Saturn's cloud tops.
Pioneer 11 made the first spacecraft flyby of Saturn in 1979.
Pioneer 11 discovered Saturn's narrow F ring.
Voyager 1 discovered Saturn's G ring and five moons.
Cassini made 22 trips through the gap between Saturn and its rings.
In 1781 William Herschel found Uranus. He first thought it was a comet or a star.
items.d: It was a new planet, not a comet and not a star.

items.t: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun.
items.d: Six planets orbit closer to the Sun than Uranus does.

items.t: Uranus is about four times as wide as Earth.
items.d: Across its middle, Uranus is about 51,100 km (31,800 miles) wide.

items.t: Uranus orbits about 19 times farther from the Sun than Earth.
items.d: That is about 2.9 billion km (1.8 billion miles) from the Sun.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 2 hours and 40 minutes to reach Uranus.
items.d: Light from the Sun has a very long trip to get there.

items.t: A day on Uranus lasts about 17 hours.
items.d: That is one full spin, shorter than a day on Earth.

items.t: One year on Uranus lasts about 84 Earth years.
items.d: That is one long loop around the Sun.

items.t: Uranus is tilted about 98 degrees, so it spins on its side.
items.d: Other planets spin more upright. Uranus looks like it is lying down.

items.t: Each pole on Uranus has a dark winter about 21 years long.
items.d: The sideways tilt makes seasons there last a very long time.

items.t: Uranus spins backward. Venus is the only other planet that does.
items.d: Most planets spin one way. Uranus and Venus spin the other way.

items.t: Uranus is named for a Greek sky god, not for a king.
items.d: Herschel wanted to honor King George. The sky god name won.

items.t: Most of Uranus is a hot, thick fluid, not solid ice.
items.d: Uranus is called an ice giant. It has a small rocky core inside.

items.t: Uranus looks blue-green because of methane gas.
items.d: The methane soaks up red light, and blue-green light is what we see.

items.t: Uranus has nine thin, dark inner rings and two outer rings.
items.d: The inner rings are mostly narrow and dark grey.

items.t: Uranus's rings were discovered on March 10, 1977.
items.d: Astronomers found them by surprise, using a telescope on an airplane.

items.t: Uranus's five biggest moons are Miranda, Ariel, Umbriel, Titania, and Oberon.
items.d: These five are the major moons of Uranus.

items.t: Most moons of Uranus are named for characters in old stories.
items.d: Most names come from Shakespeare. A couple come from Alexander Pope.

items.t: Only Voyager 2 has visited Uranus, flying by in January 1986.
items.d: No other spacecraft has flown close to Uranus.

items.t: Titania is Uranus's largest moon, about 1,600 km across.
items.d: That is about 1,000 miles from side to side.

items.t: Miranda is only about 500 km across, roughly one-seventh our Moon's size.
items.d: Our Moon is about seven times as wide as little Miranda.

items.t: Some canyons on Miranda are 12 times as deep as the Grand Canyon.
items.d: Those cracks are far deeper than Earth's famous canyon.

items.t: A rock dropped from Miranda's tallest cliff would fall for about 10 minutes.
items.d: The cliff is so high that the fall takes a long time.

items.t: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft to visit all four giant planets up close.
items.d: It passed Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, and Neptune.

items.t: Voyager 2 flew past Neptune on 25 August 1989.
items.d: It was the first human-made object to fly by Neptune.

items.t: At Neptune, Voyager 2 passed about 4,800 km above the clouds.
items.d: That is about 2,980 miles up, its closest giant-planet flyby.

items.t: Neptune is the eighth planet and the farthest from the Sun.
items.d: No planet in our solar system orbits farther out.

items.t: Neptune is the only planet you cannot see with just your eyes.
items.d: It is too dim and far away. You need a telescope to see it.

items.t: Math showed where to look for Neptune. It was found in 1846.
items.d: Le Verrier predicted the spot. Galle found it on his first night.

items.t: Galileo saw Neptune in 1612, but he thought it was a star.
items.d: He wrote it down again in 1613 and still missed what it was.

items.t: Neptune is about four times as wide as Earth.
items.d: Across its middle, it is about 49,500 km (30,800 miles) wide.

items.t: Neptune is about 30 times farther from the Sun than Earth is.
items.d: If Earth to the Sun were one step, Neptune would be 30 steps out.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 4 hours to reach Neptune.
items.d: Neptune is so far away that the light needs all that time.

items.t: A day on Neptune lasts about 16 hours.
items.d: That is how long Neptune takes to spin once.

items.t: Neptune takes about 165 Earth years to go around the Sun.
items.d: One trip around the Sun there is a very long year.

items.t: In 2011 Neptune finished its first orbit since it was found.
items.d: It was discovered in 1846, and one orbit takes about 165 Earth years.

items.t: Neptune tilts about 28 degrees, and each season lasts over 40 years.
items.d: Spring, summer, fall, and winter each last for decades there.

items.t: Neptune has the fastest winds of any planet.
items.d: They can pass 2,000 km per hour, about nine times stronger than Earth's.

items.t: In 1989, Voyager 2 saw a Neptune storm big enough to fit Earth inside.
items.d: The 1989 storm was called the Great Dark Spot, but it later disappeared.

items.t: Neptune has no solid surface to stand on.
items.d: Below the clouds there is no hard ground like Earth's.

items.t: Neptune's rocky core has about the same mass as Earth.
items.d: Mass means how much stuff is inside. Neptune's core matches Earth.

items.t: Neptune's magnetic field is about 27 times stronger than Earth's.
items.d: It is tipped about 47 degrees from the planet's spin.

items.t: Noon on Neptune would look like dim twilight.
items.d: Twilight means the dim light after sunset. Sunlight on Earth is about 900 times brighter.

items.t: Finding Uranus about doubled the known size of the solar system.
items.d: The map of known planets suddenly reached much farther out.

items.t: Methane gas in Neptune's air helps make the planet look blue.
items.d: There is only a little methane in the outer air, but it affects the color we see.

items.t: Triton is the only large moon that orbits opposite its planet's spin.
items.d: It goes around Neptune the other way from the planet's spin.

items.t: Voyager 2 saw ice geysers on Triton spray ice more than 8 km high.
items.d: That spray climbed more than 5 miles above the ground.

items.t: Part of Triton is bumpy and looks like cantaloupe skin.
items.d: That area is called cantaloupe terrain because of the melon look.

items.t: Triton's surface is about minus 235 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is minus 391 degrees Fahrenheit. Triton is about 2,700 km (1,680 miles) wide.

items.t: Pluto was found in 1930 and was called the ninth planet for many years.
items.d: In 2006, scientists reclassified Pluto as a dwarf planet.

items.t: Pluto is about 2,400 km wide. That is only about one-fifth as wide as Earth.
items.d: You could line up five Plutos to stretch across Earth.

items.t: Pluto is about 39 times farther from the Sun than Earth is.
items.d: That is about 5.9 billion km away, on average.

items.t: Sunlight takes about 5.5 hours to reach Pluto.
One year on Pluto lasts 248 Earth years.
items.d: That is how long Pluto takes to go once around the Sun.

items.t: Gravity on Pluto is only about 6 percent of Earth's gravity.
items.d: You would jump much, much higher there than you can at home.

items.t: Pluto has a thin atmosphere made mostly of nitrogen.
items.d: Nitrogen is also the main gas in the air we breathe on Earth.

items.t: Ceres was discovered in 1801 by Giuseppe Piazzi.
items.d: It was the first known object in the asteroid belt.

items.t: Ceres holds about one quarter of all the mass in the asteroid belt.
Ceres is about 2.8 times farther from the Sun than Earth is.
items.d: Sunlight takes about 22 minutes to reach it.

items.t: Ceres could be up to 25 percent water.
items.d: That might be more water than all of Earth has.

items.t: NASA's Dawn spacecraft reached Ceres in 2015.
items.d: It was the first spacecraft ever to visit a dwarf planet.

items.t: A dwarf planet orbits the Sun and is nearly round, but it has not cleared other objects from its path.
To be a full planet, an object must orbit the Sun, be mostly round, and clear its orbit of similar objects.
Five dwarf planets are officially recognized: Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris.
There may be more than a hundred dwarf planets we have not found yet.
Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto on February 18, 1930, at an observatory in Arizona.
Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto using a blink comparator and two photos of the same sky.
items.d: A planet moves, so it seems to jump from one photo to the next.

items.t: An 11-year-old girl from England, Venetia Burney, suggested the name Pluto.
Charon is the largest of Pluto's moons. It is about half as wide as Pluto.
items.d: Charon is about 1,200 km across.

items.t: Charon is the biggest known moon compared with the world it circles.
Charon circles Pluto once every 6.4 Earth days, about 19,600 km away.
The same side of Charon always faces Pluto. The two are locked together.
Eris is about the same size as Pluto, roughly 2,400 km wide.
Eris has one small moon named Dysnomia.
items.d: Dysnomia goes around Eris about once every 16 days.

items.t: One year on Eris lasts 557 Earth years.
items.d: Eris is about 68 times farther from the Sun than Earth.

items.t: Haumea is shaped like an oval football because it spins so fast.
Haumea spins once about every 4 hours.
items.d: That is one of the fastest spins of any large object in our solar system.

items.t: Haumea has two moons, Namaka and Hi'iaka.
items.d: They are named after the daughters of a Hawaiian goddess.

items.t: Haumea was the first Kuiper Belt object found to have rings.
items.d: Scientists found them in 2017 as it passed in front of a star.

items.t: Makemake was first seen in 2005. Its finders nicknamed it Easterbunny.
items.d: It was found just days after Easter.

items.t: Makemake is named after a god of the Rapanui people of Easter Island.
Makemake is about 1,430 km wide, a bit smaller than Pluto.
items.d: One year there lasts about 305 Earth years.

items.t: The Kuiper Belt starts near Neptune's orbit and reaches out to about 50 times Earth's distance from the Sun.
The Kuiper Belt is shaped like a thick donut, not a thin flat ring.
The Kuiper Belt holds millions of small icy objects.
items.d: More than 2,000 have been found and listed so far.

items.t: All of the Kuiper Belt together has no more than about 10 percent of Earth's mass.
Pluto was the very first Kuiper Belt object ever discovered.
The Kuiper Belt is named after Gerard Kuiper, who wrote about objects beyond Neptune in 1951.
Neptune's gravity stirred up the Kuiper Belt, so its icy bits never joined into a planet.
New Horizons launched on January 19, 2006, on its way to Pluto.
items.d: It left at about 58,000 km/h, the fastest launch speed relative to Earth.

items.t: A Jupiter flyby in 2007 gave New Horizons a speed boost and saved about three years.
New Horizons flew past Pluto on July 14, 2015, about 7,800 km above its surface.
New Horizons took over 15 months to send home its Pluto data.
items.d: Its weak signal meant the data had to be sent very slowly.

items.t: New Horizons uses a radioisotope power generator instead of solar panels.
In 2019 New Horizons flew by Arrokoth, the most distant object explored up close.
Arrokoth is about 35 km long, 20 km wide and 10 km thick.
Arrokoth looks like a flattened red snowman.
items.d: It has two lobes joined together.

items.t: Arrokoth's red color comes from chemicals called tholins.
Arrokoth was first spotted in Hubble telescope pictures in 2014.
items.d: Scientists were searching for a target for New Horizons.

items.t: Asteroids are rocky, airless leftovers from the early solar system.
Asteroids formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
Asteroids are sometimes called minor planets.
Most asteroids orbit the Sun between Mars and Jupiter.
The region where most asteroids orbit is called the main asteroid belt.
Vesta is the largest known asteroid, about 530 kilometers across.
Some asteroids are less than 10 meters across, smaller than a bus.
All the asteroids together have less mass than Earth's Moon.
Several robotic spacecraft have studied asteroids up close.
Vesta is the second most massive body in the main asteroid belt.
Vesta is shaped almost like a sphere.
The Dawn spacecraft orbited Vesta from July 2011 to September 2012.
Vesta has a giant crater named Rheasilvia, about 500 kilometers wide.
Some meteorites found on Earth come from the asteroid Vesta.
Vesta has a trough named Divalia Fossa that is bigger than the Grand Canyon.
The DART spacecraft launched on November 23, 2021.
DART hit the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos on September 26, 2022.
Dimorphos is a small asteroid moonlet about 160 meters across.
Dimorphos orbits a larger asteroid named Didymos, about 780 meters wide.
DART tested whether hitting an asteroid could change its motion.
A meteoroid is a space rock, from as small as dust to as large as a small asteroid.
A meteor is the streak of light made when a fast meteoroid burns in our atmosphere.
A meteoroid that reaches the ground is called a meteorite.
About 44,000 kilograms of meteoritic material falls toward Earth each day.
Almost all space material entering Earth's atmosphere turns into vapor.
On an ordinary clear night, several meteors may be visible each hour.
During a meteor shower, many more meteors can appear than usual.
Each Perseid meteor comes from a tiny piece of Comet Swift-Tuttle.
The OSIRIS-REx spacecraft launched on September 8, 2016.
OSIRIS-REx used Earth's gravity to swing toward asteroid Bennu in 2017.
OSIRIS-REx arrived at asteroid Bennu on December 3, 2018.
The OSIRIS-REx team named its chosen sampling site Nightingale.
OSIRIS-REx touched Bennu briefly in 2020 to gather dust and pebbles.
OSIRIS-REx left Bennu in May 2021 for a 2.5-year journey toward Earth.
A capsule carrying material from Bennu landed in Utah on September 24, 2023.
OSIRIS-REx delivered about 121.6 grams of material from Bennu.
Bennu is about 500 meters wide at its equator.
Bennu comes closest to Earth about every six years.
The rock that makes up Bennu formed nearly 4.6 billion years ago.
Bennu was discovered on September 11, 1999.
Bennu has a shape that looks like a spinning top.
Bennu takes about 435 days to travel once around the Sun.
A third-grade student suggested Bennu's name, inspired by an Egyptian bird.
Asteroid Ryugu is about 900 meters across.
Ryugu was discovered in May 1999.
Ryugu was named after a magical underwater palace in a Japanese folktale.
Japan's Hayabusa2 spacecraft arrived at Ryugu in June 2018.
Hayabusa2 returned its Ryugu sample capsule to Earth in December 2020.
Hayabusa2 brought about 5.4 grams of material from Ryugu to Earth.
Hayabusa was the first mission to return an asteroid sample to Earth.
Our solar system has one star, eight planets, five dwarf planets and hundreds of moons.
items.d: The star is the Sun. Everything else goes around it.

items.t: The solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago.
items.d: That is much, much older than any dinosaur.

items.t: The solar system travels around the center of the Milky Way once every 230 million years or so.
items.d: One lap around our galaxy takes a very, very long time.

items.t: One astronomical unit (AU) is the distance from Earth to the Sun, about 150 million km.
items.d: Scientists use AU to measure distances inside the solar system.

items.t: Mercury and Venus are the only planets with no moons.
items.d: Every other planet has at least one moon.

items.t: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are called the rocky, or terrestrial, planets.
items.d: They are the four planets closest to the Sun.

items.t: The Sun is about 1.4 million km across, roughly 100 times wider than Earth.
The Sun holds about 99.8% of all the mass in our solar system.
items.d: It would take more than 330,000 Earths to match the Sun's mass.

items.t: The Sun is a yellow dwarf star that is about 4.5 billion years old.
The nearest star beyond our Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.24 light-years away.
items.d: A light-year is how far light travels in one year.

items.t: In order from the Sun: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune.
items.d: Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet.

items.t: Jupiter is the largest planet and Mercury is the smallest.
Jupiter and Saturn are gas giants. Uranus and Neptune are ice giants.
The word planet comes from an ancient Greek word that means wanderer.
items.d: Long ago, people noticed planets slowly moved across the night sky.

items.t: The five dwarf planets are Ceres, Pluto, Haumea, Makemake and Eris.
Pluto was changed from a planet to a dwarf planet in 2006.
items.d: A group of astronomers called the IAU made that decision.

items.t: Venus is the hottest planet, about 467 degrees C on its surface.
items.d: That is hotter than Mercury, even though Venus is farther from the Sun.

items.t: Venus takes 243 Earth days to spin once, longer than its 225-day year.
Venus spins backward compared with Earth, so the Sun would rise in the west.
Jupiter is so big that about 1,000 Earths could fit inside it.
items.d: It is about 11 times wider than Earth.

items.t: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm wider than Earth.
items.d: Astronomers have observed it for centuries.

items.t: A day on Jupiter lasts only 9.9 hours, the shortest of any planet.
Galileo first saw Jupiter's four biggest moons in 1610.
items.d: They are Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.

items.t: Mercury is the fastest planet. It circles the Sun every 88 Earth days.
items.d: Mercury is named for the swiftest of the ancient Roman gods.

items.t: Mercury is only a little bigger than Earth's Moon.
One day on Mercury, from sunrise to sunrise, lasts 176 Earth days.
items.d: That is about as long as two Mercury years.

items.t: Neptune is the windiest planet, with winds over 1,900 km per hour.
One year on Neptune lasts about 165 Earth years.
Neptune was found in 1846 after mathematicians worked out where it should be.
items.d: Then astronomers pointed a telescope there and saw it.

items.t: Neptune is about 30 AU from the Sun, and sunlight takes about 4 hours to get there.
Saturn is less dense than water on average. It is the only planet like that.
items.d: It is mostly light gas, so it is very fluffy for its size.

items.t: Saturn's rings are made of billions of chunks of ice and rock.
Uranus is tilted so far that it spins on its side.
William Herschel discovered Uranus in 1781.
items.d: Uranus is named after the Greek god of the sky.

items.t: Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano in the solar system, about 40 km tall.
Mars looks red because the iron in its rocks and dust has rusted.
A day on Mars is about 24.6 hours, and a Martian day is called a sol.
About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by ocean.
Earth is the only place we know of that has living things.
The solar system began as a cloud of gas and dust that flattened into a disk.
items.d: The Sun formed in the middle of that disk.

items.t: Rocky planets formed close to the Sun. Gas and ice giants formed farther out.
Most asteroids orbit the Sun in a belt between Mars and Jupiter.
items.d: All of them together weigh less than Earth's Moon.

items.t: Ceres is the largest object in the asteroid belt.
items.d: It makes up about 25% of the asteroid belt's total mass.

items.t: Pluto takes 248 Earth years to go around the Sun once.
An 11-year-old girl from Oxford, England, suggested the name Pluto.
items.d: Her name was Venetia Burney.

items.t: Voyager 1 was launched in 1977 and was the first human-made object to reach interstellar space.
Each Voyager spacecraft carries a gold-plated Golden Record with greetings in 55 languages.
Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969.
Apollo 11 splashed down on July 24, 1969.
Apollo 11 carried Neil Armstrong, Michael Collins, and Buzz Aldrin.
Neil Armstrong was the first human to step onto the Moon.
Buzz Aldrin was the second person to walk on the Moon.
Michael Collins stayed in Moon orbit while Armstrong and Aldrin landed.
The Apollo 11 lunar module was named Eagle.
Apollo 11 landed at a place called Tranquility Base.
Armstrong and Aldrin spent about 22 hours on the Moon's surface.
Apollo 11's Eagle landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
Aldrin stepped onto the Moon 19 minutes after Armstrong.
The Apollo 11 moonwalk lasted about two and a half hours.
Apollo 11 brought back 21.5 kg of Moon rocks, dust, and other material.
About 600 million people watched the Apollo 11 moonwalk live on TV.
Apollo 11 samples helped scientists identify three previously unknown minerals.
Eagle's lower section was left on the Moon after Apollo 11 lifted off.
Jim Lovell commanded Apollo 13.
Fred Haise was Apollo 13's lunar module pilot.
Apollo 13 launched from Kennedy Space Center on April 11, 1970.
Apollo 13's crew used their lunar module as a lifeboat.
Ground engineers helped Apollo 13's crew make its air-cleaning equipment fit.
Apollo 13 splashed down safely in the South Pacific on April 17, 1970.
Apollo 7 was the first crewed Apollo flight and spent 10 days orbiting Earth.
Apollo 12 made the Apollo program's second Moon landing.
Apollo 15 was the first mission to drive a Lunar Roving Vehicle on the Moon.
Apollo 13 circled the Moon but did not land.
The Saturn V rocket stood 111 meters tall with an Apollo spacecraft on top.
The Saturn V rocket had three stages.
Five powerful F-1 engines drove the Saturn V's first stage.
Thirteen Saturn V rockets launched from 1967 to 1973.
The final Saturn V launch carried Skylab, the first American space station.
Saturn V was the first rocket to carry people beyond low Earth orbit.
Apollo 8 was NASA's first crewed mission to orbit the Moon.
Apollo 8 carried Frank Borman, Jim Lovell, and William Anders.
Apollo 8 launched on Dec. 21, 1968, and splashed down six days later.
Apollo 8's crew spent about 20 hours orbiting the Moon.
Apollo 17 landed in the Moon's Taurus-Littrow Valley.
Apollo 17 was the final Apollo mission to land on the Moon.
Harrison Schmitt was the first scientist to walk on the Moon.
Eugene Cernan was the last Apollo astronaut to leave footprints on the Moon.
Apollo 17 astronauts gathered a record amount of Moon material during three moonwalks.
Lunar rovers were used on Apollo 15, Apollo 16, and Apollo 17.
Apollo 17's rover reached a top speed of about 18 km/h.
Each lunar rover had a mass of about 210 kg without its cargo on Earth.
Lunar rovers traveled to the Moon folded inside the lunar module.
Apollo missions returned 382 kg of Moon rocks, pebbles, sand, dust, and core samples.
The six Apollo landings brought back about 2,200 separate Moon samples.
Moon rocks show that the Moon's crust formed about 4.4 billion years ago.
Moon Trees grew from seeds that traveled around the Moon aboard Apollo 14.
Twelve people walked on the Moon during the Apollo program.
Artemis I lifted off on November 16, 2022.
items.d: It left Launch Pad 39B at Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

items.t: Orion flew for about 25 and a half days on Artemis I.
items.d: It splashed down off the coast of San Diego on December 11, 2022.

items.t: On Artemis I, Orion traveled about 432,000 kilometres from Earth.
items.d: NASA's figure is 268,563 miles from Earth.

items.t: Orion also flew about 70,000 kilometres past the Moon's far side.
items.d: NASA's figure for that extra stretch is 43,471 miles.

items.t: Artemis I carried no astronauts. It was a big test flight.
items.d: Orion completed 161 test goals to check its systems.

items.t: Orion carried 5,600 passive sensors and 34 active detectors.
items.d: They measured space radiation on the trip around the Moon.

items.t: Near the Moon, radiation in Orion was about twice the station's level.
items.d: That is about twice the radiation on the International Space Station.

items.t: A test dummy named Moonikin Campos sat in the commander seat.
items.d: The name honors Arturo Campos, an engineer from the Apollo days.

items.t: Two test dummies, Helga and Zohar, flew to study radiation.
items.d: Only Zohar wore a protective vest. Helga did not.

items.t: About 3.4 million names flew around the Moon on Artemis I.
items.d: They were saved on a flash drive inside the Orion capsule.

items.t: Ten small CubeSats flew to space with Artemis I.
items.d: One named EQUULEUS filmed a green comet in February 2023.

items.t: Orion came home at nearly 40,000 kilometres per hour.
items.d: It dipped into the air, skipped back out, then came down again. It was a first for a US spacecraft.

items.t: Orion spent about six days in a distant orbit around the Moon.
items.d: On its trip, it passed within about 130 kilometres of the surface.

items.t: Four astronauts flew around the Moon on Artemis II.
items.d: They were Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, Christina Koch, and Jeremy Hansen.

items.t: Artemis II lasted about nine days in April 2026.
items.d: Launch was April 1, and splashdown was April 10.

items.t: Artemis II looped around the Moon on a free-return path.
items.d: A free-return path uses the Moon's pull to swing the ship back toward Earth.

items.t: Artemis II was the first crewed trip beyond low Earth orbit since 1972.
items.d: The previous one was Apollo 17, the last Apollo Moon mission.

items.t: Artemis II came within about 6,545 kilometres of the Moon's far side.
items.d: That closest point was about 4,067 miles from the surface.

items.t: Jeremy Hansen was the first non-American to travel around the Moon.
items.d: He is a Canadian Space Agency astronaut and flew on Artemis II.

items.t: Artemis II traveled about 407,000 kilometres from Earth.
items.d: That is 252,756 miles. NASA called it the farthest people had been.

items.t: NASA gave the Moon program the name Artemis in May 2019.
items.d: In old Greek stories, Artemis is the twin sister of Apollo and the goddess of the Moon.

items.t: NASA calls Mars the far goal for human explorers.
items.d: The Artemis Moon trips help prepare for that journey.

items.t: NASA plans a base near the Moon's south pole.
items.d: Astronauts would live, work, and explore from that polar base.

items.t: The SLS Block 1 rocket stands about 98 metres tall.
items.d: That is 322 feet, which is taller than the Statue of Liberty.

items.t: SLS Block 1 makes about 39 million newtons of thrust.
items.d: That is 8.8 million pounds, 15 percent more push than the Saturn V.

items.t: Two solid boosters give SLS most of its push at liftoff.
items.d: In the first two minutes they supply more than 75 percent of the thrust.

items.t: Four engines on the SLS core burn liquid hydrogen and oxygen.
items.d: Those super-cold liquids are the rocket's main fuels.

items.t: Orion's solar wings unfold until they stretch 19 metres across.
items.d: The wings are part of the European service module and make electricity.

items.t: Orion's European service module brings power, water, and air.
items.d: It supplies electricity, water, oxygen, and nitrogen.

items.t: NASA planned Gateway as the first space station around the Moon.
items.d: Partners are Canada, Europe's space agency, Japan, and the UAE.

items.t: Gateway's planned Moon orbit would take about 7 days.
items.d: It would swing from about 1,500 kilometres over the north pole out to about 70,000 kilometres over the south pole.

items.t: In March 2026, NASA said it would pause the Gateway station plan.
items.d: NASA said it would pause Gateway as designed and focus on a surface base.

items.t: A Moon lander design called Starship is about 52 metres tall.
items.d: It is about 9 metres wide, or about 30 feet across.

items.t: The lunar Starship does not need a heat shield.
items.d: It will not fly back through Earth's air, so it also has no flight fins.

items.t: The Starship lander is planned to stay about seven days on the Moon.
items.d: The visit plan includes four moonwalks.

items.t: Some ridges near the Moon's south pole stay sunny most of the time.
items.d: One ridge is in sunlight more than 92 percent of the time, good for solar power.

items.t: Some deep craters at the Moon's south pole never get sunlight.
items.d: These cold traps can hold water ice for a very long time.

items.t: NASA's LCROSS mission found water in Cabeus crater.
items.d: The debris it kicked up was nearly 5 percent water.

items.t: The Moon's spin axis is tilted only about 1.5 degrees.
items.d: Because the tilt is tiny, the poles have long shadows and near-constant light.

items.t: Odysseus launched on February 15, 2024, and landed on the Moon.
items.d: It was the first commercial lander to touch down on the Moon.

items.t: Blue Ghost landed in Mare Crisium on the Moon on March 2, 2025.
items.d: It was the first fully successful landing in NASA's private lander program.

items.t: Chang'e 4 was the first craft to land gently on the Moon's far side.
items.d: On January 3, 2019, it landed in Von Karman crater, about 180 km wide.

items.t: The Queqiao satellite relays messages to the Moon's far side.
items.d: It orbits beyond the Moon so Earth can talk with the far side lander.

items.t: Chang'e 5 brought about 1.7 kg of Moon rock and soil to Earth.
items.d: The sample capsule returned in December 2020.

items.t: Chang'e 6 was first to bring home samples from the Moon's far side.
items.d: About 1.9 kg landed by parachute in Inner Mongolia on June 25, 2024.

items.t: India's Chandrayaan-3 landed near the Moon's south pole in 2023.
items.d: Vikram the lander touched down on August 23. The rover was Pragyan.

items.t: Pragyan's laser confirmed sulfur in soil near the Moon's south pole.
items.d: It drove 101.4 metres across the south polar soil.

items.t: Japan's SLIM landed on the Moon on January 19, 2024.
items.d: Japan became the fifth country to land gently on the Moon.

items.t: SLIM was nicknamed Moon Sniper because its aim was so close.
items.d: It landed within about 100 metres of the chosen spot.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space on 12 April 1961.
items.d: His spacecraft was called Vostok 1. It launched from Baikonur Cosmodrome.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin's trip around Earth lasted 108 minutes. He went around our planet just once.
items.d: That is shorter than many movies!

items.t: Yuri Gagarin was 27 years old when he flew into space.
items.d: He was born in 1934 and flew in 1961.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin did not land inside his capsule. He ejected about 7,000 metres up and used a parachute.
Gherman Titov flew Vostok 2 in August 1961 and went around Earth 17 times.
items.d: His trip took about 25 hours.

items.t: Gherman Titov was the first person to sleep in space.
items.d: He woke up with his arms floating in front of him!

items.t: Valentina Tereshkova became the first woman in space on 16 June 1963.
items.d: She flew on Vostok 6.

items.t: Valentina Tereshkova went around Earth 48 times during her flight.
Before she was a cosmonaut, Valentina Tereshkova worked in a textile factory and jumped from planes for fun.
items.d: She was an amateur skydiver.

items.t: Valentina Tereshkova's radio call sign was Chaika, which means Seagull in Russian.
items.d: After launch she called out, "It is I, Seagull!"

items.t: Sally Ride became the first American woman in space on 18 June 1983.
items.d: She flew on the space shuttle Challenger.

items.t: Sally Ride was 32 when she flew, the youngest American in space at that time.
Sally Ride earned a physics PhD at Stanford University.
items.d: Her research studied how X-rays interact with matter between stars.

items.t: On her first flight, Sally Ride used a robotic arm to let go of a satellite and then catch it again.
Sally Ride led a program called EarthKAM, where students asked for photos of Earth taken from space.
Kalpana Chawla was the first woman of Indian heritage to fly into space.
items.d: She was born in Karnal, India, in 1962.

items.t: Kalpana Chawla first flew on the space shuttle Columbia in November 1997.
An asteroid, a Moon crater and a cargo spacecraft are named to honour Kalpana Chawla.
Rakesh Sharma became the first Indian to travel to space in April 1984.
items.d: He flew on a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft.

items.t: Asked how India looked from space, Rakesh Sharma said, "Sare Jahan Se Accha."
items.d: The words come from a famous poem.

items.t: Mae Jemison became the first African-American woman in space in September 1992.
items.d: She flew on the space shuttle Endeavour.

items.t: Before she became an astronaut, Mae Jemison was a medical doctor who worked in Liberia and Sierra Leone.
Mae Jemison studied ballet, jazz and African dance.
items.d: She loved dance as well as science.

items.t: In 2007 Peggy Whitson became the first woman to command the International Space Station.
items.d: She did it again in 2017.

items.t: Peggy Whitson became the first woman to lead NASA's Astronaut Office.
items.d: She was also the first leader who was not a pilot.

items.t: Astronaut Scott Kelly has an identical twin brother named Mark, who is also an astronaut.
While Scott Kelly was in space, his twin Mark stayed on Earth as a comparison in a spaceflight study.
Katherine Johnson was a NASA mathematician who worked out the path for Alan Shepard's 1961 space flight.
Before his orbit of Earth, John Glenn asked Katherine Johnson to check the computer's numbers.
items.d: He trusted her maths.

items.t: The film Hidden Figures tells the story of Katherine Johnson and other Black women mathematicians at NASA.
Christa McAuliffe was a school teacher picked by NASA from more than 11,000 applicants.
items.d: She was to be the first teacher in space.

items.t: Christa McAuliffe planned to teach lessons from space, including one called The Ultimate Field Trip.
Alan Shepard became the first American in space on 5 May 1961. His flight lasted about 15 minutes.
items.d: His spacecraft was called Freedom 7.

items.t: Alan Shepard hit golf balls on the Moon in 1971.
items.d: He used a golf club head attached to a tool handle.

items.t: John Glenn became the first American to orbit Earth in 1962. He went around three times.
John Glenn flew in space again in 1998 at age 77, on the space shuttle Discovery.
Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon on 20 July 1969.
Neil Armstrong said, "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."
Neil Armstrong commanded Gemini 8 in 1966, which made the first docking of two spacecraft in space.
Buzz Aldrin was the second person to walk on the Moon, about 19 minutes after Neil Armstrong.
Buzz Aldrin studied how spacecraft meet in orbit. His nickname was Dr. Rendezvous.
Buzz Aldrin described the Moon as "magnificent desolation."
items.d: Desolation means a very empty, quiet place.

items.t: Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk in history on 18 March 1965.
Alexei Leonov's spacewalk lasted about 12 minutes. A 4.8-metre tether kept him tied to his ship.
Alexei Leonov's suit puffed up like a balloon, so he let out some air to squeeze back inside.
In 1975, Alexei Leonov shook hands with American Thomas Stafford in space.
items.d: It was the Apollo-Soyuz mission.

items.t: Svetlana Savitskaya was the first woman to do a spacewalk, in July 1984.
Helen Sharman became the first Briton in space in May 1991. She visited the Mir space station.
Helen Sharman joined after hearing a radio advert: "Astronaut wanted. No experience necessary."
items.d: About 13,000 people applied.

items.t: Yang Liwei became China's first astronaut in October 2003.
The ISS circles Earth about once every 90 minutes.
The ISS travels around Earth 16 times in one day.
People have lived on the ISS without a break since November 2000.
A crew of seven people normally lives and works on the ISS.
Five space agencies from 15 countries work together to operate the ISS.
The ISS is about 109 metres long from end to end.
The ISS has a mass of about 420,000 kilograms.
The living space inside the ISS is larger than a six-bedroom house.
Eight main solar arrays provide about 75 to 90 kilowatts of power to the ISS.
The ISS was built in space using pieces delivered on 42 assembly flights.
Up to eight spaceships can connect to the ISS at the same time.
Canadarm2 is a 17-metre robotic arm that can grab visiting spacecraft.
About 13 kilometres of wire connect the ISS electrical power system.
ISS software watches about 350,000 sensors.
More than 50 computers control systems aboard the ISS.
The outside of the ISS can hold more than 20 research projects at once.
Some spacecraft can reach the ISS about four hours after launch.
The ISS laboratory has hosted nearly 3,000 research investigations.
Astronauts have taken more than 3.5 million photos of Earth from the ISS.
Astronauts on the ISS exercise for at least two hours each day.
In about one day, the ISS travels as far as a trip to the Moon and back.
The ISS passes over places where about 90 percent of Earth's people live.
The ISS truss is a 94-metre backbone that holds its solar arrays.
Water recycling cuts the need for water deliveries to the ISS by 65 percent.
Astronauts use a piston and flywheel machine to copy weight lifting in space.
The ISS has a treadmill called T2 and a cycling machine called CEVIS.
In microgravity, muscles and bones can weaken, so astronauts need exercise.
There is no shower on the ISS.
The ISS has no washing machine, so astronauts change clothes about every three days.
Space toilets use a fan for suction, and astronauts strap themselves to the seat.
Astronauts eat three meals a day. They sip drinks and soups from bags through straws.
Magnets keep forks, knives and spoons from floating away at the ISS table.
Astronauts strap onto exercise machines so they do not push themselves away.
Many astronauts attach sleeping bags to walls so they stay in one place.
items.d: Some wear earplugs because the station's fans and equipment are loud.

items.t: Before bed, ISS astronauts may email home, watch films or use ham radio.
A spacewalk usually lasts five to eight hours, depending on the job.
Safety tethers keep spacewalking astronauts connected to their spacecraft.
Astronauts train underwater for seven hours for each planned hour of spacewalking.
Spacesuits provide spacewalkers with oxygen to breathe and water to drink.
Astronauts spacewalk to test new equipment and make repairs.
The ISS Cupola has seven windows, including one that looks straight down at Earth.
Astronauts use a workstation in the Cupola to control the Canadarm2 robotic arm.
The ISS water system can recover about 98 percent of its water.
Dehumidifiers collect moisture from astronauts' breath and sweat for recycling.
Each astronaut needs about 3.8 litres of water daily for food, drinks and washing.
Sensors check recycled ISS water, and iodine helps stop microbes from growing in it.
ISS crews can choose from about 200 foods and drinks on their standard menu.
The ISS space garden is about the size of carry-on luggage and usually holds six plants.
Most rocket engines burn fuel to make hot gas. The gas shoots out the back and pushes the rocket forward.
items.d: Think of a balloon zooming around when you let the air out.

items.t: A rocket engine does not need air from outside. The rocket carries everything it needs to burn its fuel.
items.d: That is why rockets can keep working in the emptiness of space.

items.t: A rocket pushes its exhaust backward. The exhaust pushes the rocket forward.
items.d: Push one way, and you get pushed the other way.

items.t: A rocket sits still on the pad until a big enough push, called thrust, acts on it.
items.d: This is Newton's first law: things stay put until a force moves them.

items.t: Most of a rocket's mass is its propellant. The rocket gets lighter as the propellant burns.
items.d: So it speeds up more easily as the trip goes on.

items.t: The Saturn V moon rocket stood about 111 meters tall, roughly like a 36-story building.
A fully fueled Saturn V weighed about 2.8 million kilograms, about as much as 400 elephants.
At liftoff, the Saturn V made about 34.5 million newtons of thrust.
items.d: That is an enormous push, enough to lift a building-sized rocket.

items.t: The Saturn V could send about 118,000 kg into Earth orbit and about 43,500 kg all the way to the Moon.
The Saturn V was developed at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama.
The first Saturn V launch, Apollo 4, flew in 1967 with no crew on board.
Apollo 8 was the first Saturn V to carry astronauts.
Apollo 11 in 1969 was the first mission to land astronauts on the Moon. A Saturn V launched it.
A Saturn V launched the Skylab space station. That version had only two stages.
The Apollo Saturn V had three stages. Each stage burned until its fuel ran out, then dropped away.
The Saturn V's first stage lifted the rocket about 68 kilometers up.
The Space Shuttle had three main parts: the orbiter, two boosters, and a big external fuel tank.
The Shuttle orbiter was about the size of a large passenger airliner.
Ceramic tiles on the Shuttle orbiter's underside protected it from heat when it came back to Earth.
Each Shuttle orbiter was designed to fly 100 times.
In orbit, the Space Shuttle moved about 27,870 km/h.
items.d: That is faster than a bullet by many times over.

items.t: The Shuttle's three main engines burned liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen from the big external tank.
The Shuttle's external tank was the only part that could not be reused.
The Shuttle's boosters dropped off after about two minutes, parachuted into the sea, and were reused.
India's PSLV has four stages. They alternate between solid and liquid propellants.
India's PSLV is called the Workhorse of ISRO because it reliably carries satellites to low Earth orbit.
India's PSLV launched the Chandrayaan-1 Moon mission in 2008 and the Mars Orbiter in 2013.
One PSLV rocket launched 10 satellites on a single mission in 2008.
PSLV has versions with six, four, two, or no strap-on boosters.
India's GSLV rocket project began in 1990 to launch satellites to geosynchronous orbit.
ISRO began developing its own cryogenic upper stage in 1994. Its engine uses liquid hydrogen and oxygen.
Falcon 9 is a two-stage rocket. Its first stage can fly back and be used again.
The Falcon 9 first stage has nine Merlin engines. The second stage has one.
In December 2015, a Falcon 9 booster made the first upright landing after an orbital launch.
Falcon 9 boosters can land on drone ships out at sea.
Starship is a reusable spacecraft that sits on top of a giant booster called Super Heavy.
Starship is built from stainless steel. Its builders switched from carbon composites in 2018.
Launch Complex 39 at Kennedy Space Center was built as the Moonport for the Apollo program.
Huge crawlers weighing about 2,720 tonnes carried rockets to the pad at about 1.6 km/h.
A flame trench under the launch pad guides rocket exhaust away. It is about 13 meters deep and 18 meters wide.
Robert Goddard launched the first liquid-fueled rocket on March 16, 1926, in Massachusetts.
Goddard's first liquid rocket flew for only about 2.5 seconds and landed in a cabbage field.
Tsiolkovsky published the rocket equation in 1903. It shows why bigger speed changes need more propellant.
Rockets drop empty stages along the way. The leftover rocket is then lighter and easier to speed up.
NASA was established in 1958.
NASA took over from an older agency called the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics.
NASA has its headquarters in Washington, D.C.
The first Space Shuttle flight into orbit happened in 1981.
NASA's Space Shuttle program ended in 2011 after mission STS-135.
The shuttle Discovery carried the Hubble Space Telescope into space in 1990.
NASA's twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity landed on Mars in 2004.
The James Webb Space Telescope is an infrared observatory launched in 2021.
The European Space Agency, or ESA, was founded in 1975.
ESA has its headquarters in Paris, France.
ESA began with ten founding member countries.
Europe's main spaceport is in Kourou, French Guiana.
ESA's Rosetta was the first spacecraft to orbit a comet.
ESA's Huygens probe landed on Titan, a moon of Saturn.
ESA's Gaia telescope created a huge, precise 3D catalogue of objects in space.
Ulf Merbold was the first ESA astronaut to fly in space.
India's space organization took the name ISRO in 1969.
ISRO has its headquarters in Bengaluru, India.
India's first satellite, Aryabhata, was launched in 1975.
India's Mars orbiter succeeded on its first attempt.
India launched its first solar probe, Aditya-L1, in 2023.
Chandrayaan-3 landed on the Moon on August 23, 2023.
The Chandrayaan-3 Moon lander was named Vikram.
Chandrayaan-3's Pragyan rover had six wheels and a mass of 26 kilograms.
Japan formed JAXA in 2003 by joining three organizations together.
JAXA's Hayabusa was the first spacecraft to return asteroid samples to Earth.
Hayabusa visited asteroid Itokawa and returned samples to Earth in 2010.
JAXA's Hayabusa2 returned samples from asteroid Ryugu in 2020.
JAXA built Kibo, the largest module of the International Space Station.
JAXA's SLIM spacecraft made a gentle Moon landing in January 2024.
SLIM's landing made Japan the fifth country to land on the Moon.
The China National Space Administration was founded in 1993.
Chang'e 4 made the first landing on the side of the Moon facing away from Earth.
Chang'e 5 collected material from the Moon and brought it to Earth.
The Yutu rover worked on the Moon from 2013 to 2016.
Tianwen-1 made China's space agency the second to land a rover on Mars.
The name Tiangong means Heavenly Palace.
The Tiangong space station forms a T shape and usually has three crew members.
SpaceX was founded in 2002.
Falcon 1 made SpaceX the first private company to launch a liquid-fueled rocket to orbit.
Dragon became the first commercial spacecraft to deliver cargo to the ISS in 2012.
SpaceX first landed and recovered a rocket's first stage in December 2015.
SpaceX became the first private company to send astronauts to the ISS in 2020.
Falcon 9 reached orbit on its first attempt in 2010.
Falcon Heavy made its first flight in 2018.
Blue Origin was founded in 2000.
New Shepard is named after Alan Shepard, the first American in space.
New Shepard flew its first mission with people aboard in July 2021.
Rocket Lab was founded in New Zealand in 2006.
Rocket Lab's Electron rocket reached orbit on its second flight in 2018.
A satellite is anything that orbits a planet or a star.
items.d: That includes moons and planets, and also machines people send to space.

items.t: Earth is a natural satellite because it orbits the Sun.
items.d: Natural means nobody built it. Earth's path around the Sun makes it a satellite.

items.t: The Moon is a natural satellite of Earth.
items.d: Nobody launched it. It already travels around Earth on its own.

items.t: Thousands of human-made satellites orbit Earth.
items.d: People built them and launched them so they could circle the planet.

items.t: Some satellites photograph Earth to help predict the weather.
items.d: They can track a hurricane and show which way the storm is moving.

items.t: Some satellites take pictures of the Sun and faraway galaxies.
items.d: They also photograph other planets out in the solar system.

items.t: Satellites carry TV signals and phone calls around the world.
items.d: That is how a TV show or a phone call can reach someone far away.

items.t: More than 30 satellites work together to make GPS.
items.d: GPS uses them to help a phone or a map find your location.

items.t: From high up, a satellite can see a huge area of Earth at once.
items.d: That wide view is why one satellite can watch a whole storm system.

items.t: Satellites that look at space see it more clearly.
items.d: They fly above clouds, dust, and air that can blur the view of telescopes on the ground.

items.t: Most satellites have an antenna and a power source.
items.d: The antenna sends and receives messages. The power source runs the satellite.

items.t: Solar panels turn sunlight into electricity for satellites.
items.d: Those shiny panels are a common power source on satellites.

items.t: A satellite stays up when its speed balances Earth's pull.
items.d: Gravity tugs inward. Fast sideways motion keeps the satellite circling.

items.t: A geostationary satellite looks like it is standing still.
items.d: It keeps moving, but it stays above the same place on Earth.

items.t: A polar satellite can scan the whole Earth, one strip at a time.
items.d: Each loop sees a new strip, until the strips add up to the globe.

items.t: Explorer 1 was America's first human-made satellite.
items.d: It launched in 1958. Before it, the United States had no satellite in orbit.

items.t: Explorer 1 measured cosmic rays, speedy particles in space.
items.d: A sensor on the satellite counted these high-energy particles.

items.t: Explorer 6 took the first satellite picture of Earth in 1959.
items.d: It was the first photo of our planet sent home from a satellite.

items.t: In 1960, TIROS-1 sent the first TV picture of Earth from space.
items.d: A television camera on the satellite sent the view of Earth back home.

items.t: OCO-2, launched in 2014, measures carbon dioxide in the air.
items.d: Carbon dioxide is a gas in Earth's air. This satellite tracks how much there is.

items.t: Satellites watch wildfires, volcanoes, and their smoke.
items.d: From orbit they can see a smoke plume spread across a wide area.

items.t: Pictures from satellites help farmers choose crops to plant.
items.d: The information helps them match crops to the land they farm.

items.t: Some satellites watch for strong rays coming from the Sun.
items.d: They spot bursts of energy from the Sun so scientists can study them.

items.t: Low Earth orbit begins just above the top of the atmosphere.
items.d: It is the nearby part of space where many satellites travel.

items.t: NASA's Aqua satellite orbits about 705 kilometers up.
items.d: One full trip around Earth takes Aqua about 99 minutes.

items.t: Most NASA science satellites fly in low Earth orbit.
items.d: Many weather satellites use this same nearby orbit.

items.t: Thin air slowly tugs low satellites closer to Earth.
items.d: Now and then they need a boost so they do not sink too low.

items.t: A geostationary satellite orbits about 36,000 kilometers up.
items.d: At that height, one orbit matches one full spin of Earth.

items.t: A geostationary orbit is a circle above Earth's equator.
items.d: Both the round shape and the spot above the equator are required.

items.t: Higher orbits take longer. The Moon needs about a month.
items.d: A low satellite can orbit in about 99 minutes. Some orbits take about 12 hours.

items.t: Polar-orbiting satellites see most of Earth twice a day.
items.d: They pass over once in daylight and once in the dark.

items.t: Some satellites cross the equator at the same local time each day.
items.d: This is called a sun-synchronous orbit. The clock time stays about the same.

items.t: Sputnik 1 was the world's first human-made satellite.
items.d: It launched on October 4, 1957.

items.t: Sputnik 1 was about the size of a beach ball.
items.d: From side to side it measured 58 centimeters.

items.t: Sputnik 1 weighed about 84 kilograms.
items.d: It was heavy for something only 58 centimeters across.

items.t: Sputnik 1 circled Earth about once every 98 minutes.
items.d: Its path was a stretched oval, called an ellipse, not a perfect circle.

items.t: GPS has three parts: satellites, ground stations, and receivers.
items.d: A receiver, like the one in a phone, listens to the satellites.

items.t: A GPS receiver needs at least four satellites to find you.
items.d: It measures the distance to each one, then works out your spot.

items.t: GPS ground stations check that the satellites are on course.
items.d: They use radar to make sure each satellite is where we expect.

items.t: An ordinary GPS can place you within a few meters.
items.d: That is close enough to show which street or building you are near.

items.t: Special GPS tools can find a spot within a few inches.
items.d: That is about the width of your palm.

items.t: GPS can help scientists watch volcanoes.
items.d: It can also show how the ground has shifted after an earthquake.

items.t: A basic CubeSat is a cube 10 centimeters on each side.
items.d: That small size is called 1U. Bigger CubeSats stack these cubes together.

items.t: A CubeSat usually weighs about 1 to 10 kilograms.
items.d: A university in California called Cal Poly first developed CubeSats in 1999.

items.t: Telstar 1 sent the first TV signals across the Atlantic Ocean.
items.d: It launched on July 10, 1962. A July 23 show reached viewers in 16 countries.

items.t: Landsat has the longest satellite record of Earth's land.
items.d: The first Landsat launched on July 23, 1972, and the picture record kept going.

items.t: Most space junk breaks up before it can reach the ground.
items.d: Falling back into the air heats it so much that it does not survive.

items.t: Tiny flecks of paint can flake off and become space junk.
items.d: Big temperature changes and tiny hits can chip paint off a spacecraft.

items.t: Polar weather satellites circle Earth about 14 times a day.
items.d: They fly about 833 kilometers up, low enough for detailed pictures.

items.t: Some weather satellites can take a picture every 30 seconds.
items.d: GOES-R satellites can do this from their high orbit over the equator.

items.t: The two Voyager spacecraft launched in 1977.
items.d: They left Earth before many of today's grandparents were adults.

items.t: Voyager 1 and 2 are the only spacecraft ever to fly outside the Sun's protective bubble.
items.d: Scientists call that bubble the heliosphere.

items.t: Voyager 1 was the first human-made object to travel one light-day away from Earth.
items.d: Light takes one full day to cover that distance.

items.t: A team led by Carl Sagan picked what went onto the Voyager Golden Record.
The Golden Record opens with: "To the makers of music - all worlds, all times."
Each Voyager travels more than 3 times the Earth-Sun distance every year.
items.d: That is about 450 million km every single year.

items.t: In 2012, Voyager 1 became the first spacecraft to leave the Sun's bubble and measure interstellar space.
The Voyagers use special radioisotope generators for power, not solar panels.
Voyager 2 launched on August 20, 1977, about two weeks before its twin, Voyager 1.
Voyager 2 was the first spacecraft to fly past Uranus, in January 1986.
Voyager 2 was the first spacecraft to fly past Neptune, in August 1989.
Voyager 2 discovered 10 new moons around Uranus.
The Voyager Golden Record is a 30-centimetre (12-inch) gold-plated copper disk.
items.d: It is shaped like a music record and carries sounds from Earth.

items.t: The Golden Record carries spoken greetings in 55 languages.
The Golden Record holds sounds of thunder and birds, plus music from many cultures and times.
The cover of the Golden Record shows how to play it and how to find Earth.
A radio message to Voyager 1 takes about a day to arrive, and the reply takes another day.
items.d: So a chat with it would be very slow.

items.t: Each Voyager has a 3.7-metre dish antenna, to talk to Earth.
The Voyagers' power is slowly fading, so engineers switch off instruments one at a time.
In the Pale Blue Dot photo, Earth is only about one pixel in size.
It took eight years and six requests to get approval for the Pale Blue Dot photos.
Carl Sagan first suggested turning Voyager's cameras back toward Earth in 1981.
After taking the family portrait of our planets, Voyager 1 turned its cameras off for good.
Pioneer 10 launched on March 2, 1972.
Pioneer 10 was the first spacecraft to fly through the asteroid belt.
Pioneer 10 flew past Jupiter in 1973 and took about 500 pictures.
Pioneer 10 carries a metal plaque with a man, a woman and a map to our Sun.
Pioneer 11 was the first spacecraft to fly past Saturn.
Pioneer 11 sent back the first pictures of the polar regions of Jupiter.
Parker Solar Probe launched on August 12, 2018, to study the Sun up close.
At its closest, Parker Solar Probe moves at about 690,000 km/h.
items.d: That is fast enough to cross a big country in seconds.

items.t: Parker's heat shield is about 11 cm thick and handles heat of about 1,400 degrees Celsius.
In 2021, NASA said Parker had flown through the Sun's corona, the first spacecraft to touch the Sun.
Juno was the first solar-powered NASA spacecraft built to work so far from the Sun.
Juno found that Jupiter's Great Red Spot reaches about 320 km deep.
In 2004 Cassini became the first spacecraft to orbit Saturn, and it stayed for 13 years.
Cassini found jets of water ice and vapor spraying from cracks near the south pole of Enceladus.
Huygens was the first probe to land on a world in the outer solar system.
items.d: It landed on Titan, a moon of Saturn, in January 2005.

items.t: Huygens floated down through Titan's thick haze on parachutes for about 2.5 hours.
Titan has lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane near its poles.
Titan is the only known world besides Earth with a thick atmosphere rich in nitrogen.
Japan's Hayabusa was the first spacecraft to land on an asteroid and lift off again.
In September 2014, India's Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars orbit.
items.d: India became the first Asian nation to reach Mars orbit.

items.t: India's Mangalyaan was planned to last six months but worked for about 7.5 years.
Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, was launched on October 4, 1957.
Sputnik 1 was about the size of a beach ball, only 58 cm across.
Sputnik 1 circled Earth once about every 98 minutes.
The first US satellite, Explorer 1, launched on January 31, 1958.
The earliest known telescope record is Hans Lipperhey's patent request from 1608.
Galileo built his own telescope in 1609 after hearing about the Dutch invention.
Isaac Newton built the first practical reflecting telescope, which used mirrors.
Refracting telescopes use lenses. Reflecting telescopes use mirrors.
Large mirrors are lighter and easier to make smooth than large lenses.
A bigger telescope mirror gathers more light, revealing dimmer and more distant objects.
A curved telescope mirror flips an image. Extra mirrors can turn it the right way.
Hubble launched aboard Space Shuttle Discovery on April 24, 1990.
Hubble's main mirror is 2.4 metres wide.
Hubble's mirror had the wrong shape. Astronauts fixed its blurry vision in 1993.
Astronauts visited Hubble on five repair and upgrade missions. The last was in 2009.
Hubble circles Earth at a height of about 540 kilometres.
Hubble travels around Earth about once every 94 minutes.
Hubble weighed about 11,000 kilograms at launch.
The Webb telescope launched on December 25, 2021, from French Guiana.
Webb has a gold-coated main mirror that is 6.5 metres wide.
Webb's main mirror is built from 18 hexagonal pieces.
Webb uses a giant sunshield made of five layers.
Webb circles the Sun near a spot called L2, about 1.5 million kilometres beyond Earth.
Webb stays colder than about minus 223 degrees Celsius to observe infrared light.
NASA, the European Space Agency, and the Canadian Space Agency worked together on Webb.
Webb observes infrared light. Its sunshield blocks heat from the Sun, Earth, and Moon.
Kepler discovered more than 2,600 planets outside our solar system.
NASA retired Kepler in 2018 after the spacecraft ran low on fuel.
TESS launched on April 18, 2018, to search for planets around other stars.
TESS observes the sky using four wide-view cameras.
TESS travels around Earth once every 13.7 days.
TESS surveys about 85 percent of the sky.
Chandra, NASA's X-ray space telescope, launched on July 23, 1999.
X-ray telescopes work in space because Earth's atmosphere absorbs most X-rays.
Chandra uses nested glass mirrors that reflect X-rays at very shallow angles.
Spitzer, an infrared space telescope, launched on August 25, 2003.
Liquid helium kept Spitzer's instruments cold until the helium ran out in 2009.
Spitzer followed Earth around the Sun, where Earth did not block its view.
NASA switched off Spitzer in 2020 after more than 16 years of observations.
Spitzer helped reveal a system of seven Earth-size planets around the star TRAPPIST-1.
The European Space Agency's Gaia spacecraft launched on December 19, 2013.
Gaia precisely measured the positions, distances, and motions of stars.
Gaia worked near a spot called L2, about 1.5 million kilometres from Earth.
Stars in one constellation are usually far apart and are not joined together.
The constellations you can see depend on the season and your location on Earth.
The Big Dipper is a star pattern inside the larger constellation Ursa Major.
items.d: A star pattern that is not an official constellation is called an asterism.

items.t: Polaris, the North Star, seems almost still because it sits near the sky's north pole.
Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn can all be seen without a telescope.
Skyglow from too many city lights can wash out stars and the Milky Way.
Penguins use their wings like flippers.
items.d: They flap them underwater to swim after food.

items.t: American flamingos get their pink color from their food.
items.d: Tiny algae and small animals they eat contain pigments, which give their feathers color.

items.t: Bats are the only mammals that can fly by flapping their wings.
items.d: Flying squirrels glide, like a paper plane.

items.t: Dolphins come to the surface for air.
items.d: They breathe through a blowhole on top of the head.

items.t: Male humpback whales sing long songs.
items.d: Their songs repeat groups of sounds and can be heard underwater.

items.t: An elephant uses its trunk to pick up food.
items.d: Its trunk is a long nose that can grab a meal and carry it to its mouth.

items.t: A butterfly starts life as an egg.
items.d: It hatches as a caterpillar, then changes inside a chrysalis before coming out as a butterfly.

items.t: Spiders have eight legs. Insects have six.
items.d: A ladybug may look a bit like a tiny spider, but it has six legs.

items.t: Female sea turtles lay their eggs on land.
items.d: They dig a nest in the sand and cover the eggs before going back to sea.

items.t: A kangaroo joey finishes much of its early growth in a pouch.
items.d: The newborn climbs into its mother's pouch, where it drinks milk.

items.t: Crocodiles lay eggs and can guard their nests.
items.d: A mother crocodile may even carry her hatchlings to water in her mouth.

items.t: Beavers build dams from sticks, mud and other things they find.
items.d: A dam slows a stream and can make a pond behind it.

items.t: An ostrich can run fast, but it cannot fly.
items.d: It has long, strong legs that help it take big steps.

items.t: A male seahorse carries the young before they are born.
items.d: The female puts her eggs into a pouch on the male. The young grow there until he gives birth.

items.t: Polar bears have black skin under their fur.
items.d: Their fur looks white, which helps them blend in with snow and ice.

items.t: A giraffe has seven neck bones, the same number as you.
items.d: Those bones are very long, which lets the neck reach high leaves.

items.t: A blue whale is the biggest animal alive today.
items.d: The biggest ones can grow to about 30 meters long.

items.t: Whales and dolphins move their tails up and down.
items.d: Most fish swim by swinging their tails from side to side.

items.t: A whale mother feeds her baby milk.
items.d: Whales are mammals, so babies drink milk even though they live in the sea.

items.t: Hippos are the closest living relatives of whales.
items.d: Hippos are nearer cousins to whales than to pigs or horses.

items.t: A bat's wing is a hand with very long fingers.
items.d: Skin stretched between the fingers makes the wing.

items.t: Bats are not blind. Many find their way by echoes.
items.d: The bat makes clicks and listens for the sounds that bounce back.

items.t: A camel's hump stores fat, not water.
items.d: The fat is stored energy. A camel still has to drink when it can.

items.t: A dromedary camel has one hump. A Bactrian camel has two.
items.d: Both can live in dry places and travel far between drinks of water.

items.t: A camel can close its nostrils to keep out blowing sand.
items.d: Long eyelashes help keep sand out of its eyes too.

items.t: A koala is not a bear. It lives mostly in trees.
items.d: It eats eucalyptus leaves and sleeps for most of the day.

items.t: A giant panda is a bear that eats mostly bamboo.
items.d: A special wrist bone works like a thumb and helps it grip the stalks.

items.t: The elephant is the largest living animal on land.
items.d: Even a baby elephant can weigh about 100 kilograms.

items.t: An elephant's tusks are very long teeth.
items.d: Elephants use them to dig, to lift things, and to strip bark.

items.t: A rhino's horn is made of keratin, like your hair and nails.
items.d: The horn grows from the skin. It is not made of bone.

items.t: A hippo's eyes, ears, and nose sit on top of its head.
items.d: It can rest almost underwater and still see, hear, and breathe.

items.t: Every zebra has its own stripe pattern.
items.d: No two zebras match exactly, a bit like human fingerprints.

items.t: The cheetah is the fastest animal on land.
items.d: A long tail helps it balance when it turns at high speed.

items.t: Lions live together in family groups called prides.
items.d: Females in the pride rest together and help care for the cubs.

items.t: Polar bears live in the Arctic, not in Antarctica.
items.d: Penguins live in the Southern Hemisphere, so they never meet polar bears in the wild.

items.t: Chimpanzees use sticks as tools.
items.d: A chimp pokes a stick into a mound so termites climb on, then eats them.

items.t: Apes do not have tails. Most monkeys do.
items.d: Gorillas, chimpanzees, orangutans, gibbons, and people are apes.

items.t: A platypus is a mammal that lays eggs.
items.d: Its bill can sense tiny electric signals from animals in the water.

items.t: A kangaroo uses its tail like an extra leg.
items.d: When it walks slowly, it plants the tail and swings both hind legs forward.

items.t: Sloths hang upside down in trees for much of their lives.
items.d: Algae can grow in their fur and give the coat a green tint.

items.t: A sea otter can use a rock as a tool.
items.d: Floating on its back, it opens hard shells against a rock on its chest.

items.t: Sea lions have small ear flaps. True seals do not.
items.d: Sea lions can walk on land by turning their back flippers forward.

items.t: Orcas are dolphins, and they are the biggest ones.
items.d: They live in family groups and keep in touch with clicks and calls.

items.t: Dolphins find things by listening to echoes.
items.d: They make clicks, and the echoes tell them the shape and distance of objects.

items.t: Rabbits are not rodents, even though they look a bit like them.
items.d: Behind their two big front teeth is a second small pair. Rodents do not have those.

items.t: Hummingbirds can hover in place and fly backward.
items.d: Their wings beat so fast that they look like a blur.

items.t: Owls can turn their heads very far, but not all the way around.
items.d: Their eyes stay fixed in place, so the head does the turning.

items.t: An owl's feathers help it fly almost without a sound.
items.d: Soft, fringed edges break up the noise that wings usually make.

items.t: A father emperor penguin keeps the egg on his feet.
items.d: A warm fold of belly skin covers the egg for about two months.

items.t: The ostrich is the largest bird alive today.
items.d: An ostrich egg is also the largest egg of any living bird.

items.t: Ostriches do not bury their heads in the sand.
items.d: A low head usually means the bird is feeding or tending its eggs.

items.t: The bend you see in a flamingo's leg is its ankle.
items.d: The real knee is hidden high up near the body, under the feathers.

items.t: A pelican's pouch is a scoop, not a bag for saving fish.
items.d: It scoops up water and fish, drains the water, and swallows the fish.

items.t: Arctic terns travel from the Arctic to the Antarctic each year.
items.d: That round trip is one of the longest yearly journeys any animal makes.

items.t: Many geese fly together in a V shape.
items.d: Flying just behind and to the side lets a goose save energy.

items.t: Ducks rub oil on their feathers to help stay waterproof.
items.d: The oil comes from a gland near the tail, and the duck spreads it with its bill.

items.t: A parrot can copy sounds, including people's words.
items.d: Being able to copy a word does not mean the bird understands it.

items.t: Many flying birds have hollow bones.
items.d: Air spaces inside the bones keep the skeleton light for flying.

items.t: A puffin can carry several fish in its bill at one time.
items.d: Small spines in the mouth hold the fish while the puffin catches more.

items.t: A kiwi has nostrils on the tip of its beak.
items.d: It smells for worms in the soil. Kiwis live in New Zealand and cannot fly.

items.t: Weaver birds build nests by weaving grass.
items.d: In many kinds, the male weaves a hanging nest and leaves a small doorway.

items.t: A duckling follows its mother soon after it hatches.
items.d: This fast learning is called imprinting. It helps the duckling stay with its parent.

items.t: A male peacock spreads a giant fan of feathers.
items.d: He shows off for the female, called a peahen, who is mostly brown.

items.t: Honeybees dance to tell other bees where flowers are.
items.d: The direction of the dance shows the way, and dancing longer means the flowers are farther.

items.t: Honeybees store honey in six-sided wax cells.
items.d: Those six-sided shapes fit together tightly, with no gaps between them.

items.t: Butterflies can taste with their feet.
items.d: Landing on a leaf tells the butterfly if it is a good place for eggs.

items.t: Tiny scales cover a butterfly's wings.
items.d: The scales make the colors and patterns you see on the wings.

items.t: Ants lay down scent trails for the colony to follow.
items.d: That is how a line of ants can lead straight to a dropped crumb.

items.t: Leafcutter ants farm a fungus for food.
items.d: They carry leaf pieces home, and the fungus grows on the leaves.

items.t: A housefly has just one pair of wings.
items.d: Where a second pair would be, tiny knobs help the fly balance in the air.

items.t: A firefly's light comes from a chemical glow.
items.d: The light stays cool. Flashing fireflies use patterns to signal their own kind.

items.t: Crickets chirp faster on warmer nights.
items.d: Warmer air speeds up their wing muscles, so the chirps come faster.

items.t: Water striders walk on the surface of a pond.
items.d: Hair on their feet keeps them from breaking through the water's surface.

items.t: A ladybug's hard wing covers protect its thin flying wings.
items.d: The covers lift up, and the thin wings unfold when the ladybug flies.

items.t: A dragonfly can beat its front and back wings separately.
items.d: That lets it hover, turn fast, and even fly backward.

items.t: Not every spider builds a web to catch food.
items.d: A jumping spider sneaks close, then leaps onto a small insect.

items.t: A pill bug is related to crabs, not to insects.
items.d: It wears its skeleton outside and can roll into a tight ball.

items.t: A chameleon can look two ways at the same time.
items.d: Each eye swivels on its own, so one may look forward and one back.

items.t: A chameleon's colors change with mood, light, and heat.
items.d: They do not simply copy the color of whatever they are sitting on.

items.t: Many geckos can walk straight up a smooth wall.
items.d: Tiny hairs on their toes grip the wall, even on glass.

items.t: Snakes smell by flicking their tongues.
items.d: The tongue picks up scents and passes them to an organ in the mouth.

items.t: A snake can open its mouth far wider than its head looks.
items.d: The two halves of the lower jaw can spread apart and are joined by stretchy tissue.

items.t: A turtle cannot crawl out of its shell.
items.d: The shell is part of the skeleton, with ribs and backbone inside it.

items.t: A tortoise is a kind of turtle that lives on land.
items.d: Tortoises walk on sturdy feet. Sea turtles swim with flippers.

items.t: Most frogs can breathe through their skin and their lungs.
items.d: Their skin has to stay damp for the oxygen to pass through.

items.t: A tadpole slowly changes into a frog.
items.d: It begins with gills and a tail, then grows legs and lungs.

items.t: Crocodiles are more closely related to birds than to lizards.
items.d: Their family line split from lizards long before it split from the dinosaur line.

items.t: A shark's skeleton is cartilage, not bone.
items.d: Cartilage is tough and bendy, like the material in your outer ear.

items.t: The whale shark is the largest fish in the world.
items.d: It swims with its mouth open and filters tiny food from the water.

items.t: Sharks grow new teeth for their whole lives.
items.d: The teeth sit in rows. A back tooth moves up when a front one falls out.

items.t: Sharks can detect weak electricity in the water.
items.d: Sensors on the snout help them notice animals close by.

items.t: Most fish feel ripples through a line of sensors on each side.
items.d: It helps a fish notice other animals moving nearby, even in cloudy water.

items.t: A seahorse is a fish, and it swims upright.
items.d: It can wrap its curly tail around seaweed to stay in place.

items.t: Clownfish can live safely in a sea anemone's tentacles.
items.d: A special coating on their skin protects them from the stings.

items.t: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
items.d: Two hearts serve the gills. The third heart serves the rest of the body.

items.t: An octopus has no bones in its body.
items.d: That is why it can slip through a hole barely wider than its beak.

items.t: An octopus can change color to blend in with the sea floor.
items.d: It can also raise bumps on its skin to look like rocks or coral.

items.t: A cuttlefish can change color in the blink of an eye.
items.d: Small color sacs in the skin open and close to make new patterns.

items.t: A squid has eight arms and two long tentacles.
items.d: To move quickly, it shoots a jet of water out behind it.

items.t: A sea star is not a fish, even though some call it a starfish.
items.d: It has no backbone and creeps along on many tiny tube feet.

items.t: A jellyfish has no brain, no heart, and no bones.
items.d: A spread-out net of nerves helps it move through the water.

items.t: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called coral polyps.
items.d: Each polyp builds a hard little cup. Over many years, the cups can build a reef.

items.t: A hermit crab makes its home in an empty shell.
items.d: As it grows, it leaves the old shell and moves into a bigger one.

items.t: An adult flounder has both eyes on one side of its head.
items.d: A baby flounder starts with one eye on each side, and one eye moves.

items.t: Barnacles are relatives of crabs, even though they look like shells.
items.d: A barnacle sticks to a rock and waves feathery legs to catch food.

items.t: A scallop has many small eyes around the edge of its shell.
items.d: Those eyes spot changes in light, so the scallop can clap its shell and swim away.

items.t: An oyster can grow a pearl inside its shell.
items.d: If something bothers it inside, the oyster coats that bit with smooth shell.

items.t: Many salmon swim back to the stream where they were born.
items.d: They can follow the smell of their home water on the long trip back from the sea.

items.t: A goldfish can remember things for months.
items.d: The story that a goldfish forgets everything in seconds is not true.

items.t: A pufferfish swallows water to puff itself into a ball.
items.d: The round shape makes the fish much harder to swallow.

items.t: Parrotfish help make the white sand on some coral beaches.
items.d: They crunch coral as they eat, and the ground-up pieces come out later as sand.

items.t: An electric eel is a fish that makes its own electricity.
items.d: Pulses of electricity help it find food in dark, muddy rivers.

items.t: An adult sponge is an animal that usually stays fixed in one spot.
items.d: Water flows through its body, and it strains out tiny bits of food.

items.t: A group of lions is called a pride.
items.d: A pride is a lion family that lives and rests together.

items.t: A lion pride can be as small as 3 or as big as 40.
items.d: One pride might be a few lions. Another might be a whole crowd.

items.t: The lionesses in a pride are usually related.
items.d: They are family, and they share one pride.

items.t: A lion pride usually has no more than two adult males.
items.d: A pride keeps its number of adult males small.

items.t: A male lion's mane can be blond, reddish-brown, or black.
items.d: One lion may have a pale mane, and another a very dark one.

items.t: A lion cub may drink milk from other lionesses as well as its mother.
items.d: In a pride, cubs can have more than one lioness to feed them.

items.t: Lion cubs rely on the pride until they are about a year and a half old.
items.d: They need the adults in the pride through all of that time.

items.t: A lion's roar can be heard about 8 kilometers away.
items.d: That is about 5 miles. A roar can travel a very long way.

items.t: Lionesses usually do the hunting, mostly in the dark.
items.d: Night is the usual time for lionesses to hunt.

items.t: Lions rest or sleep for about 16 to 20 hours each day.
items.d: That leaves about 4 to 8 hours when they are not resting.

items.t: Wild lions live in Africa, plus a small group in India's Gir Forest.
items.d: In Africa, they live from south of the Sahara toward South Africa.

items.t: The tiger is the largest wild cat in the world.
items.d: No other wild cat grows bigger than a tiger.

items.t: No two tigers have exactly the same stripes.
items.d: Each tiger has its own pattern, a bit like a fingerprint.

items.t: Tigers enjoy water and swim well, unlike most cats.
items.d: Most cats stay away from water. A tiger is happy to swim.

items.t: A tiger's tail is about 90 centimeters long and helps it balance.
items.d: That is about 3 feet. The tail helps the tiger stay steady.

items.t: Tiger cubs grow to about four times their size in the first month.
items.d: A new cub gets much bigger before the month is over.

items.t: Some tigers live where it is very cold, in the Siberian region of Russia.
items.d: These tigers have a home in a place that gets very cold.

items.t: Tigers live across Asia, from Russia to Sumatra and Southeast Asia.
items.d: Their range runs from the far north all the way to tropical islands.

items.t: Sumatran tigers are the smallest tigers, and they live only on Sumatra.
items.d: Sumatra is an island in Indonesia. These tigers live nowhere else.

items.t: Tigers usually hunt alone, and they wait until dark.
items.d: A tiger sets out by itself when the day is over.

items.t: A cheetah can sprint at about 97 kilometers per hour.
items.d: That is about 60 miles per hour, and only for a short distance.

items.t: A cheetah can cover about 9 meters in one stride.
