items.t: Sea stars have eyespots at the tips of their arms that sense light.
A jellyfish is about 95 percent water.
Jellyfish have no brain, no blood and no heart.
items.d: A simple net of nerves lets them sense light and smell.

items.t: A jellyfish has just one opening that works as its mouth and its exit.
A jellyfish's middle layer is a thick, bouncy jelly called mesoglea.
A box jellyfish has 24 eyes, and some of them have lenses.
items.d: Its bell is shaped like a box.

items.t: A moon jelly is almost see-through. You can see four horseshoe shapes inside.
A sea urchin chews with an organ called Aristotle's lantern.
A sea urchin walks using lots of bendy tube feet and its spines.
Some sea urchins can live for more than 100 years.
Sponges are animals with no true organs, and their bodies are full of tiny pores.
items.d: Water flows through the pores, and the sponge filters food from it.

items.t: Clownfish live safely among sea anemone tentacles that sting other fish.
items.d: A mucus coating on the clownfish helps it avoid the stings.

items.t: Octopuses have rounded bodies, bulging eyes and eight long arms.
The common octopus has the scientific name Octopus vulgaris.
items.d: Scientific names help people identify the same species worldwide.

items.t: An octopus can swim backward by blasting water through a tube called a siphon.
items.d: The water pushes the octopus in the opposite direction.

items.t: Octopuses explore small openings with their arms while searching for food.
Octopuses can change colour to blend in or communicate with other octopuses.
Octopuses usually live alone in dens made from rocks.
Some octopuses arrange rocks to make a door for their den.
items.d: They can close the rock door behind them after going inside.

items.t: An octopus has three hearts, one main heart and two hearts for its gills.
Octopus blood looks blue because it contains a copper-rich protein.
About two-thirds of an octopus's nerve cells are in the nerve cords of its arms.
items.d: Its arms can perform complex movements and explore nearby objects.

items.t: Octopus arms contain no bones. Their muscles help support and move them.
An octopus has a hard, sharp beak around its mouth.
A giant Pacific octopus can have an arm span of up to about 4.8 metres.
The mimic octopus can copy the appearance of animals such as lionfish and sea snakes.
The veined octopus collects coconut shells and uses them to build a shelter.
Even a large octopus can squeeze through a gap only a little wider than 2.5 cm.
items.d: Its boneless body can fit through surprisingly narrow spaces.

items.t: A squid has eight arms and two longer tentacles around its mouth.
Squid travel by squirting water through a funnel, a method called jet propulsion.
Like octopuses, squid have three hearts.
Squid have colour-changing skin cells called chromatophores.
items.d: They control these cells to help match the colours around them.

items.t: A squid can release a cloud of ink to distract a nearby predator.
A squid's mouth contains a sharp beak made mainly from a material called chitin.
Most squid are no more than about 60 cm long.
Some squid make light and use it as camouflage.
items.d: Light underneath them can help hide their dark outline in the water.

items.t: Squid have giant nerve fibres that can be up to about 1 mm wide.
items.d: These wide fibres carry nerve signals very quickly.

items.t: Squid have advanced eyes that are similar in some ways to vertebrate eyes.
items.d: Vertebrates are animals with backbones, including fish and people.

items.t: A cuttlefish has an internal shell-like part called a cuttlebone.
Cuttlefish have unusual pupils shaped like the letter W.
Cuttlefish can rapidly change their skin colour to match their surroundings.
A cuttlefish has three separate hearts.
Cuttlefish blood has an unusual green-blue colour.
Cuttlefish are typically about 15 to 25 cm long.
Cuttlefish cannot see colour, but they can detect polarized light.
items.d: Polarized light has waves lined up in particular directions.

items.t: Cuttlefish skin has yellow-orange, red and brown-black colour cells.
A nautilus shell is divided into chambers on the inside.
A tube called the siphuncle runs through the chambers of a nautilus shell.
A nautilus can have from 50 to more than 90 tentacles.
Nautiluses have remained relatively unchanged for hundreds of millions of years.
A nautilus may live for more than 20 years.
items.d: That is a long life compared with many octopuses and squid.

items.t: Depending on the species, a nautilus shell is about 10 to 25 cm across.
A nautilus has a simple pinhole eye with no lens.
items.d: Light enters through a small opening instead of passing through a lens.

items.t: Molluscs are the second-largest animal group after arthropods.
items.d: Arthropods include insects, spiders and crabs. Snails, clams, squid and octopuses are all molluscs.

items.t: Molluscs make up about 23% of all named marine organisms.
items.d: They are the largest animal group in the sea by number of named species.

items.t: About 80% of known mollusc species are gastropods, the group containing snails and slugs.
The radula is a tooth-covered feeding ribbon found only in molluscs.
items.d: Many snails use it to scrape and move bits of food.

items.t: A mollusc's basic body plan includes a muscular foot.
items.d: In different molluscs, the foot can help with crawling, digging or gripping.

items.t: Molluscs have a body covering called a mantle, with a cavity used for breathing.
Fossils of snails, clams and squid relatives date back more than 500 million years.
Some molluscs produce pearls and the shiny material called mother of pearl.
Giant clams can grow to about 120 cm across and weigh more than 200 kg.
A peacock mantis shrimp can snap its club at about 83 km/h.
items.d: It reaches that speed from a standstill, with no running start.

items.t: Mantis shrimp eyes have 12 to 16 kinds of light-sensing cells.
items.d: Most humans have only four visual pigments.

items.t: One mantis shrimp eye can judge distance by itself.
items.d: Each eye has trinocular vision, which means it can see depth on its own.

items.t: Some mantis shrimp pairs stay together for up to 20 years.
items.d: Only some species do this, and those pairs can last a very long time.

items.t: Most mantis shrimp grow to about 10 cm long.
items.d: The zebra mantis shrimp is much bigger and can reach 38 cm.

items.t: Shrimp paddle forward, but they zip backward to get away.
items.d: Little paddles called swimmerets push them ahead. A tail flick sends them back.

items.t: Hermit crabs live in empty shells to protect soft bodies.
items.d: Most use old sea snail shells and carry the shell wherever they walk.

items.t: A hermit crab has a soft belly that curls in a spiral.
items.d: It fits the shell's spiral. Related crustaceans have hard bellies.

items.t: Hermit crabs may line up, biggest to smallest, to trade shells.
items.d: A line of up to 20 crabs can swap shells in order, one after another.

items.t: Christmas Island red crabs walk to the sea each year to breed.
items.d: They leave the forest together and head for the coast.

items.t: Some hermit crabs carry a sea anemone on the shell.
items.d: The anemone can help keep other animals away, and it gets a ride.

items.t: The coconut crab is a hermit crab that no longer uses a shell.
items.d: It has given up the shell that other hermit crabs still carry.

items.t: Antarctic krill grow about 6 cm long and weigh up to about 2 grams.
items.d: Six centimetres is about as long as a child's finger.

items.t: A krill swarm can pack 10,000 to 30,000 animals in one cubic metre.
items.d: Picture a box one metre on each side, crowded with tiny krill.

items.t: Antarctic krill mostly eat tiny plants called phytoplankton.
items.d: Phytoplankton are plant plankton that float in the sunny top of the sea.

items.t: Krill are important food for whales and many other animals.
items.d: Many whales, and lots of other sea animals, eat krill.

items.t: Krill glow yellow-green, so they are sometimes called light-shrimp.
items.d: Their light organs can flash for up to 2 or 3 seconds.

items.t: Spiny lobsters sometimes walk across the sea floor in a line.
items.d: They march one behind another in a long single file.

items.t: There are about 7,000 species of true crabs.
items.d: A species is one kind of crab. There are thousands of kinds.

items.t: Many crabs run quickly by scooting sideways.
items.d: On a beach, a crab often zips to the side instead of straight ahead.

items.t: A pea crab is only a few millimetres wide.
items.d: That is smaller than the nail on your little finger.

items.t: A crustacean's hard shell cannot stretch, so it must be shed.
items.d: It sheds the old shell while growing and forms a new, larger one.

items.t: The coconut crab is the largest land arthropod alive.
items.d: It can weigh up to 4.1 kg, about as heavy as a house cat.

items.t: A coconut crab's legs can reach about 90 cm across.
items.d: Ninety centimetres is the same as three 30 cm rulers laid end to end.

items.t: Coconut crabs can climb trees about 10 metres high.
items.d: Ten metres is about as tall as a three-storey building.

items.t: Baby coconut crabs drift at sea for 3 to 4 weeks.
items.d: They drift with other plankton in the ocean during those weeks.

items.t: The American lobster has a crusher claw and a cutter claw.
items.d: The crusher has rounded bumps. The cutter has a sharp inner edge.

items.t: Some American lobsters are blue because of a gene change.
items.d: That change makes them produce extra amounts of one protein.

items.t: Young American lobsters shed their shells about ten times a year.
items.d: Adults slow down and shed only about once every few years.

items.t: Decapod means ten-footed, like crabs, lobsters, and shrimp.
items.d: Crayfish and prawns are decapods too. They all have ten walking legs.

items.t: The Japanese spider crab has the largest leg span of any arthropod.
items.d: From claw to claw it can stretch about 3.7 metres (about 12 feet).

items.t: A Japanese spider crab can weigh up to 19 kg.
items.d: Nineteen kilograms is about as heavy as a full suitcase.

items.t: Japanese spider crabs live from 50 to 600 metres deep.
items.d: Even 50 metres is a deep dive. 600 metres is much deeper.

items.t: A barnacle is a crustacean, related to crabs and lobsters.
items.d: Crabs and lobsters are crustaceans too, even though a barnacle looks like it has a shell.

items.t: A young barnacle glues itself down headfirst.
items.d: It sticks on with a natural cement and then stays in that spot.

items.t: Adult barnacles catch food with long feathery legs called cirri.
items.d: They wave those legs through the water and strain out tiny bits of food.

items.t: Barnacles have existed for at least about 325 million years.
items.d: They go back to a time called the mid-Carboniferous.

items.t: A woodlouse is a crustacean, not an insect.
items.d: People may think it is a bug, but its real group is the crustaceans.

items.t: Count a woodlouse's legs and you will find fourteen.
items.d: They come in seven pairs, and 7 times 2 is 14.

items.t: Woodlice need damp places because they dry out fast.
items.d: They lose water quickly, so they hide where it stays moist.

items.t: Some woodlice can roll their body into a ball.
items.d: Rolled up, they make a small round shape.

items.t: Yeti crabs have hairy claws and live in the deep sea.
items.d: Their homes are hot vents and cold seeps on the deep ocean floor.

items.t: A male fiddler crab has one claw much bigger than the other.
items.d: The big one is the major claw. The smaller one is the minor claw.

items.t: Male fiddler crabs wave their big claw to signal females.
items.d: The crab lifts the claw up, then brings it back down.

items.t: A male fiddler crab can grow back a lost big claw.
items.d: The new claw grows on the same side after he next sheds his shell.

items.t: A pistol shrimp shoots a bubble at about 90 km/h.
items.d: It snaps a huge claw shut, and the snap fires the bubble out.

items.t: A pistol shrimp's snapping claw is bigger than half its body.
items.d: That oversized claw is the one that makes the famous snap.

items.t: Some pistol shrimp share a burrow with a goby fish.
items.d: The goby keeps watch while the two animals share the burrow.

items.t: Decorator crabs stick seaweed and bits onto their bodies.
items.d: Tiny hooked hairs grab and hold the disguise, a bit like a fastener.

items.t: Cleaner shrimp pick parasites off fish at cleaning stations.
items.d: The shrimp gather there and clean parasites off the fish.

items.t: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed plants.
items.d: The poison they take in from milkweed makes them taste bad to hungry animals.

items.t: A monarch butterfly has bright orange wings with black veins, a black border and white dots.
Every fall, millions of monarchs fly about 4,000 km to warm places in Mexico or California.
items.d: That is about 2,500 miles. They come from Canada and the United States.

items.t: Monarchs often return to the same forests each year, and some find the very same trees their ancestors used.
Scientists are still not sure how migrating monarchs know which way to fly.
A monarch caterpillar eats and eats for about two weeks, and it sheds its skin as it grows.
A monarch chrysalis starts green with shiny golden dots. Later it turns see-through.
items.d: After 9 to 15 days, a butterfly comes out.

items.t: Adult butterflies do not grow. They sip nectar from flowers like clover and goldenrod.
A monarch caterpillar can crawl up to 10 metres from its milkweed to find a safe spot to make a chrysalis.
The viceroy butterfly looks a lot like a monarch, but it is a bit smaller.
items.d: Both taste bad to predators, so they share the same warning look.

items.t: A monarch's wings stretch about 9 to 10 centimetres across.
A monarch egg is tiny, only about 1.2 millimetres long.
items.d: A female monarch can lay 300 to 500 eggs over a few weeks.

items.t: A monarch caterpillar grows through five stages, shedding its skin between each one.
In warm summer weather, a monarch can grow from an egg to an adult in as little as 25 days.
Monarch butterflies were raised on the International Space Station in 2009.
Butterflies live on every continent except Antarctica.
A butterfly has four wings, and all of them are covered in tiny scales.
Many blue and green butterfly colours come from tiny wing shapes that bend light, not from paint-like colour.
Butterflies taste with sensors on their feet.
A butterfly's life has four stages: egg, caterpillar, chrysalis and adult.
A butterfly drinks through a long tube called a proboscis. It coils up like a spring when not in use.
Queen Alexandra's birdwing is the largest butterfly in the world.
items.d: Females have wings that stretch more than 25 centimetres across.

items.t: Queen Alexandra's birdwing lives only in the forests of Oro Province in Papua New Guinea.
Butterflies that crowd together on damp mud are mostly males. They are collecting minerals.
items.d: This is called puddling.

items.t: The Melissa Arctic butterfly spends two winters as a caterpillar before it becomes a butterfly.
There are about 160,000 kinds of moth. That is roughly 9 out of every 10 butterflies and moths.
Most moths fly at night, while most butterflies fly in the daytime.
Moths often have feathery antennae. Butterflies have thin antennae with a little ball at the tip.
Adult luna, atlas and cecropia moths have no working mouthparts, so they cannot eat.
When clothes get holes from moths, it is the caterpillars that did it, not the adult moths.
Some moth caterpillars spin a silk cocoon. Others pupate without one.
Butterflies and moths are the second-largest group of insects, with about 180,000 known kinds.
A caterpillar has at most 5 pairs of fleshy prolegs. Tiny hooks on them help it grip.
Most caterpillars shed their skin four or five times as they grow.
Some caterpillars look like bird droppings, so birds do not want to eat them.
A silkworm cocoon is made from one long silk thread, about 300 to 900 metres long.
Silkworms are really moth caterpillars. They mostly eat white mulberry leaves.
Silkworms make their silk in glands near their mouths and wrap themselves in a cocoon.
The atlas moth has wings about 25 to 30 centimetres across. That is among the biggest of any moth.
The tips of an atlas moth's wings look like snake heads, which can scare off hungry animals.
Adult atlas moths cannot eat, and they live only one to two weeks.
The cecropia moth is the largest moth native to North America, with wings up to about 18 centimetres across.
Luna moths have long, twisted tails on their hind wings that may confuse bats hunting at night.
A peppered moth caterpillar can sense a twig's colour with its skin and change its own colour to match.
Painted lady butterflies live on every continent except Antarctica.
A blue morpho's wings are about 12 centimetres across and shimmer bright blue on top.
items.d: The blue changes as you look from different angles.

items.t: The hummingbird hawk-moth hovers at flowers and makes a humming sound, so it looks like a tiny hummingbird.
Glasswing butterflies have clear wings. Tiny pillars on the wings reduce shiny reflections.
Nearly one-third of our food depends on insect pollination, mostly by bees.
Pollinators help produce almonds, raspberries, peaches, avocados and pumpkins.
Some flowers store their pollen inside a part called the anther.
A bumblebee can shake pollen loose by quickly vibrating its chest muscles.
items.d: This special flower-shaking trick is called buzz pollination.

items.t: A bee scrapes loose pollen into its pollen basket before visiting another flower.
Buzz pollination helps about 20,000 plant species.
items.d: Blueberries, cranberries, tomatoes and potatoes are among them.

items.t: Wind pollinates some plants, but many food plants need animal pollinators.
items.d: Many fruits, nuts and vegetables depend on these helpful visitors.

items.t: There are about 250 bumblebee species around the world.
Bumblebees feed their young protein-rich pollen.
Bumblebee species have different tongue lengths for feeding from different flowers.
Most bumblebees nest underground in dry, dark colonies of about 50 to 400 bees.
Only bumblebee queens from a colony survive the winter.
A bumblebee colony's first group of young in spring is made of female workers.
Bumblebee colonies produce new queens and males in late summer.
Bumblebees can fly in cooler weather than other bees.
Bumblebees pollinate flowers from coastal plains to mountains and Arctic tundra.
A bumblebee queen often makes her nest in an old rodent burrow.
A bumblebee queen keeps her eggs warm by making heat with her flight muscles.
Bumblebee workers born early in the season help care for their younger siblings.
Termites build large, complex mounds without architects or foremen in charge.
Termites about a centimetre long can build structures about a metre in size.
A termite mound acts as a ventilation system for a colony deep underground.
Daily changes in outdoor temperature help move air through a termite mound.
Air moving through a termite mound carries smell signals about where to build.
Termite workers can find a hot part of their mound and adjust it to cool it down.
Termite mounds can be tall and narrow or small and compact.
items.d: Their shapes differ depending on the environment.

items.t: Termite mounds may inspire people to design more sustainable buildings.
Termites are not ants. They are a type of cockroach.
Worker termites gather and store food while caring for the young and the nest.
Tiny microbes in termite guts help termites digest wood.
Army ants make temporary shelters from their own bodies instead of permanent nests.
An army ant shelter can be about a metre across and hold hundreds of thousands of ants.
items.d: This living shelter is called a bivouac.

items.t: The army ant queen and her young stay near the centre of the living shelter.
At dawn, an army ant shelter breaks apart into marching columns searching for food.
Most army ant workers are blind and follow chemical scent trails.
An army ant colony can search an area about the size of six tennis courts in one day.
Army ants are not one scientific group. The name covers several ant family lines.
The biggest army ant soldiers can grow up to 12 mm long.
Ants communicate with scents, sounds and touch.
Ants live on every continent except Antarctica.
Leafcutter ants grow fungus for food by giving it freshly cut plant pieces.
Leafcutter ants can carry up to 50 times their own body weight.
Leafcutter ants stop collecting a kind of leaf if it harms their fungus garden.
The European hornet is Britain's largest social wasp.
A European hornet is about 25 to 35 mm long.
Hornets chew wood into pulp to build their nests.
Hornet workers take over the care of the nest.
A hornet queen wakes from hibernation and starts a new nest each spring.
Paper wasps make paper by mixing chewed wood and plant fibres with saliva.
items.d: They use this homemade paper to build their nests.

items.t: Scientists have named about 54,000 kinds of spiders.
items.d: That is a huge family of eight-legged animals living all over the world.

items.t: Every spider has eight legs.
items.d: Insects have six legs, so counting legs is a quick way to tell them apart.

items.t: Most spiders have eight eyes, arranged in four pairs.
items.d: The eyes sit on the top front part of the spider's head area.

items.t: Spider silk is about as strong as nylon.
items.d: Spiders make this strong thread in their own bodies.

items.t: The tiniest spiders are less than half a millimetre long.
items.d: They are very hard to spot.

items.t: Spiders make silk with body parts called spinnerets.
items.d: Their silk can come from up to six types of glands.

items.t: Spiders grow by molting, which means shedding their outer skin.
items.d: The old skin gets too tight, so the spider slips out of it.

items.t: A mother spider can lay up to 3,000 eggs in silk egg sacs.
items.d: The silk sac wraps the eggs like a little blanket.

items.t: Spiders live on every continent except Antarctica.
Spiders have no antennae, but insects do.
items.d: This is another easy way to tell a spider from an insect.

items.t: Nearly all spiders are hunters that eat mostly insects.
items.d: They also eat other spiders.

items.t: Scorpions have lived on Earth for about 430 million years.
items.d: That is long before the dinosaurs.

items.t: Scorpions glow blue-green under ultraviolet light.
items.d: People use a special black light to see the glow in the dark.

items.t: A scorpion has two grasping pincers and a narrow, segmented tail.
Most kinds of scorpions are not a serious danger to people.
items.d: Scientists know of more than 2,500 different kinds.

items.t: A mother scorpion carries her babies on her back.
items.d: They ride there while their new skin hardens.

items.t: Scorpions give birth to live babies instead of laying eggs.
Some scorpions are only about 8.5 mm long.
items.d: The biggest ones are about as long as a school ruler.

items.t: Scorpions mostly hunt insects like grasshoppers and crickets.
Some scorpions can go up to a year without eating.
Scorpions are usually active at night.
items.d: Animals that are active at night are called nocturnal.

items.t: Jumping spiders are the biggest spider family, with about 7,000 kinds.
Jumping spiders see colors and can judge distance with their eyes.
items.d: Their big front eyes help them aim a jump.

items.t: Jumping spiders trail a silk thread when they leap.
items.d: If a jump goes wrong, the spider climbs back up the thread.

items.t: Male jumping spiders can use zigzag dances to attract females.
Most jumping spiders are between 1 and 25 mm long.
Many American tarantulas flick tiny hairs off their bodies to stay safe.
items.d: The hairs can irritate skin.

items.t: Female tarantulas can live 30 to 40 years.
items.d: Some females can live for several decades.

items.t: The goliath birdeater from South America is the biggest tarantula.
Many tarantulas live in burrows in the ground.
Tarantulas have poor eyesight and rely mostly on touch.
items.d: Sensitive hairs on their bodies feel the world around them.

items.t: Tarantulas breathe with two sets of book lungs.
items.d: They use these organs to breathe.

items.t: Ticks are tiny arachnids, not insects.
items.d: Adult ticks are only about 3 to 5 mm long.

items.t: Ticks cannot jump.
Most mites are less than 1 mm long.
items.d: They are arachnids, like spiders.

items.t: Mite fossils from about 410 million years ago have been found.
Most orb-weaver spiders build vertical webs.
items.d: The spider adds a closely spaced sticky spiral to catch food.

items.t: Spiders often eat their own old web.
items.d: They get back some of the energy they used to spin it.

items.t: Some spiders travel by sailing on the wind on silk threads.
Arachnids include spiders, scorpions, ticks and mites.
items.d: They have no antennae and no wings.

items.t: Harvestmen are arachnids, but they are not true spiders.
items.d: They have no silk glands, so they cannot build webs.

items.t: One spider can make up to seven different kinds of silk.
items.d: Each type has its own job, like building webs or wrapping eggs.

items.t: Snakes are reptiles without legs.
items.d: They are a kind of reptile with no legs.

items.t: More than 4,000 snake species are known.
items.d: There are about 4,170 known kinds.

items.t: Snakes cannot blink.
items.d: A clear scale stays closed over each eye like a tiny window.

items.t: A snake's forked tongue collects scent particles.
items.d: It gathers them from the air, ground, or water.

items.t: Snakes have a special scent organ inside their mouths.
items.d: It is called Jacobson's organ, or the vomeronasal organ.

items.t: Snakes can swallow food much larger than their heads.
items.d: A meal can be much bigger than the snake's own head.

items.t: The word for shedding skin is ecdysis.
items.d: It means a snake sheds its old outer layer.

items.t: A snake may shed its skin four or five times each year.
items.d: Shedding replaces the old outer layer with a fresh one.

items.t: Most snake species are not venomous.
items.d: Only some kinds of snakes make venom.

items.t: Snakes live on every continent except Antarctica.
items.d: Antarctica is the only continent without snakes.

items.t: Some islands have no snakes at all.
items.d: Snakes are missing from many islands.

items.t: Most snakes have only one working lung.
items.d: In most snakes, only one lung is used to breathe.

items.t: Snakes use their surroundings to warm or cool their bodies.
items.d: Animals that do this are called ectothermic.

items.t: Snakeskin feels smooth and dry, not slimy.
items.d: Its scales form a dry outer covering.

items.t: Pit vipers can sense infrared heat with special facial pits.
items.d: The pits help them notice warm animals nearby.

items.t: Sea snakes are widespread in the warm Indo-Pacific oceans.
items.d: This huge region stretches across parts of the Indian and Pacific oceans.

items.t: The mainland reticulated python is the longest snake alive today.
items.d: It lives in South and Southeast Asia.

items.t: Reticulated pythons are excellent swimmers.
items.d: They have been seen far out at sea and have reached many islands.

items.t: A female reticulated python can lay 15 to 80 eggs at once.
items.d: A group of eggs laid together is called a clutch.

items.t: A reticulated python has an irregular diamond pattern.
items.d: The pattern acts as camouflage by breaking up the snake's outline.

items.t: The green anaconda is one of the world's heaviest and longest snakes.
items.d: It is the largest snake native to the Americas.

items.t: Female green anacondas are usually much larger than males.
items.d: Males average about 3 metres long.

items.t: Green anacondas give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
items.d: Their eggs develop inside the mother's body.

items.t: A green anaconda's eyes and nostrils sit on top of its head.
items.d: This placement helps it see and breathe while mostly underwater.

items.t: Green anacondas prefer shallow, slow-moving water.
items.d: They live in tropical rainforests.

items.t: Vipers have long fangs that fold back on hinges.
items.d: The hinged fangs fit inside the mouth when they are not being used.

items.t: Most vipers give birth to live young.
items.d: Their eggs stay and develop inside the mother's body.

items.t: A rattlesnake's rattle is made of hollow, linked pieces of keratin.
items.d: Keratin is also found in human hair and nails.

items.t: A rattlesnake adds a rattle segment whenever it sheds its skin.
items.d: Each time the skin is shed, a new piece is added.

items.t: A rattlesnake shakes its rattle as a warning.
items.d: The sound tells other animals to give it space.

items.t: Rattlesnakes live naturally only in the Americas.
items.d: Their range stretches from southern Canada to central Argentina.

items.t: An eastern diamondback rattlesnake can grow to about 2.4 metres.
items.d: It is the largest kind of rattlesnake.

items.t: The black mamba is named for the black inside of its mouth.
items.d: Its skin is not what gives this snake its name.

items.t: A black mamba can move at about 16 kilometres per hour for a short distance.
items.d: That is a quick burst, not a speed it keeps all day.

items.t: The black mamba is the second-longest venomous snake.
items.d: Only the king cobra grows longer among venomous snakes.

items.t: The word mamba comes from the Zulu word imamba.
items.d: Zulu is a language spoken in southern Africa.

items.t: The inland taipan is usually shy and keeps to itself.
items.d: It lives in remote, partly dry areas of central Australia.

items.t: An inland taipan becomes darker in winter and paler in summer.
items.d: Its body color changes with the seasons.

items.t: Titanoboa was an extinct snake about 12.8 metres long.
items.d: It grew up to about 12.8 metres (42 feet).

items.t: Titanoboa lived about 60 to 58 million years ago.
items.d: That is about 60 to 58 million years before today.

items.t: Titanoboa fossils were found in coal mines in Colombia.
items.d: Colombia is a country in South America.

items.t: The Barbados threadsnake is about 10 centimetres long.
items.d: It is about as thin as spaghetti and is one of the smallest snakes.

items.t: Barbados threadsnakes mainly eat termites and ant larvae.
items.d: Their tiny size lets them eat very small food.

items.t: A Barbados threadsnake lays one large egg at a time.
items.d: One egg is a very small clutch compared with many other snakes.

items.t: The king cobra is the world's longest venomous snake.
items.d: No other venomous snake grows longer.

items.t: The king cobra's scientific name means snake-eater.
items.d: Ophiophagus describes its habit of mainly hunting other snakes.

items.t: A female king cobra builds a leaf-litter nest and guards her eggs.
items.d: The king cobra is the only snake known to build an above-ground egg nest.

items.t: Flying snakes flatten their bodies into wing-like shapes.
items.d: They spread their ribs to help glide between trees.

items.t: Flying snakes can glide as far as 100 metres.
items.d: They glide through the forests and jungles where they live.

items.t: A flying snake wiggles from side to side while gliding.
items.d: Its body keeps making snake-like waves in the air.

items.t: A green sea turtle can be about 1.5 meters long.
items.d: It can weigh up to about 320 kg. That is a very big turtle!

items.t: Green sea turtles nest on the coasts of more than 80 countries.
items.d: That is a lot of beaches all around the warm parts of our world.

items.t: A mother green sea turtle returns to nest where she was born.
items.d: She may swim a long way to find that exact spot again.

items.t: A green sea turtle lays about 115 eggs in one nest and covers them with sand.
items.d: The sand keeps the eggs hidden and snug.

items.t: Baby sea turtles break out of their eggs using a tiny egg tooth.
items.d: The egg tooth helps them crack the shell after about two months.

items.t: Young green sea turtles float at sea and eat plankton. Older ones move to shallow bays.
items.d: Plankton is a mix of tiny living things drifting in the water.

items.t: A green sea turtle can rest underwater for up to five hours.
items.d: That is up to 300 minutes underwater!

items.t: Some green sea turtles have swum more than 2,600 km between feeding and nesting places.
items.d: That is a very long trip for an animal with flippers.

items.t: Green sea turtles are named for the greenish color of their fat, not their shell.
items.d: Scientists think the green color comes from all the plants they eat.

items.t: The leatherback is the biggest turtle on Earth.
items.d: It can reach about 2 meters long and weigh about 900 kg.

items.t: A leatherback's shell is leathery and feels almost rubbery.
items.d: Other sea turtles have hard shells, but not the leatherback.

items.t: Leatherback turtle ancestors lived about 100 million years ago.
items.d: That was during the age of the dinosaurs.

items.t: Leatherbacks eat mostly jellyfish.
items.d: They are big animals that eat very soft, wobbly food.

items.t: Only female leatherbacks come onto land, and only to lay eggs.
items.d: Males stay in the ocean their whole lives.

items.t: Baby sea turtles can get confused by house lights near the beach.
items.d: They may head toward the lights instead of the sea.

items.t: Galapagos tortoises can live to be over a hundred years old.
items.d: Some could have been alive when your great-grandparents were kids.

items.t: Galapagos tortoises eat grasses, cacti, fruits and leaves.
items.d: They are plant-eaters.

items.t: A Galapagos tortoise can be about 1.8 meters long and weigh about 260 kg.
items.d: That is a huge tortoise!

items.t: On hot, dry islands, tortoises have saddle-shaped shells with a high notch above the neck.
items.d: The notch lets them stretch their necks up to reach taller plants.

items.t: The Galapagos Islands are named after tortoises.
items.d: Galapago is the Spanish word for tortoise.

items.t: Baby Galapagos tortoises hatch after four to eight months and care for themselves right away.
items.d: They have no parents to look after them.

items.t: Loggerhead turtles are named for their big head.
items.d: Their head looks like a big log.

items.t: A loggerhead has powerful jaws that can crush conchs and horseshoe crabs.
items.d: Those are animals with hard shells.

items.t: Loggerhead turtles can live more than 50 years in the wild.
items.d: That is a very long life for a sea animal.

items.t: Loggerhead babies wait just under the sand until night before heading to the sea.
items.d: At nightfall, they crawl out and head toward the ocean.

items.t: Green turtles are the only sea turtles that eat mostly plants as adults.
items.d: They graze on algae and seagrasses.

items.t: The hawksbill turtle is named for its beak-like mouth.
items.d: The pointy mouth looks like the beak of a hawk.

items.t: In many places, hawksbill turtles prefer to eat sponges.
items.d: Sponges are simple sea animals that live on rocks and reefs.

items.t: Kemp's ridley is the smallest sea turtle in the world.
items.d: It is still a big animal, but small next to its giant cousins.

items.t: Kemp's ridley is the only sea turtle that routinely nests during the day.
items.d: Daytime nesting is unusual among sea turtles.

items.t: Young Kemp's ridleys drift with floating Sargassum seaweed.
items.d: The seaweed gives them a place to hide and food to eat.

items.t: Olive ridley turtles are named for the olive green color of their heart-shaped shell.
items.d: Their shell looks a bit like a heart.

items.t: Olive ridleys nest in huge groups called arribadas.
items.d: Thousands of turtles can arrive on one beach at the same time.

items.t: Leatherbacks can dive about 1,200 meters deep, deeper than any other turtle.
items.d: That is more than a kilometer straight down!

items.t: Some leatherbacks swim over 16,000 km a year between nesting and feeding places.
items.d: That is a very long trip for a turtle.

items.t: A turtle's shell has a domed top called a carapace and a flatter bottom called a plastron.
items.d: The top shell is joined to the turtle's backbone and ribs.

items.t: Turtles have no teeth. They have a hard beak instead.
items.d: Their beaks are made of a tough material called keratin.

items.t: All turtles lay their eggs on land, even sea turtles.
items.d: Even sea turtles leave the water to lay their eggs on land.

items.t: In many turtles, nest temperature decides if babies are boys or girls.
items.d: The temperature around the eggs affects whether hatchlings are male or female.

items.t: In Britain, land turtles are called tortoises and freshwater turtles are called terrapins.
items.d: The word turtle there usually means a sea turtle.

items.t: There are seven kinds of sea turtle living in the world today.
items.d: They include green, leatherback, loggerhead, hawksbill, and flatback turtles.

items.t: Sea turtles cry salty tears.
items.d: A special gland near the eye gets rid of extra salt from the sea.

items.t: Aldabra Atoll in the Seychelles is home to about 180,000 giant tortoises.
items.d: That is the biggest group of giant tortoises in the world.

items.t: Aldabra giant tortoises do a job in nature a bit like elephants.
items.d: Their role in the island ecosystem is similar to an elephant's role.

items.t: Tortoises are land turtles, and they generally eat plants.
items.d: Most kinds can live 80 to 150 years.

items.t: The alligator snapping turtle is the biggest freshwater turtle in North America.
items.d: It lives mainly in freshwater in the southeastern United States.

items.t: An alligator snapping turtle wiggles a worm-shaped tongue tip to trick fish.
items.d: Fish swim in to check out the fake worm, and the turtle snaps its mouth shut.

items.t: Desert tortoises spend at least 95 percent of their lives in burrows.
items.d: That means almost all their time is spent underground.

items.t: The pig-nosed turtle has a snout like a pig and flippers like a sea turtle.
items.d: It lives in freshwater rivers in northern Australia and New Guinea.

items.t: A peregrine falcon can dive at over 320 km/h (about 200 mph).
items.d: This fast dive is called a stoop.

items.t: A peregrine can still see separate flashes at about 129 a second.
items.d: Scientists call this flicker fusion. Fast flashes do not blur together.

items.t: Peregrine falcons lay their eggs in a simple scrape.
items.d: They usually skip a stick nest and use a cliff-edge scrape.

items.t: Peregrine falcons eat almost only medium-sized birds.
items.d: Birds of that size make up nearly their whole diet.

items.t: Female peregrines can be up to 30 percent larger than males.
items.d: In a pair, the female is the bigger bird.

items.t: The bald eagle builds the largest nest of any North American bird.
items.d: No other bird in North America makes a bigger nest.

items.t: An adult bald eagle's wingspan is about 1.8 to 2.3 metres.
items.d: That is about 5 feet 11 inches to 7 feet 7 inches across.

items.t: Fish make up most of a bald eagle's diet.
items.d: In every part of their range, fish are the main food.

items.t: Young bald eagles do not have a white head yet.
items.d: They stay dark brown with white streaks until about age five.

items.t: The bald eagle is the national bird of the United States.
items.d: It is a national symbol of the United States too.

items.t: A great horned owl's 'horns' are just tufts of feathers.
items.d: Those tufts are not real horns, and they are not ears.

items.t: A great horned owl's call is a low, loud set of hoots.
items.d: The hoots sound like ho-ho-hoo hoo hoo.

items.t: No raptor in the Americas eats a wider mix of prey.
items.d: The great horned owl's diet includes more kinds of animals than other raptors there.

items.t: Barn owls have faces shaped like a heart.
items.d: That heart-shaped face makes the barn owl easy to spot.

items.t: The barn owl group is the most widespread group of owls.
items.d: No other owl genus is spread so widely around the world.

items.t: About 99 percent of an osprey's diet is fish.
items.d: Fish make up nearly the whole menu, about 99 of every 100 meals.

items.t: An osprey plunges feet first into the water to catch fish.
items.d: Its toes lead the way into the water.

items.t: An osprey can flip its outer toes for a stronger grip.
items.d: Then it holds a fish with two toes forward and two toes back.

items.t: Ospreys can close their nostrils when they dive.
items.d: Closing them helps keep water out during the plunge.

items.t: Osprey feathers are dense and oily.
items.d: The oil helps keep the feathers from soaking up water.

items.t: Ospreys live on every continent except Antarctica.
items.d: Look in temperate and tropical lands, not on the Antarctic ice.

items.t: Ospreys that nest in North America spend winter in South America.
items.d: North American nesters travel there for the colder months.

items.t: An Andean condor's wings can span about 3.3 metres.
items.d: The maximum reach is about 10 feet 10 inches.

items.t: Andean condors stay up by riding rising warm air.
items.d: These rising currents are called thermals, so they flap much less.

items.t: Andean condors are among the longest-living birds.
items.d: Some of them live for more than 70 years.

items.t: An Andean condor's head and neck are almost featherless.
items.d: Bare skin covers most of the head and the long neck.

items.t: Harpy eagles have the largest talons of any living eagle.
items.d: Their toes and claws are bigger than those of other eagles alive now.

items.t: In some studies, sloths make up most of a harpy eagle's diet.
items.d: Where scientists have checked, sloths were the main food.

items.t: Harpy eagles live in the top layer of tropical rainforest.
items.d: They use the upper canopy of warm lowland forest.

items.t: A harpy pair usually raises one chick every 2 to 3 years.
items.d: They often wait two or three years before raising another chick.

items.t: A secretarybird's legs are unusually long for its weight.
items.d: The legs are nearly twice as long as other ground birds that weigh the same.

items.t: Only one animal with a backbone is known to eat mostly bone: the bearded vulture.
items.d: About 70 to 90 percent of its food is bone.

items.t: Bearded vultures drop bones onto rocks to break them.
items.d: Smaller pieces let them reach the soft marrow inside.

items.t: A bearded vulture digests a large bone in about 24 hours.
items.d: A big bone is broken down inside the bird in about one day.

items.t: A bearded vulture's orange color comes from iron-rich mud.
items.d: It gets the stain by dust-bathing or rubbing the mud on its body.

items.t: Turkey vultures find their food by smell.
items.d: Sniffing out a meal is uncommon among birds.

items.t: An adult turkey vulture has a small red head with few feathers.
items.d: The head is small for the body and can look almost bare.

items.t: The Philippine eagle is the national bird of the Philippines.
items.d: The country has officially declared it the national bird.

items.t: The Philippine eagle wears a shaggy, mane-like crest.
items.d: Long brown feathers form that mane around its head.

items.t: The California condor has one of the widest wingspans of any North American bird.
items.d: Its wings stretch about 3 metres from tip to tip.

items.t: Snowy owls are well known on the open Arctic tundra.
items.d: They are one of the best known birds of that wide northern land.

items.t: The snowy owl is the only owl with mainly white feathers.
items.d: Its plumage is mostly white, unlike other owls.

items.t: Snowy owls are often active during the day.
items.d: You may see them out in daylight, especially in summer.

items.t: A snowy owl's toes are covered in thick white feathers.
items.d: Those toes are extremely thickly feathered and white.

items.t: Snowy owl nesting depends on how many lemmings there are.
items.d: When lemmings are scarce or plentiful, owl breeding changes with them.

items.t: There are more than 200 species of owls.
items.d: Most are active at night and spend their time alone.

items.t: An owl's eyes are fixed in place and cannot move.
items.d: They sit in stiff tubes, so the owl turns its head to look around.

items.t: An owl can turn its head about 270 degrees.
items.d: That wide turn lets the owl look around behind its body.

items.t: Some owls have ears placed at different heights on the head.
items.d: The uneven ears help the owl pinpoint where a sound is coming from.

items.t: Special wing feathers let owls fly almost silently.
items.d: Those feathers let the owl move through the air with almost no sound.

items.t: American robin eggs are a bright blue-green color.
items.d: Each nest usually holds three to five of these pretty eggs.

items.t: American robins often run across lawns looking for earthworms.
items.d: They pick up worms and other food from the ground.

items.t: The American robin sings a cheery, carol-like song.
items.d: It is one of the birds you hear early in the morning.

items.t: A robin starts its nest with coarse grass, twigs, paper and feathers.
items.d: These materials form the base of the nest.

items.t: The American robin was named after the European robin.
items.d: Both birds have a reddish-orange chest.

items.t: The American robin is the most common landbird in North America.
items.d: That means there are more of them than almost any other land bird.

items.t: Connecticut, Michigan and Wisconsin all chose the American robin as their state bird.
The northern mockingbird is great at copying sounds.
items.d: Its scientific name even refers to this talent.

items.t: One northern mockingbird can know about 43 to 203 different song types.
items.d: That is a huge playlist for one small bird!

items.t: Mockingbirds copy more than birds. They can imitate cats, dogs, frogs and crickets.
Mockingbirds build their nests about 1 to 3 metres above the ground.
items.d: That ranges from about waist height to above a door.

items.t: Northern mockingbirds boldly guard their nests and the area around them.
items.d: They will chase away other birds and animals.

items.t: Starling flocks that swirl together in the sky at sunset are called murmurations.
A wild starling was once seen copying a sound it had heard only one time.
items.d: Starlings are very good mimics.

items.t: Starling feathers look black, but they shine with purple and green.
items.d: This shimmering effect is called iridescence.

items.t: Starlings can fly at about 60 to 80 km per hour.
Starlings poke their bills into the ground and open them to find hidden food.
A blue jay's feathers look blue because of how light bounces inside them.
items.d: There is no blue pigment. It is a trick of light.

items.t: Blue jays hide acorns so they can eat them later.
Blue jays can copy the cries of hawks very well.
A blue jay builds an open cup-shaped nest in the branches of a tree.
Thousands of blue jays have been seen migrating together in flocks.
A blue jay lifts its head crest all the way up when it is excited or aggressive.
Blue jays especially love to eat peanuts in the shell.
The common raven is the heaviest of all the perching birds.
items.d: Perching birds are also called songbirds.

items.t: Ravens can copy sounds around them, even human speech.
Young ravens are among the most playful birds.
A raven has one of the biggest brains of any bird.
Ravens have a long, wedge-shaped tail, which helps tell them from crows.
Ravens make 15 to 30 different kinds of calls.
Ravens are one of the few wild animals that make their own toys.
Eurasian magpies can recognize themselves in a mirror.
items.d: Very few animals can do this.

items.t: More than half of a magpie's body length is its tail.
Magpies build huge nests that are easy to spot in trees when the leaves fall.
Male house sparrows have bold markings on the head. Females are mostly buff-brown.
House sparrows love to take dust baths or water baths, often in groups.
House sparrows often nest in the eaves and cracks of houses.
The house sparrow is the most widely spread wild bird on the planet.
House sparrows mostly eat the seeds of cereal plants and weeds.
A house sparrow is only about 16 cm long.
items.d: That is about as long as a school ruler.

items.t: Both male and female European robins have an orange breast.
Male European robins guard their territory fiercely.
European robins sometimes sing at night, especially near bright street lights.
Robins have been on Christmas cards for over 150 years.
Young European robins are spotted brown and white. They have no red breast yet.
Some robins from Scandinavia and Russia fly to Britain and western Europe for winter.
American crows can remember and recognize people by how they look.
Young American crows often stay with their family to help raise the new chicks.
American crows can gather at night in huge groups, sometimes thousands strong.
Male American goldfinches are bright yellow in summer and olive in winter.
Parrots have two toes pointing forward and two pointing backward on each foot.
items.d: That gives every parrot foot four toes arranged in two pairs.

items.t: There are about 410 species of parrot.
items.d: They are grouped into four families and 101 groups called genera.

items.t: Parrots are among the most intelligent birds.
Many parrots can copy human speech and other sounds.
items.d: Their sound copying is called imitation or mimicry.

items.t: Most parrots mainly eat seeds, nuts, and fruit.
Almost all parrots make their nests in hollow spaces inside trees.
A climbing parrot can use its strong beak like a third foot.
items.d: Its two feet and beak can all help it hold on.

items.t: Cockatoos can raise and lower the crest of feathers on their heads.
items.d: A crest is a group of feathers that stands above the head.

items.t: The hyacinth macaw is the longest parrot, at about 1 metre long.
A large toucan's bill can be more than half as long as its body.
A toucan's huge bill is surprisingly light.
items.d: Inside, bone supports hold a light foam called keratin.

items.t: A toucan can use its bill to help control its body temperature.
Toucans eat mostly fruit.
Toucans are social birds that usually live in groups.
A toucan's tongue can grow up to 15 centimetres long.
A sleeping toucan flips its tail forward until it touches its head.
Hummingbirds are named for the humming sound made by their beating wings.
One hummingbird species beats its wings 99 times each second while hovering.
items.d: That is almost 100 beats during every second of hovering.

items.t: Hummingbirds can hover in one place in the air.
items.d: Hovering means staying nearly still while flying.

items.t: Hummingbirds can enter a deep sleep called torpor to save energy.
Wild hummingbirds live only in the Americas.
Hummingbirds are specially suited to drinking nectar from flowers.
items.d: Nectar is a sweet liquid made by flowers.

items.t: A hummingbird's cup-shaped nest is about 3.8 centimetres wide.
Hummingbirds lay the smallest eggs of any birds.
Rufous hummingbirds migrate about 6,300 kilometres between Alaska and Mexico.
items.d: They make this long journey twice each year.

items.t: The bee hummingbird is the smallest living bird.
Bee hummingbirds live naturally only in Cuba.
A female bee hummingbird weighs only about 2.6 grams.
A bee hummingbird's egg is about the size of a coffee bean.
A bee hummingbird beats its wings about 80 to 200 times per second.
A bee hummingbird builds a cup-shaped nest only about 2.5 centimetres wide.
A male bee hummingbird has a bright red throat.
items.d: The top of his head is green.

items.t: Many hornbills have a hollow bump called a casque on top of the bill.
A hornbill's first two neck bones are fused together.
items.d: This helps support the bird's heavy bill.

items.t: Hornbills have large eyelashes that act like a sunshade.
There are about 62 living species of hornbill.
The kingfisher family contains 118 species.
items.d: Scientists divide them into three smaller groups called subfamilies.

items.t: Kingfishers have long, dagger-shaped bills.
Kingfishers have excellent eyesight.
items.d: They watch carefully from a perch before swooping down toward food.

items.t: Kingfisher eggs are always white.
The laughing kookaburra is a kingfisher with a call that sounds like laughter.
Most birds-of-paradise live on New Guinea.
items.d: Others live in eastern Australia and the Maluku Islands.

items.t: The bird-of-paradise family contains 44 species.
items.d: Scientists place them in 17 groups called genera.

items.t: Many male birds-of-paradise grow very long, fancy feathers.
items.d: The special feathers may extend from the head, beak, wings, or tail.

items.t: Some male birds-of-paradise perform carefully ordered courtship dances.
Birds-of-paradise build nests from leaves, ferns, and curling vine parts.
Male peafowl are called peacocks, while females are called peahens.
Peafowl chicks can follow their mother soon after they hatch.
Indian peafowl can fly despite their large size.
The kakapo is the world's only flightless parrot.
Flamingos are pink because of the tiny shrimp-like animals they eat.
items.d: Their food gives their feathers the pink colour.

items.t: Baby flamingos are born grey and white. They take about two years to turn pink.
items.d: Their pink colour grows in slowly as they eat.

items.t: A flamingo's beak works like a strainer. It filters food out of the water.
items.d: The water is pushed out and the food stays inside.

items.t: Flamingos stir up the muddy bottom with their webbed feet to find food.
items.d: Stirring the mud helps bring food within reach.

items.t: Flamingos feed in big groups. There is safety in numbers while their heads are down.
items.d: Many eyes can spot trouble while others eat.

items.t: Flamingos in zoos can turn pale unless their food has the right supplements.
items.d: Their diet must contain the pigments that colour their feathers.

items.t: Flamingo parents take turns sitting on their single egg.
items.d: Each flamingo pair looks after just one egg at a time.

items.t: Puffins flap their wings very fast, several times every second, to fly.
items.d: Their small wings work hard to keep them in the air.

items.t: Puffins use their wings to swim underwater. They can stay under for up to about a minute.
items.d: They fly through the water to catch food.

items.t: Puffins are good diggers. They dig burrows to make their nests.
items.d: They also fix up their burrows when needed.

items.t: A puffin's bill is brightly coloured. The half near the tip is orange-red.
items.d: The orange-red part is near the end of the bill.

items.t: A puffin pair has just one white egg each year.
items.d: Puffins have a small clutch, which means they have very few eggs at once.

items.t: A baby puffin is called a puffling.
items.d: Puffins are long-lived birds that raise few chicks.

items.t: The Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back again every year.
items.d: That is one of the longest journeys of any animal.

items.t: One Arctic tern was tracked flying about 96,000 km in just ten months.
items.d: That is more than twice around the Earth.

items.t: Arctic terns see two summers every year, one in the north and one in the south.
items.d: They follow the sunshine across the world.

items.t: Many Arctic terns live for 15 to 30 years.
items.d: They make their huge trip again and again.

items.t: A mute swan is about 140 to 160 cm long. That is as long as a tall child.
items.d: It is one of the heaviest flying birds.

items.t: Baby swans, called cygnets, grow fast. In about three months they are close to adult size.
items.d: Cygnets can dive when they are about three weeks old.

items.t: Mute swans pair up with one partner and often reuse the same nest each year.
items.d: They are known as monogamous birds.

items.t: A pelican has a huge throat pouch that it uses to catch fish.
items.d: The pouch works a bit like a fishing net.

items.t: Pelicans can work together as a team to catch fish.
items.d: Teamwork helps them gather the fish.

items.t: The Dalmatian pelican is believed to be the largest pelican.
items.d: Its wings can stretch up to 3 metres across.

items.t: Brown pelicans plunge head-first into the water to catch fish.
items.d: They dive from the air to grab their meal.

items.t: Domestic pigeons come from wild rock doves.
items.d: Some are used as homing pigeons, and some are kept as pets.

items.t: Pigeon parents feed their babies a special food called crop milk.
items.d: Both the mother and father make it.

items.t: Pigeons were once used to carry messages, in peace and in war.
items.d: They are called carrier or homing pigeons.

items.t: Pigeons can sip water without tipping their heads back, unlike most birds.
items.d: They just dip their bills in and drink.

items.t: Chickens come mainly from a wild bird called the red junglefowl.
items.d: People tamed chickens about 8,000 years ago.

items.t: Hens bred for eggs can lay over 300 eggs in a year.
items.d: That is nearly one egg every day.

items.t: The wandering albatross has the longest wings of any living bird, up to 3.7 metres across.
items.d: Its wingspan can be wider than a small car is long.

items.t: Albatrosses can glide for hours without flapping their wings.
items.d: They ride the wind over the ocean.

items.t: Albatrosses spend most of their lives over the sea. They land only to nest and feed.
items.d: They are true ocean wanderers.

items.t: Albatrosses can live for over 50 years.
items.d: An albatross may spend many decades travelling over the ocean.

items.t: Albatross parents take turns on the nest while the other goes to find food.
items.d: Sharing the work helps the chick grow.

items.t: A grey heron can stand perfectly still in shallow water while it hunts.
items.d: It waits for a fish to swim close.

items.t: A grey heron can stand up to about 1 metre tall.
items.d: Its long legs help it wade.

items.t: Grey herons nest together in groups called heronries.
items.d: Many nests can be in the same trees.

items.t: A flying grey heron folds its long neck back into an S shape.
items.d: Its long neck is pulled back while it flies.

items.t: Sandhill cranes make a loud trumpeting call that can be heard from far away.
items.d: Their calls carry across wide open wetlands.

items.t: The mallard is the main ancestor of most domestic duck breeds.
items.d: Many tame ducks come from this wild duck.

items.t: Mallard ducklings can swim as soon as they hatch.
items.d: They are ready for the water almost right away.

items.t: A male mallard has a green head. The female is mostly speckled brown.
items.d: Males and females look quite different.

items.t: A female mallard makes the classic deep quack linked with ducks.
items.d: Her quack is deeper than the male mallard's call.

items.t: Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas.
items.d: They are among the highest-flying birds in the world.

items.t: Canada geese fly in a V-shaped formation.
items.d: The birds form a clear V as they travel through the sky.

items.t: Canada goose goslings can walk and swim as soon as they hatch.
items.d: They are ready to follow their parents right away.

items.t: Most Canada goose pairs stay together for life.
items.d: They raise their families together.

items.t: Tardigrades have survived exposure to outer space.
items.d: They survived being exposed to space.

items.t: Dried-out tardigrades can briefly survive from about -272°C to 149°C.
items.d: Drying out helps them endure extreme temperatures for short periods.

items.t: Tardigrades can pause their metabolism in a state called cryptobiosis.
items.d: Their body activity becomes extremely low until conditions improve.

items.t: A grown tardigrade is usually only about 0.5 millimetres long.
items.d: It is much smaller than a grain of rice.

items.t: Tardigrades live from mountaintops and deep seas to rainforests and Antarctica.
items.d: These tiny animals can be found in very different habitats.

items.t: The ocean's deepest known place is about 10,935 metres deep.
items.d: It is called Challenger Deep and lies in the Mariana Trench.

items.t: Animals that make their own light live from the ocean surface to the seafloor.
items.d: This natural glow is called bioluminescence.

items.t: Sea animals use natural light to communicate, find food, or escape.
items.d: That light can warn a predator, lure food, or send a signal.

items.t: A cheetah's highest reliably reported running speed is about 104 km/h.
items.d: Its body is built for very fast sprints.

items.t: A cheetah can speed from 0 to 97 km/h in less than three seconds.
items.d: That quick burst helps it move across open grassland.

items.t: In eastern and southern Africa, cheetahs live mostly in savannas.
items.d: The Serengeti and Kalahari are two well-known cheetah habitats.

items.t: The blue whale is the largest animal known ever to have existed.
items.d: It is larger than any known dinosaur.

items.t: The longest scientifically measured blue whale was about 30 metres long.
items.d: The longest confirmed lengths are about 29.9 to 30.5 metres.

items.t: A newborn blue whale is already about 6 to 7 metres long.
items.d: Even a blue whale calf is longer than many cars.

items.t: A blue whale's heart can weigh about 180 kilograms.
items.d: It is the largest heart known in any animal.

items.t: An average blue whale eats about 1,100 kilograms of krill each day.
items.d: Krill are small, shrimp-like sea animals.

items.t: Blue whale calls can reach about 188 decibels.
items.d: They are among the loudest sounds made by any animal.

items.t: Some Arctic terns migrate about 70,000 kilometres each year.
items.d: They fly between Arctic and Antarctic regions, the longest known animal migration.

items.t: Many Arctic terns live for about 15 to 30 years.
items.d: One recorded Arctic tern reached 31 years old.

items.t: Greenland sharks have the longest known lifespan of any animal with a backbone.
items.d: The oldest estimates reach several hundred years.

items.t: Greenland sharks grow only about 0.5 to 1 centimetre each year.
items.d: Their growth is extremely slow, just like their long lives.

items.t: Greenland sharks prefer icy water from about -1°C to 7°C.
items.d: They prefer cold water from just below freezing to about 7°C.

items.t: Male emperor penguins balance an egg on their feet to keep it warm.
items.d: The male alone cares for the egg for about 65 to 75 days.

items.t: Emperor penguins are the only penguins that breed during the Antarctic winter.
items.d: They breed in the extremely cold Antarctic winter.

items.t: One emperor penguin was recorded diving about 535 metres deep.
items.d: That is more than half a kilometre beneath the water's surface.

items.t: Emperor penguins can stay underwater for about 20 minutes while hunting.
items.d: These long dives let them hunt for food.

items.t: A very thirsty camel can drink about 140 litres of water at once.
items.d: That would fill roughly 140 one-litre bottles.

items.t: Camels have long eyelashes and nostrils that can close.
items.d: These features help keep blowing desert sand out.

items.t: A camel's spreading toes help it grip soft ground such as sand.
items.d: Widening toes give extra grip on soft ground such as sand.

items.t: Camels can lose about 25% of their body weight as water.
items.d: Most mammals can tolerate only about 12% to 14% water loss.

items.t: A fennec fox's huge ears release heat and detect animals underground.
items.d: Both jobs are useful in its hot desert home.

items.t: The fennec fox is the smallest species in the dog family.
items.d: It lives in the deserts of North Africa.

items.t: Fennec foxes are mostly active at night.
items.d: Nighttime is cooler than daytime in their desert habitat.

items.t: In firmer soil, a fennec fox den can have up to 15 entrances.
items.d: A den in firmer soil can cover up to 120 square metres.

items.t: Chameleons change colour mainly for signals and reactions to conditions.
items.d: Temperature and social messages can both affect their colours.

items.t: A chameleon's tongue can strike in as little as 0.07 seconds.
items.d: The tongue is often 1.5 to 2 times as long as the chameleon's body.

items.t: A chameleon can move and focus each eye independently.
items.d: It can watch two different things at the same time.

items.t: Nearly all chameleons have tails that can grip branches.
items.d: This grasping tail helps a chameleon hold on while climbing.

items.t: Green algae grow in sloth fur and help hide sloths among the trees.
items.d: The greenish coat acts as camouflage in the rainforest.

items.t: A sloth's digestion can take a month or longer.
items.d: It can take a month or more for a sloth to digest a meal.

items.t: Tree sloths spend most of their lives hanging upside down.
items.d: They hang upside down in tropical rainforest trees.

items.t: The mimic octopus can copy the appearance of several other sea animals.
items.d: It can resemble animals such as lionfish, sea snakes, and jellyfish to stay safe.

items.t: Wood frogs can survive when their blood and other tissues freeze in winter.
items.d: They thaw and become active again when conditions warm.

items.t: The wood frog is the only North American frog found north of the Arctic Circle.
items.d: Its ability to endure freezing helps it live in this cold region.

items.t: Bats are the only mammals capable of true powered flight.
items.d: Flying squirrels and sugar gliders glide instead of powering their flight.

items.t: Many bats find food in darkness by making sounds and listening for echoes.
items.d: This skill is called echolocation, and the sounds are too high for us to hear.

items.t: A polar bear has black skin, while its clear hairs look white.
items.d: The dark skin absorbs heat in its cold Arctic habitat.

items.t: Polar bears have a layer of fat about 5 to 10 centimetres thick.
items.d: This thick layer helps insulate them in icy Arctic conditions.

items.t: The Great Barrier Reef is home to over 1,500 fish species.
items.d: About 400 kinds of coral also live in this enormous reef habitat.

items.t: Your smallest bones are inside your ears.
items.d: These tiny bones help pass vibrations from your eardrum to the inner ear.

items.t: Your pupil is the opening in the middle of your eye.
items.d: It usually gets bigger in dim light to let more light in.

items.t: Your heart is a pump made of muscle.
items.d: Every beat pushes blood through your body.

items.t: When you breathe in, oxygen from the air can pass into your blood.
items.d: It passes through the walls of tiny air sacs in your lungs.

items.t: Your tongue and nose work together when you taste food.
items.d: When you have a stuffy nose, food may seem to have less flavor.

items.t: The equator is an imaginary line around the middle of Earth.
items.d: It divides Earth into the Northern Hemisphere and the Southern Hemisphere.

items.t: The Pacific Ocean is Earth's largest ocean.
items.d: It lies between Asia and Australia on one side and the Americas on the other.

items.t: The South Pole sits in Antarctica.
items.d: At the South Pole, a thick sheet of ice covers the land.

items.t: A map scale helps you work out real distances.
items.d: If 1 centimeter on a map stands for 1 kilometer, 3 centimeters stand for 3 kilometers.

items.t: An island is a piece of land surrounded by water.
items.d: An island can sit in a lake or river as well as in the ocean.

items.t: Word of the day: nocturnal.
items.d: A nocturnal animal is active at night. A barn owl often hunts after dark.

items.t: Word of the day: peninsula.
items.d: A peninsula is land with water around most of it. Much of Florida sits between the Gulf and the Atlantic Ocean.

items.t: Word of the day: palindrome.
items.d: A palindrome reads the same forward and backward. Try it with the word level.

items.t: Word of the day: transparent.
items.d: If something is transparent, you can see clearly through it, like through clean window glass.

items.t: Word of the day: migrate.
items.d: To migrate is to move from one place to another. Many birds do this as the seasons change.

items.t: A grown-up's skeleton has 206 bones.
items.d: Babies are born with more bones. Some of those bones join as the child grows.

items.t: Children usually have 20 baby teeth.
items.d: Baby teeth later fall out so larger adult teeth can take their places.

items.t: People can grow up to 32 adult teeth.
items.d: That count includes wisdom teeth, which do not grow in for everyone.

items.t: Tooth enamel is the hardest material in the human body.
items.d: Enamel is the tough outer layer of the part of a tooth you see.

items.t: Each of your hands has 27 bones.
items.d: The hands and feet together hold more than half of a grown-up's bones.

items.t: The femur is the longest bone in the human body.
items.d: The femur is your thigh bone. It helps you stand, walk, and run.

items.t: Your outer ears and nose tip are mostly cartilage.
items.d: Cartilage is bendier than bone, but it still holds a shape.

items.t: The left lung is a little smaller than the right lung.
items.d: That leaves room for the heart, which sits a bit left of center.

items.t: Your body temperature is usually about 37 degrees Celsius.
items.d: That is about 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

items.t: More than half of your body is water.
items.d: Water is in your blood, your muscles, and even your bones.

items.t: Your skin is your body's largest organ.
items.d: It helps hold water in, keeps out germs, and lets you feel touch.

items.t: Your body has about 600 skeletal muscles, and many move your bones.
items.d: A muscle can pull on a bone, but it cannot push.

items.t: Even identical twins have different fingerprints.
items.d: Those tiny skin ridges form before birth and stay with you for life.

items.t: You can taste sweet, salty, sour, bitter, and umami.
items.d: Umami is a savory taste, like the taste in a ripe tomato.

items.t: Word of the day: archipelago.
items.d: An archipelago is a group of islands. Hawaii is one in the Pacific.

items.t: Word of the day: delta.
items.d: A delta is low land a river builds at its mouth. The Nile has a big delta.

items.t: Word of the day: tributary.
items.d: A tributary flows into a larger river. The Missouri flows into the Mississippi.

items.t: Word of the day: humidity.
items.d: Humidity is how much water vapor is in the air. High humidity can make a warm day feel sticky.

items.t: Word of the day: glacier.
items.d: A glacier is a thick mass of ice that slowly flows. It can carve a valley as it moves.

items.t: Word of the day: erosion.
items.d: Erosion wears away rock and soil. Rain and rivers can carry the bits elsewhere.

items.t: Word of the day: oasis.
items.d: An oasis is a place in a desert where water lets plants grow.

items.t: Word of the day: strait.
items.d: A strait is a narrow waterway between two larger bodies of water. The Strait of Gibraltar is one.

items.t: Word of the day: isthmus.
items.d: An isthmus is a narrow strip of land joining two larger areas. The Isthmus of Panama is one.

items.t: Word of the day: precipitation.
items.d: Precipitation is water falling from the sky. Rain, snow, and hail all count.

items.t: Word of the day: climate.
items.d: Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years. Deserts have a dry climate.

items.t: Word of the day: pollen.
items.d: Pollen is a powder that helps flowering plants make seeds. Bees often carry it from bloom to bloom.

items.t: Word of the day: germinate.
items.d: A seed germinates when it starts to grow. Warmth and water help a bean germinate.

items.t: Word of the day: fossil.
items.d: A fossil is preserved evidence of ancient life, such as a bone, shell, footprint, or leaf print.

items.t: Word of the day: homophone.
items.d: Homophones sound alike but mean different things. See and sea are homophones.

items.t: Asia is the largest continent.
items.d: From Saudi Arabia to India, China, and Japan, those lands are part of Asia.

items.t: Australia is the smallest of the seven continents.
items.d: Australia is also one country. Europe is the next smallest continent.

items.t: Africa is the only continent in all four hemispheres.
items.d: The equator and the 0 degrees longitude line both cross it, so it reaches north, south, east, and west.

items.t: Greenland is the world's largest island.
items.d: Australia is larger, but maps count it as a continent, not an island.

items.t: The Sahara is the largest hot desert on Earth.
items.d: It stretches across North Africa, from the Atlantic Ocean to the Red Sea.

items.t: Antarctica is a cold desert.
items.d: So little new snow or rain falls each year that it counts as a desert.

items.t: The Amazon River carries more water than any other river.
items.d: It flows east across South America into the Atlantic Ocean.

items.t: The Nile River flows north to the Mediterranean Sea.
items.d: It crosses northeastern Africa and runs through Egypt.

items.t: Mount Everest is Earth's highest peak above sea level.
items.d: The top is about 8,849 meters above sea level, in the Himalayas.

items.t: The Andes are the longest mountain chain on land.
items.d: They run about 7,000 kilometers down the west side of South America.

items.t: The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon.
items.d: Over a very long time, it cut down through layers of rock in Arizona.

items.t: A fjord is a deep, narrow arm of the sea.
items.d: Glaciers carved many fjords long ago. Later the sea filled them.

items.t: The country of Ecuador is named for the equator.
items.d: The equator crosses the country, which is in South America.

items.t: Canberra is the capital of Australia.
items.d: Sydney has more people, but the capital city is Canberra.

items.t: Japan is made up of thousands of islands.
items.d: Most people live on Honshu, Hokkaido, Kyushu, or Shikoku.

items.t: Huge plates of rock under the land and sea creep very slowly.
items.d: They move only a few centimeters a year, about as fast as fingernails grow.

items.t: Latitude tells how far north or south of the equator you are.
items.d: The equator is 0 degrees latitude. The North Pole is 90 degrees north.

items.t: Longitude tells how far east or west a place is.
items.d: Zero degrees of longitude runs through Greenwich, London. That line is the prime meridian.

items.t: Maps often show five oceans on Earth.
items.d: They are the Pacific, Atlantic, Indian, Southern, and Arctic Oceans.

items.t: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest ocean.
items.d: It lies in the far north and surrounds the North Pole.

items.t: About 71 percent of Earth's surface is ocean.
items.d: Spin a globe and point anywhere. Your finger will often land on water.

items.t: About 97 percent of Earth's water is salty.
items.d: Fresh water in rivers, lakes, and ice is only a small share of all Earth's water.

items.t: Ocean tides are raised mainly by the Moon's gravity.
items.d: The Sun's gravity changes tides too, so some high tides are higher than others.

items.t: Most ocean waves are made by the wind.
items.d: The wind drags on the surface, and the water rises and falls.

items.t: About 90 percent of an iceberg hides underwater.
items.d: The ice floats, so only a small part shows above the sea.

items.t: The Mariana Trench is the deepest known part of the ocean.
items.d: The bottom there is about 11 kilometers below the surface.

items.t: Coral reefs are built by tiny animals called polyps.
items.d: Each polyp leaves a small stony cup. Millions of cups make the reef.

items.t: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest coral reef system.
items.d: It stretches more than 2,000 kilometers off Australia's northeast coast.

items.t: Earth has seasons because the planet is tilted.
items.d: When your part of Earth leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits it more directly.

items.t: Away from the equator, summer days last longer than winter days.
items.d: Earth's tilt keeps the Sun above the horizon for more hours in summer.

items.t: Heat from the Sun turns liquid water into invisible vapor.
items.d: That is evaporation. It is why wet clothes dry on a sunny line.

items.t: Clouds form when water vapor cools into tiny drops or ice.
items.d: A cold window fogs up on a chilly day for the same kind of reason.

items.t: Rain falls when drops in a cloud grow large enough.
items.d: Tiny cloud drops bump and join. When they get large, gravity pulls them down.

items.t: A rainbow appears when sunlight bends through raindrops.
items.d: To see it, keep the Sun behind you and the falling rain in front.

items.t: A fainter second rainbow shows the colors in reverse.
items.d: Its light bounces twice inside each drop, so the order of colors flips.

items.t: Snowflakes often grow with six arms.
items.d: The ice inside a snowflake builds in a six-part pattern.

items.t: You see lightning before you hear its thunder.
items.d: Light arrives almost at once. Sound takes about 3 seconds to go 1 kilometer.

items.t: Fog is a cloud resting on the ground.
items.d: Tiny water drops hang in the air and hide things that are far away.

items.t: Dew is water that collects on cool grass and leaves.
items.d: At night, vapor in the air turns to liquid on those cool surfaces.

items.t: Water boils at a lower temperature high on a mountain.
items.d: At sea level it boils at 100 degrees Celsius. Lower air pressure changes that.

items.t: Green plants make their food using sunlight, water, and air.
items.d: They take carbon dioxide from the air. This is called photosynthesis.

items.t: Leaves look green because they hold chlorophyll.
items.d: Chlorophyll catches sunlight the leaf uses to make its food.

items.t: In sunlight, green plants give off oxygen.
items.d: That oxygen mixes into the air people and animals breathe.

items.t: In autumn, many green leaves turn yellow or red.
items.d: As green chlorophyll fades, yellow shows through, and some leaves make red pigments.

items.t: A seed contains a tiny plant and a store of food.
items.d: The stored food feeds the sprout until its leaves can make food.

items.t: Roots anchor a plant and take in water from the soil.
items.d: Tiny root hairs soak up water and minerals the plant needs.

items.t: Grass can keep growing after the top is cut.
items.d: It grows from low down, near the soil, not from the tips.

items.t: In plant science, a banana counts as a berry.
items.d: It develops from one flower's ovary. Wild bananas have seeds inside their flesh.

items.t: A strawberry's tiny outside dots are little fruits.
items.d: Each little fruit, called an achene, usually holds one seed.

items.t: In plant science, a tomato is a fruit.
items.d: It grows from a flower and holds seeds, which is what makes a fruit.

items.t: A potato is a fat underground stem, not a root.
items.d: This kind of stem is a tuber. The eyes on it can sprout new plants.

items.t: Cutting an onion can make your eyes water.
items.d: The cut lets out a gas that stings, and tears wash the sting away.

items.t: Many tree trunks add one new growth ring each year.
items.d: A wide ring often means a good growing year. A thin ring can mean a hard one.

items.t: Young sunflower buds turn to follow the Sun.
items.d: Once the bloom is fully open, it usually settles facing east.

items.t: People have been writing for more than 5,000 years.
items.d: Some of the oldest marks were pictures and wedge shapes pressed in clay.

items.t: Wheels have helped move heavy loads for more than 5,000 years.
items.d: A cart with wheels rolls along. Dragging the same load is much harder.
