items.t: Paper was invented in China about 2,000 years ago.
items.d: Fibers from plants were mashed with water, spread flat, and dried.

items.t: In the 1400s, Gutenberg's press printed books much faster.
items.d: Metal letters could be moved around and used again for the next page.

items.t: The core of a pencil is graphite, not lead.
items.d: Graphite is a soft form of carbon. Clay is mixed in to change the hardness.

items.t: Zero, as a number, was developed in India long ago.
items.d: That was more than 1,000 years ago. Zero lets 101 mean one hundred and one.

items.t: In Roman numerals, V stands for 5 and X stands for 10.
items.d: IV means 4, because I before V takes 1 away. VI means 6.

items.t: A leap year gives February 29 days instead of 28.
items.d: They usually come every 4 years so the calendar stays lined up with the seasons.

items.t: One day has 24 hours, and one hour has 60 minutes.
items.d: A minute has 60 seconds. So one hour has 60 times 60, or 3,600 seconds.

items.t: The earliest bicycles had no pedals.
items.d: A rider sat over two wheels and pushed along with both feet.

items.t: Food cans came along before the can opener did.
items.d: For years, people had to cut a can open with a hammer and chisel.

items.t: Louis Braille created a writing system you can read by touch.
items.d: Raised dots stand for letters, and a fingertip can feel each pattern.

items.t: A popcorn kernel pops when water inside turns to steam.
items.d: The steam builds until the shell bursts and the inside puffs up.

items.t: Ice floats because it is less dense than liquid water.
items.d: When water freezes, it spreads out, so the same amount fills more space.

items.t: A melted candy bar led to the microwave oven.
items.d: In 1945, Percy Spencer noticed the candy melt near radar gear, then tried cooking with those waves.

items.t: In 1903 the Wright brothers flew the first controlled powered airplane.
items.d: The first flight lasted 12 seconds and traveled about 37 meters.

items.t: Hook-and-loop fasteners copy the tiny hooks on a burr.
items.d: Those hooks grab loops in fur or cloth. A Swiss inventor turned that into a fastener.

items.t: Adult male woolly mammoths were about as tall as a big African elephant, around 3 metres at the shoulder.
items.d: That is about as high as the ceiling of a tall room.

items.t: A woolly mammoth's tusks were very long and curved. Tusks are really extra-long front teeth.
A mammoth wore two layers of fur: long outer hairs on top and a shorter, warm undercoat underneath.
items.d: Like wearing a long coat over a fluffy sweater.

items.t: Woolly mammoths mostly ate grasses and small flowering plants called forbs.
Some woolly mammoths lived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic until about 4,000 years ago.
Scientists found milk in the tummy of a frozen baby mammoth. It showed what mammoth calves drank.
We know a lot about mammoths because frozen mammoth bodies have been found in Siberia and North America.
items.d: The cold kept them safe for a very long time.

items.t: Ice age artists drew woolly mammoths a lot. Only horses and bison were drawn more often.
The closest living relative of the woolly mammoth is the Asian elephant.
A woolly mammoth could probably live to be about 60 years old.
A mammoth's trunk was strong and sensitive. It worked like an extra arm with many jobs.
A newborn mammoth calf weighed about 90 kilograms.
items.d: That is about as heavy as a grown-up person.

items.t: The biggest sabre-toothed cat, Smilodon populator, had fangs about 28 cm long.
items.d: That is almost as long as a 30 cm school ruler.

items.t: The 'sabre-toothed tiger' was not closely related to tigers at all.
items.d: Scientists call its genus Smilodon.

items.t: Smilodon was very muscular, but its bite was weaker than the bite of other big cats.
Hundreds of Smilodon fossils have been found in the La Brea Tar Pits in Los Angeles.
Smilodon is the official state fossil of California.
Smilodon lived in both North America and South America.
The giant ground sloth Megatherium was about 6 metres long and as heavy as an Asian elephant.
Megatherium picked leaves, twigs and fruits from trees and bushes.
Three-toed sloths are the closest living relatives of the giant ground sloths.
items.d: Today's sloths are much smaller.

items.t: The first Megatherium skeleton was found in 1787 on the bank of the Luján River in Argentina.
Scientists use the word megafauna for animals that weigh 45 kilograms or more.
Many big ice age animals died out. Around 65 out of every 100 megafauna species vanished worldwide.
In Australia, North America and South America, every mammal heavier than 1,000 kg died out.
Africa lost fewer big animals than many other regions.
Pakicetus, an early whale relative, lived about 48 million years ago in what is now Pakistan.
Pakicetus had four long legs and could walk on land. It is a step between land mammals and whales.
Basilosaurus was an early whale about 17 to 20 metres long. It lived roughly 34 to 41 million years ago.
Basilosaurus still had tiny back legs, about 35 cm long, with three toes.
items.d: Its ancestors walked on land.

items.t: Basilosaurus means 'king lizard'. People first thought its bones came from a giant reptile.
items.d: It was really a whale.

items.t: The woolly rhinoceros was about as big as today's white rhino.
The woolly rhino had a hump on its shoulders that held lots of fat.
Ice age people painted woolly rhinoceroses on cave walls.
The Irish elk had the biggest antlers of any deer, spanning more than 4 metres across.
items.d: That is wider than a small car is long.

items.t: The Irish elk lived across northern Europe and Asia, not only in Ireland.
Glyptodon was an armadillo relative about 2 metres long. Its shell was made of hundreds of bony plates.
Glyptodon's tail was covered in rings of spiky bony plates.
Cave bears are thought to have eaten almost only plants.
Cave bears got their name because most of their bones have been found in caves.
Dire wolves were about as big as the largest grey wolves alive today.
Diprotodon was the biggest marsupial ever. It stood about 1.8 metres tall at the shoulder.
Wombats and koalas are the closest living relatives of the giant Diprotodon.
The last ice age lasted from about 115,000 to 11,700 years ago.
During the ice age, sea levels were much lower because so much water was frozen in ice.
The Bering land bridge let animals and people walk from Asia into North America.
In 1940, teenager Marcel Ravidat found Lascaux cave after his dog explored a hole.
items.d: The cave is full of ice age paintings.

items.t: Lascaux cave has more than 600 paintings that are about 17,000 to 22,000 years old.
The oldest known stone tools are about 3.3 million years old.
Stone Age people made tools from bone as well as from stone.
An African elephant's trunk is about 2 metres long.
Wild African elephants can live up to about 70 years.
Cheetahs can run about 97 to 113 km/h for short distances.
Cheetahs have black tear-like marks from their eyes to their mouths.
A cheetah can cover about 9 metres in one long stride.
items.d: Its flexible spine helps stretch its body while running.

items.t: A giraffe's tongue can grow to about 53 centimetres long.
A newborn giraffe is already about 1.9 metres tall.
Giraffe calves can run within a few hours of being born.
A platypus's soft snout has thousands of receptors that help it find prey.
A newborn koala is about the size of a jelly bean.
A koala joey stays in its mother's pouch for about seven months.
Koalas are marsupials related to kangaroos. They are not bears.
A giant anteater's tongue is about 60 centimetres long.
items.d: It can flick in and out up to 150 times in one minute.

items.t: Giant anteaters have no teeth.
Giant anteaters walk on their front knuckles.
items.d: They tuck their sharp claws into their palms while walking.

items.t: About one in every five known mammal species is a bat.
Bats are the only mammals that can truly fly for a long time.
The smallest bat weighs only about 2 grams.
items.d: It is called Kitti's hog-nosed bat.

items.t: A giant golden-crowned flying fox can have a wingspan of about 1.6 metres.
Many bats use echoes to find prey in the dark.
items.d: They make very high sounds, then listen for the sounds bouncing back.

items.t: A bat's wing has long finger bones covered by a thin membrane.
Monotremes are the only living mammals that lay eggs.
Only five kinds of monotreme live today.
items.d: They are the platypus and four kinds of echidna.

items.t: Baby monotremes are called puggles.
items.d: They drink milk from openings in their mother's skin because monotremes have no teats.

items.t: The red kangaroo is the largest living marsupial.
Red kangaroos can hop at about 60 km/h.
A kangaroo's Achilles tendons work like rubber bands.
items.d: They store and release energy to help power each hop.

items.t: A male red kangaroo can leap about 8 to 9 metres in one bound.
A newborn red kangaroo is only a few centimetres long.
items.d: It uses its front legs to climb into its mother's pouch.

items.t: A kangaroo's strong tail acts like a third leg when it stands.
items.d: Its two feet and tail form a sturdy tripod.

items.t: Every tiger has its own unique pattern of stripes.
items.d: A tiger's stripe pattern is like its own fingerprint.

items.t: Tigers are powerful swimmers and can cross rivers up to about 8 km wide.
A tiger's roar can be heard from about 3 km away.
Lions are inactive for about 20 hours each day.
Lions are the most social wild cats.
items.d: They live in groups called prides, with related females, cubs, and a few males.

items.t: Newborn lion cubs have dark spots that fade as they grow.
Giraffes are the tallest living land animals.
items.d: They can stand about 4.3 to 5.7 metres tall.

items.t: Giraffes have seven neck bones, the same number as humans.
items.d: Each giraffe neck bone is more than 28 centimetres long.

items.t: A giraffe's heart weighs about 11 kilograms.
items.d: It beats around 150 times each minute.

items.t: Echidna spines are special hairs made of keratin.
items.d: Keratin is also found in human fingernails.

items.t: Echidnas have no teeth.
items.d: They grind food between their tongue and the inside of their mouth.

items.t: A baby echidna hatches after about 10 days.
items.d: It uses a tiny egg tooth to open its leathery egg.

items.t: Koalas sleep for about 20 hours each day.
Green algae can grow in the grooves of a sloth's fur.
items.d: The green color helps the sloth blend in with leafy trees.

items.t: Three-toed sloths have eight or nine neck bones.
items.d: Most mammals, including humans, have seven neck bones.

items.t: Sloths are surprisingly strong swimmers.
items.d: They can hold their breath for up to about 40 minutes.

items.t: Wombats make cube-shaped droppings to mark their territory.
A wombat's pouch faces backward.
items.d: This helps keep soil out of the pouch while the wombat digs.

items.t: Each year the Arctic tern flies from the Arctic to the Antarctic and back.
items.d: That yearly journey is the longest migration of any bird.

items.t: Tracked Arctic terns fly about 70,900 km in a year.
items.d: That is farther than flying once around the Earth.

items.t: One tagged Arctic tern flew about 96,000 km in ten months.
items.d: People followed this bird from the Farne Islands.

items.t: Tiny hooklets on feather parts called barbules zip a feather's vanes together.
items.d: The hooklets keep the feather flat and smooth for flying.

items.t: A bar-tailed godwit can fly from Alaska to New Zealand without stopping.
items.d: Some fly the same kind of non-stop trip all the way to Australia.

items.t: One young godwit flew non-stop from Alaska to Tasmania.
items.d: The flight took about 11 days and covered at least 13,560 km.

items.t: A peregrine dive has been reliably measured at about 184 km/h.
items.d: The bird folds its wings and drops steeply through the air.

items.t: Peregrine falcons have a third eyelid that clears the eye.
items.d: It sweeps away dirt while the falcon keeps seeing.

items.t: A male bee hummingbird weighs about 2 grams.
items.d: That is about as heavy as half a teaspoon of sugar.

items.t: A bee hummingbird's nest is a cup about 2.5 cm across.
items.d: She builds it from cobwebs, bark, and lichen.

items.t: A bee hummingbird beats its wings 80 to 200 times a second.
items.d: Those fast beats let the tiny bird hover in place.

items.t: Hummingbirds can hover and fly in any direction.
items.d: They can go forward, backward, sideways, or stay still.

items.t: Word of the day: torpor
items.d: A deep rest at night. Hummingbirds can slow their energy use to about one fifteenth of normal.

items.t: One kind of hummingbird can reach up to 1,260 heartbeats a minute.
items.d: At that top rate, the heart beats 21 times each second.

items.t: The ostrich is the largest and heaviest living bird.
items.d: An adult weighs about 63 to 145 kilograms.

items.t: Ostriches are the fastest birds on land.
items.d: They can run up to about 70 km/h (about 43 miles an hour).

items.t: The ostrich lays the largest egg of any living bird.
items.d: One egg weighs about 1.5 kilograms.

items.t: A kiwi egg is huge compared with the mother's body.
items.d: It can weigh up to about one fifth of her weight.

items.t: Tiny pores in an eggshell let the chick inside breathe.
items.d: A hen's egg has about 7,500 of these breathing holes.

items.t: A father emperor penguin balances the egg on his feet.
items.d: Males alone warm the egg for about 65 to 75 days.

items.t: Emperor penguins huddle together to share warmth.
items.d: Birds on the edge slowly move inward so everyone gets a warm turn.

items.t: One emperor penguin dived 564 metres deep.
items.d: That dive lasted about 22 minutes.

items.t: The emperor penguin is the tallest and heaviest penguin.
items.d: Adults are about 110 to 120 cm long.

items.t: A father emperor penguin can feed his chick a milky food.
items.d: He makes it in his throat and feeds the chick for a few days.

items.t: Penguin wings are stiff flippers made for swimming.
items.d: Their swimming looks like flying, only through water.

items.t: Parrots have two toes forward and two toes back.
items.d: That grip helps them climb and hold on tight.

items.t: Nearly all penguins live in the southern half of the world.
items.d: The Galapagos penguin lives at the equator, and a little north of it.

items.t: All penguins have dark backs and white fronts.
items.d: From above, the dark back blends with the deep water. From below, the white belly blends with the light.

items.t: The kakapo is the heaviest parrot, and it cannot fly.
items.d: It lives in New Zealand and is the only flightless parrot.

items.t: A male kakapo's deep boom can travel a long way.
items.d: On a still night, you could hear it at least 1 km away.

items.t: The wandering albatross has the longest wingspan of any living bird.
items.d: Its wings can reach up to about 3.7 metres from tip to tip.

items.t: A wandering albatross glides about 22 metres for each metre it drops.
items.d: This shallow glide lets it travel far without much flapping.

items.t: Wandering albatrosses can live for more than 50 years.
items.d: Breeding pairs usually stay together for life.

items.t: Albatross pairs spread their wings and wave their heads.
items.d: They clap their bills and call loudly to impress a mate.

items.t: Owls can turn their heads as much as 270 degrees.
items.d: An owl's eyes are fixed, so it must turn its head to look around.

items.t: Comb-like feather edges make owl flight almost silent.
items.d: Those edges bring the sound of flapping down to almost nothing.

items.t: Unlike most owls, snowy owls often hunt during the day.
items.d: They are especially active in the daytime during summer.

items.t: Snowy owls have the longest toe feathers of any owl.
items.d: Thick white feathers cover their toes in the cold Arctic.

items.t: Birds find their way using the Sun, stars, and Earth's magnetic field.
items.d: They also follow landmarks and smells.

items.t: Geese in a V formation can save energy while flying.
items.d: The V can cut the effort by about 12 to 20 percent versus flying alone.

items.t: Word of the day: syrinx
items.d: Birds sing with this part at the bottom of the windpipe. Some can make two notes at once.

items.t: Young songbirds learn songs by listening to adult birds.
items.d: Their early practice is a lot like a baby babbling.

items.t: Lyrebirds copy the sounds around them.
items.d: They mimic birds, koalas, dingoes, and some machine sounds.

items.t: A male lyrebird fans 16 special tail feathers over his head.
items.d: He shows off the tail to impress a mate.

items.t: Common swifts can stay airborne for up to ten months.
items.d: They can drink, eat, mate, and sleep while they fly.

items.t: Kiwis are the only birds with nostrils at the beak tip.
items.d: They sniff out worms at night. Hair-like feathers hide their tiny wings.

items.t: Birds are the only dinosaurs still alive today.
items.d: Every bird, from a hummingbird to an ostrich, is a living dinosaur.

items.t: Birds have light, hollow bones that help them fly.
items.d: A beak also weighs less than a jaw full of teeth.

items.t: Bar-headed geese are some of the highest-flying birds.
items.d: They cross the Himalayas. One bird was tracked at 7,290 metres.

items.t: Every insect has six legs, and its body has three parts.
items.d: The three parts are the head, thorax, and abdomen.

items.t: Insects have a pair of antennae on their heads to sense their surroundings.
items.d: Antennae work a bit like a nose and fingers in one.

items.t: Insects are the most diverse animal group, with more than a million known kinds.
items.d: They make up more than half of all known animal species.

items.t: Giant dragonfly-like insects once had wingspans of 55 to 70 cm.
items.d: That is about as wide as a big pizza box.

items.t: The oldest known flying insects lived about 325 million years ago.
items.d: That was long before dinosaurs appeared.

items.t: Some insects change shape completely as they grow. This is called complete metamorphosis.
items.d: A caterpillar looks nothing like the butterfly it becomes.

items.t: In complete metamorphosis, a pupa stage comes between the larva and the adult.
items.d: Inside, its body is rebuilt into the adult form.

items.t: In incomplete metamorphosis, young insects are called nymphs.
items.d: They grow into adults by shedding their outer skeleton.

items.t: A butterfly's pupa has a special name. It is called a chrysalis.
items.d: The caterpillar rests inside until it is ready to come out as a butterfly.

items.t: Ants live in colonies, and the biggest super colonies can hold hundreds of millions of ants.
items.d: That is more ants than people in many countries.

items.t: Most ants in a colony are wingless female workers.
items.d: They gather food, care for the young and build the nest.

items.t: An ant queen can live up to 30 years, but a worker ant lives only about 1 to 3 years.
items.d: The queen is the longest-living ant in the nest.

items.t: More than 13,800 ant species are known.
items.d: Ants live on every continent except Antarctica.

items.t: Ants leave a scent trail called a pheromone trail, and other ants follow it.
items.d: That is how a line of ants finds the same piece of food.

items.t: Army ants do not build permanent nests.
items.d: Their whole colony travels together.

items.t: Weaver ant workers build nests in trees by joining leaves together.
items.d: Workers hold the leaves in place while others stick them.

items.t: Honey bees tell their hive mates where food is by doing a waggle dance.
items.d: The dance shows both the direction and the distance of the flowers.

items.t: A healthy honey bee hive in midsummer can hold 40,000 to 80,000 bees.
items.d: Almost all of them are workers.

items.t: A honey bee queen can lay over 2,500 eggs in one day.
items.d: She is bigger than the worker bees.

items.t: Honey bees collect nectar from flowers and turn it into honey.
items.d: They store it in wax cells for food.

items.t: A baby honey bee hatches from an egg as a tiny larva with no legs or eyes.
items.d: It is fed by worker bees until it is ready to grow up.

items.t: Honey bee larvae that eat only royal jelly grow bigger and become queens.
items.d: The food they eat decides what kind of bee they turn into.

items.t: Honeypot ant workers store liquid food in their swollen abdomens.
items.d: They can become so full that they cannot move.

items.t: Termites are not ants. They belong to the same insect group as cockroaches.
items.d: Termites and ants just look a little alike.

items.t: A termite queen can live 30 to 50 years, and some lay up to 40,000 eggs a day.
items.d: She is one of the longest-living insects.

items.t: Most worker and soldier termites are completely blind.
items.d: They find their way in dark tunnels by touch and smell.

items.t: Bumblebees have round bodies covered in soft hair.
items.d: The fuzz helps them carry pollen from flower to flower.

items.t: Some bumblebees shake pollen loose from flowers by buzzing at just the right pitch.
items.d: This trick is called buzz pollination.

items.t: A bumblebee colony is small, usually with only 50 to 400 bees.
items.d: A honey bee hive can hold many times more.

items.t: Butterfly wings have tiny scales. The name Lepidoptera means scale wing.
items.d: Moths belong to this group too.

items.t: A butterfly drinks through a long tube called a proboscis, which coils up when not in use.
items.d: It works like a curly straw.

items.t: There are about 20,000 kinds of butterflies in the world.
items.d: They come in almost every color you can think of.

items.t: Queen Alexandra's birdwing is the world's largest butterfly.
items.d: It comes from Papua New Guinea.

items.t: A butterfly cannot fly right after it comes out. Its wings must unfold and dry first.
items.d: It waits quietly for a while before its first flight.

items.t: Monarch caterpillars eat only milkweed leaves.
items.d: The plant makes monarchs taste bad to hungry predators.

items.t: A female monarch butterfly lays 300 to 500 eggs over a few weeks.
items.d: She lays them one at a time on milkweed plants.

items.t: Beetles are called Coleoptera, a Greek word that means sheath wing.
items.d: Their hard front wings cover their back like a shield.

items.t: Beetles are the largest group of insects.
items.d: About one in four known animal species is a beetle.

items.t: Some water beetles carry an air bubble under their wing cases to breathe while they dive.
items.d: It works a bit like a tiny scuba tank.

items.t: Ladybirds are beetles, not true bugs.
items.d: Most of them hunt tiny insects called aphids.

items.t: A ladybird's bright colors warn predators that it tastes bad.
items.d: Birds learn to leave it alone.

items.t: Fireflies are beetles, and they make light with a chemical reaction in their bodies.
items.d: This is called bioluminescence.

items.t: Each kind of firefly has its own flash pattern to find a mate.
items.d: It is like a secret blinking code.

items.t: Dung beetles can roll a ball of dung in a straight line, even around obstacles.
items.d: Some even use the Milky Way to find their way at night.

items.t: Bombardier beetles mix two chemicals to make a hot spray when threatened.
items.d: The spray comes in about 500 tiny pulses each second.

items.t: Most of a dragonfly's life is spent as a nymph under water.
items.d: Only the last part of its life is spent flying.

items.t: A dragonfly can hover, and it can fly in six directions.
items.d: It beats its front and back wings out of step with each other.

items.t: A dragonfly can catch up to 95% of the prey it chases.
items.d: That makes it one of the best hunters in the insect world.

items.t: Cicadas make their loud song with drum-like parts on their bodies called tymbals.
items.d: Some cicadas come out of the ground only every 13 or 17 years.

items.t: One spider can make up to seven kinds of silk, each suited to a different job.
For the same weight, spider silk is stronger than steel.
Spider silk is tougher than steel. It soaks up more energy before it snaps.
Dragline silk forms a web's rim and spokes, and it works as a spider's safety line.
The spiral threads in an orb web are made from sticky, stretchy silk.
Spiders make a stiff kind of silk for protective egg sacs.
Spiders release silk through spinnerets on their abdomens.
Scorpions glow bright blue-green under ultraviolet light.
items.d: A black light gives off ultraviolet light, also called UV.

items.t: Baby scorpions ride on their mother's back until after the first time they shed their outer covering.
More than 2,500 kinds of scorpion have been described.
Scorpions live on every continent except Antarctica.
Scorpions have existed for about 430 million years.
Scorpions give birth to live young instead of laying eggs.
Centipedes have one pair of legs on each leg-bearing body segment.
Despite their name, centipedes never have exactly 100 legs.
Centipedes always have an odd number of leg pairs.
items.d: That means their total number of legs is even, but never 100.

items.t: Different centipedes have from 15 to 191 pairs of legs.
Centipedes lose water easily because they lack a waxy waterproof coat.
Most millipede body segments carry two pairs of legs.
Many millipedes release smelly liquid from tiny pores for protection.
One kind of millipede can have more than 1,300 legs.
Many millipedes curl into a tight coil to protect their delicate legs.
Most millipedes eat rotting leaves and other plant material.
Millipedes do not bite and are mostly harmless to people.
An ancient giant millipede called Arthropleura was the largest known land animal with no backbone.
Spiders are air-breathing animals with eight limbs.
A spider has two main body parts, the cephalothorax and the abdomen.
items.d: The cephalothorax is the head and the chest joined together.

items.t: A spider may use as many as six types of silk-making glands.
Spiders can swallow only liquid food because their guts are too narrow for solids.
Spiders shed their outer covering, or molt, as they grow.
Some jumping spiders see about ten times more sharply than dragonflies.
Trapdoor spiders wait inside burrows that often have hinged lids.
The smallest spiders have bodies less than 0.4 millimetres long.
The largest and heaviest spiders belong to the tarantula group.
Ticks are arachnids, not insects.
items.d: Like spiders and scorpions, they belong to the arachnid group.

items.t: Adult ticks are only about 3 to 5 millimetres long.
Ticks have four life stages: egg, larva, nymph and adult.
Ticks belong to two main families, hard ticks and soft ticks.
Many ticks wait on plants with their legs stretched out in a pose called questing.
Ticks live around the world, especially in warm, humid places.
A snail has a ribbon-like tongue called a radula, covered with thousands of tiny teeth.
A snail's shell keeps growing throughout its life.
Snails glide on a layer of mucus using a strong, muscular foot.
Land snails are usually busiest on damp nights.
Baby land snails hatch looking like tiny adults.
items.d: They do not change into a different body shape as they grow.

items.t: Most snail species live in the sea, not on land.
Earthworms have several pairs of curved blood vessels that work like hearts.
items.d: These vessels are called aortic arches.

items.t: Earthworms have no lungs. They take in oxygen through their moist skin.
Tiny bristles called setae help an earthworm grip the soil.
items.d: The bristles grow on the worm's body segments.

items.t: Woodlice are land-living crustaceans, not insects.
items.d: They belong to the same broad animal group as crabs and shrimp.

items.t: Every bottlenose dolphin has its own special whistle that works like a name.
items.d: It makes this whistle soon after it is born.

items.t: Dolphins send out clicks and listen for the echoes. This is called echolocation.
items.d: The echoes tell them an object's shape, size, speed and distance.

items.t: Dolphins shed the outer layer of their skin about every two hours.
Bottlenose dolphins can swim up to about 35 km per hour.
The blue whale is the largest mammal in the world.
A baby blue whale weighs about 1,800 kg at birth. That is about two tons.
A grown blue whale can eat about 4 to 7 metric tons of tiny krill in one day.
items.d: Krill are small shrimp-like animals.

items.t: Great white sharks can swim up to about 24 km per hour using their powerful tails.
A great white shark can have up to 300 triangle-shaped teeth, set in several rows.
Sharks have skeletons made of cartilage, not bone.
items.d: Cartilage is the bendy stuff in your ears and the tip of your nose.

items.t: Baby great white sharks, called pups, are already about 1.5 meters long when they are born.
The hammerhead shark is named for the odd shape of its head.
A hammerhead's wide-set eyes help it scan a bigger area than other sharks can.
Hammerhead sharks can sense the tiny electrical signals that living animals give off.
items.d: This helps them find food.

items.t: Hammerhead sharks do not lay eggs. Mothers give birth to live pups.
Octopuses live in all the world's oceans, and are most common in warm tropical waters.
A frightened octopus can squirt inky fluid that darkens the water.
items.d: The cloud can confuse an animal chasing it.

items.t: An octopus can change color to blend in with its surroundings.
items.d: It can turn gray, brown, pink, blue or green.

items.t: Crabs, shrimps and lobsters are some of an octopus's favorite foods.
Octopuses usually live alone, in dens built from rocks.
An octopus can swim backward by blasting water out of a body tube called a siphon.
The clown anemonefish is only about 10 cm long, but it has a famous partnership.
items.d: It lives safely inside a sea anemone.

items.t: Clownfish live among the stinging tentacles of an anemone and are not bothered by them.
Hiding in an anemone's tentacles helps protect clownfish from hungry animals.
Clownfish nibble away parasites that bother their home anemone.
items.d: That makes them helpful housemates.

items.t: Orcas live and hunt together in family groups called pods.
An orca has about 45 teeth, each about 8 cm long.
Orcas have black backs and white bellies.
There are at least 50 different kinds of seahorses.
Seahorses use their tube-shaped snouts like vacuums to slurp up hundreds of tiny meals a day.
A mother seahorse lays her eggs in a pouch on the dad's belly. Dad carries the babies.
A newborn seahorse is about the size of a jelly bean.
Seahorses can move each eye separately from the other.
A narwhal's tusk can grow up to about 3 meters long.
A narwhal's tusk is really a long spiral tooth. Usually only males grow one.
A narwhal's tusk is packed with nerves and has tiny holes that let seawater in.
Narwhals must swim up to the surface to breathe.
items.d: They are mammals, so they breathe air, like us.

items.t: Jellyfish have been drifting in the oceans for millions of years, even before the dinosaurs.
Jellyfish are not really fish. They have no backbone.
items.d: Animals with no backbone are called invertebrates.

items.t: Jellyfish use tiny stinging cells in their tentacles to stun the food they catch.
A giant squid can grow to at least 10 meters long.
Giant squid have some of the biggest eyes in the animal kingdom, about 25 cm across.
A giant squid moves by squirting water out of a funnel on its body.
Electric eels can release powerful electric charges of about 650 volts.
Electric eels are not true eels. They are more closely related to carp and catfish.
Belugas can nod and turn their heads in all directions.
Belugas talk to each other using clicks, whistles and clangs.
The whale shark is the largest known living fish.
A baby kangaroo is called a joey.
A baby swan is called a cygnet.
A baby hare is called a leveret.
A baby owl is called an owlet.
A baby eagle is called an eaglet.
A baby goat is called a kid.
Baby bats and baby seals are both called pups.
Baby whales, giraffes and elephants are all called calves.
A baby goose is called a gosling.
A baby turkey is called a poult.
A baby porcupine can be called a porcupette.
A baby deer is called a fawn.
A baby horse is a foal. A young female is a filly, and a young male is a colt.
A baby sheep is called a lamb.
A baby pig is called a piglet.
A baby frog is called a tadpole.
A baby oyster is called a spat.
A baby wolf can be called a pup or a cub.
The male emperor penguin incubates the pair's egg by himself.
An emperor penguin egg takes about 65 to 75 days to hatch.
Male emperor penguins huddle and take turns in the warmer middle.
Emperor penguin parents take turns watching their chick and feeding at sea.
Emperor penguin chicks gather in groups called crèches.
items.d: One crèche can contain a dozen to several thousand chicks.

items.t: A male seahorse carries eggs in a pouch near the front of his tail.
A male seahorse releases about 100 to 1,000 young in most species.
Some cuckoos lay their eggs in the nests of other birds.
A newborn kangaroo is about the size of a lima bean.
A joey usually stays in its mother's pouch for about nine months.
A group of kangaroos can be called a mob, court or troupe.
A platypus is a mammal that usually lays two small, leathery eggs.
A mother platypus raises her young in a grass-lined nesting burrow.
items.d: The burrow can be as long as 30 metres.

items.t: Platypus babies lap milk from their mother's fur because she has no teats.
Beaver lodges have underwater entrances and an air vent at the top.
Beaver dams hold back flowing water and form ponds.
A beaver family may welcome up to four babies, called kits, in spring and summer.
Naked mole-rat colonies average 75 to 80 animals.
items.d: Their tunnel networks can stretch 3 to 5 kilometres.

items.t: In a naked mole-rat colony, only one female queen has babies.
A honey bee colony usually has one queen and tens of thousands of female workers.
A honey bee larva fed only royal jelly develops into a queen.
Young worker bees called nurse bees feed larvae and clean the hive.
Honey bee eggs are laid one at a time in wax honeycomb cells.
items.d: Worker bees build and shape the honeycomb.

items.t: A wolf pack is mainly a family made of parents and their offspring.
A lion pride is a group of related lions and their offspring.
items.d: The females form the steady core of the pride.

items.t: A lioness usually gives birth to one to four cubs in a hidden den.
Lion cubs can drink milk from any nursing female in their pride.
An African elephant calf is born after about 22 months of pregnancy.
Young female elephants help mothers care for calves in their family group.
items.d: This shared care is called allomothering.

items.t: An octopus can turn gray, brown, pink, blue, or green.
items.d: Matching the colours around it helps the octopus hide.

items.t: An octopus can squirt a cloud of dark ink.
items.d: The ink darkens the water and confuses whatever is too close.

items.t: An octopus has three hearts.
items.d: One heart moves blood around the body. Two hearts send blood to the gills.

items.t: An octopus has blue blood.
items.d: A copper-rich protein carries oxygen, which makes the blood look blue.

items.t: The veined octopus uses coconut shells to build a shelter.
items.d: It gathers old shells and puts them together. That is a kind of tool use.

items.t: Octopuses are among the smartest animals without a backbone.
items.d: Experiments show they can remember things for a short time and a long time.

items.t: Even a big octopus can slip through a gap a little over 2.5 cm wide.
items.d: That gap is only about 1 inch across.

items.t: Some octopuses can let an arm go and grow a new one.
items.d: Letting the arm go helps them get free. The arm can grow back.

items.t: The mimic octopus can copy lionfish, sea snakes, and jellyfish.
items.d: It changes its shape, colour, and movement to look like those animals.

items.t: Most bat sounds are too high for people to hear.
items.d: Their calls go from about 14,000 to over 100,000 vibrations a second.

items.t: A bat's clicks get much faster as it closes in on a meal.
items.d: The clicks rise from about 10 to 20 a second to about 200 a second.

items.t: Dolphins send a tight beam of high clicks ahead of them.
items.d: Toothed whales, including dolphins, aim the beam where the head points.

items.t: A platypus bill has almost 40,000 electric sensors.
items.d: The sensors pick up faint electric signals from small animals nearby.

items.t: Sharks are the most electricity-sensitive animals known.
items.d: Jelly-filled pores called ampullae of Lorenzini sense tiny electric fields.

items.t: The elephantnose fish sends out weak electric pulses.
items.d: Nearby objects bend those pulses, and the fish reads the bends.

items.t: Bumblebees can sense static electric charges on flowers.
items.d: They notice whether a charge is there and the pattern it makes.

items.t: An electric eel can make up to about 860 volts.
items.d: That is the strongest electricity made by any electric fish.

items.t: An electric eel is not a true eel.
items.d: It is a knifefish, only a distant cousin of true eels.

items.t: An electric eel must gulp air about every two minutes.
items.d: It breathes air at the surface, even though it lives in water.

items.t: An electric eel stacks about 6,000 special muscle cells.
items.d: Each cell makes a small voltage. Together, like battery cells, they add up.

items.t: Chameleons change colour mainly to signal and to control heat.
items.d: Matching the background can happen, but it is not the main reason.

items.t: A chameleon can shoot out its tongue in as little as 0.07 seconds.
items.d: That quick tongue can catch an insect before it hops away.

items.t: A chameleon can look at two things at the same time.
items.d: Each eye can move and focus all by itself.

items.t: In winter sleep, a bear cools only about 3 to 5 degrees C.
items.d: Many hibernators cool by about 32 degrees C or more. Bears stay warmer.

items.t: A hibernating Arctic ground squirrel can reach about minus 2.9 degrees C.
items.d: That is below freezing, yet the squirrel can warm back up.

items.t: The common poorwill is a bird that can hibernate.
items.d: Most birds only take short deep rests. A long winter sleep is unusual for birds.

items.t: Platypus fur can glow cyan and green in ultraviolet light.
items.d: The fur soaks up ultraviolet light and sends it back out as colour.

items.t: A platypus shuts its eyes and ears underwater.
items.d: With eyes and ears closed, it finds food by sensing electricity.

items.t: Axolotls can regrow legs, tails, and parts of the eye and heart.
items.d: A new leg grows over several months, and it does not leave a scar.

items.t: A tiny piece of a planarian can grow into a whole new worm.
items.d: A bit with as few as 10,000 cells can finish the job in one to two weeks.

items.t: A starfish can drop a damaged arm and grow a new one.
items.d: The lost arm slowly grows back over time.

items.t: Salamanders and newts can regrow more parts than other four-legged animals.
items.d: They can regrow limbs, tails, jaws, and parts of their eyes.

items.t: Some lizards can drop the tail, and the tail keeps wiggling.
items.d: The wiggling tail gets the attention, so the lizard has time to run off.

items.t: A cuttlefish can change its skin colour in about one second.
items.d: The change can help it hide, signal friends, or warn others to stay back.

items.t: A worried cuttlefish can let out a cloud of dark ink.
items.d: The ink can work like smoke, or form a decoy shaped a bit like the cuttlefish.

items.t: Wood frogs can freeze solid in winter and still wake in spring.
items.d: They can remain frozen for about 190 days, then thaw and hop again.

items.t: A freezing wood frog makes sugar that works like antifreeze.
items.d: The liver turns stored glycogen into glucose to help protect its cells.

items.t: A wood frog can live with about 65 to 70 percent of its body water frozen.
items.d: Ice can form in most of its body water, and the frog can still recover.

items.t: Pangolin scales are made of keratin, just like your fingernails.
items.d: The scales overlap and cover the pangolin in a tough coat.

items.t: A pangolin can curl into a tight ball when it feels unsafe.
items.d: The hard scales face outward and act like armour.

items.t: A large pangolin can stick its tongue out as far as 40 cm.
items.d: That is about 16 inches, longer than a 30 cm school ruler.

items.t: Sea otters smash shells open by hitting them with rocks.
items.d: Using a rock this way makes the sea otter one of the few mammals that use tools.

items.t: Archerfish spit water to knock insects off plants above the surface.
items.d: A strong jet can hit an insect about 3 metres above the water.

items.t: Monarch caterpillars store bitter chemicals from milkweed.
items.d: The chemicals remain in the butterfly and make it taste awful.

items.t: Eastern North American monarchs fly to central Mexico for winter.
items.d: The trip is about 1,900 to 4,500 km (1,200 to 2,800 miles). The round trip takes several generations.

items.t: A crow named Betty bent a straight wire into a hook.
items.d: In a lab test, nine of ten successful tries used a hook she bent herself.

items.t: A bombardier beetle can spray a mist almost as hot as boiling water.
items.d: It mixes chemicals in its body. The mix nears 100 degrees C and pops out loudly.

items.t: A box jellyfish has 24 eyes.
items.d: The eyes are in four clusters, with six eyes on each cluster.

items.t: An Arctic fox can turn fully white in winter and brown in summer.
items.d: The whole coat changes colour with the seasons.

items.t: Dogs were the first animal people tamed, more than 14,000 years ago.
items.d: That was even before people started farming.

items.t: A dog has about forty times more smell receptors than a person.
items.d: That is why dogs are so good at sniffing out hidden things.

items.t: Dogs can hear sounds up to four times better than people can.
items.d: A dog may hear a car coming long before you do.

items.t: Dogs see a world of mostly yellows, blues and grays.
items.d: Dogs see fewer colors than people do.

items.t: There are around 450 official dog breeds, more than any other mammal.
items.d: From tiny lap dogs to giant farm helpers, dogs come in many shapes.

items.t: People first started living with cats in the Near East about 9,500 years ago.
A cat has dozens of whiskers that it can move.
items.d: Whiskers help a cat feel its way around.

items.t: Cats sleep 12 to 16 hours a day.
items.d: Many cats average 13 to 14 hours, more than half the day.

items.t: Cats can hear about 10.5 octaves of sound, more than people or dogs.
items.d: People and dogs hear about 9 octaves.

items.t: Cats can pull their claws in and push them out when they need them.
items.d: That keeps the claws sharp and tucked away while walking.

items.t: A cat that falls a short way can twist its body and land on its paws.
Cats can see with about one sixth of the light that people need.
items.d: That helps them see in very dim light.

items.t: Hamsters have stretchy cheek pouches that reach back to their shoulders.
items.d: They stuff food in and carry it home to their burrows.

items.t: Pet hamsters are nocturnal, which means they are busiest at night.
items.d: That is why a hamster wheel squeaks while you sleep.

items.t: Syrian hamsters usually live only two to three years.
A hamster's front teeth never stop growing.
items.d: Chewing keeps them from getting too long.

items.t: People in China first bred goldfish for bright colors more than 1,000 years ago.
A pet goldfish can live more than 10 years.
items.d: With good care, it can be a friend for a long time.

items.t: Goldfish have no stomach, so they make lots of waste and need clean water.
Goldfish can tell different people apart.
items.d: A goldfish may learn who feeds it.

items.t: People began taming horses about 6,000 years ago in Central Asia.
items.d: That was around 4000 BCE.

items.t: Horses can sleep both standing up and lying down.
A baby horse, called a foal, can stand and run soon after it is born.
A mother horse carries her baby for about 340 days before it is born.
items.d: That is nearly a whole year.

items.t: Horses are measured in hands. One hand is about 10 cm (4 inches).
items.d: A horse that is 15 hands tall is about 152 cm to the shoulder.

items.t: A pet or farm horse usually lives about 25 to 30 years.
A cow has one big stomach with four parts.
Cows bring food back up and chew it again. This is called chewing the cud.
Taurine cattle were first tamed about 10,500 years ago from wild aurochs.
A cow can see almost all the way around, about 330 degrees.
items.d: People see much less, so a cow notices a lot around it.

items.t: Chickens were first tamed about 8,000 years ago.
Some hens bred for eggs can lay over 300 eggs in a year.
Chickens have a pecking order, where some birds are the bosses of others.
Pigs are about as smart as dogs.
Pigs cool down by rolling in mud or water.
items.d: Mud helps them stay cool on a hot day.

items.t: Mother pigs dig a hollow in the ground the size of their body to make a nest.
Sheep were among the first animals people ever tamed.
Sheep wool is the most widely used animal fiber, and it is cut off by shearing.
Most lambs can stand up within an hour of being born.
Sheep like to stay in a flock and strongly prefer being in a group.
Sheep can remember the faces of about 50 other sheep for over two years.
There are more than 200 kinds of sheep, and their wool can be white to dark brown.
Guinea pigs were first kept by people in the Andes mountains of South America.
Guinea pigs cannot make their own vitamin C, so they must get it from food.
A guinea pig's front teeth never stop growing, so it chews to wear them down.
Rabbits have two sets of front teeth, one behind the other.
Rabbits can see almost all the way around, nearly 360 degrees.
European rabbits live in underground tunnel networks called warrens.
items.d: This is true of European rabbits.

items.t: A rabbit mother can have four to twelve babies in one litter.
items.d: Baby rabbits are called kits.

items.t: The Sun is our solar system's only star. It is about 150 million km from Earth.
The Sun is about 100 times wider than Earth.
The Sun's core is hotter than 15 million degrees Celsius.
The Sun has no moons, but eight planets travel around it.
The Sun is about 4.5 billion years old.
Life on Earth depends on energy from the Sun.
At its equator, the Sun spins around once in about 25 Earth days.
The Sun is a huge ball of hydrogen and helium held together by gravity.
Mercury is both the smallest planet and the closest planet to the Sun.
If Earth were a nickel, Mercury would be about as big as a blueberry.
Mercury travels around the Sun in just 88 Earth days, faster than any other planet.
One full day and night on Mercury lasts about 176 Earth days.
Venus is the hottest planet, even hotter than Mercury.
Venus spins slowly in the opposite direction from most planets.
Venus takes 243 Earth days to spin around once. That is longer than a Venus year.
Venus was named for the ancient Roman goddess of love and beauty.
After the Moon, Venus is the brightest object in Earth's night sky.
Venus has phases, just like the Moon.
Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the fifth largest planet.
Earth is the only planet in our solar system with liquid water on its surface.
Earth has one moon.
Earth has no rings.
Earth's atmosphere protects us from meteoroids. Most burn up as they pass through it.
Earth spins around once every 23.9 hours.
Mars looks red because iron minerals in its dirt have rusted.
Mars was named for the ancient Roman god of war.
If Earth were a nickel, Mars would be about as big as a raspberry.
Olympus Mons on Mars is the largest volcano in the solar system.
Mars has the solar system's largest canyon. It is about 3,900 km long.
Mars has two potato-shaped moons. They have too little mass for gravity to make them round.
A year on Mars lasts 687 Earth days.
Jupiter has the shortest day of any planet, about 9.9 hours.
About 1,000 Earths could fit inside Jupiter if it were hollow.
Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth. It has lasted for hundreds of years.
Jupiter's moon Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system.
Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system. It is even bigger than Mercury.
Evidence shows that Jupiter's moon Europa has a vast ocean beneath its icy crust.
Jupiter has faint rings. The Voyager 1 spacecraft discovered them in 1979.
Saturn is about nine times wider than Earth.
If Earth were a nickel, Saturn would be about as big as a volleyball.
Saturn is less dense than water, so it could float in an enormous bathtub.
A day on Saturn lasts only about 10.7 hours.
Saturn's rings contain billions of small chunks of ice and rock coated with dust.
Saturn has seasons because its axis is tilted, much like Earth's.
Uranus is tilted so far that it appears to spin sideways.
Uranus was the first planet discovered with the help of a telescope.
The moons of Uranus are named for characters created by Shakespeare and Alexander Pope.
Uranus has the most extreme seasons in the solar system because of its unusual tilt.
Methane gas in Uranus's atmosphere helps give the planet its blue-green color.
Winds on Uranus can reach about 900 km per hour.
The International Space Station zooms around Earth at about 8 kilometres every second.
items.d: That is about 28,000 km every hour, so fast it circles Earth in about 90 minutes.

items.t: Astronauts on the space station see 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets every single day.
items.d: The station circles Earth about every 90 minutes, so day and night keep flipping.

items.t: A crew of seven people from different countries can live on the International Space Station.
items.d: They live and work together high above Earth.

items.t: The International Space Station is bigger inside than a six-bedroom house.
items.d: It is about 109 metres long from end to end.

items.t: People have lived on the International Space Station without a break since November 2000.
items.d: Crews take turns, so someone has always been on board.

items.t: Astronauts exercise at least two hours every day in space.
items.d: Without exercise, their muscles and bones would get weak.

items.t: The space station has a robotic arm called Canadarm2 that is about 17 metres long.
items.d: It helps move big pieces of the station, like a giant crane.

items.t: Voyager 1 and Voyager 2 were both launched in 1977.
items.d: They have been travelling through space for decades.

items.t: Voyager 1 entered interstellar space in 2012. Voyager 2 followed in 2018.
items.d: Interstellar space is the space between the stars.

items.t: Each Voyager carries a golden record with sounds and pictures of Earth.
items.d: A team led by scientist Carl Sagan chose what went on each record.

items.t: Voyager 1 was the first human-made object to travel one light-day from Earth.
items.d: That is as far as light travels in one whole day.

items.t: Apollo 11's lunar module landed on the Moon on July 20, 1969.
items.d: It was named Eagle, after the eagle on the mission badge.

items.t: Neil Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin and Michael Collins were the crew of Apollo 11.
items.d: Collins stayed in orbit while the other two landed on the Moon.

items.t: Apollo 11 astronauts brought home about 21.5 kg of Moon rocks and dust.
items.d: Scientists studied them to learn about the Moon's history.

items.t: About 600 million people watched the first Moon walk live on TV.
The Apollo 11 crew splashed down in the Pacific Ocean on July 24, 1969.
items.d: Their capsule landed in the sea with parachutes.

items.t: Sputnik 1, launched on 4 October 1957, was the first artificial satellite to orbit Earth.
Sputnik 1 was a shiny metal ball about 58 cm across.
items.d: It was about as wide as a big beach ball.

items.t: Sputnik 1 sent out radio beeps that people on Earth could hear with radio receivers.
items.d: It circled Earth about once every 96 minutes.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin was the first person to travel into space, on 12 April 1961.
items.d: He flew in a spacecraft called Vostok 1.

items.t: Yuri Gagarin's space flight lasted 108 minutes and went once around Earth.
Valentina Tereshkova orbited Earth 48 times in nearly three days.
items.d: She is the only woman to have flown a solo space mission.

items.t: Sally Ride became the first American woman in space in 1983, on the shuttle Challenger.
Sally Ride used the shuttle's robotic arm to release a satellite and then catch it again.
The Hubble Space Telescope was launched into orbit in 1990 on the space shuttle Discovery.
items.d: It is named after the astronomer Edwin Hubble.

items.t: Hubble was built so astronauts could fix it in space.
items.d: Five shuttle missions repaired and upgraded it.

items.t: Webb's main mirror is 6.5 metres wide and made of 18 gold-coated hexagons.
items.d: The gold helps it reflect infrared light very well.

items.t: Webb travels around the Sun about 1.5 million km from Earth.
Webb's sunshield is about the size of a tennis court and keeps the telescope cold.
items.d: It has five thin layers.

items.t: NASA's space shuttles flew 135 missions between 1981 and 2011.
The five shuttles that flew in space were Columbia, Challenger, Discovery, Atlantis and Endeavour.
Ingenuity was the first helicopter to fly on another planet, on Mars in April 2021.
items.d: It weighed only about 1.8 kg.

items.t: Ingenuity carried a tiny piece of cloth from the Wright brothers' 1903 airplane to Mars.
Curiosity, a Mars rover about the size of a car, landed on Mars on August 6, 2012.
Curiosity was lowered to Mars by a rocket-powered sky crane on ropes.
The Curiosity rover zaps rocks with a laser to find out what they are made of.
The Perseverance rover landed in Jezero Crater on Mars on February 18, 2021.
Perseverance has microphones, and it recorded the sound of wind on Mars.
Perseverance collects rock samples that a future mission might bring back to Earth.
Philae made the first soft landing on a comet on 12 November 2014.
items.d: It was carried there by the European spacecraft Rosetta.

items.t: Parker Solar Probe was launched in 2018 to study the Sun. Its heat shield is made of carbon.
In 2021, Parker Solar Probe became the first spacecraft to enter the Sun's outer atmosphere, the corona.
Skylab, launched in 1973, was the first space station of the United States.
Mir was the first space station built in pieces while in orbit.
items.d: It was put together from 1986 to 1996.

items.t: Alexei Leonov made the first spacewalk on March 18, 1965. It lasted about 12 minutes.
In space there is no air, so a spacesuit gives an astronaut everything needed to breathe.
Twelve people walked on the Moon during six Apollo landings.
items.d: The last landing was Apollo 17 in December 1972.

items.t: Apollo 8 was the first crewed mission to orbit the Moon.
items.d: Astronaut William Anders took the famous Earthrise photo.

items.t: A volcano is an opening where lava, small rocks, and steam reach Earth's surface.
Melted rock is magma underground. After it erupts, it is called lava.
Magma can hold trapped gas, a bit like the fizz inside a sealed soda bottle.
Cinder cones are the simplest type of volcano.
Shield volcanoes grow from runny lava flows and have wide, gently sloping sides.
items.d: From far away, their shape looks like a warrior's shield.

items.t: Volcanoes can be active, dormant, or extinct.
items.d: Dormant means sleeping.

items.t: Some eruptions blast material high into the sky. Others produce slow lava flows.
Hot spots are very hot areas deep inside Earth where lighter magma rises.
Underwater volcanoes can form where tectonic plates pull apart and magma rises.
Io, one of Jupiter's moons, has volcanic plumes erupting from its surface.
Magma rises because it is lighter than nearby solid rock.
items.d: It can gather underground in spaces called magma chambers.

items.t: What magma is made of helps decide how explosive an eruption will be.
Thin, runny magma lets gas escape easily, making eruptions gentler.
Thick magma traps gas more easily, so pressure can build inside it.
Volcanic mudflows form when hot volcanic material mixes with water, snow, or ice.
Earth's crust is about 30 km thick on average beneath land.
Earth's crust is only about 5 km thick beneath the ocean.
The mantle is Earth's biggest layer. It is about 2,900 km thick.
items.d: This rocky layer is mostly solid, but it moves very slowly.

items.t: Earth's outer core is made of liquid iron and nickel.
Earth's inner core is a solid ball made of iron and nickel.
An earthquake happens when two blocks of Earth suddenly slip past each other.
Earth has four main layers: crust, mantle, outer core, and inner core.
Earth's outer shell is split into moving plates, like pieces of a giant puzzle.
Most earthquakes happen along faults near the edges of tectonic plates.
items.d: A fault is a break between blocks of rock.

items.t: Rough plate edges can stick while the rest of each plate keeps moving.
items.d: This stores energy until the edges finally slip.

items.t: When a fault slips, seismic waves carry energy away in every direction.
items.d: These waves make the ground shake.

items.t: A small quake can be called a foreshock only after a larger quake follows it.
A main earthquake is followed by smaller earthquakes called aftershocks.
Scientists need readings from at least three seismograph stations to locate an earthquake.
One whole step up in earthquake magnitude means 10 times greater wave height on a seismogram.
One whole step up in earthquake magnitude means about 32 times more energy is released.
Most fossils begin when a plant or animal is quickly buried by sediment.
Soft body parts usually decay before fossilizing, while hard bones or shells may remain.
Many fossils form when minerals fill tiny spaces in buried remains.
items.d: This can preserve teeth, bones, shells, and wood.

items.t: A trace fossil records what an animal did instead of preserving its body.
items.d: A fossil footprint is one example.

items.t: Fossils of land animals are much scarcer than fossils of animals that lived in water.
The fossil record is incomplete, so it shows only part of life's long history.
Soft tissues rarely become fossils, but rare examples can reveal lots about ancient life.
Earth's rigid outer shell has seven or eight major plates and many smaller ones.
Tectonic plates move about as fast as your fingernails grow.
Plate boundaries come in three main types: convergent, divergent, and transform.
items.d: Plates can move together, apart, or slide past each other.

items.t: Earth's continents were once joined in one huge land mass called Pangaea.
The Ring of Fire around the Pacific Plate is Earth's most active volcanic zone.
The Ring of Fire stretches for about 40,000 km around the Pacific Ocean.
About two-thirds of the world's active or dormant volcanoes are in the Ring of Fire.
About 90% of the world's earthquakes happen within the Ring of Fire.
The Mohs scale ranks how well minerals resist scratches, from 1 to 10.
Diamond is the hardest mineral on the Mohs scale, with a ranking of 10.
Khufu's Great Pyramid is the largest of the three main pyramids at Giza.
items.d: It is the biggest one in the famous pyramid group.

items.t: Each year the Nile flooded and left rich soil that farmers used for crops.
items.d: When the water went down, the soil it left was good for planting food.

items.t: The Nile River flows from south to north.
items.d: Face north, and the water is moving the same way you are looking.

items.t: Hatshepsut was a woman pharaoh who ruled Egypt for 21 years.
items.d: She was the ruler of Egypt for 21 years, a long time to lead a country.

items.t: Ramesses II built more monuments to himself than any other pharaoh.
items.d: A monument is something big, like a statue or temple, made so people remember you.

items.t: The Great Pyramid was the tomb of the pharaoh Khufu.
items.d: A pharaoh was the king of ancient Egypt, and this pyramid was made for him.

items.t: The Great Pyramid was built around 2600 BC and took about 26 years.
items.d: If builders started when a baby was born, that child would be 26 at the end.

items.t: The Great Pyramid once stood about 147 metres tall (about 481 feet).
items.d: About 49 floors of 3 metres each would reach that height, because 49 times 3 is 147.

items.t: The Great Pyramid was built from about 2.3 million stone blocks.
items.d: Together, those blocks weighed about 6 million tonnes.

items.t: For more than 3,700 years, the Great Pyramid was the tallest thing people had built.
items.d: Year after year, nothing built by people stood taller than this pyramid.

items.t: Thousands of workers called up for the job built the Great Pyramid.
items.d: Conscript means people who were called up by the ruler to do a job.

items.t: When it was new, the whole Great Pyramid was covered in smooth white limestone.
items.d: Casing stones made every side smooth and white.

items.t: More than one million animal mummies have been found in Egypt, and many are cats.
items.d: A great number of those animal mummies are cats.

items.t: Tutankhamun became pharaoh when he was only about 8 or 9 years old.
items.d: That is about the same age as you.

items.t: A team led by Howard Carter found Tutankhamun's tomb in 1922.
items.d: Excavators are diggers who uncover old things. Carter led them.

items.t: Tutankhamun's tomb held more than 5,000 objects.
items.d: That is a huge number of objects to find in one tomb.

items.t: The Rosetta Stone was found in July 1799 near Rosetta, in the Nile Delta.
items.d: A French army officer found the stone in the Nile Delta.

items.t: The Rosetta Stone repeats one message in hieroglyphs, Demotic, and Greek.
items.d: Hieroglyphs and Demotic are two Egyptian scripts. The bottom text is Greek.

items.t: The Rosetta Stone's message is a decree from 196 BC praising King Ptolemy V.
items.d: A decree is an official message. This one was written to honor the king.

items.t: In 1822, Jean-Francois Champollion announced in Paris how to read hieroglyphs.
items.d: He shared the key that let people read ancient Egyptian writing again.

items.t: The Rosetta Stone has been on show at the British Museum almost nonstop since 1802.
items.d: It has been there for more than 200 years, with only a few short breaks.

items.t: The Nile is about 7,000 kilometres long, one of the longest rivers on Earth.
items.d: At 30 kilometres a day, walking along it would take more than 200 days.

items.t: Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt were joined into one land around 3150 BC.
items.d: The two lands became one country more than 5,000 years ago.

items.t: Hatshepsut is the second woman confirmed to have ruled Egypt as pharaoh.
items.d: She ruled in her own right, with the full power of a pharaoh.

items.t: Hatshepsut built a famous temple at Deir el-Bahari, across from Luxor.
items.d: It stands opposite the city of Luxor.

items.t: Hatshepsut's trading trip to Punt brought back 31 living myrrh trees.
items.d: Punt was a land they visited for trade, and the trees were still alive.

items.t: Hatshepsut was often shown wearing a false beard, a sign of pharaoh power.
items.d: The beard was not her own hair. It was a symbol that she held royal power.

items.t: Ramesses II ruled for 66 years, one of the longest reigns of any pharaoh.
items.d: A reign is the time a ruler is in charge. His lasted 66 years.

items.t: Howard Carter began working in Egypt when he was only 17.
items.d: He was a teenager, already helping to copy pictures painted in tombs.

items.t: The Great Sphinx has a human head and the body of a lion.
items.d: It is one giant statue with a person's face and a lion's body.

items.t: The Great Sphinx is about 73 metres long and about 20 metres high.
items.d: From paw to tail, the body is about 73 metres long.

items.t: The Great Sphinx was carved from the solid rock of the Giza plateau.
items.d: Workers cut it from one mass of stone that was already in the ground.

items.t: The Sphinx's nose was not shot off by cannon fire. That story is a myth.
items.d: It is a popular tale, but cannon fire did not destroy the nose.

items.t: The Great Sphinx was carved between about 2600 BC and 2500 BC.
items.d: That makes it more than 4,500 years old.

items.t: The Valley of the Kings holds at least 63 tombs, across the Nile from Luxor.
items.d: The tombs sit on the west bank of the river, opposite modern Luxor.

items.t: The Step Pyramid of Djoser at Saqqara rises in six giant steps.
items.d: Each step is smaller than the one below it, like a stone staircase.

items.t: Imhotep, Djoser's vizier, is credited with designing the Step Pyramid.
items.d: A vizier was the pharaoh's top official, like the lead planner.

items.t: The Step Pyramid is the earliest colossal stone building in Egypt.
items.d: Colossal means giant. It was Egypt's first truly huge building of stone.

items.t: Word of the day: papyrus
items.d: Papyrus is a plant. People made writing sheets from its stem. The word paper comes from it. A letter could be written on papyrus.

items.t: Papyrus sheets were first made in Egypt as far back as the third millennium BC.
items.d: The third millennium BC means the years from about 3000 BC to 2000 BC.

items.t: Egyptians also used papyrus reeds to build boats.
items.d: The plant was useful for more than paper. People built reed boats from it.

items.t: Senet was an Egyptian board game with 30 squares in three rows of 10.
items.d: Three rows of 10 squares make 30 squares, because 3 times 10 is 30.

items.t: A senet game was found in Tutankhamun's tomb.
items.d: Finding the game in his tomb shows it was packed among his things.

items.t: Listing everything in Tutankhamun's tomb took Howard Carter nearly 10 years.
items.d: He wrote careful notes on each object, and the job lasted almost 10 years.

items.t: In 1968, Abu Simbel's temples were moved to higher ground to save them.
items.d: The whole temples were shifted to higher ground so Lake Nasser would not cover them.

items.t: Abu Simbel's Great Temple has four giant statues of Ramesses II.
items.d: Each statue is about 20 metres tall (66 feet), carved in the 13th century BC.

items.t: Cleopatra is the only ruler of her dynasty known to have learned the Egyptian language.
items.d: A dynasty is a ruling family. She was born in Alexandria and ruled from 51 BC to 30 BC.

items.t: Queen Nefertiti's famous painted bust is at the Neues Museum in Berlin.
items.d: She was the queen of Akhenaten. A bust shows the head and shoulders, and hers is painted.

items.t: The ancient Olympic Games are traditionally dated to 776 BC.
items.d: They were held at Olympia in Greece.

items.t: Ancient Olympic winners got a crown of olive leaves, not a gold medal.
items.d: A wreath of leaves was the prize for being the best.

items.t: The ancient Greeks held the Olympics every four years. That gap was called an Olympiad.
items.d: An Olympiad also became a way to count time.

items.t: Ancient Olympic athletes ran, wrestled, boxed and raced chariots.
items.d: Pankration was another event.

items.t: The word stadium comes from the stadion, a short sprint that was the first Olympic event.
items.d: So every stadium is named after a footrace.

items.t: Cynisca of Sparta was the first woman to win at the ancient Olympics, with a chariot team she owned.
A Roman legion had about 5,000 soldiers on foot. It was split into ten smaller groups called cohorts.
A Roman legionary usually signed up for 25 years of service.
items.d: That is a very long time to be a soldier.

items.t: Roman soldiers were builders too. They made roads, bridges, ports and even whole new cities.
The Romans built more than 400,000 km of roads. That is about ten times around Earth.
items.d: Earth is about 40,000 km around, so 400,000 km wraps around 10 times.

items.t: The Appian Way is one of the oldest and most important Roman roads.
items.d: Milestones along it showed travelers the numbered miles.

items.t: Ancient Greece had about 1,500 city-states, each called a polis.
items.d: City-states used different systems of rule, including democracy and aristocracy.

items.t: Greek city-states founded colonies. This spread Greek language, religion and art.
Spartan boys began their training at age seven, in a school system called the agoge.
The word democracy comes from Greek and means people power.
Cleisthenes grouped Athenians into ten groups by where they lived, not by how rich they were.
Socrates was a Greek thinker from Athens who taught by asking short questions.
items.d: He never wrote books. We know him from what his students wrote.

items.t: Plato founded the Academy, a school of ideas in Athens.
items.d: Many of his writings are conversations, called dialogues.

items.t: Aristotle tutored a boy named Alexander, who grew up to be Alexander the Great.
Aristotle was the first person to study biology in an organized way.
Archimedes was born in the seaport city of Syracuse, Sicily.
items.d: He was a Greek thinker who loved math and machines.

items.t: Archimedes explained buoyancy: fluid pushes up with the weight of the fluid an object moves aside.
items.d: That is why a boat floats.

items.t: The Colosseum is the largest ancient amphitheatre ever built, and the largest still standing.
The Colosseum could hold about 50,000 to 80,000 people.
The Colosseum had a retractable awning, the velarium, to keep sun and rain off the crowd.
Augustus was the first Roman emperor. He ruled from 27 BC to AD 14.
items.d: The month of August is named after him.

items.t: Augustus began the Pax Romana, a long period of relative peace in the Roman world.
Roman aqueducts sloped only a tiny bit, about 1 part in 4,800, so water flowed without pumps.
items.d: Gravity did all the work.

items.t: The aqueducts of Rome added up to over 415 km. Some still bring water to Rome today.
Pompeii had at least 31 bakeries, each with a wood-burning oven.
items.d: The town was buried by ash when Mount Vesuvius erupted in AD 79.

items.t: Julius Caesar created the Julian calendar, which the Romans used.
Julius Caesar wrote Commentaries about events in Gaul.
Julius Caesar crossed the Rubicon river with his army, openly defying the Roman Senate.
Romans called breakfast ientaculum, lunch prandium and dinner cena.
Most Roman citizens visited a public bath at least once a day.
Many Romans lived in apartment blocks called insulae.
The Romans spoke Latin.
items.d: Many words in English, French, Spanish and Italian come from Latin.

items.t: The Parthenon was a temple of Athena on the Acropolis in Athens.
After Alexander's conquests, Greek culture spread into North Africa and Western Asia.
Hadrian's Wall in Britain stretches about 117 km. Work began in AD 122.
Hadrian's Wall became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1987.
items.d: Three Roman legions built most of it in about six years.

items.t: Roman legionaries carried a big rectangular shield called a scutum.
Many Roman bridges were built so well that people still use them today.
Sparta had two kings ruling at the same time.
The Greek alphabet developed in the Archaic period of ancient Greece.
Roman soldiers spent most of their time on training and daily jobs, not on fighting.
Aristotle taught at a building in Athens called the Lyceum.
Vikings were the first Europeans known to reach North America.
Vikings began settling Iceland in the 9th century.
Vikings used an alphabet of angular letters called runes.
Many everyday English words came from the Vikings' Old Norse language.
Horned Viking helmets are a myth. There is no evidence that Vikings wore them.
Viking longships were fast and agile, using both sails and oars.
Longship builders overlapped the wooden planks that formed the hull.
items.d: This building method is called clinker-building.

items.t: Some longships had dragon-shaped carvings on their bows.
items.d: These decorated vessels were sometimes called dragonships.

items.t: The Gokstad Viking ship is nearly 24 metres long.
Longships used oars near coasts and on rivers to speed up quickly.
A Viking longship could reach about 28 kilometres per hour.
items.d: That is about 15 knots in good conditions.

items.t: Oak was a favourite wood for longships because it was strong and resisted rot.
A boy training to become a knight could become a page at about age seven.
A page training to be a knight could become a squire at about age 14.
Knights were expected to be brave, skilled and courteous.
The joust was the most popular contest at many knights' tournaments.
A motte was a flat-topped mound of earth used as the base of some castles.
A bailey was a protected yard inside a castle where the household lived.
A moat was a ditch around a castle that made tunnelling and moving towers harder.
The keep was a castle's main living place, often a great tower.
Curtain walls were tall, thick walls surrounding a castle's bailey.
A portcullis was a gridded wooden gate strengthened with metal.
items.d: It could be lowered to block a castle entrance.

items.t: Norman builders put up many castles in England after 1066.
Complete suits of plate armour appeared in Europe by about 1420.
A full suit of plate armour weighed about 15 to 25 kilograms.
A person wearing plate armour could still run, jump and move freely.
Chain mail was made from many tiny linked rings of iron or steel.
Warriors usually wore a shirt of chain mail beneath their plate armour.
Jousting was very popular with Norman-English knights.
A tilt barrier kept jousting horses apart so they would not collide.
Jousting is the official state sport of Maryland in the United States.
L'Anse aux Meadows is a Viking site at the northern tip of Newfoundland, Canada.
L'Anse aux Meadows became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1978.
The Norse settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows dates to about the year 1000.
Tree rings show that Vikings cut wood at L'Anse aux Meadows in 1021.
Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found the Viking site at L'Anse aux Meadows.
items.d: They were Norwegian. Helge was an explorer and Anne Stine was an archaeologist.

items.t: More than 800 Norse objects have been uncovered at L'Anse aux Meadows.
The Bayeux Tapestry is nearly 70 metres long but only about 50 centimetres tall.
The Bayeux Tapestry shows events from England and Normandy in the 11th century.
The Bayeux Tapestry is really an embroidery because its pictures were stitched.
The Bayeux Tapestry contains the first known picture of Halley's Comet.
The final scenes of the Bayeux Tapestry are missing.
Traditional English longbows were made from yew wood.
Some luxury medieval books used vellum made from stretched calf skin.
A manuscript is truly illuminated only if its decoration includes gold or silver.
The Book of Kells is the best-known illuminated manuscript in the English-speaking world.
Medieval craft workers trained as apprentices, then journeymen, then masters.
Guilds controlled who was allowed to trade in many medieval towns.
Guilds kept shared funds to help members who were ill or elderly.
Roald Amundsen and his team of five were the first people to reach the South Pole, on 14 December 1911.
items.d: They had 16 sled dogs with them.

items.t: Amundsen led the first expedition to sail through Canada's Northwest Passage.
items.d: It is an icy sea route through the far north of Canada.

items.t: Roald Amundsen learned to use sled dogs to carry goods across the ice.
items.d: Strong dogs can pull heavy loads over snow, which helped him in the race to the Pole.

items.t: Robert Scott's team reached the South Pole on 17 January 1912 and found the Norwegians had been there first.
items.d: They found Amundsen's tent nearby.

items.t: Three men walked through the Antarctic winter to collect emperor penguin eggs at Cape Crozier.
items.d: Scientists wanted the eggs to learn how penguins grow.

items.t: Apsley Cherry-Garrard called the winter egg trek 'the worst journey in the world'.
items.d: He used those words as the title of his book about the expedition.

items.t: Apsley Cherry-Garrard joined Scott's expedition as an assistant zoologist with no science training.
items.d: A zoologist studies animals.

items.t: Ernest Shackleton named his ship Endurance after his family motto.
items.d: The ship's first name was Polaris.

items.t: Endurance sank in the Weddell Sea on 21 November 1915.
items.d: The Weddell Sea is off the coast of Antarctica.

items.t: Sea ice covers the Weddell Sea all year round.
items.d: It lies off the coast of Antarctica.

items.t: The wreck of the Endurance was found on 5 March 2022.
items.d: It had been lost for more than 100 years.

items.t: The wreck of the Endurance lies about 3,000 metres deep, and it was still in very good shape.
items.d: That is about 3 km down on the seabed.

items.t: Shackleton's crew reached Elephant Island, a remote island where nobody lived and ships rarely came.
items.d: It is near Antarctica.

items.t: Shackleton and five men sailed the small lifeboat James Caird about 1,300 km to South Georgia.
items.d: That is about 800 miles across the Southern Ocean.

items.t: Ernest Shackleton chose Frank Wild as his second-in-command.
items.d: The second-in-command is the person who helps the leader.

items.t: Shackleton brought all the men stranded on Elephant Island home safely.
items.d: The group was rescued without loss of life.

items.t: Marco Polo was born around 1254 in Venice.
items.d: Venice is famous for its canals.

items.t: Marco Polo set off for Asia in 1271 when he was 17, with his father and uncle.
items.d: The trip took them across lands far from home.

items.t: Kublai Khan made Marco Polo a foreign emissary.
items.d: An emissary is someone sent to carry out jobs for a ruler.

items.t: Marco Polo returned to Venice in 1295 after 24 years away.
items.d: He had left when he was a teenager.

items.t: Marco Polo told his travel stories to Rustichello da Pisa, who wrote them down in a book.
items.d: The book is called The Travels of Marco Polo.

items.t: Ferdinand Magellan's fleet had five ships and about 270 men.
items.d: Their goal was to sail across the seas to reach Asia.

items.t: Ferdinand Magellan gave the Pacific Ocean its name.
items.d: Pacific means calm or peaceful.

items.t: Magellan's ship Victoria, led by Juan Sebastian Elcano, finished the trip around the world in 1522.
items.d: Only about 18 or 19 of the first crew got back to Spain.

items.t: Christopher Columbus was born in the Republic of Genoa.
items.d: He later sailed for Spain.

items.t: Columbus left Spain in August 1492 with three ships, the Nina, the Pinta and the Santa Maria.
items.d: Each ship was small compared with ships today.

items.t: Columbus landed on an island in the Bahamas on 12 October 1492.
items.d: It was his first landing in the Americas.

items.t: On 29 May 1953, Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary were the first confirmed to reach the top of Everest.
items.d: Tenzing was a Sherpa mountaineer.

items.t: Expedition leader John Hunt said Hillary and Tenzing reached Everest's top together, as a team.
items.d: He described their achievement as teamwork.

items.t: A 2020 survey by Nepal and China measured Mount Everest at about 8,849 metres tall.
items.d: That is almost 9 km above sea level.

items.t: Mount Everest is named after Sir George Everest, a British surveyor in India.
items.d: A surveyor measures land and mountains.

items.t: The Nepali name for Mount Everest, Sagarmatha, means roughly 'head in the sky'.
items.d: The mountain's peak is very high.

items.t: Challenger Deep is named after HMS Challenger, a British Royal Navy survey ship.
