items.d: The ship's crews explored the oceans.

items.t: In January 1960 the submarine Trieste made the first trip down to Challenger Deep.
items.d: Trieste was a deep-diving vessel called a bathyscaphe.

items.t: Challenger Deep is at the southern end of the Mariana Trench and is about 10,935 metres deep.
items.d: That is about 11 km below sea level.

items.t: President Thomas Jefferson sent Lewis and Clark on an expedition soon after the Louisiana Purchase of 1803.
items.d: The purchase gave the US a huge new area of land.

items.t: The Corps of Discovery was a group of soldiers and volunteers led by Meriwether Lewis and William Clark.
items.d: They set out in May 1804.

items.t: Lewis's Newfoundland dog, Seaman, was the only animal to finish the whole Lewis and Clark trip.
items.d: Seaman was a big, strong dog.

items.t: The Lewis and Clark team first saw the Pacific Ocean on 7 November 1805.
items.d: They had travelled for about a year and a half to get there.

items.t: Between 1405 and 1433, Zheng He led seven treasure voyages across Asia.
items.d: His fleets sailed from China.

items.t: A giraffe brought to China from Malindi was seen as a qilin, a lucky mythical creature.
items.d: Zheng He's ships carried it home.

items.t: Ibn Battuta set off from Tangier at age 21 and travelled for about 30 years.
items.d: He was born there in 1304 and travelled from 1325 to 1354.

items.t: Ibn Battuta travelled about 117,000 km over about 30 years.
items.d: Earth's distance around is about 40,000 km.

items.t: Hiram Bingham led the 1911 Yale expedition that made Machu Picchu famous around the world.
items.d: A local man, Melchor Arteaga, led him to the site.

items.t: Fridtjof Nansen made the first crossing of Greenland's interior on skis in 1888.
items.d: Greenland is covered by a huge sheet of ice.

items.t: Nansen's ship Fram was frozen into Arctic ice and drifted along with it.
items.d: The plan was to let the moving ice carry the ship.

items.t: Fridtjof Nansen won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1922 for helping people made homeless by World War I.
items.d: He was an explorer, and he also helped others.

items.t: Charles Darwin was 22 when he joined HMS Beagle for a voyage that began in December 1831.
items.d: The voyage ended in October 1836.

items.t: The Beagle voyage was planned for about two years, but it lasted almost five.
items.d: It sailed around the world.

items.t: In 2014 Malala Yousafzai won the Nobel Peace Prize at age 17.
items.d: She was the youngest person ever to win a Nobel Prize.

items.t: The United Nations called 12 July 2013 Malala Day, her 16th birthday.
items.d: On that day she gave a speech about education for children.

items.t: Malala Yousafzai campaigns for education, especially for girls.
items.d: She also speaks up for children's rights, including the right to learn.

items.t: At 15, Greta Thunberg began a school strike for the climate in Sweden.
items.d: In 2018 she began alone outside parliament, where Sweden's leaders meet.

items.t: Greta Thunberg's strike grew into the worldwide Fridays for Future movement.
items.d: It spread from one solo strike to people in countries around the world.

items.t: In August 2019 Greta Thunberg sailed across the Atlantic to New York.
items.d: She left from Plymouth, England, and the trip ended in New York City.

items.t: In 1930 Gandhi led the Dandi Salt March, a walk of about 400 km.
items.d: About 400 km is about 250 miles. The march protested a British tax on salt.

items.t: Gandhi led India's freedom movement through nonviolent resistance.
items.d: Nonviolent resistance means standing up for change without hurting people.

items.t: Gandhi was first called Mahatma, meaning great-souled, in 1914.
items.d: The title was first used for him in South Africa.

items.t: Nelson Mandela spent 27 years in prison, starting on Robben Island.
items.d: Robben Island is where his long prison time began.

items.t: Nelson Mandela was set free from prison in 1990.
items.d: President F. W. de Klerk released him that year.

items.t: In 1994 Nelson Mandela became South Africa's first Black head of state.
items.d: A head of state is a country's top leader. He won the first election open to every adult.

items.t: Nelson Mandela received more than 250 honours, including the Nobel Peace Prize.
items.d: A honour is a special award for doing great things. He won more than 250 of them.

items.t: In 1955 Rosa Parks refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery.
items.d: This happened in Montgomery, Alabama. She stayed seated when told to move.

items.t: The Montgomery bus boycott that followed Rosa Parks lasted 381 days.
items.d: A boycott means people join together and stop using something. This one lasted more than a year.

items.t: In 1963 Martin Luther King Jr. gave the 'I Have a Dream' speech.
items.d: He was a leader of the March on Washington, where he gave that speech.

items.t: Martin Luther King Jr. won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964.
items.d: He was honoured for fighting racial inequality with nonviolent resistance.

items.t: The US holiday for Martin Luther King Jr. was first observed in 1986.
items.d: The holiday honours his nonviolent work against racial inequality.

items.t: Kailash Satyarthi shared the 2014 Nobel Peace Prize with Malala Yousafzai.
items.d: Sharing a prize means both people were honoured together that year.

items.t: Kailash Satyarthi started Bachpan Bachao Andolan to protect children.
items.d: The name means Save Childhood Movement. It works to keep children safe.

items.t: Kailash Satyarthi's team freed over 138,000 children in India from child labour.
items.d: Child labour means children are forced to work. His team helps them become free.

items.t: In 1980 India gave Mother Teresa the Bharat Ratna, its highest civilian award.
items.d: A civilian award is for people who are not in the military. This is India's top one.

items.t: Mother Teresa won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1979.
items.d: She was honoured for her work to overcome poverty and distress.

items.t: In 1977 Wangari Maathai founded the Green Belt Movement to plant trees.
items.d: It is a group that cares for nature. Its main work is planting trees.

items.t: In 2004 Wangari Maathai became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.
items.d: No African woman had received the Nobel Peace Prize before her.

items.t: Wangari Maathai was the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a PhD.
items.d: A PhD, or Doctor of Philosophy, is one of the highest university degrees.

items.t: In 1913 Rabindranath Tagore won the Nobel Prize in Literature.
items.d: He was the first non-European, and the first Indian, to win any Nobel Prize.

items.t: Rabindranath Tagore wrote the national anthems of India and Bangladesh.
items.d: He wrote the words and composed the music for both countries' special songs.

items.t: Rabindranath Tagore founded Visva-Bharati University.
items.d: A university is a school for older students. He created this one.

items.t: Mary Kom won an Olympic bronze medal in boxing at London 2012.
items.d: Flyweight is a boxing group based on weight. Her medal came in that event.

items.t: Mary Kom has won the World Amateur Boxing Championship six times.
items.d: She grew up in rural Manipur, India, then became a world champion boxer.

items.t: At Tokyo 2020, Neeraj Chopra's javelin throw of 87.58 m won gold.
items.d: A javelin is a long spear. Athletes try to throw it as far as they can.

items.t: Neeraj Chopra was the first Indian to win Olympic gold in athletics.
items.d: Athletics means track and field events, like running, jumping, and throwing.

items.t: Sachin Tendulkar played his first Test cricket match in 1989, at age 16.
items.d: A Test is a long cricket match between countries. His was against Pakistan on 15 November 1989.

items.t: Sachin Tendulkar scored 100 centuries in international cricket.
items.d: A century means 100 runs in one innings. He did that 100 times for India.

items.t: Sachin Tendulkar was part of India's 2011 Cricket World Cup winning team.
items.d: Across six World Cups for India, this was his first win.

items.t: P. V. Sindhu is the first Indian woman to win two Olympic medals.
items.d: She won badminton silver at Rio 2016 and bronze at Tokyo 2020.

items.t: In 2019 Sindhu was the first Indian to win gold at the badminton World Championships.
items.d: She won gold at the World Championships, the big world badminton contest.

items.t: B. R. Ambedkar led the committee that wrote India's Constitution.
items.d: A constitution is the basic set of rules for a country.

items.t: Savitribai Phule is widely regarded as India's first woman teacher.
items.d: Widely regarded means many people agree she was the first.

items.t: In 1848 Savitribai Phule helped found a school for girls at Bhide Wada, Pune.
items.d: Bhide Wada is the place in Pune where that girls' school began.

items.t: Harriet Tubman escaped slavery on 17 September 1849.
items.d: Slavery means people were owned and forced to work. She got herself free.

items.t: Harriet Tubman made about 13 trips and rescued about 70 enslaved people.
items.d: She went back again and again so others could reach freedom too.

items.t: Helen Keller lost her sight and hearing from illness at 19 months old.
items.d: She was younger than two. The illness left her unable to see or hear.

items.t: Anne Sullivan was Helen Keller's teacher and lifelong companion.
items.d: A companion is someone who stays with you. Anne taught Helen and stayed.

items.t: In 1904 Helen Keller earned a college degree at Radcliffe.
items.d: She was the first person who was deaf and blind to earn a Bachelor of Arts.

items.t: Jesse Owens won four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics.
items.d: He won the 100 m, the 200 m, the long jump, and the 4x100 m relay.

items.t: Most of Frida Kahlo's paintings are small pictures of herself.
items.d: These are called self-portraits. She painted them at a small size.

items.t: Frida Kahlo's family home, La Casa Azul, is now a museum.
items.d: La Casa Azul means the Blue House. It is the Frida Kahlo Museum.

items.t: In 1960 Ruby Bridges, age six, was the first African American child at William Frantz Elementary.
items.d: The school is in New Orleans. U.S. marshals walked with her to school each day.

items.t: Atoms are incredibly tiny, about 100 picometers across.
items.d: That is far too small to see, even with a normal microscope.

items.t: Every atom has a nucleus in the middle, made of protons and usually neutrons.
items.d: Tiny electrons form a swarm around it.

items.t: Almost all of an atom's mass is packed into its tiny nucleus.
items.d: The swarm of electrons around it weighs very little.

items.t: Protons have a positive charge, and neutrons have no charge at all.
items.d: Electrons are negative.

items.t: Hydrogen atoms have one proton. Oganesson atoms have 118 protons.
items.d: The number of protons tells you which element it is.

items.t: Mendeleev used his periodic table to predict properties of elements not yet found.
items.d: He left gaps for them and guessed their properties.

items.t: There are 118 known elements. The first 94 occur naturally on Earth.
items.d: The rest are made by scientists.

items.t: The noble gases sit in group 18. They were not found yet when Mendeleev made his table.
items.d: Helium and neon are noble gases.

items.t: An element's atomic number is the number of protons in its nucleus.
items.d: Carbon has 6 protons, so its atomic number is 6.

items.t: Elements in the same group of the periodic table tend to behave in similar ways.
items.d: That is why the table is so useful to chemists.

items.t: In a solid, particles cannot move around freely. They only jiggle in place.
items.d: That is why a rock keeps its shape.

items.t: A liquid takes the shape of its container, and it is almost impossible to squash.
items.d: Juice fills a cup, then fills a bottle the same way.

items.t: Liquids are very hard to squash, but gases can be squashed. Gas molecules are far apart.
items.d: A bike pump squeezes air into a smaller space.

items.t: Plasma forms when it is so hot that electrons break away from their atoms.
items.d: It is a fourth state of matter, after solid, liquid and gas.

items.t: About 99% of ordinary matter in the universe is plasma.
items.d: Here on Earth, solids, liquids and gases are far more common.

items.t: Stars are almost pure balls of plasma.
items.d: Our Sun is one of them.

items.t: Lightning and glowing neon signs both contain plasma.
Pure water is neutral. It has a pH of 7 at 25 degrees Celsius.
items.d: Acids are below 7 and bases are above 7.

items.t: Lemon juice tastes sour because it has citric acid. Its pH is about 2.2.
items.d: Its low pH means the juice is acidic.

items.t: Each step on the pH scale is a tenfold change in hydrogen ions.
items.d: A liquid at pH 3 has ten times more hydrogen ions than one at pH 4.

items.t: Red cabbage and hibiscus flowers contain pigments that work as natural pH indicators.
items.d: They change color depending on how acidic a liquid is.

items.t: When an acid reacts with a base, it is called neutralization. The products are a salt and water.
Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate. It is not the same thing as baking powder.
items.d: They are different kitchen ingredients.

items.t: Quartz sand, also called silica, is the main raw material for making glass.
items.d: Beach sand and glass are close relatives.

items.t: Glass is an amorphous solid. Its atoms are not in a neat repeating pattern.
items.d: A salt crystal is neat. Glass is more jumbled.

items.t: Borosilicate glass resists cracking when its temperature changes suddenly.
items.d: Handy for glass dishes that go in a hot oven.

items.t: Obsidian is natural glass from volcanoes. It breaks into very sharp edges.
items.d: People long ago used it to make cutting tools.

items.t: Lightning striking sand can melt it into glass shaped like branching roots.
items.d: These are called fulgurites.

items.t: Plastics are materials made mainly of polymers.
The first fully synthetic plastic was invented in New York in 1907.
Thermoplastics can be heated and reshaped again and again without changing chemically.
The word plastic comes from a Greek word meaning able to be shaped or molded.
A mixture has two or more substances that can be separated by physical methods.
items.d: You can pick raisins out of a trail mix.

items.t: Mixtures can be separated by filtering, freezing, or distilling.
items.d: A coffee filter separates grounds from liquid.

items.t: In a chemical reaction, the amount of each element stays the same. Atoms just rearrange.
items.d: Nothing is lost. Atoms are not created or destroyed.

items.t: Reactions that release heat are exothermic. Reactions that absorb heat are endothermic.
items.d: Burning a candle gives out heat.

items.t: A catalyst speeds up a reaction and is not used up, so it can work again.
Atoms of the same element can have different numbers of neutrons. These are called isotopes.
items.d: Carbon always has 6 protons, but not always the same neutrons.

items.t: Only two elements are liquid at 0 degrees Celsius: bromine and mercury.
Hydrogen and helium, the lightest elements, were made in the Big Bang.
Gold's chemical symbol, Au, comes from aurum, the Latin word for gold.
Gold is the most malleable metal. One gram can be beaten into a sheet of one square meter.
items.d: That sheet would be thinner than a hair.

items.t: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at standard temperature and pressure.
Helium is the second most common element in the observable universe, after hydrogen.
Oxygen gas makes up about 21% of Earth's atmosphere.
items.d: Most of the rest is nitrogen.

items.t: The oxygen in Earth's air is made by photosynthesis.
items.d: Plants, algae and some bacteria release it.

items.t: Diamond is a form of the element carbon, with atoms in a crystal pattern.
items.d: Pencil graphite is also made of carbon.

items.t: Volcanic eruptions carried diamonds up to the surface, inside rocks called kimberlites.
Light travels about 300,000 km every second through empty space.
items.d: In one second, light could travel around Earth more than seven times.

items.t: Sunlight takes a little over 8 minutes to reach Earth.
items.d: The sunlight you see began its trip more than 8 minutes ago.

items.t: Light moves more slowly through water or glass than through empty space.
Water droplets split, bend, and reflect sunlight to make a rainbow.
In a main rainbow, red is outside and violet is inside.
A double rainbow has a faint second arc with its colours reversed.
Every rainbow is really a full circle.
items.d: From the ground, you usually see only the upper part of the circle.

items.t: To see a rainbow, look for water ahead with the low Sun behind you.
A glass prism can split white light into a spectrum of colours.
A prism bends blue light more than red light.
The daytime sky looks blue because air scatters blue light more than red light.
Sunsets look red because much of the blue light has scattered away.
items.d: Light from a low Sun travels through a longer path of air.

items.t: William Herschel discovered invisible infrared light in 1800.
People give off infrared light that thermal cameras can detect.
Remote controls commonly use infrared light to command appliances.
Infrared is often called heat radiation.
Sound travels through air at about 343 metres per second at 20°C.
Sound travels faster in water than in air.
items.d: In fresh water at 20°C, it travels about 1,481 metres per second.

items.t: Sound travels faster through warm air than through cold air.
An echo is a sound that bounces off a surface and returns a moment later.
A clear echo needs a reflecting surface more than about 17 metres from the sound source.
Bats, dolphins, and whales use echoes to navigate.
items.d: This way of locating things is called echolocation.

items.t: Sonar technology finds things by using echoes.
A passing siren sounds higher as it approaches and lower as it moves away.
items.d: This change in pitch is called the Doppler effect.

items.t: People typically hear sounds from about 20 to 20,000 hertz.
items.d: Hertz measures how many sound vibrations happen each second.

items.t: Dogs can hear pitches up to about 45,000 hertz, much higher than people can.
Some bats can hear pitches as high as 200,000 hertz.
A freely falling object speeds up by about 9.8 metres per second each second.
items.d: This is what happens when air resistance is ignored.

items.t: You would weigh about 0.5% more at the poles than at the equator.
items.d: Earth's gravity is slightly stronger near the poles.

items.t: Gravity near the space station is almost 90% as strong as it is on the ground.
items.d: Astronauts float because they and the station are falling around Earth together.

items.t: Friction is a force that resists surfaces sliding against each other.
Friction can change movement energy into heat.
items.d: Rubbing two surfaces together can make them warmer.

items.t: Oil and other lubricants reduce friction between surfaces.
Break a bar magnet in two, and each piece has a north and south pole.
Opposite magnetic poles attract each other.
items.d: A north pole and a south pole pull together.

items.t: A compass needle is a magnet that lines up with Earth's magnetic field.
Iron, nickel, and cobalt are strongly attracted to magnets.
The six simple machines include the lever, pulley, wedge, screw, wheel and axle, and inclined plane.
Simple machines change the size or direction of a force to make jobs easier.
An object stays still or moves in a straight line at a steady speed unless a force acts on it.
items.d: This idea is Newton's first law of motion.

items.t: Force equals mass times acceleration.
items.d: This rule is Newton's second law of motion, often written as F = ma.

items.t: When two things push on each other, their forces are equal and opposite.
items.d: This idea is Newton's third law of motion.

items.t: Water pushes up on an object with a force equal to the weight of water it displaces.
items.d: This is called Archimedes' principle.

items.t: Steel ships float because their air-filled shape makes them less dense overall than water.
Heat naturally flows from a hotter object to a colder object.
Metals such as copper and gold conduct heat well.
Air conducts heat poorly, so trapped air can act as insulation.
Kinetic energy is the energy an object has because it is moving.
If the same object doubles its speed, it has four times as much kinetic energy.
Ada Lovelace wrote steps for a machine to calculate special numbers. Many call it the first published program.
items.d: Her notes were published in 1843.

items.t: Ada Lovelace imagined that a machine might one day make music, not just do sums.
items.d: She wrote this in the 1840s, long before any modern computer existed.

items.t: Ada Lovelace added notes to an article about a machine. Her notes were three times longer than the article.
ENIAC, finished in 1945, was a giant computer that weighed about 27 tonnes.
items.d: That is heavier than about five elephants.

items.t: ENIAC used about 18,000 glass parts called vacuum tubes to do its sums.
items.d: Today a tiny chip does far more with no glowing tubes at all.

items.t: Six women programmed ENIAC.
items.d: They included Kay McNulty, Betty Jean Jennings and Betty Holberton.

items.t: Computers use binary, a number system with only two digits: 0 and 1.
items.d: Counting in binary goes 0, 1, 10, 11, 100.

items.t: A single binary digit is called a bit. The word is short for binary digit.
In binary, 101 means 4 + 0 + 1, which is 5.
items.d: Each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8 and so on.

items.t: Computers use binary because two states, like on and off, are easy to build with electric circuits.
items.d: A switch is either on (1) or off (0).

items.t: A byte is usually a group of eight bits.
items.d: Computer memory is often counted in bytes.

items.t: One byte can hold 256 different values, from 0 to 255.
items.d: That is because 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 = 256.

items.t: In 1947, a real moth was found stuck in a computer relay and taped into the team's log book.
items.d: The team jokingly called it the first actual bug they had found.

items.t: Grace Hopper is often credited with creating the first compiler, a tool that translates computer code.
Grace Hopper helped create COBOL, a programming language that reads a bit like English.
items.d: She was nicknamed Grandma COBOL.

items.t: Tim Berners-Lee proposed the World Wide Web in 1989 while he worked at a science lab called CERN.
The very first website went online in December 1990. It explained the web project itself.
The World Wide Web was given away free. It had no patent and no fees, so anyone could use it.
The web and the Internet are not the same. The web is a system of linked pages built on the Internet.
items.d: The Internet is the network of wires and computers underneath.

items.t: The first message sent over ARPANET in 1969 was just 'lo'. The computer crashed after two letters of 'login'.
items.d: It went from a computer at UCLA to one at Stanford Research Institute.

items.t: ARPANET was an early network that sent data as small pieces called packets.
items.d: Today the Internet still breaks data into packets.

items.t: On 1 January 1983, ARPANET switched to TCP/IP, the shared language of the Internet.
In 1936, Alan Turing described an imaginary machine that helped form the theory of computing.
In 1950, Alan Turing proposed a test using written conversation with a person and a machine.
items.d: If a judge could not tell them apart, the machine could be said to think.

items.t: In 1997 a chess computer called Deep Blue beat the world champion Garry Kasparov in a six-game match.
items.d: It could look at about 200 million chess positions every second.

items.t: Douglas Engelbart and Bill English built the first computer mouse prototype in 1964.
items.d: It was shown to the public on 9 December 1968.

items.t: The computer that helped guide Apollo to the Moon had only 2,048 words of working memory.
items.d: A modern phone has millions of times more.

items.t: On Apollo 11 the computer gave alarms but kept the most important jobs running, so the landing went on.
Margaret Hamilton's MIT team wrote software for the Apollo spacecraft.
items.d: She received the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 2016.

items.t: Scratch is a coding language where you snap together blocks. It is made mainly for ages 8 to 16.
items.d: It comes from the MIT Media Lab.

items.t: The Python programming language is named after a comedy show, Monty Python's Flying Circus, not the snake.
Python was made to be easy to read. It uses indentation, not curly brackets, to group lines of code.
items.d: Guido van Rossum released the first version in 1991.

items.t: DNS is called the phone book of the Internet. It turns a website name into a number address computers use.
The first working transistor was made in 1947 at Bell Labs.
items.d: A transistor can work as a switch controlled by electricity.

items.t: Some advanced microprocessors hold tens of billions of transistors on one chip.
items.d: Early computers needed thousands of big glass tubes instead.

items.t: In 1837 Charles Babbage designed the Analytical Engine, a mechanical computer. It was never finished.
items.d: It was planned to use punched cards for its programs.

items.t: Machine learning lets a computer find patterns in data and use them on new data.
items.d: Arthur Samuel first used the term 'machine learning' in 1959.

items.t: In supervised machine learning, a computer learns from examples that come with the right answers.
items.d: Showing it many labelled cat photos teaches it what a cat looks like.

items.t: In March 2016 a program called AlphaGo beat Go champion Lee Sedol in four of five games.
items.d: Go has far more possible moves than chess, so it is much harder for computers.

items.t: Phishing is a trick where a message pretends to be from someone you trust, to get your private information.
Warning signs of a scam message include spelling mistakes, a strange sender address, and pressure to act fast.
items.d: If unsure, ask a grown-up before you click.

items.t: Multi-factor sign-in uses two or more proofs: something you know, something you have, or something you are.
items.d: A password plus a code sent to your phone is an example.

items.t: Encryption scrambles a message into secret code. Only someone with the right key can unscramble it.
The Caesar cipher hides a message by shifting each letter a set number of places along the alphabet.
items.d: With a shift of 1, A becomes B and CAT becomes DBU.

items.t: An algorithm is a clear list of steps to solve a problem, a bit like a recipe.
The word algorithm comes from the name of al-Khwarizmi, a Persian scholar from about 1,200 years ago.
A pixel is the smallest dot of a picture on a screen. The word comes from picture element.
items.d: A megapixel is one million pixels.

items.t: Many screens make each pixel from three tiny parts: red, green and blue.
items.d: Mixing different amounts of their light makes many colours on the screen.

items.t: Linux was started by a student named Linus Torvalds in 1991. It is free for anyone to use and improve.
items.d: Its mascot is a penguin named Tux.

items.t: The Golden Gate Bridge opened to the public on May 27, 1937.
The Golden Gate Bridge is about 2.7 kilometres long.
The Golden Gate Bridge has a 1,280-metre span between its towers.
The Golden Gate Bridge is painted a reddish-orange called International Orange.
Each Golden Gate Bridge tower contains about 600,000 rivets.
The Burj Khalifa is about 830 metres tall.
The Burj Khalifa officially opened on January 4, 2010.
The Burj Khalifa has 57 elevators and 8 escalators.
The Burj Khalifa rests on 192 foundation piles, each 1.5 metres wide.
The Burj Khalifa's design was based on the flower of the Hymenocallis, a desert plant.
Hoover Dam is about 221 metres tall.
Hoover Dam was built from 1931 to 1936.
Hoover Dam stands in the Black Canyon of the Colorado River.
Hoover Dam holds back a reservoir called Lake Mead.
About 2.48 million cubic metres of concrete were used to build Hoover Dam.
The Channel Tunnel is a railway tunnel about 50 kilometres long.
items.d: It runs beneath the English Channel.

items.t: The Channel Tunnel has an underwater section about 38 kilometres long.
The Channel Tunnel opened in 1994.
The Channel Tunnel has two rail tunnels and a separate service tunnel.
When Channel Tunnel digging teams met, their paths were off by only 30 centimetres.
items.d: The two teams met underground in 1990.

items.t: The Eiffel Tower is 330 metres tall, including its antenna.
The Eiffel Tower was built from 1887 to 1889.
The iron in the Eiffel Tower weighs about 7,300 tonnes.
About 2.5 million rivets join the Eiffel Tower's 18,038 iron parts.
The Eiffel Tower has been completely repainted at least 19 times.
Sunlight can heat the Eiffel Tower and move its top by up to 18 centimetres.
items.d: The top shifts away from the Sun.

items.t: The Three Gorges Dam is about 2.3 kilometres long.
The Three Gorges Dam crosses the Yangtze River in China.
The main body of the Three Gorges Dam was completed in 2006.
A ship lift at the Three Gorges Dam can raise ships weighing up to 3,000 tonnes.
The Sydney Opera House officially opened on October 20, 1973.
Danish architect Jorn Utzon designed the Sydney Opera House.
The Sydney Opera House roofs are made from large concrete shells.
More than one million white and cream tiles cover the Sydney Opera House shells.
The Brooklyn Bridge opened on May 24, 1883.
items.d: It was the first fixed crossing over New York's East River.

items.t: The Brooklyn Bridge is about 1.8 kilometres long, including its approaches.
John A. Roebling designed the Brooklyn Bridge.
The Brooklyn Bridge's two towers are 85 metres tall.
A parade of 21 elephants crossed the Brooklyn Bridge in 1884.
The Millau Viaduct is about 2.5 kilometres long.
The Millau Viaduct reaches 343 metres from the ground to the top of its highest mast.
The Millau Viaduct's seven masts are each 87 metres high.
The Panama Canal is an artificial waterway about 82 kilometres long.
Locks on the Panama Canal lift ships to Gatun Lake, then lower them again.
Gatun Lake is man-made and sits 26 metres above sea level.
items.d: The lake forms part of the Panama Canal route.

items.t: The Leaning Tower of Pisa tilts because it was built on soft ground.
The Leaning Tower of Pisa has seven bells, one for each note in a major scale.
The Large Hadron Collider sits in a tunnel about 27 kilometres around.
About 10,000 superconducting magnets steer particles in the Large Hadron Collider.
The cacao tree was first grown by people in South America, in what is now Ecuador.
items.d: That was thousands of years ago, long before any chocolate bar.

items.t: Long ago, cocoa beans were used as money in some ancient civilizations.
items.d: Imagine paying for your lunch with beans!

items.t: The first recorded shipment of cocoa beans to Europe arrived in 1585.
items.d: Before that, most Europeans had never tasted chocolate.

items.t: Chocolate was once mostly a drink for rich people. New machines later made solid milk chocolate for everyone.
items.d: That change started in the 1800s.

items.t: About 60 percent of the world's cocoa is grown in two West African countries, Ivory Coast and Ghana.
items.d: Many chocolate treats start with beans from there.

items.t: Modern pizza developed in Naples, Italy.
Tomatoes could not be on pizza until the 1500s, because tomatoes came from the Americas.
items.d: Europeans had never seen a tomato before then.

items.t: In 2017, UNESCO added the art of making Neapolitan pizza to its list of cultural heritage.
items.d: That means the skill of making it is treasured around the world.

items.t: People traded spices like cinnamon and black pepper in India and the Middle East about 4,000 years ago.
Nutmeg first came from the Banda Islands in Southeast Asia.
In medieval Europe, spices were some of the most wanted and most expensive goods you could buy.
items.d: Pepper and cinnamon were treasures back then.

items.t: Saffron was the most exclusive spice of all, prized for its golden colour as well as its flavour.
The city of Venice controlled the spice trade with the Middle East for hundreds of years.
Before 1500, nobody grew potatoes outside South America.
items.d: Now potatoes are eaten in almost every country.

items.t: Corn, also called maize, came from the Americas. The Spanish brought it to the Old World.
Tomatoes were brought to Spain from the Americas, then spread to other European countries.
items.d: Italian pasta sauce had no tomatoes until after that.

items.t: Chili peppers came from the Americas. Portuguese traders brought them to India, where they became important.
The Spanish were the first Europeans to grow cacao, starting in 1590.
Sugarcane came from the Indian subcontinent. It was later brought to the Spanish West Indies.
Coffee reached the Americas around the year 1720, brought from Africa and the Middle East.
Rice was first farmed in China, somewhere between about 8,200 and 13,500 years ago.
Rice is the main food for more than half of the people in the world.
items.d: That is billions of people eating rice.

items.t: China and India together grow about half of all the rice in the world.
Long-grain rice usually cooks up dry and fluffy, with grains that stay separate.
items.d: It is useful in dishes where you want separate grains.

items.t: Short-grain rice turns sticky when cooked. It is used a lot in Japanese cooking.
items.d: Sticky rice is easy to shape into rice balls.

items.t: Noodles about 4,000 years old were found in northwestern China.
items.d: They are the oldest noodles ever found.

items.t: The oldest written mention of noodles is in a Chinese book from almost 2,000 years ago.
Ramen came from Chinese noodle dishes. It became common in Japan after World War II.
Sushi's ancestor was fish fermented with rice in Southeast Asia to help preserve freshwater fish.
In 1824, a cook named Hanaya Yohei in Edo, now Tokyo, is credited with making nigiri sushi.
items.d: Nigiri is a small block of rice with a slice of fish on top.

items.t: In old Edo, cooks started using vinegared rice instead of slow fermenting. That made sushi a fast food.
Tea drinking may have begun in Yunnan, China, where people first used it as medicine.
A Chinese legend says a ruler named Shennong invented tea. It is a story, not proven history.
Portuguese traders and priests brought tea drinking to Europe in the 1500s.
To meet demand for tea, Britain began growing it on big farms in India and Ceylon.
items.d: Ceylon is now called Sri Lanka.

items.t: After water, tea is the most widely drunk beverage in the whole world.
There are over a thousand different types of cheese in the world.
To make cheese, special enzymes make milk clump into curds. The liquid that is left over is called whey.
Blue cheeses, like Roquefort, get their blue veins from mold cultures added on purpose.
items.d: This mold is safe to eat in blue cheese.

items.t: The oldest known evidence of bread-making is about 14,500 years old, found at a site in Jordan.
Sourdough bread is made by letting dough ferment for a long time with wild yeasts and bacteria.
items.d: The tiny living things make the dough rise.

items.t: The word curry probably comes from kari, a Tamil word for a spiced dish eaten with rice.
The story of ice cream may have begun in ancient Persia, about 2,500 years ago.
The ice cream cone became popular in the United States at the 1904 World's Fair in St. Louis.
Gelato is an Italian frozen dessert made with more milk and less fat than ice cream.
Mooncakes are traditionally eaten in China during the Mid-Autumn Festival.
items.d: The festival is a time to enjoy the full moon with family.

items.t: A salted egg yolk inside a mooncake stands for the full moon.
Carbohydrates, proteins and fats are the three big nutrients your body needs in large amounts.
Leonardo da Vinci painted the Mona Lisa on white poplar wood from about 1503 to 1506.
items.d: It is oil paint on a wood panel. White poplar is the pale wood he used as the board.

items.t: In French, the Mona Lisa is called La Joconde, a name that means happy.
items.d: It is a pun on Giocondo, the married name of Lisa, the woman in the picture.

items.t: Vincent van Gogh made about 2,100 artworks, including about 860 oil paintings.
items.d: Most of them were made in just the last two years of his life.

items.t: Picasso and Georges Braque started Cubism, which shows many sides of an object at once.
items.d: A cubist face can show the front and the side together, built from shapes.

items.t: Word of the day: origami
items.d: Origami means paper folding. Ori means to fold, and kami means paper. Try folding a crane.

items.t: The paper crane is the best-known origami model.
items.d: You fold one square sheet into a bird with wings and a beak.

items.t: Word of the day: kirigami
items.d: Kirigami means paper cutting in Japanese. A paper snowflake you cut out is kirigami.

items.t: When Henri Matisse had to stay in bed, he made art by cutting painted paper.
items.d: He cut shapes with scissors from paper he had painted, then arranged the shapes.

items.t: Leonardo da Vinci was born in 1452 in or near Vinci, a hill town in Italy.
items.d: The town gave him his name. Da Vinci means from Vinci.

items.t: The Louvre in Paris began in the late 1100s as a fortress of King Philip II.
items.d: A fortress is a strong building. Long after, this one became a famous art museum.

items.t: I. M. Pei designed the Louvre's glass pyramid. It opened in 1989.
items.d: Pei proposed the glass pyramid in 1984. People enter the museum through it.

items.t: Michelangelo finished the marble statue David in 1504. He was about 29.
items.d: He carved David from one huge block of Carrara marble, a stone from Italy.

items.t: Michelangelo painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling from 1508 to 1512.
items.d: The ceiling has more than 300 painted figures. He worked for about four years.

items.t: Jackson Pollock put canvases on the floor and poured or splashed paint on them.
items.d: This is his drip technique. He used liquid house paint so it could pour and splash.

items.t: Frederic Auguste Bartholdi designed the Statue of Liberty.
items.d: Gustave Eiffel built the metal frame inside the copper statue.

items.t: France gave the Statue of Liberty as a gift. It was dedicated on 28 October 1886.
items.d: The people of France gave it to the United States. Dedicated means the opening day.

items.t: The Statue of Liberty was reddish-brown copper, then turned green.
items.d: Within about 20 years it turned green. That layer is verdigris, and it protects the copper.

items.t: Screens and printers mix colors in different ways.
items.d: Screens add red, green, and blue light. Printers use cyan, magenta, yellow, and black ink.

items.t: Painters learn red, yellow, and blue as the primary colors.
items.d: You can mix lots of colors from these three. Some colors still cannot be made that way.

items.t: Word of the day: ultramarine
items.d: It is a deep blue from lapis lazuli stone. The name means beyond the sea. Painters ground the stone to make paint.

items.t: Long ago, real ultramarine blue could cost as much as gold.
items.d: Painters saved this rare blue for special robes. A human-made version came in 1826.

items.t: A zoetrope and a flip book both make still drawings seem to move.
items.d: Spin or flip the drawings quickly, and your eyes blend them into motion.

items.t: Hand-drawn animation often uses 12 to 24 drawings for every second.
items.d: At 12 drawings a second, one minute needs 12 times 60, which equals 720 drawings.

items.t: In stop motion, real objects are moved a little and photographed frame by frame.
items.d: When the frames play fast, the still object looks like it is moving by itself.

items.t: Hokusai used Prussian blue in The Great Wave, a blue that does not fade easily.
items.d: The pigment came from Holland starting in 1820. It helped the famous print keep its color.

items.t: Impressionism got its name from Monet's 1872 painting Impression, Sunrise.
items.d: In 1874 a critic used the name to make fun of a show. Painters kept the name.

items.t: Word of the day: en plein air
items.d: En plein air means outdoors. Impressionist painters worked outside to catch changing sunlight.

items.t: The Great Pyramid was built for Pharaoh Khufu and took about 26 years.
items.d: Building started around 2600 BC. Khufu was a king of ancient Egypt.

items.t: The Great Pyramid is made of an estimated 2.3 million blocks.
items.d: Counting one block each second would take more than 26 days with no breaks.

items.t: The Great Pyramid was the tallest human-made structure for over 3,700 years.
items.d: For a very long time, nothing people built stood taller than the Great Pyramid.

items.t: The Great Sphinx has a human head and a lion's body, carved from limestone.
items.d: It was cut from the rock of the Giza ground about 4,500 years ago.

items.t: Gothic style began in northern France in the 1100s, with pointed arches.
items.d: A flying buttress is a stone support on the wall. It allowed taller walls and bigger stained-glass windows.

items.t: The Taj Mahal in Agra, India, is white marble set with semi-precious stones.
items.d: The stones are fitted into the marble to make patterns. Shah Jahan ordered the work in 1631.

items.t: Jorn Utzon of Denmark designed the Sydney Opera House. It opened in 1973.
items.d: Utzon was the Danish architect. The opera house officially opened on 20 October 1973.

items.t: The Sydney Opera House roof has 1,056,006 tiles in white and cream.
items.d: Some tiles are glossy white and shiny. Others are matte cream and look softer.

items.t: In 1974, farmers digging a well near Xi'an, China, found the Terracotta Army.
items.d: Their digging uncovered the clay soldiers on 29 March 1974.

items.t: The Terracotta Army has more than 8,000 soldiers, and no two look exactly alike.
items.d: Each clay figure has its own features. Every soldier looks a little different.

items.t: The soldiers of the Terracotta Army were first painted in bright colors.
items.d: Artists used many colors on the clay. The figures were colorful when they were new.

items.t: In 1931, Salvador Dali painted melting watches in The Persistence of Memory.
items.d: The pocket watches look soft and droopy. He finished the picture in August 1931.

items.t: Cave artists made hand pictures by pressing a hand on the wall and coloring around it.
items.d: They blew or spread paint around the hand. Lift the hand, and its shape remains.

items.t: A warty pig painted in a cave in Sulawesi is at least 45,500 years old.
items.d: The cave, Leang Tedongnge, is in Indonesia. People made animal art that long ago.

items.t: Hokusai's The Great Wave off Kanagawa is a woodblock print from about 1831.
items.d: Artists carve a wooden block, ink it, and press paper on it. Mount Fuji is in the background.

items.t: Tyrian purple dye came from sea snails. Thousands were needed for a tiny bit of dye.
items.d: Twelve thousand snails gave no more than 1.4 grams of pure purple dye.

items.t: Egyptian blue is considered the first human-made pigment, created in ancient Egypt.
items.d: People mixed sand, copper, and lime to make the blue, instead of only finding a natural color.

items.t: Egyptian blue gives off infrared light, which our eyes cannot see.
items.d: Scientists use the glow to find this blue on old objects that look unpainted.

items.t: Word of the day: pointillism
items.d: Pointillism is painting with tiny dots of color. Step back, and your eye blends the dots.

items.t: Word of the day: fresco
items.d: Fresco means fresh in Italian. Paint on wet plaster sinks in, so the picture becomes part of the wall.

items.t: Rembrandt's The Night Watch is not a night scene. Dark varnish made it look like one.
items.d: Painted in 1642, it measures about 363 cm by 437 cm and hangs in the Rijksmuseum.

items.t: At age 18, in 1856, William Perkin accidentally made the purple dye mauveine.
items.d: He was trying to make malaria medicine. His find became the first purple dye made in large amounts.

items.t: Rodin's The Thinker was first called The Poet. He planned it in 1880.
items.d: It began as one figure for a large doorway. Later the statue became famous on its own.

items.t: In Norse myths, Thor has a mighty hammer called Mjolnir.
items.d: Thor is the god of thunder, storms and strength.

items.t: Thor rides in a chariot pulled by two goats.
items.d: That is a very unusual way to travel across the sky!

items.t: Thursday is named after the Norse god Thor.
items.d: Thor's day became Thursday.

items.t: Thor's wife in the old Norse stories is Sif, a goddess with golden hair.
Odin, a Norse god, has two ravens named Huginn and Muninn that sit on his shoulders.
In Norse myths, Odin rides an eight-legged horse called Sleipnir.
items.d: Imagine a horse with eight legs!

items.t: In the stories, Odin gave up one eye to gain wisdom.
Odin carries a spear called Gungnir in Norse myths.
Wednesday is named after the Norse god Odin in many languages.
items.d: Odin was also called Woden, so Wednesday means Woden's day.

items.t: In Greek myths, Zeus is the king of the gods who live on Mount Olympus.
Zeus's weapon in Greek myths was the thunderbolt.
items.d: He is often shown with an eagle too.

items.t: Zeus's parents in Greek myths were the Titans Cronus and Rhea.
The Romans called the Greek god Zeus by the name Jupiter.
items.d: The planet Jupiter is named after him.

items.t: In Greek myths, Medusa had living snakes instead of hair.
items.d: The story says anyone who looked at her turned to stone.

items.t: In the myth, the winged horse Pegasus sprang from Medusa's body after the hero Perseus defeated her.
In the Greek myth, Perseus gave Medusa's head to Athena, who put it on her shield.
The Minotaur of Greek myth had a bull's head and tail and a man's body.
In Greek myth, the Minotaur lived at the center of a maze called the Labyrinth.
In the myth, the clever builder Daedalus designed the Labyrinth for King Minos of Crete.
The Greek hero Theseus is the one who beat the Minotaur in the myth.
In Greek legend, the Greeks used a giant wooden horse to sneak into the city of Troy.
items.d: Warriors hid inside it.

items.t: In the Trojan Horse story, Odysseus is said to have planned the trick.
The most detailed Trojan Horse story was written by the Roman poet Virgil.
items.d: His poem is called the Aeneid.

items.t: Cerberus, from Greek myth, was usually a three-headed dog.
items.d: Some tales give him a snake for a tail.

items.t: In Greek myth, bringing Cerberus out of the underworld was the last of Heracles' twelve labours.
The twelve Olympians were the main gods of ancient Greece, and they lived on Mount Olympus.
Athena was the Greek goddess of wisdom, crafts and strategy in war.
The Greek god Ares was called Mars by the Romans.
items.d: The planet Mars is named after the Roman name.

items.t: Ra was the ancient Egyptian god of the Sun, often shown as a falcon.
Egyptian myth says Ra carried the Sun across the sky in a boat each day.
A sphinx is a mythical creature with a human head and a lion's body.
In Greek myth, the sphinx asked travelers a riddle and challenged them to answer.
items.d: She appears in the story of Oedipus.

items.t: The Great Sphinx of Giza in Egypt is the largest and most famous sphinx.
items.d: Egyptian sphinxes had no wings, but Greek ones did.

items.t: The phoenix is a bird from Greek myth that gains new life by rising from the ashes of the one before it.
The Ramayana is a Hindu epic poem traditionally credited to the sage Valmiki.
items.d: It has nearly 24,000 verses.

items.t: In the Ramayana, Ravana, king of Lanka, kidnaps Sita.
Amaterasu is the sun goddess in Japanese myths.
items.d: One tale says she hid in a cave.

items.t: In Japanese folklore, a kitsune is a fox spirit that can take human form.
items.d: More tails means an older, more powerful kitsune.

items.t: Anansi is a trickster from West African folktales who is usually a spider.
items.d: The tales come from Ghana.

items.t: In some Native American stories, the Thunderbird makes thunder by flapping its wings.
items.d: In some tales it makes lightning by flashing its eyes.

items.t: The Brothers Grimm, Jacob and Wilhelm, were German folklorists who collected folk tales.
items.d: Their first book came out in 1812.

items.t: The Brothers Grimm helped make Cinderella and Hansel and Gretel famous.
The Greek tale of Rhodopis is often considered the earliest known Cinderella-style story.
The glass slipper comes from Charles Perrault's version of Cinderella.
items.d: The Grimm version, Aschenputtel, is different.

items.t: Cinderella has thousands of versions told all around the world.
Hans Christian Andersen, a Danish writer, was born in Odense, Denmark, in 1805.
Hans Christian Andersen's story The Little Mermaid made him famous around the world.
In Andersen's The Emperor's New Clothes, a child says the emperor is not wearing any clothes.
In Norse myths, Yggdrasil is a giant sacred tree at the center of the cosmos.
In Norse myth, a squirrel named Ratatoskr runs up and down the world tree Yggdrasil.
At Diwali, people light small oil lamps called diyas.
items.d: Candles and lanterns are lit too, so homes shine for the festival.

items.t: Families decorate floors with colorful patterns called rangoli at Diwali.
items.d: People draw the patterns on the floor to dress the home for the festival.

items.t: Diwali is also marked with fireworks.
items.d: The fireworks join the oil lamps, candles, and lanterns of the festival.

items.t: Diwali celebrations usually last five or six days.
items.d: Lights, floor patterns, and fireworks fill those days.

items.t: Diwali falls on a different date each year.
items.d: It usually comes between mid-October and mid-November.

items.t: Chinese New Year celebrations last until the Lantern Festival.
items.d: The Lantern Festival is on the 15th day of the new year.

items.t: Red paper-cuts and couplets decorate doors and windows at Chinese New Year.
items.d: The red decorations are a bright part of getting the home ready.

items.t: Lion dances are performed at Chinese New Year.
items.d: The dance is an old custom meant to ward off evil spirits.

items.t: Children receive red envelopes with money at Chinese New Year.
items.d: These gifts are known as lai see in some Chinese communities.

items.t: At Holi, people throw colored water and powder at each other.
items.d: Friends end the day covered in bright color. It is a happy, messy festival.

items.t: On the night before Holi, people light big bonfires.
items.d: The bonfire ceremony is called Holika Dahan.

items.t: Holi marks the arrival of spring in India and Nepal.
items.d: When spring arrives, Holi brings people outdoors to share color.

items.t: Holi usually falls in March, around the full moon.
items.d: Its date follows the full moon in the month of Phalguna.

items.t: Word of the day: hanami
items.d: Hanami means enjoying flowers, usually cherry blossoms. In Japan, people go out to enjoy hanami.

items.t: Hanami began in Japan's Nara period, from 710 to 794.
items.d: People first admired plum blossoms. Cherry blossoms became the favorite later.

items.t: Word of the day: yozakura
items.d: Yozakura means viewing cherry blossoms at night. People enjoy yozakura by lantern light in a park.

items.t: A playful Japanese saying goes, dumplings rather than flowers.
items.d: It teases friends who care more about snacks than about the blossoms.

items.t: In 1912, Japan gave 3,000 cherry trees to the United States.
items.d: The trees were planted in Washington, D.C.

items.t: Cherry blossoms usually last no more than two weeks.
items.d: The flowers stay only a short time, so the viewing season is brief.

items.t: A kilt is a knee-length garment that wraps around the waist.
items.d: This Scottish clothing style was first recorded in the 16th century.

items.t: Word of the day: sett
items.d: A sett is the checked pattern of a tartan. You can spot the sett on a kilt.

items.t: Word of the day: sporran
items.d: A sporran is a pouch worn at the waist, and the Gaelic word means purse. People wear a sporran with a kilt.

items.t: Word of the day: Hogmanay
items.d: Hogmanay is the Scots name for New Year's Eve. People in Scotland celebrate Hogmanay as the old year ends.

items.t: First-footing is a New Year custom in Scotland.
items.d: The first person to step through a friend's door after midnight is the first-foot.

items.t: People link arms for the last verse of Auld Lang Syne.
items.d: At Hogmanay, friends link arms when that last verse starts.

items.t: Songkran is the Thai New Year, known for big public water fights.
items.d: The public splashing is a symbol of cleansing for the new year.

items.t: Songkran is celebrated on 13 April each year.
items.d: 14 and 15 April are holidays too, so the New Year stretches over several days.

items.t: At Songkran, people gently pour water on the hands of elders.
items.d: This custom is called Rod Nam Dam Hua, and it asks for a blessing.

items.t: Oktoberfest began in 1810 to celebrate a royal wedding in Bavaria.
items.d: Crown Prince Ludwig married Princess Therese, and the public joined the celebration.

items.t: Oktoberfest is held on the Theresienwiese, or Therese's Meadow.
items.d: People in Munich often call the festival grounds the Wiesn.

items.t: Word of the day: jeogori
items.d: The jeogori is the basic top of a Korean hanbok. Both men and women wear the jeogori.

items.t: Bright hanbok colors were generally worn by children and girls.
items.d: Middle-aged men and women more often wore quieter, muted colors.

items.t: Word of the day: seolbim
items.d: Seolbim means new clothes and shoes worn for the Korean New Year holiday.

items.t: A sari can be from 4.1 to 8.2 metres of cloth.
items.d: That equals 4.5 to 9 yards. Different saris use different lengths in that range.

items.t: A sari wraps around the waist, with the loose end over one shoulder.
items.d: One long piece of cloth becomes a full outfit when it is draped this way.

items.t: There are more than 80 recorded ways to wear a sari.
items.d: The same cloth can be folded and draped in many different styles.

items.t: Word of the day: kimono
items.d: Kimono means thing to wear. A person wraps a kimono around the body like a robe.

items.t: A broad sash called an obi holds a kimono closed.
items.d: The obi wraps around the middle and keeps the robe in place.

items.t: In everyday wear, a kimono crosses left side over right.
items.d: That is the usual way to wrap the front panels.

items.t: Word of the day: yukata
items.d: A yukata is the most informal kimono. People wear this light robe in the summer.

items.t: Nowruz, the Persian New Year, follows the spring equinox.
items.d: The equinox is a day when daytime and nighttime are about the same length.

items.t: Nowruz families set out a Haft-sin table with seven things.
items.d: In Persian, each item's name begins with the letter sin.

items.t: Nowruz holidays last thirteen days.
items.d: The holiday ends with outdoor picnics on a day called Sizdah Bedar.

items.t: The haka is a traditional Maori dance from New Zealand.
items.d: People perform the haka to welcome important guests.

items.t: Hanukkah lasts eight nights and begins on 25 Kislev.
items.d: Kislev is a month name. A hanukkiah has eight lights plus the shamash, used to light the others.

items.t: In the Maori hongi, people press their noses together.
items.d: Often their foreheads touch as well. It is a greeting of the Maori people.

items.t: The hongi shares the ha, the breath of life, between two people.
items.d: When noses touch, each person shares a little of their breath.

items.t: The Thai wai is a bow made with palms pressed together.
items.d: Hands held higher, and a deeper bow, show greater respect.

items.t: Namaste is said with palms pressed together and fingers pointing up.
items.d: Palms touch, fingers point up, and the word greets someone with respect.

items.t: Eid al-Fitr marks the end of Ramadan, a month of daytime fasting.
items.d: To fast means to pause eating. Many people do this from dawn until sunset.

items.t: The Lydians were among the first people to use gold and silver coins.
items.d: Lydia was an ancient kingdom in what is now Turkey.

items.t: The first stamped metal coins were made around 650 to 600 BC.
items.d: That is more than 2,600 years ago.

items.t: Paper money was first used in China, during the Song dynasty.
items.d: Those early notes were called jiaozi.

items.t: The word money comes from the Latin word moneta, which meant coin.
Barter means swapping goods or services directly, with no money at all.
items.d: You give a bag of apples and get a pair of socks.

items.t: When money becomes unstable, people often go back to bartering.
items.d: Swapping things you have for things you need can work without coins.

items.t: The Bank of England was set up in 1694 to be the government's banker.
The Bank of England has a nickname: The Old Lady of Threadneedle Street.
items.d: The name comes from a cartoon drawn in 1797.

items.t: The Bank of England is the world's second oldest central bank, after Sweden's.
A coin is a small object, usually round and flat, that people use to pay for things.
Around 600 BC, the kingdom of Lydia made coins from electrum, a mix of gold and silver.
King Croesus of Lydia made some of the first gold coins with a standard purity.
Coins are made in big numbers at a place called a mint.
items.d: Having lots of the same coins makes trading much easier.

items.t: A banknote may last about four years, while a coin can last about 30.
items.d: That is why coins are used for small, everyday payments.

items.t: Early metal coins were invented to make weighing precious metal easier.
items.d: A stamp on the coin showed how much metal it held.

items.t: In China, people found the remains of a bronze coin factory about 2,600 years old.
items.d: It is described as the world's oldest known coin factory.

items.t: Early Chinese banknotes were printed on paper made from mulberry bark.
Watermarks and security threads are added while banknote paper is being made.
items.d: Hold a banknote to the light and look for a hidden picture.

items.t: Some banknotes have clear windows covered with shiny holographic foil.
items.d: These features are very hard for fakers to copy.

items.t: Plastic banknotes last longer than paper ones and are harder to fake.
Australia produced the first polymer banknote, made from a plastic called polypropylene.
In 1996, Australia became the first country with a full set of plastic banknotes.
Many cards keep information in a magnetic stripe that a machine can read.
items.d: Swipe the stripe and the machine reads the data stored on it.

items.t: Chip cards are harder to copy, so they help stop fraud.
Governments collect taxes to pay for things everyone shares.
items.d: Roads, schools and parks are paid for this way.

items.t: The first known tax system was in ancient Egypt, about 5,000 years ago.
items.d: It began around 3000 to 2800 BC.

items.t: In ancient Egypt, the word for labor was a synonym for taxes.
items.d: People could pay their taxes by working.

items.t: Ancient Rome auctioned off the job of collecting taxes.
Interest is extra money a borrower pays back on top of what was borrowed.
items.d: Borrow 100 coins, repay 105: the 5 extra coins are interest.

items.t: Venice's Arsenal fitted ships along a canal, a bit like an early assembly line.
A moving assembly line once cut the time to build one car to just 93 minutes.
One car assembly line built cars faster than the paint of the day could dry.
items.d: So the maker had to limit the number of paint colors.

items.t: A stock exchange is a marketplace where people buy and sell shares of companies.
The Amsterdam Stock Exchange is often called the oldest modern stock market.
Stock exchanges let small investors own shares in the same companies as big investors.
The Royal Mint, which makes coins for the UK, was founded in the year 886.
The famous scientist Isaac Newton became warden of the Royal Mint in 1696.
Piggy banks are used to teach children about saving money.
The oldest known pig-shaped savings banks come from Java, from the 12th century.
In the Javanese language, one word means both savings and piggy bank.
items.d: The word is celengan.

items.t: The Fort Knox depository is a fortified vault building in the United States.
items.d: It holds over half of the country's gold reserves.

items.t: The US Treasury built the Fort Knox gold vault building in 1936.
Cowrie shells were used as money for centuries in Africa.
The cowrie was the shell most widely used around the world as shell money.
Ghana's money, the cedi, is named after cowrie shells.
On Yap, people used round stones, some of them huge, with holes in the middle as money.
The biggest known Yap stone is 3.6 metres wide and weighs about 4,000 kg.
Yap stones were rarely moved. Everyone just agreed who owned them.
items.d: Even a stone lost at sea was still counted as owned.
